Palenque, known in the Itza' language as Lakamha, meaning big water, stands in the Mexican state of Chiapas near the Usumacinta River, 150 metres above sea level. It is a medium-sized site, smaller than Tikal, Chichen Itza or Copán, but holds some of the finest Maya architecture, sculpture and bas-relief carving. The Palace, the largest complex, measures 97 by 73 metres at its base and has a four-story tower. An aqueduct with a three-metre-high vault diverts the Otulum River under the main plaza.

The Temple of the Inscriptions holds the second longest glyphic text known from the Maya world. In 1952 Alberto Ruz Lhuillier lifted a slab in its floor and found a stairway to the tomb of Pakal, whose sarcophagus held the richest jade collection seen in a Maya tomb, including a mosaic mask. John Lloyd Stephens and Frederick Catherwood visited in 1840. Archaeologists estimate that only about 10 percent of the city has been uncovered. Palenque National Park was designated in 1981.
palermo: Palermo lies in a basin formed by the Papireto, Kemonia and Oreto rivers, which the Arabs named the Conca d'Oro, the Golden Basin, in the 9th century. A mountain range forms a cirque around the city and faces the Tyrrhenian Sea, and historically it made the interior of Sicily hard to reach. Monte Pellegrino, which stands apart in front of the sea, is the historically most important of the mountains, and Goethe called its cliff the most beautiful promontory in the world. Cave drawings at nearby Addaura show settlement perhaps around 8000 BCE.

The original inhabitants were the Sicani, who according to Thucydides arrived from the Iberian Peninsula. In the 8th century BCE the Phoenicians built a settlement on the natural harbour, one of their three main colonies in Sicily along with Motya and Soluntum, and the city later passed to Carthage. As Panormus it was part of the Roman Republic and Empire for over a thousand years. The Vandals under Geiseric took it in 440 CE, and in late 535 Belisarius laid siege to the city, which had refused to surrender, and eventually prevailed. From 831 to 1072 Palermo was under Arab rule and for the first time the capital of Sicily.

After the Norman conquest it became the capital of the Kingdom of Sicily, which lasted from 1130 to 1816. Spain ruled the city from 1479 until 1713, with brief interruptions, and Austria from 1720 to 1734. Charles III chose Palermo for his coronation as King of Sicily, but the royal court resided in Naples. In 1866 Palermo was the seat of a week-long popular rebellion against annexation by the Savoy kingdom, which was crushed under martial law, and the Teatro Massimo opened in 1897.

Allied bombing in 1942 and 1943 destroyed the harbour and much of the city, with heavy civilian casualties, until the Allied invasion of Sicily captured it on 22 July 1943. In 1946 Palermo became the seat of the Regional Parliament, and in 1948 the element technetium was discovered at its university.

Palermo is the capital and largest city of Sicily. Its inhabitants speak Italian and the Palermitano dialect of Sicilian. The city is the main seat of the World Heritage Site Arab-Norman Palermo and the Cathedral Churches of Cefalù and Monreale, and its markets of Vucciria, Ballarò and Capo are known for fruit, vegetables and fish. Its patron saint is Saint Rosalia, whose feast day is 15 July.
palermo-cathedral: The cathedral is dedicated to the Assumption of the Virgin Mary and is the church of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Palermo. Walter Ophamil, the Norman archbishop of Palermo and minister of King William II, had it erected in 1185 on the area of an earlier Byzantine basilica. By tradition that church was founded by Pope Gregory I, and the Arabs turned it into a mosque after conquering the city in the 9th century. A Qur'an verse is carved on a column of the southern portico, which belonged to the original basilica and the mosque. Ophamil is buried in the crypt.

The building mixes styles because of centuries of additions. The upper orders of the corner towers date from the 14th and 15th centuries, and the Gothic-Catalan southern portico was erected around 1465. Charles III and Victor Amadeus II of Sardinia were both crowned in the cathedral, the latter in December 1713.

The present neoclassical appearance comes from work between 1781 and 1801, supervised by Ferdinando Fuga and Giuseppe Venanzio Marvuglia. Marvuglia's changes were more radical than Fuga's plans, and the great retable by Gagini was destroyed, its sculptures moved elsewhere in the building. In 1801 the astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi, who discovered the asteroid Ceres, built a meridian line on the floor, where an image of the sun, projected through a small hole in a dome, crosses a bronze line at solar noon. It was meant to standardise time and to fix the date of the spring equinox for Easter.

In the first two chapels of the right aisle stand the tombs of Roger II, his daughter Constance I of Sicily, her husband Emperor Henry VI and their son Emperor Frederick II, with the burials of Constance of Aragon and Peter II of Sicily. The four main sarcophagi are of porphyry and are described as the first medieval free-standing secular tombs in the West. Odo of Bayeux, half-brother of William the Conqueror, was buried in the cathedral in 1097. The chapel of Saint Rosalia, patron of Palermo, holds a 17th-century silver urn that is an object of devotion.
palermo-stone: The Palermo Stone is one of seven surviving fragments of a stele known as the Royal Annals of the Old Kingdom. The stele listed the kings of Egypt from the First Dynasty through to the early part of the Fifth Dynasty and noted significant events in each year of their reigns. It may originally have been about 60 centimetres high and 2.1 metres wide, and is made of a hard black stone, probably basalt. The Palermo fragment is irregular and shield-shaped, 43.5 centimetres high, 25 wide and 6.5 thick at most.

Its front has six horizontal registers of hieroglyphs. The first lists the names of predynastic kings of Lower Egypt, identified by the Red Crown. Later registers give the annual events for kings of the First to Fourth Dynasties, and the back continues down to Neferirkare Kakai, third ruler of the Fifth Dynasty. Where a king is named, his mother's name is also recorded, such as Betrest, mother of Semerkhet, and Meresankh I, mother of Seneferu.

The annals record the height of the annual Nile flood, festivals such as the Sed festival, taxation, sculpture, buildings and warfare. They name pharaohs including Djer, Den, Semerkhet, Nynetjer, Peribsen, Khasekhemwy, Djoser, Huni, Sneferu, Khufu, Djedefre, Shepseskaf, Userkaf, Sahure and Neferirkare Kakai, and they preserve names of royal family members of the first five dynasties not otherwise recorded.

New Kingdom king lists such as the Turin Canon and the Abydos king list name Menes, probably Narmer, as the first king of the First Dynasty. The top register of the annals names at least fourteen earlier rulers, which may be preserved through oral tradition or may be fictitious; their identification with historical persons is controversial. The historian Manetho may have used information like that of the stele for his chronology.

The stele's original location is unknown, and no fragment has a secure archaeological provenance. A Sicilian lawyer, Ferdinand Guidano, bought the Palermo Stone in 1859, and his family presented it to the Palermo Archaeological Museum on 19 October 1877. Five fragments are in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, four acquired between 1895 and 1914 and one bought in 1963, and one small fragment is in the Petrie Museum in London. A visiting French archaeologist recognised its importance in 1895, and Heinrich Schäfer published it fully in 1902.

The date of the text is uncertain. It was probably made in the Fifth Dynasty, but it has been suggested that it was carved much later, perhaps in the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, though it would still rest on an Old Kingdom original. It is also unknown whether the fragments come from one stele or from separate copies, and some small Cairo fragments may not be genuine.
palestine-liberation-organization: At its first summit meeting in Cairo in 1964 the Arab League initiated the creation of an organisation to represent the Palestinian people. The Palestinian National Council convened in Jerusalem on 28 May 1964, and the PLO was founded on 2 June 1964, with the stated complementary goals of Arab unity and the liberation of Palestine. It initially sought an Arab state over the entire territory of the former Mandatory Palestine, and launched guerrilla attacks on Israel from Jordan, Lebanon, Egypt and Syria. In 1968 the founding charter was replaced by a revised version calling for a Palestinian state in which Christians, Muslims and Jews would have equal rights.

Fatah's founder, Yasser Arafat, was elected chairman in Cairo on 4 February 1969. In September 1970, in the events known as Black September, Jordan assaulted the PLO's armed groups, and by July 1971 it had been expelled to Lebanon. Israel drove it out in the 1982 Lebanon War; about 8,000 fighters evacuated Beirut, and the PLO moved to Tunis. In 1974 the United Nations General Assembly granted it observer status, on 22 November. In 1988 the National Council proclaimed a Palestinian Declaration of Independence in Algiers, and the PLO endorsed a two-state solution.

In the Oslo Accords of 1993, signed on 20 August and publicly on 13 September, the PLO recognised Israel's right to exist and accepted United Nations Security Council Resolution 242, and Israel recognised the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people. The accords created the Palestinian Authority, with Arafat at its head, to govern Gaza and Jericho. In 1996 the PLO nullified the parts of its charter that called for Israel's destruction.

The PLO is formally an umbrella organisation of resistance movements, political parties and popular organisations. It was designed as a government in exile, with a parliament, the Palestinian National Council, as its highest authority and an elected Executive Committee. The Council has 740 members and the Committee 18. The Oslo Accords created a separate Palestinian Authority for the occupied territories, which came to replace the PLO as the prime Palestinian political institution.
palk-strait: The strait stretches for about 137 km and is between 64 and 137 km wide. Its waters are shallow: around the shoals of Ram Setu they are typically only 1 to 3 metres deep, the central part is typically around 20 metres deep, and the greatest depth is 35 metres. To the north, in the Bay of Bengal, the waves are mostly swells, while in Palk Bay to the south they are mostly smaller wind waves. In the Hindu epic Ramayana the shoals are part of a bridge built by the vanara army of Rama to rescue his wife Sita from the Asura king Ravana.

During the Last Glacial Period, when sea levels fell to as much as 120 metres below their present values, the whole of the shallow strait was dry land. It was submerged again as the sea rose during the Holocene, by around 7,000 years ago.

The construction of a shipping channel through the strait was first proposed to the British government of India in 1860. Pamban Island was linked to the Indian mainland by the Pamban Bridge, opened for traffic on 24 February 1914. Trains ran from Madras to Dhanushkodi at the southern tip of the island, where a ferry crossed to Talaimannar on Mannar Island and another train carried passengers on to Colombo. The railway line to Dhanushkodi was destroyed in the 1964 Dhanushkodi cyclone together with a passenger train, killing around 200 people. A ferry between Rameswaram and Talaimannar continued into the 1970s and was discontinued by the Indian government in 1984.

The shallows, small islands and reefs make the strait difficult for large ships, though fishing boats and small craft navigate it. The Sethusamudram Shipping Canal Project, commissioned by the Government of India in 2005 to dredge a channel, met opposition on religious grounds. A road bridge beside the Pamban Bridge was opened in 1988, and a new railway bridge was completed in 2024 after rail traffic on the old bridge was suspended permanently in February 2023 over concerns about its stability. A combined undersea tunnel and bridge linking India and Sri Lanka, the Palk Strait Bridge, was first discussed in 2002 and has been examined several times since.
pallava-script: The Pallava script, or Pallava Grantha, is named after the Pallava dynasty of southern India and is attested since the 4th century CE. It evolved from Tamil-Brahmi and was used to write Old Tamil and Sanskrit, the court languages of the Pallavas, so it has glyphs for the sounds of both languages. Its main characteristics are aesthetically matched and fuller consonant glyphs, a feature also visible in the writing systems of the Chalukya, Kadamba and Vengi at the time of the Ikshvakus. It was the first significant development of Brahmi in India, combining rounded and rectangular strokes and adding typographical effects, and it suited civic and religious inscriptions.

Each consonant has an inherent /a/, which is sounded if no vowel sign is attached. When two consonants follow one another without an intervening vowel, the second takes a subscript form and is attached below the first. The usual description rests on examples from the 7th century CE, and some letters have an uncertain sound value because they occur little in Southeast Asia. The epigrapher Arlo Griffiths argues that the name is misleading, because not all the scripts it covers are connected with the Pallava dynasty, and he advocates calling them Late Southern Brāhmī scripts.

During Pallava rule the script travelled with priests, monks, scholars and traders into Southeast Asia, and it evolved into scripts such as Balinese, Baybayin, Javanese, Kawi, Khmer, Lanna, Lao, Mon-Burmese, New Tai Lue, Sundanese and Thai. In India the Chozha-Pallava script, which gave rise to the modern Tamil script, and the Grantha script both descend from it. After the Pallava dynasty was absorbed through the conquest by Aditya I in 897 CE, the Chozha-Pallava script replaced both Pallava and Grantha for Tamil texts, while Grantha stayed in use for Manipravalam texts. The Kadamba-Pallava script evolved into early forms of Kannada and Telugu. The script is not yet part of Unicode, although Anshuman Pandey made a proposal to encode it in 2018.
palm-oil: Palm oil is an edible vegetable oil taken from the reddish pulp of the fruit of the African oil palm, Elaeis guineensis, which is native to the wetlands of western Africa. Humans have used oil palms for about 5,000 years. In the late 1800s archaeologists found in a tomb at Abydos, dating to 3,000 BCE, a substance that they concluded was originally palm oil. It has long been used as a cooking oil in West and Central African countries, where it features in dishes such as egusi soup and okra soup, and European merchants trading with West Africa occasionally bought it for the same purpose.

The oil is naturally red because of its high beta-carotene content, and it takes its name from palmitic acid, a saturated fatty acid that it contains in unusually high concentration. It should not be confused with palm kernel oil, which comes from the kernel of the same fruit, or with coconut oil. It is traditionally and still industrially produced by milling the fruit; since the 1990s some has also been cold-pressed, and this artisanal oil keeps its red colour. Refined, bleached and deodorized palm oil, the basic form sold on commodity markets, contains no carotenes. Because it is highly saturated it is solid at room temperature in temperate regions, which makes it a cheap substitute for butter or hydrogenated fats in pastry and baked goods.

Palm oil became sought after by British traders during the Industrial Revolution as an industrial lubricant for machinery, and it formed the basis of soaps such as Lever Brothers' Sunlight and the American Palmolive. It is now used in food, in personal care products and as a biofuel.

Its production has drawn criticism. Forests have been cleared in parts of Indonesia and Malaysia for oil palm monoculture, reducing the habitat of the three surviving orangutan species, and journalists and researchers have reported violations of indigenous land rights in fast-growing producing regions. Supporters point out that an oil palm plantation yields about ten times more oil per hectare than soybean, sunflower or rapeseed. The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil was established in 2004 to promote global standards for its sustainable production.
palma-cathedral: The Cathedral of Santa Maria of Palma, known as La Seu, stands on the seashore of Palma between the Royal Palace of La Almudaina and the Episcopal Palace. In 1229 King James I conquered Palma, then called Madina Mayurqa, from its Almohad rulers. He at once re-established the Diocese of Mallorca, and works began on the site of the city's largest mosque; Bishop Pere de Morella consecrated the site in 1230. The earliest surviving part is the Chapel of the Holy Trinity, finished in 1327 as a burial place for the kings of Mallorca. The last traces of the mosque disappeared in 1386, and the bell tower was finished in 1498, about when the naves and vaults were completed.

The cathedral has three parallel naves with matching apses, which most scholars attribute to the influence of the cathedrals of Barcelona and Santa Maria del Mar. It has no transept or ambulatory. It is 121 metres long and 40 metres wide, and its pillars are one twelfth the width of the vault, against one sixth at Reims. The great east rose window, nearly 14 metres across, is the second-largest Gothic rose window in the world after that of Strasbourg.

In the royal chapel at the end of the central nave stand the marble tombs of the Mallorcan kings James II and James III beside the white marble Episcopal Throne of 1346. Sixteen chapels line the nave and show nearly all the styles used in Mallorca since the cathedral was begun, from the Plateresque Chapel of Sant Jeroni to the Churrigueresque Chapel of Our Lady of the Crown.

After the Tridentine Council the cathedral was richly decorated with Baroque murals and altarpieces. In the middle of the 19th century structural problems led to a French-inspired neo-Gothic rebuilding of the west front, giving it its present gable. Antoni Gaudí was invited in 1903 to oversee a restoration and moved the choir stalls and screen from the centre of the nave to the sides of the presbytery. He designed a large canopy over the altar and opened bricked-up windows. His work has been criticised for destroying Mudejar and Baroque decoration, and it stopped in 1914 after disputes with the local authorities.

The most recent major works, from 2001 to 2006, were those of the Mallorcan artist Miquel Barceló in the Chapel of Sant Pere and the Holy Sacrament, where he covered the apse in Italian ceramic with scenes of the loaves and fishes and the wedding at Cana. The project drew strong criticism.
palmyra: Palmyra lies in central Syria, 215 kilometres north-east of Damascus, in an oasis surrounded by palms. Two mountain ranges overlook it, and to the south and east it is exposed to the Syrian Desert. A small wadi, al-Qubur, crosses the area, and south of it rises the Efqa spring. Pliny the Elder, writing in the 70s CE, described the town as noted for its desert location, the richness of its soil and the springs that made agriculture and herding possible.

The city entered the written record about 2000 BCE, when Puzur-Ishtar the Tadmorean agreed to a contract at an Assyrian trading colony at Kültepe. At the beginning of the 11th century BCE Tiglath-Pileser I of Assyria recorded a defeat of the Arameans of Tadmar. The Hebrew Bible places a desert city Tadmor under Solomon, but its description does not fit the archaeology, since Palmyra was then a small settlement. Under the Seleucids, between 312 and 64 BCE, it became prosperous. In 217 BCE a force led by Zabdibel fought for Antiochus III at the Battle of Raphia.

Palmyra was autonomous before 273 CE and attached to the Roman province of Syria. It became a Roman colonia in the third century and a monarchy in 260. Its wealth, drawn from caravan trade, paid for the Great Colonnade, the Temple of Bel and the tower tombs of the Valley of Tombs, where the most recent tower is dated to 128. The Palmyrenes spoke Palmyrene Aramaic, used Greek in commerce and diplomacy, and worshipped Semitic, Mesopotamian and Arab deities.

Aurelian razed the city in 273, and Diocletian later restored it at a reduced size. The Palmyrenes became Christian in the fourth century. Khalid ibn al-Walid took the city for the Rashidun Caliphate in 634, and in the following centuries the inhabitants adopted Islam and Arabic. The Timurids reduced it to a small village in 1400. In 1932, under French Mandatory rule, the inhabitants were moved to the new village of Tadmur, and the ancient site was opened to excavation.

The ruins include the Temple of Bel, the Great Colonnade, a senate building and the funerary monuments of the Valley of Tombs, over a kilometre of necropolis with more than 50 monuments. Palmyrene funerary art is known above all for the bust reliefs that sealed burial chambers, which stress clothing, jewellery and a frontal pose. The site was damaged in the Syrian civil war, which began in 2011.
palmyrene-empire: After the murder of the Roman emperor Alexander Severus in 235, generals fought over the empire while the frontiers were raided by Carpians, Goths and Alemanni and attacked by the Sassanids. Shapur I of Persia defeated the Romans at the Battle of Edessa in 260 and captured the emperor Valerian. The Palmyrene leader Odaenathus, nominally loyal to Valerian's son Gallienus, raised an army of Palmyrenes and Syrian peasants and beat Shapur near the Euphrates. In 261 he defeated the usurpers Quietus and Macrianus. He received the title Governor of the East and styled himself King of Kings.

Odaenathus and his son Hairan were assassinated in 267, by a cousin according to Joannes Zonaras and the Historia Augusta, which names him Maeonius. His ten-year-old son Vaballathus inherited the throne, with his mother Zenobia as regent. She took the real power, kept her husband's titles, secured the borders with Persia and pacified the Tanukhid tribes in Hauran.

In the spring of 270 Zenobia set out with her generals Septimius Zabbai and Septimius Zabdas. Zabdas sacked Bosra and secured Roman Arabia. In October 270 a Palmyrene army of 70,000 invaded Egypt and declared Zenobia queen of Egypt. The Roman general Tenagino Probus retook Alexandria but was besieged at the fortress of Babylon and killed himself after capture. In 271 Palmyrene forces occupied Ancyra in Galatia, the empire's furthest extent, although an attempt on Chalcedon failed.

Zenobia at first kept up a show of subordination, issuing coins in the name of the emperor Aurelian with Vaballathus as king, but toward the end of 271 Vaballathus and his mother took the title of Augustus. In 272 Aurelian marched through Anatolia, defeated Zenobia at the Battle of Immae and again at Emesa, and besieged Palmyra. Zenobia left to seek help from the Persians but was caught near the Euphrates, and the city capitulated. Most high-ranking officials were executed, and the fates of Zenobia and Vaballathus are uncertain. In 273 the Palmyrenes rebelled under Septimius Apsaios and proclaimed a relative of Zenobia, Antiochus, as Augustus. Aurelian spared Antiochus but razed the city.

Historians disagree about the revolt's motive. Andreas Alföldi saw native ethnic opposition to Rome, Irfan Shahîd a pan-Arab movement, and Mark Whittow a reaction to Rome's inability to protect Palmyra from the Persians. Warwick Ball argued that Zenobia and Vaballathus were contenders for the Roman throne, and Fergus Millar holds that the evidence is not yet enough to decide. Modern Syrian nationalists have treated the empire as a Syrian state that sought to free the Levant from Roman rule.
pamir-mountains: The Pamirs stand at a junction with several other great ranges: the Tian Shan, the Karakoram, the Kunlun, the Hindu Kush and the Himalayas. Much of the range lies in the Gorno-Badakhshan region of Tajikistan. To the south they border the Hindu Kush along Afghanistan's Wakhan Corridor, to the north they join the Tian Shan along the Alay Valley of Kyrgyzstan, and to the east they extend to the range that includes China's Kongur Tagh. The highest peak of the core is Ismoil Somoni Peak, 7,495 metres, known from 1932 to 1962 as Stalin Peak and from 1962 to 1998 as Communism Peak.

About 12,500 square kilometres, roughly a tenth of the Pamirs, is glaciated, and the Vanch-Yakh Glacier, 77 kilometres long, is the longest glacier outside the polar regions. Winters are long and bitterly cold and summers short and cool. Annual precipitation of about 130 mm supports grassland but few trees.

The lapis lazuli found in Egyptian tombs is thought to come from the Pamir area of Badakhshan. About 138 BCE Zhang Qian reached the Fergana Valley northwest of the Pamirs, and Ptolemy vaguely describes a trade route through the area. From about 600 CE Buddhist pilgrims travelled on both sides of the Pamirs to reach India from China, and in 747 a Tang army was on the Wakhan River. In Old and Middle Chinese the range was called the Onion Range, after the wild onions growing there. The Northern Silk Road, about 2,600 kilometres long, connected the Chinese capital Chang'an with Kashgar and crossed the Pamirs towards the west.

In 1838 Lieutenant John Wood reached the headwaters of the Pamir River. The British and Russians agreed in 1873 that the Afghan frontier would run along the Panj. Russian military-scientific expeditions mapped most of the Pamirs between 1871 and about 1893. In 1892 a Russian battalion under Mikhail Ionov camped near the present Murghab, and in 1893 the Russians built a fort there. The last blank areas around the Fedchenko Glacier were mapped in 1928 by the German-Soviet Alay-Pamir Expedition.

Sheep herding in the upper meadows is the main source of income of the region, and coal is mined in the west. The Pamir Highway, one of the highest international roads in the world, runs from Dushanbe in Tajikistan to Osh in Kyrgyzstan and is the main supply route of the isolated region.
pamiris: Eastern Iranian tribes, mainly Saka, along with Tocharian and probably Dardic tribes and pre-Indo-European populations, took part in the formation of the Pamiris. Between the 7th and 2nd centuries BCE the Pamir Mountains were inhabited by tribes that written sources call Sakas. The Soviet anthropologist Lev Gumilev proposed a Hephthalite origin. From the mid-3rd century BCE the Western Pamirs formed the eastern outpost of the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, and from the mid-1st century CE of the Kushan Empire, while nomadic cattle breeding developed in the Eastern Pamirs.

Turkic and later Mongol movements into Central Asia pushed settled Iranian populations into the canyons of the mountains. Between the 10th and 16th centuries Wakhan, Shughnan and Rushan, with Darvaz, were governed by local feudal dynasties and were in effect independent. In the late 18th century Shah Wanji Khan ruled the Shughnan principality, and after his death Shughnan and Wakhan again paid tribute to the rulers of Badakhshan.

In 1895 Badakhshan was divided between Afghanistan and the Emirate of Bukhara. On 2 January 1925 the Soviet government created the Gorno-Badakhshan Autonomous Oblast. Literacy there rose from 2 per cent in 1913 to almost 100 per cent in 1984. After the Soviet Union fell, Gorno-Badakhshan remained part of Tajikistan, and in 1991 the Pamiri group La'li Badakhshan was formed in Dushanbe to represent cultural interests and press for autonomy. During the civil war of 1992 to 1997 the Pamiris were, with the Gharmis, part of the United Tajik Opposition.

A United Nations investigation reported that in December 1992 people carrying identity cards showing Pamiri or Gharmi origin were seized from buses in Dushanbe and killed or disappeared. The self-proclaimed Autonomous Republic of Badakhshan existed until November 1994.

Pamiri languages belong to the Eastern Iranian group and are largely not mutually understood. The Shughni-Rushani group and Wakhi are the most widely spoken, and Shughni serves traditionally as a lingua franca. In the 1930s Pamiri intellectuals began an alphabet based on the Latin script for Shughni, but repression in the Great Purge curtailed work in Pamiri languages. Tajik, which the Pamiris call forsi, is used between them and with neighbours.

Before Islam, Zoroastrian customs were dominant, and Zoroastrian temples were active in Shughnan and Wakhan until the late Middle Ages. Ismaili Islam is associated with the stay of Nasir Khusraw, who died in 1088, in Shughnan. Pamiri Isma'ilis call their faith Dīn-i Panj-tanī, the religion of the five, and keep the lamp ritual Chirāgh-Rāwshan. The Soviet census called them Mountain Tajiks, and in China they are classed as Tajiks, while many Pamiri intellectuals see themselves as a separate people.
pampanga: Pampanga lies on the northern shore of Manila Bay and is bordered by Tarlac, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Bataan and Zambales. Its capital is San Fernando, the regional centre of Central Luzon. Angeles City, the largest city in the area, has governed itself since it received its charter in 1964. The province covers about 2,002 square kilometres and has a rainy season from May to October and a dry season for the rest of the year. The Candaba Wetlands give shelter to migratory birds that visit the Philippines from further north in Asia.

The Kingdom of Tondo before colonisation had Kapampangan peoples at its core. The Spanish named the area La Pampanga after the natives they found living along the banks (pampáng) of the Pampanga River. It was organised as a province on 11 December 1571, the first Spanish province on Luzon. The old province covered much of Central Luzon, including parts of the modern provinces of Tarlac, Bataan, Zambales, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan and Aurora, and it was divided into pueblos for administration and taxation.

On the eve of the Philippine Revolution in 1896 it was one of eight provinces placed under martial law for rebelling against Spain, and it is represented on the Flag of the Philippines by one of the eight rays of the sun.

Japanese planes bombed Clark Field on 8 December 1941, which began the invasion of the province. After the Second World War the Hukbalahap rebels fought government forces from 1946 to 1954. Under a 1947 agreement the United States held Clark Air Base until November 1991, when the Philippine Senate rejected a renewal. In June 1991 the eruption of Mount Pinatubo had buried towns and villages under lahar floods.

During the People Power revolution, 20,000 people blocked the Bamban Bridge on 25 February to stop loyalist troops reaching Manila, and the Marcos family was flown from Clark to exile in Hawaii. The former base became the Clark Special Economic Zone, created in 1993.

Pampanga has 19 municipalities and three cities. Its people are the Kapampangans, who speak Kapampangan, one of the Central Luzon languages, and the province is predominantly Roman Catholic. Farming and fishing are the main industries, with rice, corn, sugarcane and tilapia as major products. San Fernando is known for the handcrafted lanterns called parols made each Christmas season. Clark International Airport serves the province.
pamphylia: Pamphylia lay in the south of Asia Minor between Lycia and Cilicia, extending from the Mediterranean to Mount Taurus, all within the modern Antalya province of Turkey. Pisidia bounded it on the north. It was a country of small extent, with a coastline of only about 120 km and a breadth of about 50 km. Under Roman administration the term was extended to include Pisidia and the whole tract up to the frontiers of Phrygia and Lycaonia. The name comes from the Greek for of mingled tribes or races, and Herodotus derived it from a Dorian tribe, the Pamphyloi.

Herodotus and Strabo record that the Pamphylians descended from Greeks who came with Calchas and Amphilochos after the Trojan War. Some modern scholars suggest that they migrated from Arcadia and the Peloponnese in the 12th century BCE. Britannica describes them as a mixture of aboriginal inhabitants, immigrant Cilicians and Greeks. In the Late Bronze Age the region lay on the western edge of the Hittite sphere of influence. In the historical era the population spoke Pamphylian, an idiosyncratic dialect of Greek that was seemingly influenced by neighbouring Anatolian languages and shares features with Arcadian and Cypriot.

After Cyrus defeated Croesus, Pamphylia passed to the Persian Empire, and Darius placed it in his first tax-district with Lycia, Ionia and others. Between 468 and 465 BCE the Athenians under Cimon defeated the Persians at the Eurymedon and added Pamphylia to the Delian League.

Persia retook it near the end of the Peloponnesian War, and after Alexander the Great defeated Darius III it passed back to Greek rule. After the defeat of Antiochus III in 190 BCE it was annexed by the Romans to the dominions of Eumenes of Pergamum. Some of its people then joined the Pisidians and Cilicians in piracy, with Side as the chief slave market of these raiders. After the death of Amyntas, king of Galatia, it became a district of a Roman province.

Its archaeological sites include Perga, Aspendos, Side, Sillyon and Etenna. At Aspendos a Roman bridge over the Eurymedon was reconstructed by the Seljuks and follows a zigzag course over the river. Notable Pamphylians include the mathematician Apollonius of Perga, the benefactress Plancia Magna of Perga and the historian Philip of Side.
pamplona: Pamplona lies at about 450 metres above sea level in a rounded valley, the Basin of Pamplona, on the flood plain of the Arga river, a tributary of the Ebro. The basin links the mountainous north of Navarre with the Ebro valley, and its position at a crossroads has served as a commercial link between those very different parts of the region. The historical centre stands on the left bank of the Arga.

Early settlement there goes back to the late Bronze Age or early Iron Age. In the winter of 75 to 74 BCE the area served as a camp for the Roman general Pompey in the war against Sertorius, and he is considered the founder of Pompaelo. Later research found that it was already the chief town of the Vascones, who called it Iruña, meaning the city. During the Visigothic period it became an episcopal see, and a staging ground for the Christianization of the area. The Franks raided it in 541.

From the 11th century economic recovery revived urban life, and the pilgrimages to Santiago de Compostela renewed commercial and cultural exchange with Christian Europe. In the 12th century two new boroughs, San Cernín and San Nicolás, were added to the original nucleus, the Navarrería, and the population there was swelled by Occitan merchants and artisans. Charles III decreed the union of the three places under a single municipality in 1423.

After the Castilian conquest of Navarre in 1512, Pamplona remained the capital of the semi-autonomous kingdom, which kept its own institutions and laws, but it became a Castilian-Spanish outpost. In 1513 King Ferdinand V ordered the demolition of the medieval castle and the city's monasteries and the building of a new castle nearby. Its southern walls were destroyed only in 1915.

Pamplona is the capital of the Chartered Community of Navarre. Its Gothic cathedral, of the 14th century, has an outstanding cloister, and the citadel and three of the four sides of the city walls survive. The city is known for the running of the bulls during the San Fermín festival, held each year from 6 to 14 July and brought to literary renown by Ernest Hemingway's novel The Sun Also Rises of 1926.
pan-africanism: Pan-Africanism aims to strengthen solidarity among all indigenous peoples of Africa and all peoples of African descent. It is said to originate in the struggles of sub-Saharan Africans against enslavement and colonization, from resistance on slave ships to plantation uprisings and the Back to Africa movements of the 19th century. Its core belief is that African people, on the continent and in the diaspora, share a common history and a common destiny.

The end of the 19th century produced an intercontinental political movement, alongside numerous slave insurrections in the New World, of which the Haitian Revolution is the best known. Ethiopianism gave a religious form to the same outlook. In London the Sons of Africa, addressed by Quobna Ottobah Cugoano in 1791, wrote letters to Granville Sharp, William Pitt and King George III.

Modern Pan-Africanism began around the start of the 20th century, led first by people of the diaspora. Henry Sylvester Williams, a barrister, established the African Association around 1897 and called the First Pan-African Conference, held in London's Westminster Hall in 1900, to protest the seizure of colonial lands and racial discrimination. The Pan-African Congress series followed, with meetings in Paris in 1919, London in 1921 and 1923, New York in 1927 and Manchester in 1945, pressing the cause of decolonisation.

Ghana's independence in March 1957 made Kwame Nkrumah its first prime minister and president, and he became a leading advocate of the unity of independent Africa and of regional integration for the whole continent. Under him Pan-Africanism moved beyond a movement of black Africa to a political discourse of regional unity. Pan-African thought influenced the founding of the Organisation of African Unity in 1963, since succeeded by the African Union. Most newly independent states opposed Nkrumah's wish for political union because they saw it as a threat to their sovereignty, and Félix Houphouët-Boigny was a staunch opponent.

The movement has produced many organisations and symbols, among them Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association, which adopted the red, black and green flag on 13 August 1920 in New York, and Robert Sobukwe's Pan Africanist Congress in apartheid South Africa. Flags in Malawi, Kenya and South Sudan draw on those colours, while green, yellow and red come from Ethiopia's 1897 flag. Women such as Amy Jacques Garvey and Claudia Jones were prominent, although scholarship has given them little attention. Critics, among them the journalist Philip Ochieng in 1971, have called it a movement of a self-interested educated elite that did not concern ordinary Africans.
pan-arabism: Pan-Arabism, in Arabic al-waḥda al-ʿarabiyyah or Arab unity, calls for the unification of all Arab peoples in a single nation-state from the Atlantic Ocean to the Arabian Sea. It is closely tied to Arab nationalism, which holds that the Arabs form one nation. Its origins are often traced to the Nahda, the Arab awakening of the late 19th century in the Arab regions of the Ottoman Empire. Jurji Zaydan, a Levantine Christian émigré in Egypt, argued that Arabic-speaking regions from the Maghreb to the Persian Gulf form one people whose linguistic bond outweighs religious and territorial ones.

As a political project it was first pressed by Sharif Hussein ibn Ali of Mecca, who sought a unified Arab state in the Mashreq. The Hussein-McMahon Correspondence of 1915 and 1916 produced a promise by the United Kingdom of support if the Arabs revolted, but the Sykes-Picot Agreement of 1916 divided parts of the region between the United Kingdom and France. A more formal ideology appeared in the 1930s among Syrian thinkers, and Michel Aflaq and Zaki al-Arsuzi helped found the Arab Ba'ath Party.

Abdullah I of Jordan hoped to unite Syria, Palestine and Jordan as Greater Syria, and distrust of this plan helped lead to the founding of the Arab League in 1945. Egypt had shown little interest in pan-Arabism before the 1950s. Under Gamal Abdel Nasser, Arab nationalism and Arab socialism became state policy. The United Arab Republic of Egypt and Syria, formed in 1958 on the initiative of Syrian leaders, was the first merger of two independent Arab states. It was a unitary state, which critics saw as a small country annexed by a larger one, and it ended in 1961 when Syrian army officers staged a coup and withdrew.

Other attempts followed. The Arab Federation of Jordan and Iraq, also founded in 1958, collapsed after six months. The United Arab States, a confederation with Yemen, dissolved in 1961. The union of seven emirates as the United Arab Emirates and of North and South Yemen are rare cases of actual unification.

The decline of pan-Arabism is attributed to pan-Islamism, sectarian and social differences, rivalry among Arab leaders and military defeat. Israel's victory in the 1967 Six-Day War and the failure of Egypt and Syria to generate economic growth damaged its credibility. By the mid-1970s, according to The Continuum Political Encyclopedia of the Middle East, the idea of Arab unity had become less apparent in Arab politics, though it remained a goal for the masses. By the late 1980s it was eclipsed by nationalist and Islamist ideologies.
pan-geng: Pan Geng, personal name Zi Xun, was a Shang dynasty king, best known for moving the capital to its final location at Yin. Sima Qian lists him in the Records of the Grand Historian as the nineteenth Shang king, succeeding his older brother Yang Jia, while oracle-bone inscriptions unearthed at Yinxu identify him as the eighteenth. Both the Bamboo Annals and the Records of the Grand Historian give him a reign of about 28 years.

The Bamboo Annals summarise the main events. He was enthroned in the year Bingyin with Yan as his capital. In the seventh year the Ying vassal came to Yan to pay homage. In the fourteenth year he moved the capital to Beimeng and renamed it Yin, in the fifteenth he reviewed his army at the new capital, and in the nineteenth he assigned his minister Fen to Yayu. The Records of the Grand Historian give a different account of the move. It says the people of Yin, tired of being moved, first opposed it, but were satisfied once the system of government of the founder Tang was adopted, and the move proved prosperous.

On his death he was given the posthumous name Pan Geng and was succeeded by his younger brother Xiao Xin. A chapter of the Book of Documents titled "Pan Geng" is held by tradition to be a speech by this king, but its language differs so much from that of his time that it is most likely not a product of his era. Wang Anshi, replying to an accusatory letter from Sima Guang, cited Pan Geng as an example of undaunted perseverance in pursuing a goal, the movement of the capital, against the opposition of both officials and common people.
pan-islamism: Pan-Islamism advocates the unity of Muslims under one Islamic state, often a caliphate or an international organisation with Islamic principles. It differs from pan-Arabism by focusing on religion rather than ethnicity, and it takes the ummah, the Muslim community, as the focus of allegiance. Classical scholars such as al-Mawardi and al-Ghazali discussed the ummah in a political sense, and the ideology draws on the early Islam of Muhammad and the Rashidun Caliphate. Many scholars see its doctrines in earlier states such as Islamic Iberia and the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires.

In the 18th century reformers such as Shah Wali Allah of Delhi, Muhammad Ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab and Uthman dan Fodio called for puritanical renewal. They are regarded as precursors of modern pan-Islamism, but their influence stayed local, in South Asia, Arabia and West Africa, since they did not call for an international Islamic entity.

In the last quarter of the 19th century Sultan Abdul Hamid II promoted pan-Islamism in the Ottoman Empire, after Ottomanism, to prevent secession movements among the empire's Muslim peoples. The movement's major thinkers were Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, Muhammad Abduh and Rashid Rida, who opposed European penetration of Muslim lands. Afghani feared that nationalism would divide Muslims and sought the replacement of rulers subservient to foreigners by strong patriotic ones. His student Abduh preferred gradual reform through education and distanced himself from Afghani's political path.

Rida believed unity required restoring a caliphate that applied the Sharia, and in the 1920s he set out his doctrine in al-Khilafa aw al-Imama al-'Uzma. His journal Al-Manar promoted Islamic revival and anti-British revolt. Lothrop Stoddard noted in 1921 that the pan-Islamic press had grown from about 200 journals in 1900 to over 1000 by 1914.

After the abolition of the caliphate in 1924, pan-Islamism mobilised traditionalist and reform movements alike. After the Second World War, Arab nationalist parties such as the Ba'ath and Nasserist parties took power in Egypt, Libya, Iraq and Syria, and Islamists faced repression. Sayyid Qutb was imprisoned and later executed, and Nasser took control of the mosques. After the Arab defeat in the Six-Day War, pan-Islamism regained ground against pan-Arabism. Nasser dropped his opposition to a pan-Islamic platform, and the first summit of Muslim heads of state met at Rabat in 1969, leading to the Organisation of Islamic Conference.

During the Cold War Saudi Arabia and allied states led the pan-Islamist effort against communism. The Iranian Revolution of 1979 and the Afghan mujahideen's success against the Soviet Union in 1989 raised the popularity of Islamists. Sunni thinkers such as Abul Ala Maududi embraced a new caliphate, while Ruhollah Khomeini envisaged a united Islamic state led by a Shia scholar of law.
panama-canal: The idea of a canal across the Isthmus of Panama dates back to 1513, when the Spanish conquistador Vasco Núñez de Balboa first crossed the isthmus and noted the possibility in his journal. The earliest proposal for action dates to 1534, when the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V ordered a survey for a route through the Americas to ease the voyage of ships between Spain and Peru. In 1668 the English physician and philosopher Sir Thomas Browne proposed the isthmus as the most convenient place for such a canal.

The French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps, who had built the Suez Canal, and the engineer Philippe Bunau-Varilla led the French attempt, begun in 1881. A concession from the Colombian government, obtained in 1878 and valid for 99 years, allowed the company to dig and exploit a canal. The French stopped in 1889 because investors lost confidence after engineering problems and a high death rate among workers. The United States took control of the canal property on 4 May 1904, inheriting a depleted workforce and a mass of equipment, much of it in poor condition.

The canal is an artificial waterway 82 kilometres long that connects the Caribbean Sea with the Pacific Ocean at the narrowest point of the isthmus. Because of the shape of the isthmus its general direction from the Atlantic to the Pacific is from north-west to south-east. Locks at each end lift ships up to Gatun Lake, an artificial lake 26 metres above sea level, created in 1913 by damming the Chagres River; locks at the other end lower them again. At its creation Gatun Lake was the largest human-made lake in the world. The original locks are 33.5 metres wide and admit ships of the Panamax size. A third, wider set of locks, built between 2007 and 2016, takes larger vessels.

The United States built the canal under the Isthmian Canal Commission, which also controlled the Panama Canal Zone. In 1907 Stevens resigned as chief engineer and President Theodore Roosevelt appointed Major George Washington Goethals of the US Army Corps of Engineers, who finished the work in 1914, two years ahead of the target date. The canal opened on 15 August 1914.

It shortened voyages between the oceans and spared ships the long and hazardous route around the southern tip of South America. Traffic rose from about 1,000 ships in 1914 to 14,702 vessels in 2008. The United States kept control of the canal and the Panama Canal Zone until the Torrijos–Carter Treaties of 1977 provided for its handover to Panama. After a period of joint American and Panamanian control, the Panamanian government took over in 1999, and the canal is now run by the Panama Canal Authority.
panama-canal-zone: The Panama Canal Zone, also known simply as the Canal Zone, was a concession of the United States in the Isthmus of Panama that existed from 1903 to 1979. It consisted of the Panama Canal and an area generally extending five miles on each side of the centreline, but excluding Panama City and Colón. Its capital was Balboa. The territory covered 553 square miles and spanned two provinces of Panama, Colón and Panamá. The lakes created to assure a steady supply of water for the locks were included. The zone had no formal boundary restrictions on Panamanians, and in Panama City one could enter it simply by crossing a street.

Proposals for a canal across the isthmus go back to 1529, when Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón suggested four routes, but Spanish officials judged the work beyond 16th-century technology. The zone was created on 18 November 1903 from Panamanian territory by the Hay–Bunau-Varilla Treaty. Panama received US$10 million and annual payments of US$250,000, and the zone was formally turned over on 4 May 1904. American construction concluded in August 1914 with the opening of the canal to commercial traffic. An executive order of Woodrow Wilson placed governance under the Secretary of War, giving the canal an essentially military arrangement.

During construction and into the 1940s the labour force was divided into a gold roll and a silver roll. In practice race decided the placing: American and northern European white workers went on the gold roll, and Black and southern European workers, the Black workers mostly from Barbados and Jamaica, on the silver roll. Until 1945 the zone operated under a Jim Crow system, with separate entrances at the post office. Black workers were banned from unionising after the strike of 1920, and segregation in housing and schooling persisted.

The zone, a political exclave with its own courts, police and civil government that cut Panama geographically in half, became a cause of conflict. Major rioting occurred on 21 May 1958 and 3 November 1959, and serious rioting in January 1964 led the United States to ease its controls, allowing Panamanian flags to fly beside the American flag. The Torrijos–Carter Treaties, agreed in 1977, abolished the zone on 1 October 1979, when most of its land was transferred to Panama. The Panama Canal Commission was created to ease the transition, and the canal was fully turned over to Panama in 1999.
panama-city: Pedro Arias Dávila, also called Pedrarias, founded the city on 15 August 1519. Within a few years it became a launching point for the exploration and conquest of Peru, and the expeditions that conquered the Inca Empire set out from it in 1532. It was also a transit point for the gold and silver sent back to Spain through the isthmus, on a route that led to the fairs of Nombre de Dios and Portobelo.

On 28 January 1671 the privateer Henry Morgan attacked the city with a band of 1,400 men, looted it and set it on fire. The ruins, known as Panamá Viejo, still stand and are now a World Heritage Site. The city was rebuilt on a peninsula about 8 kilometres to the southwest, the site now called the Casco Viejo, which was planned as a walled city against further pirate attacks.

The Panama Railroad ran fully from 1855, and between 1848 and 1869 about 375,000 people crossed the isthmus from the Atlantic to the Pacific and 225,000 in the other direction, which brought the city prosperity. Panama declared independence from Colombia on 3 November 1903. The Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty of that year gave the United States a strip of land ten miles wide for a canal, and the canal was completed in 1914. William Gorgas, the chief sanitary officer, ordered the fumigation of homes and the cleansing of water, and yellow fever was eradicated by November 1905. Tension over the Canal Zone broke out on 9 January 1964, remembered as Martyrs' Day, and in 1999 the United States transferred full control of the canal to Panama.

Panama City is the capital and largest city of the Republic of Panama, at the Pacific entrance of the Panama Canal. About 410,354 people live in the city proper and over a million in the Panamá District. It is the country's political and administrative centre and a hub of banking and commerce. Panamá Viejo and the Casco Viejo, which UNESCO designated a World Heritage Site in 2003, hold the city's colonial past, and the old quarter mixes Spanish colonial, French, Antillean and art deco buildings.
panama-papers: Mossack Fonseca was a Panamanian law firm and corporate service provider whose services included incorporating and operating shell companies in friendly jurisdictions on behalf of clients. It managed more than 300,000 companies over the years, with the number of active companies peaking at more than 80,000 in 2009, and its clients came from more than 100 countries. It worked with more than 14,000 banks, law firms and other intermediaries. Owning an offshore company is generally legal, and the reasons for it can be lawful, such as estate planning or holding funds in dollars.

An anonymous source calling itself John Doe leaked the documents to the journalist Bastian Obermayer of the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung. The paper asked the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists for help in analysing 2.6 terabytes of data. Journalists from 107 media organisations in 80 countries worked on them for more than a year, and the first stories appeared on 3 April 2016 together with 150 of the documents. The source insisted on encrypted communication and never met the reporters. In a statement released on 6 May, the source cited income inequality as the reason for the leak.

The firm told its clients on 1 April that its email had been hacked. Security experts noted that it had not encrypted its emails and appeared to be running a three-year-old version of the Drupal web software with known vulnerabilities.

The leak covered 214,488 offshore entities, over 210,000 of them in twenty-one jurisdictions, more than half in the British Virgin Islands. Reporters found that some of the shell companies seemed to have been used for fraud, tax evasion and evading international sanctions; more than 30 clients were at some point blacklisted by the US Treasury. Initial reports named five then-heads of state or government, and officials and associates of leaders in more than forty other countries. Mossack Fonseca said that nothing in the documents suggested it had done anything illegal.

Panama objected to the name Panama Papers, fearing damage to the country's image. Its attorney general announced an investigation on 4 April, and on 12 April prosecutors searched the firm's offices for 27 hours. President Varela announced a commission led by the Nobel laureate Joseph Stiglitz. The ICIJ's director, Gerard Ryle, called the leak probably the biggest blow the offshore world had ever taken.
pancasila: In 1942 Japan occupied the Dutch East Indies and later promised future self-government. On 1 June 1945, the last day of the first session of the Investigating Committee for Preparatory Work for Independence, the nationalist Sukarno proposed five principles as the philosophical basis of an independent Indonesia. He named them Pancasila, from the Sanskrit pañca, five, and śīla, principles, and rejected the earlier name Panca Dharma because dharma means obligation. His original five were Indonesian nationalism, internationalism, deliberative consensus, social welfare, and a divinity that upholds religious freedom. The formulation was a compromise between advocates of an Islamic state and of a secular state.

A Committee of Nine drafted a preamble, the Jakarta Charter, and moved the principle of divinity to first place. Its first sila originally obliged its Muslim adherents to carry out Islamic law. On 18 August 1945 the Preparatory Committee for Indonesian Independence deleted that clause, leaving belief in the One and Only God, to ensure national unity.

The five principles are belief in the One and Only God, just and civilised humanity, the unity of Indonesia, democracy led by wisdom in deliberation among representatives of the people, and social justice for all the people of Indonesia. Their legal formulation is in the fourth paragraph of the preamble of the constitution. Sukarno suggested that the five could be compressed into three, socio-nationalism, socio-democracy and belief in God, and further into one, gotong royong, or mutual cooperation. The national motto, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, often translated as unity in diversity, belongs to the same effort to unite a diverse archipelago.

In the Constitutional Assembly elected in 1955 the Pancasila Bloc held 53.3 per cent of the seats and the Islamic Bloc 44.8 per cent, and the debate could not be resolved. On 5 July 1959 Sukarno dissolved the assembly by decree and reimposed the 1945 Constitution. Under Suharto's New Order Pancasila was promoted as the supreme national ideology, with a mandatory indoctrination programme from 1978, and in 1983 adherence was made mandatory for all organisations. Critics say the New Order used its vagueness to legitimise authoritarian acts. After 1998 the coercive apparatus was dismantled, while Pancasila remained the foundational state ideology. Some scholars criticise it as overly vague; defenders argue that its generality gives the flexibility needed to manage Indonesia's diversity.
panchmahal-district: Panchmahal district occupies the eastern end of Gujarat. It is bordered by Dahod district to the north-east and east, Vadodara to the south-west, Chhota Udaipur to the south-east, Kheda to the west and Mahisagar to the north. The name joins panch, five, with mahal, a word of Arabic origin used for a province, estate or division. The district was originally the Pavagadh Panch Mahals, five mahals administered from Pavagadh: Godhra, Kalol, Halol, Dahod and Jhalod.

The district's history centres on the city of Champaner and the nearby Pavagadh Hill. Champaner was established in 647 in the territory of King Vanraj Chavda. In the 13th century the Delhi Sultanate under Alauddin Khalji took the city from the Chauhan rulers, and their rule lasted until 1484, when Sultan Mahmud Begada of Gujarat captured it. Under the Mughal Empire, from 1575 to 1727, Godhra became the centre of the district. The author of the Mirat-i Sikandari, writing in 1611, called the region's mangoes the best in the kingdom and said sandalwood grew abundantly and was used to build houses. In October 1997 Dahod was separated as a district of its own.

Forest covered 23.26 per cent of the land in 2011, nearly all of it reserved forest, with mahuda, teak and khakhra among the common trees. Quartz, trap and quartzite are quarried for road material, manganese is mined, and the district has the most extensive graphite deposits in Gujarat. Agriculture employed 75.88 per cent of the working population in 2011, mainly in rice, maize, wheat, castor and tur, and gram is a characteristic second crop in the east. Industry is concentrated in Godhra, Kalol and Halol.
pancho-villa: Villa told conflicting stories about his early life. According to most sources he was born on 5 June 1878 as José Doroteo Arango Arámbula, the eldest of five children of a sharecropper, Agustín Arango, and Micaela Arámbula. He grew up on the Rancho de la Coyotada, one of the largest haciendas in Durango, and had little schooling beyond basic literacy. He worked as a sharecropper, muleskinner, butcher, bricklayer and foreman for a US railway company. His dictated memoirs say that he became a hill-country thief after killing a hacienda owner who had raped his sister; the record shows that on 22 September 1894 he shot the man in the foot.

Villa joined the rebellion that Francisco Madero called in 1910 against President Porfirio Díaz, after Abraham González reached out to him in Chihuahua, and Madero promoted him to colonel. After Madero was murdered in the coup of February 1913, Villa joined Venustiano Carranza's Constitutionalist Army against Victoriano Huerta. That year local commanders elected him provisional governor of Chihuahua against Carranza's wishes, and he carried out a significant land reform, confiscating estates and expelling their owners. In 1914 Carranza diverted him from a direct advance on Mexico City, and Carranza's army entered the capital first in August.

After Huerta's fall, Villa and Emiliano Zapata allied against Carranza after the Convention of Aguascalientes, and a civil war followed. Álvaro Obregón decisively defeated Villa in 1915, and he split his remaining forces into guerrilla bands. At Namiquipa he rounded up the wives of men who had formed a home guard and allowed his soldiers to rape them, although some historians argue that crimes he did not commit were attributed to him.

On 9 March 1916 nearly 100 of his men attacked Columbus, New Mexico, in which 18 Americans and about 80 Villistas died. President Wilson sent 5,000 soldiers under General Frederick Funston, and John Pershing's force, using aircraft and trucks, pursued Villa fruitlessly until February 1917.

After Carranza's fall in 1920 Villa negotiated an amnesty with the interim president Adolfo de la Huerta and received a landed estate on condition that he retire from politics. On 20 July 1923 he was shot dead in an ambush in Parral, most likely on the orders of Plutarco Elías Calles and President Obregón. His body was stolen from its grave in 1926 and the head removed. In 1976 his remains were reburied in the Monument to the Revolution in Mexico City.

He is generally regarded in Mexico as a hero who stood up to the United States, the subject of corridos, films and novels, while some American media call him a murderer. His biographer Friedrich Katz judged that his time as governor of Chihuahua might in some ways be called the first welfare state in Mexico.
pandara-vanniyan: Kulasegaram Vairamuthu Pandara Vanniyan was a native of the Vanni and is said to have reigned there from 1785. Much about his family is unclear, but reports give him a sister, Nallanachal Vanniyan, and two younger brothers who served as his minister and his commander. He married into the family of Kumarasinghe Maha Vanniya of Nuwara Wewa, and so gained political power in the southern Vanni as well as the north. He is said to have lived at Kumulamunai, in the present Mullaitivu District.

The Vanni served as a buffer zone between the north and south of Sri Lanka. After the Portuguese captured the Jaffna Kingdom in 1621 the region was under their nominal control, and around 1782 the Dutch defeated the Vanniar chieftains.

Pandara Vanniyan is said to have defeated the Dutch officer Lieutenant von Driberg several times. Against the British, the Vanniars carried on a predatory warfare in Mannar and Trincomalee and reached the Jaffna Peninsula, and the British built forts to keep them at bay. In alliance with the Kandy Kingdom he rose to expel the British from his district. On 25 August 1803 he attacked the Government House at Mullaitivu, drove out the garrison under Captain Edward Mudge of the 19th Regiment and seized the fort and its cannons. He then overran the northern districts as far as Elephant Pass.

He turned from conventional warfare to guerrilla tactics, but the British organised a three-pronged attack from Jaffna, Mannar and Trincomalee. Von Driberg, who had stayed on after the British ousted the Dutch, defeated him on 31 October 1803 at Katsilaimadu, capturing a cannon given to him by the Kandyan king Sri Wickrema Rajasinghe. His houses were burned and his people dispersed into the jungle and out of the Vanni.

No longer a ruler, Pandara Vanniyan withdrew to areas near the Kandy Kingdom. Accounts of his end differ: by one he died fighting the British, by another he remained there until September 1810, when British forces ambushed him, and later died of his injuries. Von Driberg set up a granite monument at Katsilaimadu recording the defeat; in 2010 it was found broken. Prime Minister Ranasinghe Premadasa declared him a national hero in 1982, and a statue stands in Vavuniya. Tamil nationalists honour him as an epic hero, and he is the subject of a novel by M. Karunanidhi and of a play by Mullaimani Ve Cuppiramaniyam that won a prize from the Ceylon Art Council in 1964.
pandavas: The name Pandava means descendants of Pandu. According to the Adi Parva of the Mahabharata, Pandu was crowned king of the Kuru kingdom although he was younger than his blind brother Dhritarashtra. Cursed by a sage to die if he touched a wife in desire, he withdrew to the forest with his wives Kunti and Madri. Kunti had received a boon from the sage Durvasa allowing her to have a son by any god, and at Pandu's request she used it and shared her mantra with Madri.

Yudhishthira was fathered by the god Dharmadeva, Bhima by Vayu, Arjuna by Indra and the twins Nakula and Sahadeva by the Ashvins. After Pandu's death Kunti brought the boys to Hastinapura, where they were raised with their cousins the Kauravas, the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra.

Duryodhana, the eldest Kaurava, resented his cousins. When Yudhishthira was named crown prince, Duryodhana and his uncle Shakuni had a palace of flammable lac built at Varnavarta, but Vidura warned the Pandavas and they escaped by a tunnel. Arjuna then won the hand of Draupadi, princess of Panchala, in an archery contest, and all five brothers married her. Dhritarashtra partitioned the kingdom and gave them barren Khandavaprastha, which they built into the city of Indraprastha.

Shakuni then drew Yudhishthira into a game of dice, in which he lost his kingdom, his brothers, himself and Draupadi. In a last game the loser was to spend twelve years in exile and a thirteenth in disguise, and the Pandavas lost. They spent that year as servants at the court of King Virata of Matsya, and when they returned the Kauravas refused to give back the kingdom.

The Kurukshetra War lasted eighteen days. All hundred Kauravas and their army were killed, and the Pandavas, aided by Krishna, won at great cost. Yudhishthira was crowned, and the brothers ruled Hastinapura for thirty-six years before setting out with Draupadi for Mount Kailash.

The Harivamsa Purana, of the 8th century CE, tells the Jain version of their story. In the Garhwal region of Uttarakhand villagers perform the Pandav Lila, a ritual re-enactment of episodes from the epic in song, dance and recitation.
pandita-ramabai: Ramabai Dongre was born on 23 April 1858 into a Marathi-speaking Chitpavan Brahmin family. Her father, Anant Shastri Dongre, a Sanskrit scholar, taught her Sanskrit at home, and he had also taught her mother, Lakshmi, against the prevailing custom. The family earned a meagre living by reciting the Purana at pilgrimage sites across India. Orphaned at sixteen during the Great Famine of 1876 to 1878, Ramabai and her brother Srinivas continued to travel and recite Sanskrit scriptures. Her fame reached Calcutta, where her address in the senate hall of the university was well received, and in 1878 the University of Calcutta conferred on her the titles Pandita and Sarasvati.

After Srinivas died in 1880 she married Bipin Behari Medhvi, a Bengali lawyer of the Kayastha community, in a civil ceremony on 13 November 1880. The marriage was inter-caste and inter-regional and thought improper at the time. Their daughter Manorama was born in 1881, and Medhvi died of cholera on 4 February 1882.

Ramabai moved to Pune and founded the Arya Mahila Samaj to promote women's education and deliverance from child marriage. She gave evidence to the Hunter Commission on education, urging that teachers be trained, women school inspectors appointed and Indian women admitted to medical colleges. In 1883 she went to Britain, where she was refused a place in medical training because of progressive deafness, and there she converted to Christianity, citing her disillusionment with what she saw as orthodox Hinduism's low regard for women. She kept some independence from her Anglican mentors, retaining her vegetarian diet and rejecting the doctrine of the Trinity.

From 1886 she spent two years in the United States, lecturing and publishing The High-Caste Hindu Woman, and raised the equivalent of 60,000 rupees for a school in India. She returned in 1889 and founded Sharada Sadan in Pune for child widows. When several students converted she lost the backing of Pune's Hindu reformers, and she moved the school to Kedgaon as the Mukti Mission. During the famine of 1896 she toured Maharashtra's villages in bullock carts and brought thousands of outcast children, widows and orphans into its shelter. By 1900 it had 1,500 residents.

Ramabai translated the Bible into Marathi from the original Hebrew and Greek. She met opposition from conservative upper-caste elites in Maharashtra, among them B. G. Tilak, who attacked her work in his paper Kesari. She received the Kaisar-i-Hind Medal in 1919. Her daughter Manorama died in 1921, and Ramabai died of septic bronchitis on 5 April 1922, aged 63. Scholars of Pentecostalism have pointed to a revival at the Mukti Mission in June 1905 as part of the global revivals from which the movement arose. The mission still operates.
pandya-dynasty: The Pandyas, also called the Pandyas of Madurai, were one of the three great kingdoms of Tamilakam, with the Cholas and the Cheras; their rulers were known together as the three crowned rulers, the mu-ventar. The dynasty existed since at least the 5th to 3rd centuries BCE, and its origin and timeline are difficult to establish. Early Pandya chieftains ruled Pandya Nadu, which included the inland city of Madurai and the southern port of Korkai. Greek accounts, the edicts of the Maurya emperor Ashoka and Tamil-Brahmi coins and inscriptions suggest their continuity from the 3rd century BCE.

Tamil legend tells that three brothers, Cheran, Cholan and Pandyan, ruled together at Korkai, and that the two others then left to found their own kingdoms. The Silappatikaram says the Pandya emblem was a fish. Medieval Pandya kings claimed descent from the Lunar Race, and tradition holds that the Sangams, the academies of Tamil poets, were held at Madurai under their patronage.

The early Pandyas faded into obscurity with the rise of the Kalabhra dynasty. Kadungon revived the kingdom in the late 6th century, and from the 6th to the 9th century the Chalukyas of Badami or the Rashtrakutas, the Pallavas of Kanchi and the Pandyas dominated south India, often invading the Chola country, the Chera country, Venadu and Sri Lanka. The Pandyas declined with the rise of the Cholas of Thanjavur in the 9th century and were in constant conflict with them.

They entered a golden age under Maravarman I and Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I in the 13th century. Jatavarman I, about 1251, expanded the kingdom into the Telugu country as far as Nellore, into south Kerala, and conquered northern Sri Lanka. Maravarman Kulasekhara I defeated an alliance of the Hoysalas and the Cholas in 1279 and invaded Sri Lanka, from where the Tooth Relic of the Buddha was carried away. Rule was shared among several royals, one holding primacy.

An internal crisis coincided with the Khalji invasion of south India in 1310-11. Sultanate raids followed, with the loss of south Kerala in 1312, of north Sri Lanka in 1323 and the establishment of the Madurai Sultanate in 1334. Later Pandyas ruled from Tenkasi and Tirunelveli.

Early Pandya rulers are traditionally associated with Jainism and later with Shaivism. Pandya Nadu was home to major temples, among them the Meenakshi Temple in Madurai, which were large employers and landowners and also served as banks, schools and dispensaries. The Pandyas issued silver punch-marked and copper coins bearing the fish, their emblem. The dynasty is considered one of the longest-ruling in the world, in power from roughly 500 BCE to 1618 CE, though its extent varied greatly.
panfilo-de-narvaez: Pánfilo de Narváez was born in Castile and was a relative of Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar. Bartolomé de las Casas described him as tall and somewhat blonde inclined to redness. He took part in the Spanish conquest of Jamaica in 1509 and went to Cuba in 1511 to join its conquest under Velázquez. He led expeditions to the eastern end of the island with Las Casas and Juan de Grijalva, and Las Casas, an eyewitness, reported that Narváez presided over the massacre of Caonao, where Spanish troops killed a village full of people who had come to meet them with food.

In 1519 Velázquez sponsored Hernán Cortés's expedition to Mexico but, doubting his loyalty, recalled it. Cortés disobeyed. Velázquez named Narváez governor of Mexico and sent him with 1,400 men in 19 ships to intercept Cortés. Narváez landed at Veracruz and made camp at the Totonac town of Cempoala. Cortés returned to the coast with perhaps as few as 250 men. Although Narváez's remaining 900 outnumbered them three to one, he was outmanoeuvred, lost an eye and was captured at the Battle of Cempoala on 27 May 1520. After two years in prison he was sent back to Spain.

Charles V then appointed him adelantado of Florida. He sailed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda on 17 June 1527 with five ships and 600 men, and after a hurricane in Cuba set out again in February 1528. Storms drove him to Florida's west coast, where he landed in April 1528 with 300 men near Tampa Bay, among hostile people. The party divided, with about 100 men and 10 women on the ships and 300 men and 42 horses marching north. Narváez never saw the ships again.

Finding no gold, his men built four rafts near the St. Marks River to reach Pánuco. A storm drowned most of the remaining 240 men near Galveston Island, and Narváez and a small group were carried out to sea and never seen again. Four men survived: Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, Andrés Dorantes de Carranza, Alonso del Castillo Maldonado and the Moroccan slave Estevanico. Cabeza de Vaca's account of their journey on foot across the present-day southwestern United States and northern Mexico was the first book to describe the people, animals and plants of inland North America.
panjikent: Panjakent, also written Penjikent, lies in the Sughd province of Tajikistan on the river Zeravshan. The ruins of the old town are on the outskirts of the modern city. Downstream, on the tugay-vegetated floodplain of the river, lies the Sarazm Important Bird Area. The ancient town stood about 90 km from Samarkand, to which it was a vassal state.

Ancient Panjakent, known as Panchekanth, was a small but flourishing town of the Sogdians in pre-Islamic Central Asia. The Sogdians settled in city states in the Zeravshan valley and the surrounding oases, clustered mostly around Samarkand. These states had strong rivalries, their own traditions and ruling families, and a very decentralised political system. The town grew in the 5th century, when established businessmen and landowners made their livelihoods there. In 722 Arab Muslim forces besieged and took it, and its last ruler, Divashtich, fled into the upper Zeravshan but was captured and sentenced to death.

For around fifty years the town was ruled by new administrators, and towards the end of the 8th century the town on the upper terraces was depopulated and relocated. Records of a Penjikent rulership written in Sogdian were found not far away on Mount Mug. According to Arab geographers, in the 10th century Panjakent had a formal Friday mosque, which distinguished a town from a village; it was the easternmost city of Sogd and became well known for its walnuts.

The ruins have yielded numerous murals, and many are now displayed in the Hermitage Museum and in the National Museum of Antiquities of Tajikistan in Dushanbe. They show details of dress and daily life, and a great variety of influences: Greek decorative styles meet the Iranian narratives of the Shahnameh and the epic cycle of Rostam, scenes of festivities alternate with combats, and local cults mix with Iranian and Hindu deities. One painting shows Shiva with a halo and a sacred thread, clad in a tigerskin and seated on a cushioned seat supported by two bulls, with attendants in Sogdian dress.

The production of paintings began in the 5th century and stopped in 722 with the Arab invasion, when many works were damaged or destroyed. The Russian archaeologist Boris Marshak spent more than fifty years excavating the ruins. He stayed on as director of the excavation after Tajik independence and through the civil war of 1992 to 1997, and worked with the government of Tajikistan to protect the site.
pannonhalma-archabbey: Pannonhalma Archabbey, formally the Territorial Abbey of Saint Martin on Mount Pannonhalma, stands on a hill 282 metres high near the town of Pannonhalma and is one of the oldest historical monuments in Hungary. Saint Martin of Tours is believed to have been born at the foot of the hill, which was once called the Mount of Saint Martin. It is the second largest territorial abbey in the world, after the one at Monte Cassino. Its sights include the basilica with its crypt, the cloisters, a monumental library with 400,000 volumes and a Baroque refectory with several trompe-l'œil paintings.

Prince Géza founded it in 996 as the first Hungarian Benedictine monastery, in honour of Saint Martin of Tours, and it soon became the centre of the Benedictine order. Géza's son, King Stephen I, donated estates and privileges, and Astrik served as its first abbot. The Charter of the Tihany Benedictine Abbey, of 1055, the oldest surviving document to use the Hungarian language, is still preserved in the library. In 1096 Duke Godfrey of Bouillon, leading one of three crusader armies, spent a week there negotiating safe passage through Hungary with King Coloman. The first buildings were destroyed in 1137 and rebuilt, the present church dates from the early 13th century, and in 1486 the abbey was reconstructed in Gothic style under King Matthias.

It became an archabbey in 1541 and was fortified because of Ottoman incursions. During the occupation of Hungary by the Ottoman Empire the monks had to abandon the abbey for varying periods. A major Baroque construction was under way in the time of Archabbot Benedek Sajghó (1722–1768), and the abbey received its present form in 1832, with the library and a classicist tower. It was closed in 1786 and reopened in 1802. In 1950 the communist state confiscated the properties of the order and its schools, which were not returned until communism ended.

The abbey and its surroundings were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1996, a year after the complex was entirely reconstructed and renovated for the millennium. Its archives hold one of the richest collections of documents from the first centuries of Hungarian statehood, among them the interpolated charter of Saint Stephen of 1001–1002 and the founding charter of Tihany. A Benedictine high school, a College of Theology named after Saint Gerard of Csanád and a winery are among its present uses.
pannonia: Pannonia was a province of the Roman Empire bounded on the north and east by the Danube, on the west by Noricum and upper Italy, and on the south by Dalmatia and upper Moesia. It included western Hungary, western Slovakia, eastern Austria, northern Croatia, north-western Serbia, northern Slovenia and northern Bosnia and Herzegovina.
