After the final extension of the castle about 1254 the town was extended and walls were built round its edge; they survive on their medieval foundations. Many of the original burgage plots also survive.

Monkton Priory, on a hill across the river, was founded in 1098 by Arnulf de Montgomery and granted by him to the Benedictine order. Monkton Hall beside it is regarded as the oldest domestic building in Pembrokeshire and possibly in Wales. The first stone building in the town was a defensive tower on a cliff edge, now called the Medieval Chapel. During the English Civil War the county was largely in the hands of Parliament, which aimed to prevent communication with Ireland.

Pembroke was an ancient borough, with evidence of charters back to at least 1168, and became a municipal borough in 1836. Pembroke Dock grew from the early nineteenth century and came to rival the old town. The borough council was abolished under the Local Government Act 1972, and in 1974 the area joined the new district of South Pembrokeshire in Dyfed. In 1986 the community was divided into Pembroke Dock and a smaller Pembroke.

Pembroke has historic buildings, town walls and the castle. The millpond is held by the town's main bridge over the River Pembroke, which also acts as a dam. The town is twinned with Bergen in Lower Saxony and with Pembroke in Malta.
pembrokeshire: Pembrokeshire is bordered by Ceredigion to the north-east, Carmarthenshire to the east and otherwise by the sea. Its coast, formed by the complex geology of the area, includes high sea cliffs, wide sandy beaches, the ria of Milford Haven and offshore islands such as Ramsey, Skomer and Caldey, which are home to seabird colonies. The interior is relatively flat and gently undulating, except for the Preseli Mountains in the north. Most of the coast is protected by the Pembrokeshire Coast National Park, the only park in the United Kingdom established primarily because of its coastline, and it can be walked on the Pembrokeshire Coast Path.

Human habitation dates back between 125,000 and 70,000 years, and there are many prehistoric sites, particularly in the Preseli Mountains, including Pentre Ifan and other Neolithic remains. Roman influence was limited, with a few forts, coins and roads, and much of the area stayed beyond sustained Roman control. In the sub-Roman period the Irish Déisi settled and merged with local populations to form the Kingdom of Dyfed, which became part of Deheubarth in the 10th century. The region saw Viking raids and limited settlement.

In the Middle Ages the Normans built several castles, such as Pembroke and Cilgerran, and St David's Cathedral became an important pilgrimage site. Until the 12th century a great extent of the county was virgin woodland, and clearance in the lowland south began under Anglo-Flemish colonisation. Because of immigration, including the influx of Flemish people, the south has fewer Welsh speakers than the north. The rough boundary between the two regions is the Landsker Line, and the south has been called Little England beyond Wales; George Owen of Henllys remarked on the distinction as early as 1603.

During the Industrial Revolution the county stayed relatively rural, except for Milford Haven, which was developed as a port and Royal Navy dockyard. Slate quarrying was a significant industry in the 19th and early 20th centuries, and coal was mined between the 14th and 20th centuries, the last mine closing at Kilgetty in 1950. Since the 1950s petrochemical and liquefied natural gas industries have developed along the Milford Haven Waterway. The county town is Haverfordwest, and St Davids is the smallest city in the United Kingdom. Under the Local Government (Wales) Act 1994 Pembrokeshire became a unitary authority in 1996, after the abolition of Dyfed. It has more than 1,600 listed buildings.
pemex: Asphalt and pitch had been worked in Mexico since the time of the Aztecs, and small quantities of oil were first refined into kerosene around 1876 near Tampico. By the early 20th century subsidiaries of the British Pearson and American Doheny companies were extracting and refining oil in commercial quantities, which drew the attention of the Mexican government, which claimed all mineral rights for the state under its constitution.

In 1938 President Lázaro Cárdenas sided with oil workers who were striking against the foreign-owned companies for higher pay and social services. On 18 March 1938, citing Article 27 of the Constitution of 1917, he expropriated the resources and facilities of the United States and Anglo-Dutch companies. He asked the nation for the moral and material support needed to face the consequences of a decision that, he said, the government would neither have sought nor desired. Pemex was established by his decree of 7 June 1938. Expropriation was not outright confiscation, since the government promised compensation, but many foreign governments retaliated by closing their markets to Mexican oil until demand for petroleum in the Second World War ended the boycott.

Pemex became a lasting symbol of Mexican nationalism. In 1979 its Ixtoc 1 exploratory well in the Bay of Campeche suffered a blowout that caused one of the largest oil spills in history; the company spent 100 million dollars on the clean-up and avoided most compensation claims by asserting sovereign immunity. On 19 November 1984 a series of explosions at a Pemex liquefied petroleum gas storage facility at San Juan Ixhuatepec, near Mexico City, killed about 500 to 600 residents and injured up to 7,000 more, and it is counted among the deadliest industrial accidents in history.

Annual production fell each year between 2004 and 2007. Presidents Vicente Fox and Felipe Calderón proposed opening the sector to private investment, and the proposals met opposition in Congress. In 2008 the Mexican Congress created the National Hydrocarbons Commission to increase oversight of the company. Later events included a pipeline explosion at Tlauhuelilpan, Hidalgo, on 18 January 2019, in which at least 137 people died while gathering fuel from an illegal tap. In 2021 Pemex took over the operation of the Zama oil field, which Talos Energy had discovered in 2017, and Talos disputed the decision. The Dos Bocas refinery opened in 2024.
penang: Penang is divided into two parts by the Penang Strait, which is only 3 kilometres wide at its narrowest point. Penang Island to the west holds the capital, George Town, and Seberang Perai lies on the mainland to the east, where the state borders Kedah and Perak. Penang Island covers 295 square kilometres and has a hilly, mostly forested interior, with Penang Hill, 833 metres high, as the state's highest point. George Town began as a small settlement at the island's northeastern tip. The name comes from the Malay Pulau Pinang, meaning areca palm island.

Remains found in Seberang Perai show that around 5,000 to 6,000 years ago nomadic Melanesians lived there in the Neolithic era. Pali inscriptions on the Cherok Tok Kun megalith suggest that the Bujang Valley civilisation, based in what is now Kedah, held authority over parts of Seberang Perai by the 6th century. The whole of Penang later formed part of Kedah, which came under Siamese suzerainty by the late 18th century. Penang's modern history began in 1786, when Francis Light of the British East India Company obtained the island from Sultan Abdullah Mukarram Shah of Kedah in exchange for military aid.

Light founded the Port of Penang as a free port alongside George Town, and Penang later joined Malacca and Singapore in the Straits Settlements. A Royal Charter of 1807 led to the founding of a Supreme Court at Fort Cornwallis. During the Second World War the Japanese army took Penang without a struggle on 19 December 1941, and the British regained control in 1945. The state merged with the Federation of Malaya, which became independent in 1957.

Penang is a state of Malaysia, linked across the strait by the Penang Bridge and the Second Penang Bridge. It is one of four Malaysian states without a hereditary monarchy, and its head of state is a Governor appointed by the King of Malaysia. The unicameral State Legislative Assembly has 40 seats and meets in George Town. Its people include Chinese, Malays, Indians, Eurasians and Siamese. After the free port status was withdrawn in 1969, Chief Minister Lim Chong Eu set up the Bayan Lepas Free Industrial Zone in 1972, and the economy shifted from entrepôt trade to electronics manufacturing.
pencil: The word pencil comes from the Old French pincel and the late Latin penicillus, a little tail, and first meant an artist's fine brush of camel hair, which was also used for writing. The Romans used a stylus, a thin metal stick for scratching papyrus or wax tablets. The graphite from Cumbria was called plumbago, Latin for lead ore, and the mistake lives on in the name lead for a pencil core. The German Bleistift and the Irish peann luaidhe both mean lead pen. Because graphite could line the moulds for cannonballs, the Crown took over the mines and guarded them, and flooded them when enough had been stored. The graphite for pencils had at first to be smuggled out.

A pencil leaves marks by abrasion, a trail of solid core material that clings to the paper, which sets it apart from pens that dispense liquid ink. Most cores are graphite mixed with a clay binder, and the ratio of graphite to clay decides how hard the core is. The commonest casing is thin wood, usually hexagonal in section. Other cores include charcoal and carbon for fuller blacks, wax-based coloured cores and greasy cores that write on glass or porcelain. Copying pencils, invented in the late 19th century, held a dye that dissolved into coloured ink when moistened, so that the writing could be pressed onto another sheet.

England kept a monopoly on pencils until a method of reconstituting graphite powder was found in Germany in 1662, and square English pencils were still cut from natural graphite into the 1860s. Keswick still has a pencil factory and the Derwent Pencil Museum. Under the naval blockade of the Napoleonic Wars France could import neither English graphite nor the poorer German substitute, which led Nicolas-Jacques Conté to his clay method.

American colonists imported their pencils from Europe. Benjamin Franklin advertised them in 1729, and George Washington used a three-inch pencil when surveying the Ohio Country in 1762. William Munroe of Concord, Massachusetts, made the first American wood pencils in 1812, and Ebenezer Wood of Acton automated the work, building the first hexagonal casings. Eberhard Faber built a factory in New York. By the end of the 19th century more than 240,000 pencils were used each day in the United States. Hymen Lipman received the first patent for an attached eraser on 30 March 1858.
penda-of-mercia: Penda was a son of Pybba of Mercia and is said to have been an Icling, with a lineage traced back to Wōden in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. The Historia Brittonum says Pybba had twelve sons, of whom Penda and Eowa of Mercia were best known to its author. The time at which Penda became king is uncertain. Bede mentions an earlier Mercian king, Cearl, as a contemporary of the Northumbrian king Æthelfrith, and it is unclear whether the two were related or rivals. The origin of the name Penda is unknown, with suggestions divided between Celtic and Germanic origins.

Penda took the Severn Valley in 628 after the Battle of Cirencester. In October 633 he joined the Welsh king Cadwallon ap Cadfan of Gwynedd in defeating Edwin of Northumbria at the Battle of Hatfield Chase, where Edwin was killed. He was probably the lesser partner. On 5 August 642 he defeated Oswald of Northumbria at the Battle of Maserfield, probably in alliance with men of Powys. According to Bede, Oswald's body was dismembered, and Oswald came to be revered as a saint. After this Penda was probably the most powerful Anglo-Saxon ruler of his time.

He fought the East Angles repeatedly, killing their king Egric and the former king Sigebert, and in 654 killed King Anna. When Cenwalh of Wessex repudiated Penda's sister, Penda drove him into exile in East Anglia in 645, where he stayed three years. Penda placed his son Peada as ruler in Middle Anglia. Peada married Oswiu's daughter Alhflaed after agreeing to be baptised, and Bede says Penda tolerated Christian preaching among his Mercians. In 655 he invaded Bernicia with a large army reported as thirty warbands, including Cadafael ap Cynfeddw of Gwynedd. He was killed at the Battle of the Winwaed by Oswiu, on 15 November 655.

After the Winwaed, Oswiu briefly dominated Mercia, allowing Peada to rule its southern part. Penda's sons Wulfhere and Æthelred later ruled Mercia in succession after Northumbrian control was overthrown in the late 650s. Descendants of Penda held the kingship until the death of his grandson Ceolred in 716. His reign marked Mercia's emergence from obscurity, and it has been said that the hostility of Bede obscured his importance as an overking whose hegemony included lesser rulers of Anglo-Saxon and British origin, Christian and non-Christian alike.
pendulum-clock: Galileo Galilei investigated pendulums around 1602 and discovered that they are isochronous, swinging with a period independent of the size of the swing. In 1637 he described to his son Vincenzo a mechanism to keep a pendulum swinging, which Vincenzo partly built in 1649. Christiaan Huygens had the first clock built by Salomon Coster and described it in his manuscript Horologium of 1658. By 1659 pendulum clocks were made by the French clockmaker Nicolaus Hanet and by Ahasuerus Fromanteel in England.

A mechanical pendulum clock has a power source, a gear train, an escapement that gives the pendulum timed impulses, the pendulum itself and a dial. The early clocks had verge escapements and swings of 80 to 100 degrees. In 1673 Huygens showed that wide swings made the clock inaccurate. Robert Hooke's anchor escapement of around 1658 reduced the swing to 4 to 6 degrees and became standard, and the seconds pendulum, about 0.994 m long, came into wide use. William Clement made the first long narrow cases around 1680, called grandfather clocks, and minute hands appeared from around 1690.

The deadbeat escapement, invented by Richard Towneley in 1675 and popularised by George Graham around 1715, gradually replaced the anchor. Heat made rods expand and clocks slow in summer, which Graham's mercury pendulum of 1721 and John Harrison's gridiron pendulum of 1726 compensated. By the mid-18th century precision clocks kept time to a few seconds a week.

Until the 19th century clocks were handmade and expensive, and their ornament made them status symbols of the wealthy. Factory production of parts gradually brought them within reach of middle-class families. During the Industrial Revolution, work shifts and train services depended on pendulum clocks, and regulators in businesses and railway stations were used to set other clocks. Astronomical regulators in naval observatories were used to set marine chronometers for finding longitude.

From 1909 the US National Bureau of Standards based its time standard on Riefler pendulum clocks, and in 1929 it changed to the Shortt-Synchronome clock, accurate to better than one second a year. In the 1930s and 1940s synchronous electric clocks began to replace them in homes. Behind the Iron Curtain, where quartz technology was unavailable, Feodosii Fedchenko's AChF-3 clock of 1955 reached the accuracy of quartz clocks.
peng-dehuai: Peng Dehuai was born on 24 October 1898 in the village of Shixiang, Xiangtan County, Hunan, into a poor peasant family. His grand-uncle had fought in the Taiping Rebellion and told him of its ideals, that everyone should have enough food, women should not bind their feet and land should be redistributed equally. Poverty forced him to stop his education at ten, and he worked as a manual labourer. In March 1916 he joined a Hunan warlord army as a private, and over ten years rose to major in the armies of several warlords. One of his commanding officers, a Nationalist veteran of the 1911 revolution, led him to sympathise with the Kuomintang's aims of social reform and national reunification.

In 1926 his forces joined the Kuomintang, and he took part in the Northern Expedition. After the Wuhan government's defeat he joined the Chinese Communist Party, allying himself with Mao Zedong and Zhu De. He helped defend the Jiangxi Soviet and joined the Long March: of the 18,000 men under his command at its start in October 1934, only about 3,000 reached Shaanxi in October 1935. In the war against Japan he argued that the Red Army should genuinely fight the Japanese, against Mao's wish for token resistance. After 1945 he commanded the Northwest Field Army, and defeated the Kuomintang in Northwest China.

North Korea invaded South Korea on 25 June 1950, and Peng was among the few senior leaders who backed Mao's proposal to intervene. He directly commanded the Chinese People's Volunteer Army for the first half of the war. Convinced that the army had to be more professional and better equipped, he became Minister of National Defense in 1954 and began to reform it on the Soviet model. In January 1955 he attacked and occupied a chain of islands held by the Kuomintang off Zhejiang. He resisted Mao's personality cult during the 1950s.

The Great Leap Forward, begun in 1958, caused a man-made famine in which tens of millions starved by 1959. At the Lushan Conference of July 1959 Mao invited criticism and promised not to attack anyone personally, and Peng, critical of Mao's leadership, spoke. Mao won the confrontation, labelled Peng the leader of an anti-Party clique and in September replaced him with Lin Biao, who reversed his reforms.

Peng lived under constant surveillance near Beijing. In 1966 Jiang Qing directed Red Guards in Sichuan to arrest him, and they abducted him in chains on 25 December 1966. He died on 29 November 1974. The party leadership concealed his death for years, and his wife, Pu Anxiu, learned of it only on returning to Beijing in 1978, when the news was first publicly disclosed.
penghu: Penghu is an archipelago of 90 islands and islets in the Taiwan Strait, about 50 kilometres west of the main island of Taiwan across the Penghu Channel, covering 141 square kilometres. It is the remnant of a Miocene shield volcano, and its layers of basalt are interbedded with sandstone and mudstone. The largest city, Magong, stands on the largest island. Finds of red cord-marked pottery show that Austronesians from south-western Taiwan visited about 5,000 years ago, though they did not settle permanently.

The islands first appear in the written record in the Tang dynasty. Han Chinese from southern Fujian began to establish fishing communities in the 9th and 10th centuries, and by 1171 settlers were cultivating land there, when raiders landed and plundered their fields and the Song government began regular patrols. In November 1281 the Yuan dynasty set up the Penghu Patrol and Inspection Agency under Tong'an County. Wang Dayuan described thirty-six islands in his Daoyi Zhilüe of 1349, with grass but no trees, flocks of goats and a salt tax. In the 15th century the Ming ordered the islands evacuated under a maritime ban, and fishing communities returned in the late 16th century. The Ming established a permanent military presence from 1597.

After the Dutch were defeated by the Portuguese at the Battle of Macau in 1622, they seized Penghu and built a fort, demanding trade with China. They raided the Fujian coast until 1624, when the governor of Fujian sent 40 to 50 warships with 5,000 troops and the Dutch withdrew to Fort Zeelandia on Taiwan. The Qing overthrew the Kingdom of Tungning of the Zheng family in 1683 after the Battle of Penghu and made the islands a sub-prefecture of Taiwan Prefecture. French forces captured Penghu in March 1885 and left four months later, Admiral Amédée Courbet dying of cholera there on 11 June 1885.

Japan occupied Makung in March 1895, and Penghu was ceded with Taiwan in the Treaty of Shimonoseki that April. Under Japanese rule Makō was a major naval base. The administration passed to the Republic of China on 25 October 1945.

Penghu County is divided into one city and five rural townships, with its seat at Magong, and its people are mostly descendants of settlers from Tong'an in Fujian who speak Taiwanese Hokkien. The islands depend on sea and air transport and have long relied on fishing. Penghu National Scenic Area covers most of the archipelago, known for its columnar basalt, and tourism is a main source of income.
peninsular-war: The Treaties of Tilsit of July 1807 ended the War of the Fourth Coalition. Napoleon was irritated that Portugal, Britain's oldest ally in Europe, remained open to trade with Britain, and Prince John of Braganza, regent for his mother Queen Maria I, had declined to join the Continental System. French troops under Junot, with Spanish cooperation, set out for Lisbon on 19 November 1807 and occupied it on 30 November. The prince regent fled to Brazil with his family, court and treasure aboard an Anglo-Portuguese fleet. In February 1808 French divisions crossed the Pyrenees and occupied Navarre and Catalonia, and Napoleon then forced the abdications of Ferdinand VII and Charles IV and installed his brother Joseph Bonaparte on the Spanish throne.

On 2 May 1808 the citizens of Madrid rose against the French, and the next day the French army shot hundreds of them, as Francisco Goya's painting The Third of May 1808 shows. Spaniards rose across the country, and guerrilla warfare, from which English took the word, spread. In July 1808 the Spanish army in Andalusia defeated the French at the Battle of Bailén. Arthur Wellesley, later the Duke of Wellington, landed in Portugal in August and beat Junot at Vimeiro. Napoleon himself invaded in November 1808, but the Spanish armies, though often beaten, regrouped and kept French troops tied down.

The Cortes, besieged by 70,000 French troops, took refuge at Cádiz in 1810, while Wellington built the Lines of Torres Vedras to protect Lisbon. In 1812, as Napoleon invaded Russia, an allied army defeated the French at Salamanca on 22 July, and Joseph abandoned Madrid. The Coalition defeated Joseph's army at Vitoria in 1813, and Marshal Soult led a fighting withdrawal across the Pyrenees in the winter of 1813 to 1814. Wellington attacked Soult at Orthez on 27 February 1814.

The war drained France: its communications and supplies were strained, and its units were repeatedly isolated or harassed by Spanish partisans. Napoleon called it the Spanish ulcer. It allowed the rest of Europe to challenge him again. The Cortes of Cádiz promulgated the Spanish Constitution of 1812, later a cornerstone of European liberalism. Yet the war destroyed the social and economic fabric of both Spain and Portugal, and the civil wars between liberals and absolutists that followed ushered in revolts in Spanish America that led to the independence of all of Spain's colonies on the American mainland. The siege of Zaragoza alone left an estimated 64,000 corpses, 10,000 of them French.
penne-abruzzo: Penne stands on several hills on the Adriatic side of Abruzzo, between the valleys of the Tavo and Fino rivers, about 20 km from the sea. It lies 31 km from Pescara, 35 km from Chieti and 67 km from Teramo, and opens the way to the Gran Sasso and Monti della Laga national park through the regional natural reserve of the Lake of Penne. The old town is built almost entirely of brick, which gave it the name Città del mattone, the Town of Bricks, and in the past earned it the title of the small Siena.

The site has been occupied since at least the mid-Neolithic period. It was a seat of government of the Vestini people by 300 BCE at the latest. The Vestini and other Italic tribes were defeated by the Romans in the Social War and became Roman citizens; the town was known as Pinna Vestinorum under the Roman Republic.

In the Middle Ages Penne was held by the Lombards as part of the Duchy of Spoleto, and from around 1130 it belonged to the Kingdom of Sicily. In 1538 Emperor Charles V gave it to his daughter Margaret of Parma as a gift for her wedding to Ottavio Farnese. Under Margaret, Penne became a centre of power in Abruzzo and many palaces and civic buildings were erected. In 2006 the town received the Silver Medal of Civic Merit for what it suffered in the Second World War.

The Duomo, the church of San Massimo, was built on a 10th-century crypt that may stand on an ancient temple of Vesta; it was badly damaged by bombing in 1944 and restored in 1955. It now houses the Diocese Museum, with a crypt dating from the 8th century. Other buildings include the 12th-century church of Santa Maria in Colleromano and the Cistercian convent founded there in 1197, and Renaissance and Baroque palaces such as the Palazzo Scorpio, once the home of Margaret. Four old gates survive, among them the Porta San Francesco, rebuilt in 1780. Penne is listed among the most beautiful villages of Italy and had 12,451 inhabitants at the census of 2014.
pennine-alps: The Pennine Alps, called the Valais Alps when the term is applied to the northern Swiss part, lie in the canton of Valais in south-western Switzerland and in the Aosta Valley and Piedmont of Italy. Their names are Alpes Pennines in French, Walliser Alpen in German, Alpi Pennine in Italian and Alpes Poeninae in Latin. Together with the Bernese Alps and the Graian Alps, which include the Mont Blanc massif, the Pennines are among the three highest major subranges of the Alps.

The range straddles the border between Switzerland and Italy. The Italian side is drained by the Dora Baltea, Sesia and Toce rivers, all tributaries of the Po, and the Swiss side by the Rhône. The Great St Bernard Tunnel runs under the Great St Bernard Pass from Martigny in Switzerland to Aosta in Italy.

The main watershed between the Mediterranean Sea and the Adriatic Sea runs from west to east along the border. East of Mont Vélan, the first high summit beyond the St Bernard Pass, the chain contains many four-thousanders, among them the Matterhorn and Monte Rosa. The valleys on both sides are similar, generally running perpendicular to the main chain and descending into the Rhône Valley to the north and the Aosta Valley to the south. Unlike many ranges, the higher peaks, such as Grand Combin, Weisshorn, Mischabel and Weissmies, often lie outside the main chain, between the northern valleys. There are 126 peaks over 2,106 metres.

The main glaciers include the Gorner, Corbassière, Findel, Zmutt, Zinal, Otemma, Allalin and Ferpècle glaciers. Regional nature parks lie on both sides of the main water divide: the Parco Naturale Alta Valsesia, the Mont Mars Nature Reserve and the Regional park of Binn valley.
pennines: From the Tyne Gap in the north the range extends south through the North Pennines, the Yorkshire Dales, the South Pennines and the Peak District, and ends near the valley of the River Trent. It is divided in two by the Aire Gap, a wide pass formed by the valleys of the Aire and Ribble, and it has western spurs such as the Rossendale Fells and the Forest of Bowland. Most of it is high moorland cut by more fertile river valleys, and the highest point is Cross Fell in eastern Cumbria at 893 metres. For much of its length it is the main watershed of northern England, dividing rivers that flow west to the Irish Sea from those that reach the North Sea.

The range is a broad anticline of Carboniferous limestone overlain with Millstone Grit, and the limestone has formed large cave systems, such as Gaping Gill, and the pavements of Malham Cove. The Pennine Way, 268 miles long, is Britain's oldest long-distance footpath.

The Pennines contained Bronze Age settlements, and evidence remains of Neolithic settlement, including stone circles and henges such as Long Meg and Her Daughters. The uplands were controlled by the Brigantes, a federation of small tribes that cooperated on defence and external affairs and evolved an early form of kingdom. The Romans dominated them and exploited the Pennines for natural resources. The range was an obstacle to Anglo-Saxon expansion westwards, though the Anglo-Saxons travelled through the valleys.

In Norse times Viking Danes settled in the east and Norwegian Vikings in the west, and they influenced place names, culture and genetics. When England was unified the Pennines were incorporated. They were never a distinct political polity but were divided between neighbouring counties, a major part lying in the West Riding of Yorkshire.

The Pennines are sparsely populated by English standards, with the larger towns and cities in the foothills and lowlands around them, among them Manchester, Leeds, Sheffield and Bradford. Gaps such as the Tyne Gap, the Stainmore Gap and the Aire Gap allow communication across the range. Three trans-Pennine canals were built during the Industrial Revolution, the Huddersfield Narrow Canal with its Standedge Tunnel, the Rochdale Canal and the Leeds and Liverpool Canal, and the first Woodhead Tunnel was completed in 1845. The range is protected by national parks and national landscapes, including the Yorkshire Dales and the Peak District.
pennsylvania: Pennsylvania is officially the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. It lies in the Mid-Atlantic, Northeastern, Appalachian and Great Lakes regions, and is bordered by Delaware, Maryland, West Virginia, Ohio, New York, New Jersey and, across Lake Erie, the Canadian province of Ontario. The Mason-Dixon line forms its southern boundary. The Appalachian Mountains run through its centre, and about 59 per cent of the state is forested. Of the original Thirteen Colonies, it is the only one that does not border the Atlantic Ocean, though it has waterfront on Lake Erie and the tidal Delaware River.

Humans lived in what is now Pennsylvania for thousands of years before the colony was founded. The Meadowcroft Rockshelter in Jefferson Township holds the earliest known signs of human activity in the state and perhaps in all of North America, and may pre-date the Clovis culture. By 1000 CE the native population had developed agricultural techniques and a mixed food economy. Between 1638 and 1655 a south-eastern portion of the state was part of New Sweden, a Swedish colony.

In 1681 a royal land grant gave the territory to William Penn, son of the man after whom it is named. The colonial Province of Pennsylvania was known for relatively peaceful relations with native peoples, an innovative system of government and religious pluralism. Philadelphia hosted the First and Second Continental Congress; the latter formed the Continental Army under George Washington in 1775 and unanimously adopted the Declaration of Independence the following year. On 12 December 1787 Pennsylvania was the second state to ratify the United States Constitution, after Delaware. It has been known as the Keystone State since 1802, for its central place among the original colonies.

The capital is Harrisburg, and the largest cities are Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. The 2020 census counted 13,011,844 residents. The state has had five constitutions, in 1776, 1790, 1838, 1874 and 1968. Its industrial past gave it the lesser nicknames of the Coal State, the Oil State and the Steel State, and its five manufacturing centres were Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Erie, Scranton-Wilkes-Barre and the Lehigh Valley.
pensacola: Pensacola stands on the north side of Pensacola Bay in the Florida Panhandle, a seaport protected by the barrier island of Santa Rosa, which connects to the Gulf of Mexico. It lies 59 miles (95 km) east of Mobile, Alabama, and 196 miles (315 km) west of Tallahassee. In the Age of Sail it was the busiest port on the Gulf Coast, having the deepest harbour. The area was first inhabited by Muskogean-speaking peoples. The Pensacola people lived there at the time of European contact and probably gave the bay and then the city its name, while Creek people came regularly from present-day southern Alabama to trade.

Spanish expeditions reached the bay early: Pánfilo de Narváez in 1528 and Hernando de Soto in 1539, who recorded the name Bay of Ochuse. Tristán de Luna founded a short-lived settlement in 1559, six years before St. Augustine, but it was abandoned after a severe hurricane and not resettled until 1698, when the Spanish established a presidio from which the modern city gradually developed. Control then changed several times: Spain until 1719, France from 1719 to 1722, and Spain again until 1763.

Spain ceded Florida to Britain in 1763 after the French and Indian War, and nearly all the Spanish population left by ship for Veracruz and Cuba. The British made Pensacola the capital of West Florida, strengthened the defences around Fort San Carlos de Barrancas with the Royal Navy Redoubt, and in 1764 set up a colonial assembly under the first governor, George Johnstone. West Florida declined the invitation to send delegates to the First Continental Congress, and during the American War of Independence its colonists remained overwhelmingly loyal to the Crown. Britain held Pensacola until 1781, and Spain ruled it again from 1781 to 1821.

In the final stages of the War of 1812 American troops attacked the Spanish and British garrisons, which surrendered after two days; the United States took the city again in 1818. In 1819 the Adams–Onís Treaty recognised American control of Florida in exchange for American recognition of Spanish control of Texas. A Spanish census of 1820 counted 181 households. The Confederate States held it from 1861 to 1862, and in 1860 it was Florida's largest city, with 2,876 people.

Pensacola is the county seat and only city of Escambia County and is nicknamed the City of Five Flags, for the five governments that have ruled it: Spain, France, Great Britain, the United States and the Confederate States. Naval Air Station Pensacola, commissioned in 1914 as the first naval air station of the United States Navy, trained naval aviators including John H. Glenn and Neil Armstrong, and the city is called the Cradle of Naval Aviation. The University of West Florida lies north of the centre.
people-power-revolution: Ferdinand Marcos was elected president in 1965 and re-elected in 1969, and on 23 September 1972 he declared martial law under Proclamation No. 1081. He dissolved Congress, shut down critical media and ordered the arrest of opponents, among them Senator Ninoy Aquino. His spending relied heavily on debt, and after the recession of 1981 the economy declined, contracting by 6.8% in 1983 and by 7.3% in each of 1984 and 1985. On 21 August 1983 Aquino was assassinated as he disembarked at Manila International Airport after three years in exile. The killing outraged many Filipinos and led to non-cooperation and civil disobedience.

The election of 7 February 1986 pitted Marcos against Aquino's widow, Corazon Aquino. The Commission on Elections gave Marcos 10,807,197 votes to her 9,291,761, whereas the poll watcher NAMFREL's returns from 70% of precincts had her ahead by 7,835,070 to 7,053,068. On 16 February Aquino held a rally at Luneta Park, attended by about two million people, and announced a nonviolent civil disobedience campaign and a boycott of businesses linked to Marcos.

Officers of the Reform the Armed Forces Movement had planned a coup, and the revolt began on 22 February around Camp Crame and Camp Aguinaldo. Crowds filled Epifanio de los Santos Avenue, or EDSA. On 24 February helicopters of the 15th Strike Wing under Colonel Antonio Sotelo, sent to attack Camp Crame, landed there instead, a turning point against Marcos. On 25 February some 20,000 people blocked the Bamban Bridge and stopped loyalist reinforcements. Marcos held a rival inauguration while preparing to flee, and he and his family were flown by helicopter to Clark Air Base and then to exile in Hawaii.

Aquino issued Proclamation No. 3, a provisional constitution, and abolished the Batasang Pambansa pending a plebiscite on a new constitution. Officers of the movement that had launched the failed coup were dissatisfied with her rise to power and attempted further coups during her term. The revolution inspired later nonviolent changes of government, including those in East Germany and other former Soviet Bloc countries. In 2001 a similar EDSA uprising led to the resignation of President Joseph Estrada, and the radio broadcast of the revolution was inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2003.
peoples-action-party: Lee Kuan Yew, Toh Chin Chye and Goh Keng Swee took part in the Malayan Forum, a London-based student group opposed to colonial rule in Malaya in the 1940s and early 1950s. After returning to Singapore they met regularly to discuss independence and looked for like-minded people, among them the journalist S. Rajaratnam, English-educated left-wing students and Chinese-educated union and student leaders. The party was registered on 21 November 1954. Its first Central Executive Committee brought together trade unionists, lawyers and journalists, with Lee as secretary-general and Toh as founding chairman.

The party won the 1959 general election, the first to produce a fully elected parliament and a cabinet with full internal self-government. Lee became the first Prime Minister, a post he held for 31 years. Lee sought to reposition the party towards the centre and in 1961 expelled its leftist faction, which reorganised as Barisan Sosialis. Singapore joined Malaysia in 1963, and the party acted as an opposition at the federal level. Relations with the United Malays National Organisation worsened when each contested seats in the other's sphere, and Tunku Abdul Rahman forced Singapore to leave Malaysia on 9 August 1965.

Barisan Sosialis resigned from Parliament in 1966, after several of its leaders had been arrested in Operation Coldstore as alleged communists. Most opposition parties boycotted the 1968 election, so the party won every seat, and from 1965 to 1981 it was the only party in Parliament. It lost its first seat in a 1981 by-election in Anson to the Workers' Party. Lee stepped down as Prime Minister in 1990 in favour of Goh Chok Tong, and Lee Hsien Loong became Prime Minister in 2004.

Early on the party followed a Leninist form of organisation. Power lies in the Central Executive Committee under the secretary-general, who by convention has been the Prime Minister since 1959. The party recruits candidates by invitation, through talent spotting among the civil service, armed forces, academia, the professions and business, and says this prevents nepotism and primary elections. Members vote along the party line once a decision is made. Its youth wing was formed in 1986 as the Youth Committee and renamed the Young PAP in 1993.

The party describes its aims as pragmatism, meritocracy, multiracialism and Asian values, in analysts' account, and it supports free-market policies together with state-owned enterprises. Its symbol, a red flash and blue circle on white, was inspired, Lee Kuan Yew acknowledged, by that of the British Union of Fascists, though the colours were changed. At rallies members wear white shirts and trousers to signify incorruptibility.
peoples-army-of-vietnam: The People's Army of Vietnam was first conceived in September 1944 as the Information, Communication and Education Unit of the Liberation Army, meant to educate, recruit and mobilise the Vietnamese to drive out the French colonial and Japanese occupiers. Under the guidelines of Hồ Chí Minh, Võ Nguyên Giáp was given the task of establishing the brigades, and the Propaganda Unit of the Liberation Army came into existence on 22 December 1944. Its first formation had thirty-one men and three women, armed with two revolvers, seventeen rifles, one light machine gun and fourteen breech-loading flintlocks, and it fought its first engagements at Khai Phat and Na Ngan against French soldiers in late 1944.

In 1954 Hồ Chí Minh's administration formally named the Viet Minh's main armed wing Quân đội nhân dân Việt Nam, the Military of the people of Vietnam. In Ho's words the name stressed an army from the People, fighting for the People and serving the People.

During the French Indochina War the army was often called the Việt Minh. Its first regiment, the 102nd Capital Regiment, was created on 7 January 1947 for operations around Hanoi, and its first division, the 308th, followed. In late 1951 five new divisions were created, and the 351st Division became its first artillery division. Before the Battle of Dien Bien Phu it received 24 captured US 105 mm howitzers supplied by the Chinese People's Liberation Army. In 1954 four of its divisions, supported by this artillery, defeated the French Union forces at Dien Bien Phu, ending 83 years of French rule in Indochina.

In the Vietnam War its opponents called it the North Vietnamese Army, to tell it from the southern Viet Cong, though both worked under the same command structure. In 1976, after reunification, the Liberation Army of South Vietnam was disbanded and merged with it. It had forces in Laos to secure the Ho Chi Minh trail and support the Pathet Lao, aided the Khmer Rouge in toppling Lon Nol's government in 1975, and in 1978 helped topple Pol Pot's Democratic Kampuchea. It also fought in border wars with China.

The People's Army of Vietnam is the armed wing of the Communist Party of Vietnam and the core component of the Vietnam People's Armed Forces. It includes the Ground Force, the Navy, Air Defence and Air Force, the Border Guard and the Coast Guard. It is administered by the Ministry of National Defence under the party's Central Military Commission, which holds most power over the military, although the President of Vietnam is commander-in-chief on paper. Conscription applies in principle to every male aged 18 to 27.
peoples-court-germany: The People's Court (Volksgerichtshof) was established on 24 April 1934 by decree of Reich Chancellor Adolf Hitler. The immediate cause was the Reichstag fire trial before the Reich Court of Justice, in which all but one of the defendants were acquitted, though Hitler had already called in Mein Kampf for a "national tribunal" to execute "tens of thousands" of people he regarded as traitors. The law that created it moved treason, high treason, major sabotage and assassination of members of the government from the Reich Court of Justice and made the penalties substantially more severe. H. W. Koch names three features of German history behind it: the stab-in-the-back myth, the Enabling Act and the Führerprinzip.

A decree of 18 April 1936 made the court, described as a temporary expedient, a full court. Otto Georg Thierack, formerly vice-president of the Reich Court of Justice, became president on 1 May 1936. Its judges gained the red robes of the supreme court, and its jurisdiction grew to include misprision of treason, economic sabotage, Wehrkraftzersetzung, evading military service, sedition and espionage. In August 1942 Thierack became Reich Minister of Justice and Roland Freisler, a Nazi Party member since 1923, took the presidency and kept the most important cases for himself. Joseph Goebbels told the court that it was to start not from the law but from the decision that the man must be got rid of.

Each senate had five judges, two trained and three lay judges, about two thirds of whom came from Nazi organisations and one third from the armed forces. The court rejected judicial independence, due process, appeal and the right to counsel, and punished "criminal mentality" regardless of written law. Before the war it sentenced on average two per cent of defendants to death, but it treated members of the KPD and SPD more harshly. Between 1941 and 1943 death sentences by the People's and Special Courts rose from 1,292 to 5,336. Freisler died in an air raid in early 1945, and no trials are documented after April 1945.

Estimates of the court's work differ: Müller counts at least 14,319 defendants and at least 5,191 executions, and Wachsmann and Hoffmann 5,179 executions. Victims included the White Rose members Sophie Scholl, Hans Scholl, Alexander Schmorell, Willi Graf, Christoph Probst and Kurt Huber, and the seventeen-year-old Helmuth Hübener. After the war Ernst Lautz, chief prosecutor, was sentenced to ten years and the judge Oswald Rothaug to life in 1947. At least 29 of its judges and 69 prosecutors later worked in the West German court system. On 25 January 1985 the Bundestag declared it an instrument of judicial murder and state terrorism, and in 1998 all its judgments were annulled by federal law.
peoples-democratic-party-of-afghanistan: The party was formed at a unity congress of factions of the Socialist Party of Afghanistan on 1 January 1965. Twenty-seven men met at Nur Muhammad Taraki's house in Kabul and elected him Secretary General, with Babrak Karmal as Deputy Secretary General. Its secret constitution described its ideology as the practical experience of Marxism–Leninism, but in public it used labels such as national democratic and socialist. Four members won seats in the 1965 parliamentary election, and the party was known for its ties to the Soviet Union.

In 1967 the party split into the Khalq faction of Taraki, drawing mostly on rural Pashtuns, and the Parcham faction of Karmal, drawing on urban supporters. Soviet mediation reunited them in 1977. The party helped Mohammad Daoud Khan overthrow King Mohammad Zahir Shah in 1973, but relations with him worsened, and in the Saur Revolution of 1978 the party seized power, with Taraki as prime minister.

The government pursued rapid reform: separating mosque and state, a literacy campaign, land reform and the emancipation of women. It also launched a repression that killed thousands, mostly at Pul-e-Charkhi prison, where estimates of those executed between April 1978 and December 1979 run as high as 27,000. Olivier Roy estimated that between 50,000 and 100,000 people disappeared in the Taraki–Amin period. In December 1979 Soviet special forces killed Hafizullah Amin at the Tajbeg Palace, and Karmal became leader as the Soviet–Afghan War began. Mohammad Najibullah replaced Karmal as general secretary in May 1986. After the Soviet withdrawal in 1989, Najibullah renamed the party the Homeland Party in June 1990 and dropped Marxism–Leninism. Mujahideen took Kabul in 1992 and banned the party.

The party was organised on the model of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, with a Politburo, usually of seven to nine members, as its main executive body between sessions of the congress and the Central Committee. From 1982 it spread into the countryside, though it was organised in only about 2,000 of an estimated 25,000 villages. Its successors included the Watan Party, formed in 1997, and the National United Party of Afghanistan, registered in 2003.
peoples-liberation-army: The People's Liberation Army (PLA) traces its origins to the left-wing units of the National Revolutionary Army of the Kuomintang, which broke away in 1927 in an uprising against the nationalist government as the Chinese Red Army. In 1925 the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) had renamed its Central Military Department the Central Military Commission; it was first led by Zhang Guotao and from 1926 by Zhou Enlai. During the First United Front it was less a unified command than an administrative liaison with other armed communist groups.

During the Second Sino-Japanese War the communist units were reintegrated into the National Revolutionary Army as the New Fourth Army and the Eighth Route Army. The two were reconstituted as the PLA in 1947.

After the People's Republic was established in 1949, the army was reorganised. An Air Force leadership structure was set up in November 1949 and a Navy structure the following April. The early PLA consisted overwhelmingly of peasants and treated soldiers and officers in an egalitarian way; formal ranks were not adopted until 1955. The sociologist Alessandro Russo describes this as a break with traditional Chinese hierarchies. The first Military Service Law of 1955 created compulsory service.

Its engagements include the Chinese Civil War, the Second Sino-Japanese War, the incorporation of Xinjiang in 1949 and of Tibet in 1950, the Korean War under the banner of the Chinese People's Volunteer Army (1950–1953), the Taiwan Strait crises of 1954–1955 and 1958, the Sino-Indian War of 1962, the Sino-Soviet border conflict of 1969 and the Sino-Vietnamese War of 1979. It has also sent units, often engineers and logistics troops, on United Nations peacekeeping missions in Lebanon, the Republic of the Congo, Sudan, Ivory Coast and Haiti.

The PLA is the armed wing of the CCP, which holds that the party commands the gun. It is governed by the Central Military Commission, which exists as a party body and a state body with identical membership. Regiments, brigades and larger units have party committees and political commissars, who are officially equal to commanders in status. Operational control is divided between the service headquarters and theatre commands, grouped by geography.

The PLA now has four services, the Ground Force, Navy, Air Force and Rocket Force, and four arms established on 19 April 2024. Women took part extensively in combat during the revolutionary period and the civil war; after 1949 their role shrank mostly to support, medical and logistics duties.
pepi-i: Pepi I Meryre, also written Pepy I, was the third king of the Sixth Dynasty and ruled for over 40 years, possibly 49 or 50, toward the end of the Old Kingdom. He was the son of Teti, the founder of the dynasty, and of Iput, who may have been a daughter of Unas, the last ruler of the Fifth Dynasty. He came to the throne after the brief reign of Userkare. The later historian Manetho claims that Teti was assassinated by his bodyguards, and the Egyptologist Naguib Kanawati supports the claim, noting the growing number of guards at court and the deliberate erasure of the names of several officials, among them the vizier Hezi.

Egypt's government had been decentralising since the Fifth Dynasty, with provincial families marrying into the royal house and holding high office. Pepi answered with a vast building programme, raising temples to local gods and many chapels for his own cult throughout Egypt, and he became the most prolific builder of the Old Kingdom. He recruited officials of non-noble origin and extended a network of warehouses from which taxes and labour could be collected. Probably after his twentieth year he faced a conspiracy in the harem, and he strengthened his position by marrying two daughters of Khui, the nomarch of Abydos, Ankhesenpepi I and Ankhesenpepi II, and making Khui's wife Nebet and her son Djau viziers.

He sent military campaigns against Nubia, Sinai and the southern Levant, landing troops on the Levantine coast from Egyptian transport boats. Trade with Byblos, Ebla and the oases of the Western Desert flourished, and he launched mining and quarrying expeditions to Sinai and beyond. He had at least six consorts and at least four sons. Ankhesenpepi I probably bore Merenre Nemtyemsaf I, who succeeded him, and Ankhesenpepi II was the mother of Pepi II Neferkare.

Pepi built his pyramid complex at Saqqara, originally 52.5 metres tall, with at least six further pyramids for his consorts. Its walls carry the most extensive corpus of Pyramid Texts from the Old Kingdom, appearing for the first time in some consorts' pyramids as well. The complex was called Pepi Mennefer and gave its name to the nearby capital, Memphis. His cult continued into the Middle Kingdom and stopped early in the Second Intermediate Period; in the New Kingdom his monuments began to be quarried for stone, and in the Mamluk era they were almost entirely dismantled.
pepi-ii: Pepi II Neferkare, whose second name means beautiful is the Ka of Re, came to the throne at the age of six after the death of Merenre Nemtyemsaf I. He was long thought to be the son of Pepi I, but many Egyptologists now hold that his father was Merenre, who married Pepi II's mother Ankhesenpepi II after Pepi I's death; stone blocks found at Saqqara in the 1999 to 2000 season support this. His mother most likely ruled as regent in his early years, perhaps helped by her brother Djau, who had been a vizier. A statuette in the Brooklyn Museum shows him as a child in full regalia on her lap.

The king sent expeditions into Nubia for ivory, ebony and other goods. A letter he wrote as a child to Harkhuf, the governor of Aswan, is preserved on Harkhuf's tomb: the king promised a great reward if a captured pygmy were brought back alive, and the inscription has been called the first travelogue. Copper and turquoise were mined in Sinai, alabaster quarried at Hatnub, and his name appears in inscriptions at Byblos. He had several wives, and three of them, Neith, Iput II and Udjebten, had minor pyramids in his own complex at Saqqara.

Later tradition remembered the length of his reign. The Turin King List gives 90 or more years and Manetho a still longer figure, but the latest contemporary evidence dates from about his 62nd year, and some Egyptologists suggest no more than 64 years. Others point out that missing later dates do not exclude a longer reign. His pyramid, 78.5 metres at the base, followed the standard format and was no larger than those of his predecessors.

The Old Kingdom declined sharply in his time. Nomarchs, the regional representatives of the king, had been gaining power since before him, and during his reign wealth and authority passed to high officials, who built large tombs in the provinces; the nomarchs were free from taxation and their positions became hereditary. Late in his reign he divided the office of vizier between Upper and Lower Egypt, a further decentralisation away from Memphis. Some scholars suggest that an aging ruler, not replaced because of his divine status, led to a succession crisis and stagnation. With no dominant central power, local nobles raided each other's territories, and the Old Kingdom ended within a couple of years of his reign, leading to the First Intermediate Period.
pepin-i-of-aquitaine: Pepin was the second son of Emperor Louis the Pious and his first wife, Ermengarde of Hesbaye. In August 817 his father assigned each of his sons a kingdom within the Empire, and Pepin received Aquitaine, which had been Louis's own subkingdom under Charlemagne. The only coin issue bearing Pepin's name was struck around this time, probably at Louis's wish. In 822 he married Ingeltrude, daughter of Theodobert, count of Madrie.

The court poet Ermoldus Nigellus accompanied Pepin on a campaign into Brittany in 824. Around 827-8 Louis sent him to support Bernard of Septimania against an incursion into the Iberian March, but his army arrived too late, and its co-leaders, Hugh of Tours and Matfrid of Orléans, were deposed.

Pepin rebelled in 830 with his elder brother Lothar I, perhaps in reaction to that deposition. He marched with Gascons to Paris with Neustrian support and captured his father at Compiègne, but the rebellion broke up when Louis agreed to remove Bernard from power. In 832 Pepin escaped from his father's prison in Trier and fled to Aquitaine, and took Limoges. In 833 Lothair joined, and with the help of Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, the sons deposed their father. Lothair's conduct alienated Pepin, who stood beside his father when Louis was restored on 1 March 834 and was himself restored.

Pepin died scarcely four years after that settlement and was buried in the Church of St. Radegonde in Poitiers. His sons, Pepin II and Charles, later Archbishop of Mainz, were minors, and Louis the Pious awarded Aquitaine to his youngest son Charles the Bald, but the Aquitainians elected the younger Pepin as Pepin II. His brother Charles also briefly claimed the kingdom. Both died childless.
pepin-ii-of-aquitaine: Pepin II, called the Younger, was the eldest son of Pepin I of Aquitaine and Ingeltrude, daughter of Theodobert, count of Madrie, and a grandson of the Emperor Louis the Pious. In 832 Louis had appointed his own son Charles the Bald, Pepin's uncle and about the same age, as king of Aquitaine, nominally dispossessing the elder Pepin. When Pepin I died in 838, the nobles of Aquitaine, keen to establish their independence from the empire, elected the young Pepin king. Charles contested the kingship, and Louis disinherited his grandson fully at Crémieu and again at Worms in two later divisions of the empire.

Louis demanded that the Aquitainians send Pepin to Aachen to learn the ways of good governance, but they refused. Pepin held Aquitaine in complete control until 841, when he went to the aid of his uncle Lothair I at the Battle of Fontenoy. There he defeated Charles the Bald, but Lothair was routed by Louis the German, another son of the emperor. Pepin returned to Aquitaine and continued the war against Charles.

In 844 Pepin asked for help from Jarl Oscar, a Viking adventurer, and guided his forces up the Garonne to Toulouse, which gave them the chance to scout the land for plunder. In 845 he welcomed Seguin of Bordeaux, who had defected from the emperor's side, and made him dux Wasconum to help in the fight against Sans II Sancion of Gascony. Oscar seized Bordeaux, then held by Charles, in 847 with the aid of disaffected citizens. The loss of the city to a heathen pirate, together with Pepin's heavy drinking and loose living, eroded his support among the nobles until by 848 he had none.

Sans II captured Pepin in 851 or 852 and handed him over to Charles, who held him in the monastery of Saint Médard in Soissons. In 854 Pepin escaped with the help of some of the aristocracy and recovered part of his old authority and lands, while Vikings established in the Loire valley ravaged Poitiers, Angoulême, Périgueux, Limoges, Clermont and Bourges as Charles was busy with him. In 864 Pepin joined the Vikings, rumoured to have turned from Christianity to the worship of Woden, and took part in an attack on Toulouse. He was captured again later that year, deposed by the Edict of Pîtres and imprisoned in Senlis.
pepin-of-herstal: Pepin II, known as Pepin of Herstal, was the son of the Frankish statesman Ansegisel and the grandson and namesake of Pepin I the Elder, through the marriage of Pepin I's daughter Begga to Ansegisel. That marriage united the houses of the Pippinids and the Arnulfings, which created what would be called the Carolingian dynasty. He was probably born at Herstal in modern Belgium, where his centre of power lay, which gave him his byname. He was the grandfather of Pepin the Short and the great-grandfather of Charlemagne.

Pepin became Mayor of the Palace in Austrasia in 680. With Martin, duke of Laon, he fought the Neustrian mayor Ebroin, who had designs on all Francia and defeated the Austrasians at the Battle of Lucofao but was assassinated in 681. Pepin made peace with his successor Waratton. Waratton's successor Berchar and the Neustrian king Theuderic III then made war on Austrasia, and were decisively defeated at the Battle of Tertry in 687. Pepin followed them to Paris and forced a peace, with the condition that Berchar leave office. He became mayor in all three Frankish kingdoms, Austrasia, Neustria and Burgundy, and began calling himself Duke and Prince of the Franks.

The Neustrians barely tolerated an Austrasian overlord, but Pepin turned to Germany. Over the next years he subdued the Alemanni, the Frisians and the Franconians, and between 690 and 692 Utrecht fell, giving the Franks control of trade routes on the Rhine to the North Sea. He supported the missionary work of Willibrord. In 695 he placed his son Drogo in the Burgundian mayorship and his other son Grimoald in the Neustrian one.

Around 670 Pepin had married Plectrude, mother of Drogo and Grimoald II, both of whom died before their father. His mistress or second wife Alpaida bore him Charles Martel and Childebrand. Just before his death Plectrude convinced him to disinherit Alpaida's sons in favour of his grandson Theudoald, a young child. Pepin died suddenly on 16 December 714, at the age of 79, at Jupille. Charles had gained favour among the Austrasians through his military prowess and the booty he brought, and despite Plectrude's imprisoning of him he became sole mayor of the palace, and de facto ruler of Francia, after a civil war of more than three years. Pepin's statesmanship further decreased Merovingian royal authority and secured acceptance of his family's right to rule.
pepin-of-italy: Pepin was born Carloman in 777, the second son of Charlemagne and his wife Hildegard, and had an older brother, Charles the Younger, and a half-brother, Pepin the Hunchback. In 781 Charlemagne and Hildegard took him to Rome at the request of Pope Adrian I, with his younger brother Louis the Pious and his sisters Rotrude and Bertha. His parents had delayed his baptism so that the pope could perform it. Adrian baptised him, renamed him Pepin, and crowned him king of the Lombards, later styled king of Italy, while Louis was crowned king of Aquitaine. The name was probably chosen to recall his grandfather Pepin the Short, remembered as a firm ally of the papacy.

Although only four years old, Pepin was brought to Lombardy to live under advisers provided by Charlemagne, the most important of whom were Adalard of Corbie, Waldo of Reichenau, the Lombard duke Rotchild and Angilbert. His court was based chiefly at Verona, with palaces also at Mantua and at Pavia, the traditional Lombard capital. He was king in his own name, but Charlemagne took a strong hand in Italy into Pepin's adulthood and sometimes issued laws directly.

Pepin took part in his father's campaign against Tassilo III of Bavaria in 786. In 796 he led a campaign against the Avar Khaganate, took its stronghold and precipitated the collapse of the Avar state, which allowed the Frankish realm to expand eastward; the Latin poem De Pippini regis Victoria Avarica commemorates the victory. He also led several raids against the Duchy of Benevento and, in 810, a campaign against the Republic of Venice. In 806 Charlemagne's Divisio Regnorum confirmed Pepin in Italy and gave him most of Bavaria and Alamannia.

Pepin died on 8 July 810. Over 810 and 811 his sister Rotrude, his aunt Gisela, his half-brother Pepin and his brother Charles also died, possibly victims of an epidemic that had spread from cattle. Charlemagne then declared Pepin's son Bernard ruler of Italy and Louis the heir to the rest of the empire. Pepin had married Theodrada, a cousin of his father, and Louis later used the closeness of the relation to portray the marriage as illegitimate in order to sideline Bernard. Bernard's male-line descendants ruled as counts of Vermandois into the eleventh century, the longest-surviving direct male line of Charlemagne. Pepin also had five daughters and was an ancestor of Hugh Capet.
pepin-the-short: Pepin was the son of the Frankish prince Charles Martel and his wife Rotrude, and was educated by the monks of the Abbey Church of St Denis near Paris. When Charles Martel died in 741 he divided rule between Pepin, who became Mayor of the Palace of Neustria, and his elder brother Carloman, who took Austrasia. Their half-brother Grifo demanded a share; the brothers besieged him at Laon and imprisoned him in a monastery. In 743 Carloman raised Childeric III, the last Merovingian, to the throne as a figurehead.

Carloman entered a monastery in 747, leaving Pepin sole mayor of the palace. Grifo escaped and fled to Duke Odilo of Bavaria, married to Pepin's sister Hiltrude, and Pepin put down his revolt. Holding the power of a king while Childeric had only the title, Pepin asked Pope Zachary whether it was proper that kings of the Franks no longer had royal power. The pope, hard pressed by the Lombards, replied that the one who wields power should be called king. Childeric was confined to a monastery and Pepin was elected by an assembly of nobles and anointed in 751.

In 754 Pope Stephen II anointed him again at the Basilica of St Denis, together with his sons Charles and Carloman, and gave him the title Patricius Romanorum, the first recorded crowning of a civil ruler by a pope. Pepin made war on the Lombard king Aistulf and confirmed the papacy in possession of Ravenna and the Pentapolis, the Donation of Pepin, which formed the legal basis of the Papal States.

Around 752 Pepin turned to Septimania, received the submission of Nîmes, Maguelone, Béziers and Agde, and took Narbonne in 759. In Aquitaine he fought Duke Waiofar from 760, capturing strongholds, deporting Gascon garrisons with their families and burning villas and vineyards. By 767 he held Toulouse and Bordeaux, the nobles accepted peace, and Waiofar was killed by his own followers in 768.

Pepin died in 768 and was buried at the Basilica of Saint Denis. The realm was divided under Salic law between Charlemagne and Carloman I. He was among the most powerful rulers of his time, but his reign is largely overshadowed by that of Charlemagne.
percheron: The Percheron comes from the valley of the Huisne in western France, part of the former province of Perche, which gave the breed its name. Its exact origins are unknown. Foundation stock may have included mares captured by Clovis I from the Bretons, or Barb stallions brought from Spain by the Moors in the 8th century. Barb stallions were certainly crossed with local mares in the 8th century, and more Oriental blood came with the Comte du Perche on his return from the Crusades. Breed historians agree that the terrain and climate of Perche shaped it most.

After the age of the armoured knight, breeders sought horses able to pull heavy stagecoaches at a fast trot, the Diligence Horse, gray being preferred for its visibility at night. When railways replaced the coaches a heavier type arose for farm work and hauling goods. The breed nearly became extinct when horse breeding was suppressed during the French Revolution. Jean le Blanc, foaled in 1823, is the stallion to which all Percherons trace their ancestry, and the breed grew to a draft horse averaging about 910 kilograms. The French stud book was created in 1893.

Edward Harris II of Moorestown, New Jersey, first imported Percherons to the United States in 1839. After the American Civil War demand for large draft horses grew, and about 7,500 were exported in the 1880s. In the 1930s Percherons made up over 70 per cent of purebred draft horses in the United States, but mechanisation after World War II caused a steep decline, and only 85 were registered there in 1954.

The Percheron is the best known and most numerous French draft breed. It was used to improve the Ardennes and Vladimir Heavy Draft horses and to create the Spanish-Norman. By the end of the 19th century Percherons made up most of the driving horses of Paris. They are still used for draft work and forestry, and for parades, sleigh rides and carriage work.
perdiccas: According to the 2nd-century historian Arrian, Perdiccas was the son of the Macedonian nobleman Orontes, a descendant of the independent princes of the province of Orestis. His date of birth is unknown, but he seems to have been of an age with Alexander. In 336 BCE, when Pausanias assassinated King Philip II of Macedon, Perdiccas was among those who chased the assassin down and killed him. He was a somatophylax, or bodyguard, and a hetairos, an elite cavalry commander, of Alexander, and he distinguished himself at the conquest of Thebes in 335 BCE, where he was heavily wounded, and at Gaugamela, before following Alexander into India.

After Alexander died on 11 June 323 BCE at Babylon, Perdiccas was very influential, as his second-in-command and the holder of the signet ring Alexander had given him. The army divided, with the aristocratic cavalry officers on one side and the infantry on the other. Perdiccas proposed waiting for Alexander's wife Roxana, who was pregnant, to give birth, and when Aristonous proclaimed him king he hesitated and the moment was lost. In the Partition of Babylon a compromise made him regent of the empire for the disabled Philip III and the infant Alexander IV, and supreme commander of the army. To secure power he had thirty infantry leaders trampled by war elephants and then executed Meleager.

His authority was never secure. He distributed satrapies, sent away officers who threatened him and attached Cleomenes of Naucratis to Ptolemy in Egypt, probably to limit Ptolemy's power. Agreeing to marry Nicaea, daughter of Antipater, he later considered Cleopatra of Macedon, Alexander's sister, a match that would have given him a claim to the throne. Ptolemy diverted Alexander's body to Egypt, and Perdiccas, regarding it as an act of war, invaded Egypt while Antipater, Craterus and Antigonus moved against him.

When the invasion foundered, his soldiers mutinied, and his officers Peithon, Antigenes and Seleucus murdered him in his tent, probably about three years after he took the regency. The army went over to Ptolemy. News of Eumenes' victory over Craterus at the Hellespont, which would have restored his authority, arrived the next day.

Ancient accounts are largely negative, calling him arrogant and imperious, and Diodorus Siculus called him a man of slaughter; this may owe much to the rivalry with Ptolemy, whose lost account lies behind Arrian. Waldemar Heckel sees a tale of lofty ideals combined with excessive ambition, and calls him a great but flawed man. His death has been seen as the end of the empire as Alexander envisioned it.
perdiccas-ii-of-macedon: Perdiccas II was the oldest son of King Alexander I of Macedon and had four brothers: Alcetas, Amyntas, Menelaus and Philip. Menelaus became the father of the later king Amyntas II, and the grandson of Amyntas became king Amyntas III. Perdiccas married at least two women during his reign, Simache and Cleopatra. Simache was the mother of Archelaus and Aeropus II. Plato, through speakers in the Gorgias, accuses her of having been a slave of Alcetas, but this is doubtful, since Archelaus was treated as legitimate.

Cleopatra, who was possibly a Lyncestian or even an Argead, bore Perdiccas a son. According to Plato, Archelaus drowned this boy in a well when he was seven, because he was regarded as the legitimate heir. There is strong evidence that Cleopatra later married her stepson Archelaus, though historians such as Nicholas Hammond dispute this.

The unexpected death of Alexander I caused a dynastic crisis. Perdiccas took the throne as the oldest son, but Philip and Alcetas each obtained a local realm. He annexed the territory of Alcetas at an unknown date. Philip's hold on the Axios Valley was harder to overcome: Philip allied himself with King Derdas I of Elimiotis and with Athens, and Perdiccas answered by stirring up revolt in Athenian tribute cities, including Potidaea. Athens sent troops and ships, took Therma and besieged Pydna. It then allied with Perdiccas, who broke the treaty at once and marched to Potidaea. That fighting, together with the Battle of Sybota, led directly to the Peloponnesian War.

In 429 the Thracian king Sitalces invaded Macedonia with Philip's son Amyntas, supposedly with 150,000 men, and ravaged Mygdonia, Crestonia and Anthemus. The invasion faltered for want of supplies and because the Athenian fleet never came. Sitalces' nephew Seuthes persuaded him to leave after Perdiccas secretly promised a large dowry and the hand of his sister Stratonice.

In 424 Perdiccas helped the Spartan general Brasidas take Amphipolis from Athens, a blow to the Athenians, who relied on Macedonian timber. The Illyrians then changed sides in the Battle of Lyncestis, the Macedonians fled, and the angry Spartans plundered the Macedonian baggage train. Perdiccas allied with Athens in 423, joined the Spartan-Argive alliance by 417, and a few years later broke with the Peloponnese and aided Athens against Amphipolis. He died about 413 BCE, leaving his son Archelaus as heir.
pereiaslav: Pereiaslav lies near the confluence of the Alta and Trubizh rivers, some 95 km south-east of Kyiv, in Boryspil Raion of Kyiv Oblast. It was one of the key regional centres of power in the Middle Ages and the capital of a principality.

Pereiaslav is first mentioned in a 911 treaty with the Byzantine Empire. Vladimir I, grand prince of Kiev, built a large fortress there in 992 to protect the southern limits of Kievan Rus' from raids by steppe nomads. The city was the capital of the Principality of Pereyaslavl from the mid-11th century until the Tatars demolished it in 1239 during the Mongol invasions.

In the 14th century it was annexed by the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and later formed part of the Kiev Voivodeship, which became part of the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland in 1569. In the later 16th century it became a regimental city of the Zaporozhian Host. In 1654 Bohdan Khmelnytskyi held the Pereiaslav council, where the Zaporozhian Cossacks voted for a military alliance with the Tsardom of Russia and accepted the Pereiaslav Agreement, which brought their lands under Russian rule. It established the Cossack Hetmanate in left-bank Ukraine, subject to the Tsardom. By the Truce of Andrusovo in 1667 Pereiaslav became part of Russia.

A Jewish community is first recorded in 1620. Its members were among the first killed in the Khmelnytskyi uprising, and the chronicler Nathan Hannover lists Pereiaslav among the communities that died as martyrs. Sholem Aleichem was born in the town in 1859 and studied at its Russian gymnasium until 1876. A pogrom took place there from 30 June to 2 July 1881, and another in June 1919 killed 20 people. In autumn 1941 about 800 Jewish residents were shot on the outskirts.

In October 1943 the Soviet government renamed the town Pereiaslav-Khmelnytskyi to stress Khmelnytskyi's role in the Pereiaslav Agreement, and made it a museum and tourism centre. The Ukrainian parliament restored the historic name Pereiaslav in 2019. It has more than 20 museums, including the Museum of Folk Architecture and Household Traditions, and landmarks such as St Michael's Church dating from the 17th century and the Ascension Monastery, with a cathedral built between 1695 and 1700.
perekop: Perekop is a village on the Perekop Isthmus, which connects the Crimean peninsula to the Ukrainian mainland. It is known for the Or Qapı fortress, which served as the gateway to Crimea. The original name was that of the Greek settlement of Taphros, meaning a dug-out locality, whose people were called Taphrians. The Crimean Tatar name Or Qapı means trench gate. In the Middle Ages the place was known as Tuzla. The Slavic name Perekop means an over-dug locality.

Because of its key position Perekop endured many sieges. During the Russo-Turkish War of 1735 to 1739 the Russian field marshal Burkhard Christoph von Münnich stormed the fortifications on 17 June 1736 and left the Tatar fortress in ruins, a serious blow to the independence of the Crimean Khanate. The town was virtually wiped out in the Siege of Perekop by the Red Army in 1920, a key episode of the Russian Civil War, whose success allowed the Bolsheviks to drive Pyotr Wrangel's White Army from Crimea. Twelve years later the Soviets founded the new town of Krasnoperekopsk, 32 kilometres to the south.

In World War II German forces occupied Perekop from 27 September 1941 to 1 November 1943. Its capture, by the Wehrmacht in 1941 and by the Red Army in 1943, was used to cut Crimea off from Ukraine. The village lies within Armiansk Municipality, and the Ukrainian census of 2001 counted 894 inhabitants.
pereslavl-zalessky: Pereslavl-Zalessky lies in southern Yaroslavl Oblast, near the border with Moscow Oblast, on the main Moscow–Yaroslavl road. It stands on the south-eastern shore of Lake Pleshcheyevo, at the mouth of the Trubezh River, 140 kilometres north-east of Moscow and 123 kilometres south-west of Yaroslavl. The climate is humid continental, with long, cold and snowy winters and short, warm and rainy summers.

George I of Vladimir founded the town in 1152 as a projected capital of Zalesye, a name that means beyond the woods. The inhabitants of the nearby town of Kleshchin were relocated to it. Between 1175 and 1302 Pereslavl was the seat of a principality. In 1302 it was inherited by the prince of Moscow after the childless death of Ivan, son of Dmitry of Pereslavl. The Mongols devastated it many times between the mid-13th century and the early 15th century, and it suffered again in the Polish invasion of 1611–1612.

Between 1688 and 1693 Peter the Great built his fun flotilla on Lake Pleshcheyevo for his own amusement, among it the small boat that could be considered the forerunner of the Russian fleet. A scale model of it is now in the Central Naval Museum. In 1708 the town became part of the Moscow Governorate. Among those associated with the town are the saint Nicetas Stylites, who founded the Monastery of St Nicetas in the 12th century, and Alexander Nevsky, prince and saint, born in 1221.

The town is part of the Golden Ring of Russia and had a population of 41,925 at the 2010 census. Its monuments include the white stone Savior's Cathedral of 1152–1157, the Church of Metropolitan Peter of 1585, and the Troitse-Danilov, Nikitsky, Feodorovsky and Goritsky monasteries, built between the 16th and 19th centuries. The Museum-Preserve of Pereslavl-Zalessky is in the Goritsky Monastery. About two kilometres from the town the Kleshchin earthworks, the remains of an old defensive wall, can still be walked along.
pergamon: Pergamon lies on the north edge of the Caicus plain in Mysia, in north-west Turkey, 26 kilometres from the Aegean coast. The city was centred on a mesa of andesite 335 metres high that formed its acropolis. Three natural terraces on its south side give a route to the top. The Selinus River flows to the west of the acropolis and the Cetius to the east. In Hellenistic times the town of Elaia at the mouth of the Caicus served as its port.

Settlement can be detected from the late 8th century BCE, through pottery imported from the west. The earliest mention in literature is in Xenophon's Anabasis, since the march of the Ten Thousand ended at Pergamon in 400 to 399 BCE, when the city belonged to the family of Gongylos of Eretria, a Greek favourable to the Achaemenid Empire. Lysimachus, King of Thrace, took possession in 301 BCE, and his lieutenant Philetaerus enlarged the town. When the kingdom of Thrace collapsed in 281 BCE, Philetaerus became an independent ruler and founded the Attalid dynasty, which ruled until 133 BCE.

Eumenes I gained territory down to the coast after the Battle of Sardis in 261 BCE against Antiochus I. In 238 BCE his successor Attalus I defeated the Galatians, to whom Pergamon had paid tribute, and declared himself leader of an independent kingdom. Under Eumenes II and Attalus II the city expanded, with a new street network, wall and marketplace.

In 88 BCE Mithridates VI Eupator made Pergamon his headquarters in his first war against Rome. The Romans deprived it of its status as a free city and made it pay tribute, but it remained a prominent city, and Augustus granted it a neocorate, the first centre of the imperial cult in the province of Asia. The Arabs captured it in 663/4 CE, after which settlement shrank to the acropolis, and attacks in 1109 and 1113 after the Seljuk invasion largely destroyed it. Manuel I Komnenos rebuilt it around 1170, and it fell to the Karasids shortly after 1300 and then to the Ottomans.

The ruins stand north-west of the modern city of Bergama.
