After French occupation it was administered by the United States from 1945 to 1948, and was rebuilt over the following twenty years. The rubble was heaped on the Wallberg hill, where a monument stands.
pha-that-luang: Pha That Luang, meaning Great Stupa, stands about 4 km from the centre of Vientiane at the end of Pha That Luang Road. According to tradition, Buddhist missionaries from the Mauryan Empire were sent by Emperor Ashoka, among them Bury Chan, also called Praya Chanthabury Pasithisak, and five Arahanta monks, who brought a relic believed to be the Buddha's breastbone and enshrined it in the stupa.

In the 16th century King Setthathirat moved his capital from Luang Prabang to Vientiane and ordered the construction of the temple in 1566. Its bases were each 69 metres long, and the stupa stood 45 metres high, surrounded by 30 smaller stupas.

In 1641 Gerrit van Wuysthoff, an envoy of the Dutch East India Company, visited Vientiane and was received ceremonially at the temple by King Sourigna Vongsa. He wrote that he was particularly impressed by the enormous pyramid, whose top was covered with gold leaf weighing about a thousand pounds. The stupa was repeatedly plundered by the Burmese, Siamese and Chinese.

It was destroyed in the Thai invasion of 1828. Not until 1900 did the French restore it to its original design, working from detailed drawings made in 1867 by the French architect and explorer Louis Delaporte. That first attempt was unsuccessful, and the stupa had to be redesigned and rebuilt in the 1930s.

The monument rises in three levels. The first measures 223 by 226 feet (68 by 69 metres), the second 157 feet (48 metres) along each side, and the third 98 feet (30 metres) along each side. From ground to pinnacle it is 147.6 feet (45.0 metres) high.

The area around the stupa is gated to keep out traffic, though visitors could once drive around the whole complex. The encircling walls are roughly 279 feet (85 metres) long on each side and contain Lao and Khmer sculptures, including one of Jayavarman VII.
phags-pa-script: The ʼPhags-pa script, also written Phagspa, is an alphabet designed by the Tibetan monk Drogön Chögyal Phagpa (1235-1280) for Kublai Khan (r. 1264-1294), the founder of the Yuan dynasty, as a unified script for the written languages within the Yuan. The Mongol rulers wanted a universal script for the languages of the peoples they had subjugated. The Uyghur-based Mongolian alphabet did not fit Middle Mongol perfectly, and it would have been impractical to extend it to a language with a very different phonology such as Chinese.

Around 1269 Kublai Khan therefore asked Phagpa to design a new alphabet for the whole empire. He extended his native Tibetan alphabet to cover Mongol and Chinese, and the result was 38 letters, later counted as 41 basic letters, known by names such as square script.

The script descends from the Tibetan script and belongs to the Brahmic family, but it is unusual in being written from top to bottom. Although it is an alphabet, it is written like a syllabary or abugida, with the letters of a syllable linked into syllabic blocks.

Unlike Tibetan, all its letters are written in the order in which they are spoken and in line, and vowels are not diacritics. Short /a/ is not written except at the start of a word, which makes the script transitional between an abugida, a syllabary and a full alphabet. Letters 1-30 follow the traditional order of the thirty basic Tibetan letters. It was written in a standard blocky form, a still blockier Tibetan form and an elaborate seal form used on imperial seals.

It was used to write and transcribe varieties of Chinese, Tibetic languages, Mongolian, Uyghur, Sanskrit and probably Persian. It never gained wide acceptance, even among the Mongol elite, but it remained an official script of the Yuan dynasty until the early 1350s, when the Red Turban Rebellion began. It then served mainly as a phonetic gloss for Mongols learning Chinese characters, and its actual use lasted about a hundred years before it fell out of use with the Ming dynasty. In the 20th century it appeared on Tibetan currency, and it was used for Tibetan seal inscriptions from the Middle Ages and for inscriptions on the doors of Tibetan monasteries. It was added to the Unicode Standard in July 2006.
phaistos: The ancient city lay about 5.6 km east of the Mediterranean and 62 km south of Heraklion, at modern Faistos. The form Pa-i-to appears in Linear A texts and on 62 Linear B tablets found at Knossos. Phaistos was one of the three largest cities of Minoan Crete, with Knossos and Malia, and a road system linked it to the other cities. It was also connected to Hagia Triada, which has a smaller palace that may have been a residence of the rulers of Phaistos, and to Gortyn.

The site was first inhabited around 3600 BCE, slightly later than Knossos. The first palace dates to the Middle Minoan IB period, around 2000 BCE, and it was destroyed and rebuilt three times over about three centuries. Each rebuilding expanded on the last, on several levels joined by halls and stairs, and the palace was about two thirds the size of Knossos. It held religious and political areas, storage, housing and a theatre. It was destroyed around 1400 BCE and never rebuilt, perhaps by a large earthquake. Grape pips found in storage vessels indicate wine production.

The site was reoccupied in the Geometric Age, in the 8th century BCE. Phaistos then struck its own currency, the stater, and allied with other Cretan cities and with Eumenes II of Pergamon. Around the end of the 3rd century BCE the Gortynians destroyed it.

Federico Halbherr and his student Luigi Pernier excavated the site from 1900 to 1904. The Phaistos Disc was found in 1908 in a basement room on the north side of the palace, with a Linear A tablet. Italian teams under Doro Levi, Vincenzo La Rosa and, from 2007, Fausto Longo have continued work, and 61 Linear A inscribed items have been found. In 2025 UNESCO designated the site a World Heritage Site.
phaistos-disc: The disc was recovered intact on 3 July 1908 by the Italian archaeologist Luigi Pernier in the first Minoan palace at Phaistos, near Hagia Triada on the south coast of Crete. It lay in the basement of room 8 in building 101, northeast of the main palace, in the main cell of an underground temple depository. Dating is uncertain. Yves Duhoux places it between 1850 and 1600 BCE, Jeppesen after 1400 BCE, and Louis Godart accepts any date in Middle or Late Minoan times, spanning most of the second millennium BCE.

The unusual features led some scholars to suspect a forgery of 1908, and thermoluminescence dating has never been carried out. Andrew Robinson would welcome it but does not endorse the forgery arguments. Later finds with similar signs support authenticity, and the disc is now generally accepted as genuine.

The disc is of fine-grained fired clay, about 16 centimetres across and almost 2 centimetres thick, slightly egg-shaped, concave on one side and convex on the other. Some writers have said that the clay does not look local. It was intentionally fired, unlike tablets and seals that were baked only by accident. Each side carries a single spiral of signs made by pressing a separate stamp for each sign into the soft clay, so the disc can be seen as an early example of movable-type printing.

There are 45 distinct signs, numbered by Sir Arthur Evans, many of them showing humans, birds, plants and a boat. A scored spiral line separates the turns, and short radial lines divide the text into groups conventionally called words, 31 on one side and 30 on the other. The text is generally agreed to run clockwise from the edge toward the centre. Evans at one point argued the opposite, and later changed his mind.

Many have tried to decipher it. Most assume a syllabary, given 45 signs in so short a text, but alphabetic and logographic readings have also been proposed, and claimed languages include Greek, Luwian, Hittite and a Semitic language. Others have taken it for a prayer, a board game or a geometric theorem. Scholars regard decipherment as unlikely without more examples of the signs, and any reading without external confirmation is unlikely to be accepted. At first most scholars, including Evans, argued for a non-Cretan origin, but later finds with similar signs made a Cretan origin more popular. The signs were added to Unicode in 2008, and the disc serves as the logo of the Greek research centre FORTH.
phalanx: The first use of the word comes from Homer, who in the Iliad uses it of hoplites fighting in an organised battle line, to set formation combat apart from the individual duels common in his poems. Ancient Greek writers used it more broadly for any massed infantry formation. Historians have not agreed on how the Greek formation relates to earlier ones, since the shield wall and spear hedge were widely known.

Traditionally the hoplite phalanx has been dated to the 8th century BCE in Sparta, but this is under revision. It was perhaps devised in the 7th century BCE, after the city of Argos introduced the aspis, the shield that made the formation possible. The Chigi vase, dated to 650 BCE, shows hoplites with aspis, spear and javelins.

In the hoplite phalanx of c. 800–350 BCE the men lined up in close order, locked their shields together and projected the spears of the first few ranks over the front rank of shields. Each hoplite carried his shield on his left arm, which protected the man to his left, so the man at the extreme right was only half protected and the whole line tended to drift to the right. Each hoplite supplied his own equipment; his main weapon was a spear, the dory, about 2.4 metres long.

The Macedonian phalanx and those of the Hellenistic successor states developed from it. The phalangites carried the sarissa, a pike at least 14 feet long and more probably 18, which was wielded with both hands. Hoplite phalanxes were usually eight ranks deep or more, Macedonian ones usually sixteen, and sometimes thirty-two.

Battles between phalanxes took place on open, flat plains, where it was easier to keep formation, and usually ended when one side fled. The most widely accepted reading of the sources is the othismos, a pushing match in which the rear ranks kept pressure on the front; no Greek art shows it, and the theory remains unresolved. At Marathon in 490 BCE the Athenians thinned their phalanx to lengthen their front, and at Leuctra the Theban general Epaminondas deepened his left flank to fifty ranks.

The formation was weakest against lighter, more flexible troops, as at Lechaeum, where an Athenian force led by Iphicrates routed a Spartan mora. A Macedonian phalanx was very vulnerable on its flanks and rear and could lose cohesion on broken ground, as at Cynoscephalae and Pydna, where Roman legionary centuries engaged the phalangites hand to hand. After Alexander the Great the phalanx slowly declined, and as Rome conquered most of the Hellenistic successor states the armies that used it ceased to exist.
phalaris: Phalaris was tyrant of Akragas, the modern Agrigento in Sicily, from approximately 570 to 554 BCE. He was entrusted with building the temple of Zeus Atabyrius on the citadel and used his position to make himself tyrant. Under his rule the city seemed to attain considerable prosperity: he supplied it with water, adorned it with fine buildings and strengthened it with walls. On the northern coast the people of Himera elected him general with absolute power, despite the warnings of the poet Stesichorus. According to the Suda, he made himself master of the whole island.

He was said to be cruel to excess, and cannibalism was even alleged, with the claim that he ate suckling babies. He supposedly ordered a sculptor named Perilaus to make a hollow brazen bull that could hold a man, who was shut inside while a fire was lit beneath. A general uprising headed by Telemachus, an ancestor of Theron of Acragas, overthrew him.

In some versions of the legend Phalaris was burned alive in his own bull. Pindar, who lived less than a century afterwards, links the instrument of torture with his name, and Lucian mentions it in two satirical dialogues, Phalaris A and Phalaris B. A brazen bull certainly stood at Agrigentum, and the Carthaginians carried it off to Carthage. It was probably Scipio Aemilianus who returned it, with other stolen works of art, to the Sicilian cities after destroying Carthage around 146 BCE. In medieval times Phalaris gained a literary fame as the supposed author of a collection of letters. In 1699 Richard Bentley published a Dissertation on the Epistles of Phalaris, proving that they were misattributed and had been written around the 2nd century CE.
phalsbourg: Phalsbourg is a commune in the Moselle department in the Grand Est region of north-eastern France. It lies high on the west slopes of the Vosges, 40 kilometres north-west of Strasbourg, and commands one of the passes of the Vosges, which gave it military importance. Its population is about 4,700. In 1911 it had an Evangelical and a Roman Catholic church, a synagogue and a teachers' seminary, with industries making gloves, straw hats and liqueurs, and quarrying.

The land first belonged to the principality of Lützelstein, under the overlordship of Luxembourg and then the bishops of Metz and Strasbourg, before passing to the house of Veldenz, all within the Holy Roman Empire. In 1570 George John I, Count Palatine of Veldenz, founded the town of Pfalzburg as a refuge for Reformed Protestants expelled from the Duchy of Lorraine and as an administrative centre for his holdings. The cost forced him to sell it to Lorraine in the years after 1583. His successor founded nearby Lixheim for Reformed refugees in 1608, and also had to sell it to Lorraine, in 1623.

From 1629 to 1660 Pfalzburg and Lixheim formed the Principality of Pfalzburg for Henriette of Lorraine and her three successive husbands. Lorraine ceded the town to France in the Treaty of Vincennes in 1661. The military engineer Vauban rebuilt its fortifications in 1680. They resisted the Allies in 1814 and 1815, and held out against the Germans for four months in 1870 until the town fell on 12 December. The fortifications have since been razed. The town was German again, as Pfalzburg, from 1871 to 1918.

The United States Air Forces in Europe built an air base near the town in 1953 and returned it to the French government in 1967. It is now used by a French army helicopter regiment. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe visited the town on 23 June 1770 and mentioned his stay in his autobiography Dichtung und Wahrheit. A summer theatre festival lasting a week has been held there since 1980.
pham-van-dong: Phạm Văn Đồng was born on 1 March 1906, according to an official report, into a family of civil servants in Quảng Ngãi Province on the central coast. In 1925 he joined fellow students in a sit-in mourning the patriotic scholar Phan Chu Trinh. In 1926 he went to Guangzhou for a training course run by Nguyen Ai Quoc, later Ho Chi Minh, and joined the Vietnamese Revolutionary Youth League. Arrested in 1929, he was sentenced by the French colonial authorities to ten years and served on Poulo Condor Island until the Popular Front's amnesty of 1936.

In 1940 he went secretly to China with Võ Nguyên Giáp, joined the Indochinese Communist Party and was tasked with building a base at the border. After the August Revolution of 1945 he became minister of finance of the new Democratic Republic of Vietnam, and in 1946 headed its delegation at Fontainebleau, where talks failed because France set no firm date for a referendum in Cochinchina. He became Deputy Prime Minister in July 1949. In May 1954 he led the delegation to the Geneva Conference on Indochina and signed the accords with the French premier Pierre Mendès France.

Đồng was minister of foreign affairs from September 1954 and prime minister from 1955 until he retired in 1987, over thirty years. After Ho Chi Minh's strokes in the early 1960s he became the face of North Vietnam in the war with the United States, speaking to foreign diplomats and journalists.

On 8 June 1964 he met the Canadian diplomat J. Blair Seaborn in Hanoi, who carried an offer from President Johnson of aid and recognition in exchange for an end to attempts to overthrow the South Vietnamese government, with a warning of bombing. Đồng called the terms unacceptable and demanded an end of American assistance to the south, its neutrality and a coalition government including the National Liberation Front. He died in Hanoi on 29 April 2000, aged 94.
phanagoria: Phanagoria was the largest ancient Greek city on the Taman Peninsula, spread over two plateaus along the eastern shore of the Cimmerian Bosporus. It stood on an island in the ancient archipelago of Corocondamitis and covered 75 hectares, of which one third has since been submerged by the sea. It was a large emporium for the traffic between the coast of the Maeotian marshes and the countries south of the Caucasus, and Strabo described it as noteworthy for its trade. The site lies a short distance west of Sennoy in Krasnodar Krai, Russia.

The city was founded by Teian colonists who fled Asia Minor after their conflict with the Persian king Cyrus the Great, and took its name from one of them, Phanagoras. In the 5th century BCE it thrived on trade with the Scythians and the Sindi. In the early 4th century BCE the Bosporan Kingdom subjugated it, and it became the kingdom's eastern capital, with Panticapaeum the western one. By the first centuries CE it was the kingdom's main centre.

In the Mithridatic Wars it allied with the Roman Republic and withstood a siege by Pharnaces II of Pontus, and an insurrection against Mithridates VI of Pontus broke out there shortly before his death. Its loyalty to Rome kept it dominant until the 4th century, when the Huns sacked and destroyed it.

By the 7th century it was the capital of Old Great Bulgaria between 632 and 665 under Kubrat. It later became at least nominally a Byzantine dependency, with a Khazar tudun in the town, and in 704 the deposed emperor Justinian II settled there for a time. After the 10th century it could not compete with neighbouring Tmutarakan. In the late Middle Ages the Genoese colony of Matrega was built on its ruins, and it was made a Catholic metropolitan archdiocese in 1349 and suppressed around 1400. There has been no permanent settlement on the site since.

The site was identified in the 18th century when marble statue bases with dedications to Aphrodite were found, and Hecataeus and Strabo mention a sanctuary of Aphrodite there as the largest in the Pontic region. Exploration began in 1822. A vast necropolis with thousands of burials surrounds the city, including royal kurgans with painted burial chambers. The palace of Mithridates VI was found in 2009, and underwater work has revealed fragments of buildings. Archaeologists have also found a synagogue and a Jewish quarter.
phanariotes: The Phanariots emerged as a class of wealthy Greek merchants, mostly of noble Byzantine descent, in the second half of the 16th century. After Mehmet II captured Constantinople in 1453 he repopulated the city, and the quarter of Phanar was settled with Greeks from Mouchlion in the Peloponnese and, after 1461, with citizens of the Empire of Trebizond. The Ecumenical Patriarch was recognised as head of the empire's Orthodox subjects, and the Phanariots built their houses near his court and dominated the patriarchate's administration, often intervening in the choice of bishops and patriarchs.

As the Ottoman Empire turned to diplomacy in the 17th century, the Porte needed negotiators who knew Western languages and left the task to Greeks. From 1669 until the Greek War of Independence in 1821, Phanariots made up most of the dragomans to the Ottoman government and to foreign embassies. Their fortunes also rested on tax collection, trade monopolies, court supply and the Black Sea wheat trade.

From 1711 to 1716 onward, Phanariots were appointed princes of Moldavia and Wallachia, usually after serving as dragoman of the Porte or of the Fleet. The change followed the actions of Dimitrie Cantemir, who sided with Russia in 1710 to 1713, and of Ștefan Cantacuzino, who allied with the Habsburg commander Prince Eugene of Savoy.

A new prince obtained office by a large bribe, borrowed from creditors who came with him, and sought to recoup it quickly. Thirty-one princes from eleven families ruled in the Phanariot epoch, and Constantine Mavrocordatos ruled ten times. After the Treaty of Kuchuk-Kainarji in 1774, Russia could intervene for Orthodox subjects, and the deposition of two princes in 1806 was the cause of war between Russia and the Ottomans in 1806 to 1812.

The princes' part in the revolts of 1820 and 1821, and the Filiki Eteria uprising, led the Porte to stop appointing princes from the Phanar. Scarlat Callimachi was the last Phanariot ruler in Bucharest.

Many Phanariots patronised Greek culture, education and printing and founded academies. Constantine Mavrocordatos abolished serfdom in Wallachia in 1746 and in Moldavia in 1749, and Alexander Ypsilantis, who reigned from 1774 to 1782, began legal reforms. Condemnation of the Phanariots is a theme of Romanian nationalism, while some families, among them the Rosetti family, came to identify as Romanian. The name Neo-Phanariots is sometimes given to Greek families who rose to prominence in the 19th century, one of whose posts was Prince of Samos.
pharaoh: The word pharaoh derives from the Egyptian pr ꜥꜣ, meaning great house, which named the royal palace and was long used only in phrases referring to the court. Under the New Kingdom it became a form of address for the king himself. The earliest confirmed use for a ruler is a letter to Akhenaten (reigned c. 1353–1336 BCE), and an inscription referring to Thutmose III (c. 1479–1425 BCE) may be earlier. The first dated attachment of the title to a king's name is in year 17 of Siamun, in the tenth century BCE.

Scholars nevertheless use the word for every ruler of Egypt from the First Dynasty (c. 3150 BCE) to 30 BCE. Early kings bore up to three titles, the Horus name, the Sedge and Bee name and the Two Ladies name; the Golden Horus name, the nomen and the prenomen were added later, and by the Middle Kingdom the formal titulary had five names.

The king was the intermediary between the gods and the people. He owned all the land of Egypt, enacted laws, collected taxes and commanded the army, and he officiated at religious ceremonies and chose the sites of new temples. Officials acted only in his name, by delegated power. From the Pyramid Texts his task was summed up in a maxim, bring Maat and repel Isfet, that is, promote order and repel chaos.

Regalia expressed the office. The red crown, the Deshret, stood for Lower Egypt and the white crown, the Hedjet, for Upper Egypt; the double crown, the Pschent, is first documented in the middle of the First Dynasty. The rearing cobra, the uraeus, appears from the reign of Den. No ancient Egyptian crown has ever been found, not even in the tomb of Tutankhamun.

Egyptians often regarded the pharaoh as divine. In the Early Dynastic Period he was the incarnation of Horus; by the time of Djedefre in the 26th century BCE he was held to have no human father, his mother having been impregnated by the sun god Ra. Under the New Kingdom he was thought to possess the living royal ka of Amun-Re, received at his coronation. Temple texts called Darius the Great (522–486 BCE) a divine being, and such descriptions continued for Alexander the Great and the Ptolemaic rulers.

Herodotus reports that Egyptian priests rejected the divinity of the king, and rabbinic literature later depicted Pharaoh as a man who falsely proclaimed himself a god. Through the Hebrew Bible and the Qur'an, which spells the title firʿawn, it became the usual name for the kings of ancient Egypt.
pharisees: The name Pharisee comes from the Greek Pharisaios, from an Aramaic word meaning set apart. It may refer to their separation from Gentiles and sources of ritual impurity, or from irreligious Jews. The Pharisees emerged largely from the scribes and sages and were active from the middle of the 2nd century BCE until the destruction of the Temple in 70 CE. Josephus first mentions them in connection with Jonathan Apphus, successor of Judas Maccabaeus.

The Pharisees held that all Jews had to observe the purity laws, which applied to the Temple service, outside the Temple. They also stood out for their adherence to the laws and traditions of the Jewish people in the face of assimilation. Josephus considered them the most expert and accurate expositors of Jewish law, and estimated that there were about 6,000 of them before the fall of the Second Temple.

Under the priestly Hasmonean dynasty the Pharisees did not support the wars of expansion or the forced conversion of the Idumeans. The rift widened when a Pharisee named Eleazar insulted the ruler John Hyrcanus at his table. Hyrcanus's son Alexander Jannaeus sided openly with the Sadducees, and the resulting riot and brief civil war ended in a bloody repression of the Pharisees. His widow, Salome Alexandra, was favourably inclined towards them, and under her reign their influence grew greatly, especially in the Sanhedrin, which they came to dominate.

After the Jewish–Roman wars the Zealots were crushed, the last dying at Masada in 73 CE, and the Sadducees, whose teachings were tied to the Temple, disappeared with its destruction. Of the major sects of the Second Temple period, only the Pharisees remained.

Josephus says the Pharisees held that people have free will but that God also foresees human destiny. The sources differ on their view of the afterlife: according to the New Testament they believed in the resurrection of the dead, while Josephus says they held the soul to be immortal. They applied Jewish law to everyday life, in a form of Judaism that did not depend on the Temple and in which leaders were determined by scholarly achievement rather than birth. The standard view is that they accepted an Oral Torah alongside the written Scripture, though Anthony J. Saldarini argued that there is no direct evidence for this.

Their view of law as a way for ordinary people to engage with the sacred in daily life let them answer the questions raised by the loss of the Temple, and their responses formed Rabbinic Judaism. The Pharisees appear in the New Testament in conflict with Jesus, but Nicodemus and Gamaliel were Pharisees, and Paul the Apostle declared himself one.
pharnabazus-ii: Pharnabazus II was a son of Pharnaces II of Phrygia, grandson of Pharnabazus I and great-grandson of Artabazus I. He and his male ancestors, the Pharnacid dynasty, had governed the satrapy of Hellespontine Phrygia from Dascylium since 478 BCE. He married Apama, daughter of the Persian king Artaxerxes II, and their son Artabazus also became a satrap of Phrygia. According to some accounts his granddaughter Barsine may have become Alexander the Great's concubine. Theodor Nöldeke's research traced his descent from Otanes, one of Darius's associates in the murder of Smerdis.

Pharnabazus was first recorded as satrap in 413 BCE, when Darius II ordered him to send in the tribute of the Greek cities of the Ionian coast, which Athenian interference had kept him from collecting. Like Tissaphernes of Caria he negotiated with Sparta and fought Athens, though rivalry between the two satraps hindered the war, and Pharnabazus was by far the more energetic and upright.

He may have been responsible for the assassination of the Athenian general Alcibiades in 404 BCE, probably at the instigation of the Spartans, and of Lysander in particular. In 399 BCE his cavalry is said to have killed about 500 of the Ten Thousand Greek mercenaries, and he arranged with the Spartan admiral Anaxibius for the rest to be shipped to Byzantium.

The Spartan king Agesilaos ravaged Hellespontine Phrygia in 396 and 395 BCE, and Pharnabazus met him in person; Agesilaos withdrew to the plain of Thebe. Persian payments to Sparta's Greek rivals helped start the Corinthian War, which recalled Agesilaos in 394 BCE. Pharnabazus commanded the Achaemenid fleet at Cnidus that year, where, with the Athenian admiral Conon, he annihilated the Spartan fleet.

In 393 BCE the two sailed to Melos, raided Pherae and the Messenian coast, and seized Cythera, leaving a garrison and an Athenian governor. At Corinth he gave Sparta's rivals funds, and he gave Conon 80 triremes and money to help rebuild the long walls of Athens. He then received the king's daughter in marriage and was recalled, replaced by Tiribazus.

Artaxerxes II reassigned him to command an expedition against rebellious Egypt, which gathered 200,000 Persian troops, 300 triremes, 200 galleys and 12,000 Greeks under the Athenian general Iphicrates. It landed near Mendes in 373 BCE but moved too slowly, and Nectanebo I strengthened his defences, flooding the land near Pelusium and blocking channels of the Nile. Mutual distrust between Pharnabazus and Iphicrates kept the invaders from reaching Memphis, and the Nile flood completed the failure. This ended Pharnabazus's career, and Datames replaced him. Pharnabazus is one of the main characters of Xenophon's Hellenica and appears in his Anabasis and in Thucydides.
pharnaces-i-of-pontus: Pharnaces I was the fifth king of Pontus. Of Persian and Greek ancestry, he was the son of King Mithridates III of Pontus and his wife Laodice, and he succeeded his father. He had two siblings, a brother, Mithridates IV of Pontus, and a sister, Laodice, who both succeeded him on the throne. He was born and raised in the Kingdom of Pontus. The date of his accession cannot be fixed with certainty.

He was on the throne before 183 BCE, the year in which he reduced the important city of Sinope, which the kings of Pontus had long wanted. The Rhodians sent an embassy to Rome to complain, without effect. Pharnaces also became involved in disputes with Eumenes II of Pergamon, which led to repeated embassies to Rome and partial hostilities. In the spring of 181 BCE, without waiting for his ambassadors to return, he attacked Eumenes II and King Ariarathes IV of Cappadocia and invaded Galatia with a large force.

Roman deputies appointed by the Senate arrived to inquire into the dispute. Negotiations at Pergamon led nowhere, since the Romans rejected the demands of Pharnaces as unreasonable, and the war resumed. It continued, apparently with interruptions, until the summer of 179 BCE, when Pharnaces could not cope with the combined forces of Eumenes II and Ariarathes IV. He bought peace by giving up all his conquests in Galatia and Paphlagonia except Sinope. He was still on the throne in 170 BCE and certainly dead by 154 BCE, when his brother appears as king. The historian Polybius accuses him of an arrogant and violent character.

Pharnaces married a Seleucid princess named Nysa, a daughter of Queen Laodice IV and King Antiochus IV Epiphanes, through the diplomacy of Demetrius I Soter. They had two children: Mithridates V of Pontus and a daughter, Nysa of Cappadocia, also known as Laodice. Honorific statues and inscriptions survive that were dedicated to Pharnaces and Nysa. He made a benefaction to the people of Athens, of unknown nature, and the Athenians on Delos honoured both with a gold crown and bronze statues, in an inscription dated to 160 or 159 BCE.
pharnaces-ii-of-pontus: Pharnaces II was the youngest child of Mithridates VI of Pontus and his first wife and sister, Queen Laodice. He was born and raised in Pontus and was raised as his father's successor. In the early 1st century BCE Mithridates allied with the Sarmatian tribes, and Pharnaces probably through this alliance married an unnamed Sarmatian noblewoman. She bore him a son Darius, a daughter Dynamis and a son Arsaces. After his death Mark Antony made his sons Pontic kings for a time, and his daughter and her family succeeded him as rulers of the Bosporan Kingdom.

Mithridates planned an invasion of Italy, a scale of expedition that put many soldiers off, and Castor of Phanagoria and many castles on the Black Sea's eastern shore rebelled. Pharnaces then led his own rebellion. In Appian's account he won over Roman deserters and other camps, Mithridates fled, and the troops proclaimed Pharnaces king; Mithridates then died. Pharnaces sent the body to Pompey with an offer of submission, and Pompey named him friend and ally of the Romans and gave him the Cimmerian Bosporus, except Phanagoria, which was left independent for being first to rebel.

In 47 BCE, with Caesar besieged in Alexandria, Pharnaces invaded Anatolia. He took Colchis, Lesser Armenia, parts of Cappadocia and cities of Bithynia and Pontus. Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus, whom Caesar had sent, was defeated near Nicopolis in Lesser Armenia, and Pharnaces overran Pontus. He stopped when he learned that Asander, whom he had left in charge of the Bosporus, had revolted. Caesar then reached him near Zela. Plutarch and Appian say Caesar announced the victory with the words veni, vidi, vici; the Roman line was briefly thrown into confusion by his scythed chariots before his army prevailed, and Pharnaces escaped.

Pharnaces fled to Sinope with 1,000 cavalry and surrendered it to Domitius, who let him leave but killed his horses. He sailed to the Cimmerian Bosporus, gathered Scythians and Sarmatians and took Theodosia and Panticapaeum. Asander defeated him, short of horses and with men unused to fighting on foot, and Pharnaces was killed. He was fifty years old and had been king of the Bosporus for fifteen years. He is the subject of Vivaldi's opera Farnace of 1727, from a libretto by Antonio Maria Lucchini, and appears in Mozart's Mitridate.
pharnavaz-i-of-iberia: Pharnavaz I was a king of Kartli, the ancient Georgian kingdom known as Iberia in classical antiquity. The Georgian Chronicles credit him with founding the kingship of Kartli and the Pharnavazid dynasty, while other chronicles, such as The Conversion of Kartli, make him the second Georgian monarch. Most scholars, going by medieval evidence, place his rule in the 3rd century BCE. He is not directly attested in non-Georgian sources, and his story is full of imagery from folk tradition. According to the c. 800 chronicle The Life of Kings, he traced his descent from Kartlos, the mythical ancestor of the Georgians. His name is based on the Persian word farnah, the divine radiance that ancient Iranians believed marked a legitimate ruler.

In the royal annals Pharnavaz lost his family at the age of three, when Azon, installed by Alexander the Great, usurped his inheritance. After a dream and the discovery of a hidden treasure in a cave while hunting, he raised an army with the help of Kuji of Colchis and defeated and killed Azon, becoming king at 27. He is said to have acknowledged the suzerainty of the Seleucids, and to have patterned his administration on the Persian kingdom. The annals credit him with dividing Iberia among regional governors called eristavis, under a commander-in-chief, the spaspet. Strabo gives the Iberian army as 70–80,000. Modern scholars treat the reform as most likely a back-projection of the medieval pattern onto the distant past.

He is also said to have raised the idol Armazi on a mountain ledge, built a fortress of the same name, fortified Mtskheta, and rebuilt the cities destroyed by Alexander. He allied with North Caucasian peoples, marrying a Durdzuk woman and marrying his sister to a Sarmatian chief. The annals say he created the Georgian script and made Georgian the official language. They give him a reign of 65 years and say that he was buried in front of Armazi and worshipped.

His son Sauromaces I succeeded him. According to the annals, Pharnavaz's grave is undisclosed, and one of the last kings said to have visited it was Mirian III. The Bagrationi dynasty claimed descent from him, and Georgian kings presented themselves as heirs of the kingdom he founded. Some modern scholars have identified him with the Pharasmanes whom Arrian describes visiting Alexander the Great, though others suggest the Greek copyists confused two names.
phidias: Phidias was the son of Charmides of Athens, and the ancients believed that his masters were Hegias and Ageladas. Little is known of his life apart from his works. No original work can be attributed to him with certainty, and what survives is numerous Roman copies of varying fidelity. His earliest works were dedications commemorating the Greek victory at Marathon. His first commission was a group of national heroes with Miltiades as the central figure, and at Delphi he made a great bronze group that included the gods Apollo and Athena, several Attic heroes and Miltiades the Younger.

On the Acropolis of Athens Phidias made the Athena Promachos, a colossal bronze statue of Athena that was visible far out at sea. According to Pausanias he also made the bronze Athena Lemnia for the Athenians living on Lemnos, which Pausanias called the best of all his works to see. In the Hippias Major Plato says that he seldom, if ever, worked in marble, and in antiquity he was known for bronze and for chryselephantine statues, made of gold and ivory.

Plutarch writes that he superintended the great works Pericles ordered on the Acropolis. Inscriptions show that the marble blocks for the pediments of the Parthenon reached Athens only in 433 to 434 BCE, so most of its sculptural decoration may have come from his workshop, with pupils such as Alcamenes and Agoracritus. The ancients thought two works outshone all the others: the Athena Parthenos in the Parthenon and the Statue of Zeus in the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, of about 432 BCE. The Zeus sat on a throne decorated with sculpture, with a body of ivory and a robe of gold, and small copies on coins of Elis give a notion of its pose.

Plutarch says that his friendship with Pericles led the enemies of Pericles to attack him through Phidias. Phidias was accused of keeping some of the gold meant for the Athena Parthenos, and is said to have proved his innocence by weighing the gold robe. He was then accused of impiously portraying himself and Pericles on the statue's shield, which was apparently true. Plutarch records that he was imprisoned and died in jail, while Philochorus says the Eleans put him to death after he finished the Zeus. The historical value of these accounts is debatable.

Excavations at Olympia between 1954 and 1958 uncovered his workshop where Pausanias said it stood, with tools, terracotta moulds and pottery, and a cup inscribed as belonging to Phidias, though its authenticity is disputed. The finds allowed archaeologists to reconstruct how the statue was made. Since about 1910 the Greek letter phi has been used as the symbol of the golden ratio, after Phidias.
philadelphia: Philadelphia lies on the Atlantic Seaboard Fall Line, which separates the Atlantic Plain from the Piedmont. The Delaware and Schuylkill rivers are its principal natural bodies of water. The city encompasses about 142.7 square miles, 6 per cent of it water, and its highest point, in Chestnut Hill, is about 446 feet above sea level. The city has been coterminous with its county since 1854.

Before Europeans arrived in the early 17th century, the Lenape, also known as the Delaware Indians, lived in the village of Shackamaxon, in present-day Philadelphia. Most Lenape were pushed out of the region during the 18th century as the Thirteen Colonies expanded, a loss made worse by intertribal conflicts, newly introduced diseases, mainly smallpox, and conflicts with Europeans. In the 1860s the federal government sent most of those remaining in the eastern United States to the Indian Territory, in present-day Oklahoma.

William Penn, an English Quaker and advocate of religious freedom, founded Philadelphia in 1682, and it became the capital of the colonial Province of Pennsylvania. It hosted the First Continental Congress in 1774 and the Second Continental Congress, which formed the Continental Army, elected George Washington as its commander and adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776. The British Army occupied the city for nine months, from September 1777 to June 1778. The Constitution of the United States was ratified at the Philadelphia Convention. The city served as the national capital on several occasions until 1800, when the new capital at Washington, D.C. was completed.

Philadelphia is the most populous city in Pennsylvania and the sixth most populous in the United States, with about 1.6 million people in the 2020 census. Independence National Historical Park, which holds Independence Hall and the Liberty Bell, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the city has 67 National Historic Landmarks. It claims many firsts in the United States, among them the first library (1731), hospital (1751), medical school (1765) and zoo (1874).
philetaerus: Philetaerus was born in Tieium, a small town on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia. His father Attalus was Greek and his mother Boa came from Paphlagonia. After the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE he became involved in the Wars of the Diadochi, first serving Antigonus in Phrygia.

He then shifted his allegiance to Lysimachus, who made him commander of Pergamon after Antigonus was killed at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE. Lysimachus kept a treasury of nine thousand talents of silver there. Philetaerus was a eunuch from infancy; Attalus I, the first Attalid king, explained that as a baby he was crushed in a crowd at a burial while his nurse was carrying him, though scholars differ on the reason.

Philetaerus served Lysimachus until 282 BCE, when, perhaps because of court intrigues involving Lysimachus's third wife Arsinoë, he deserted him and offered himself and the fortress of Pergamon, with its treasury, to Seleucus. Seleucus defeated and killed Lysimachus at the Battle of Corupedium in 281 BCE and was himself killed a few months later by Ptolemy Ceraunus, a brother of Arsinoë, at Lysimachia.

Though nominally under Seleucid control, Philetaerus, especially after the death of Seleucus, had considerable autonomy. With his wealth he increased his influence beyond Pergamon and was a benefactor of neighbouring cities and of temples, including those at Delphi and Delos. He gave troops, money and food to Cyzicus to defend it against the invading Gauls, which won prestige and goodwill for himself and his family.

In his rule of nearly forty years he built the temple of Demeter on the acropolis of Pergamon, the temple of Athena, the city's patron deity, and Pergamon's first palace, and he added considerably to its fortifications. He never married and had no children, and he adopted his nephew Eumenes I, the son of his brother Eumenes, who succeeded him on his death in 263 BCE. With the exception of Eumenes II, all later Attalid rulers put Philetaerus's bust on their coins in tribute to the founder of the dynasty.
philibert-tsiranana: According to his official biography Tsiranana was born on 18 October 1912 at Ambarikorano in northeastern Madagascar, to Catholic cattle ranchers of the Tsimihety people. After his father died in 1923, his brother suggested that he attend a primary school, and he became a teacher. In 1946 he joined the Group of Student Communists and became a founding member of the Party of the Disinherited of Madagascar, PADESM. He was in France during the Malagasy Uprising of 1947 and so escaped its suppression. There he noticed that only 17 of 198 Malagasy students were coastal people, and he founded associations to close the cultural gap between the coastal peoples and those of the highlands, which the Merina resented.

Tsiranana joined the French Socialist party in 1955 and was elected deputy for the western region to the French National Assembly in January 1956. On 28 December 1956 he founded the Social Democratic Party at Majunga, which benefited from the support of the colonial administration as it transferred executive power. He favoured strong autonomy rather than early independence, arguing that independence too early would bring economic dependence, and wished to remain close to France. A constitution modelled largely on that of France was adopted on 29 April 1959, with a president who was both head of state and head of government, and on 1 May Tsiranana was elected the first president of the Malagasy Republic, with 113 votes and one abstention.

To establish his image as father of independence he recalled the three deputies exiled to France after 1947, Joseph Ravoahangy, Joseph Raseta and Jacques Rabemananjara, in July 1960, and brought two of them into his government. He declared that his country belonged to the Western world, and French advisers remained close to his government; he told the French living on the island that they were Madagascar's nineteenth tribe. He also built links with West Germany and the United States. His own Malagasy Socialism, a pragmatic development policy, did not have a large economic effect.

From 1967 Tsiranana faced mounting criticism, and his health, troubled by cardiovascular disease, declined. Many Malagasy felt that political independence had not brought economic independence, since the French controlled the economy and most senior technical posts. In the presidential election of 30 January 1972 he ran without opposition and won 99.72 percent of the vote. The opposition then took to the streets, and after farmer and student protests he granted full powers to Ramanantsoa, which ended the First Republic. After Richard Ratsimandrava was assassinated in 1975, Tsiranana was among 296 people charged, and was released for lack of evidence. He died on 16 April 1978 and is remembered as the Father of Independence.
philip-duke-of-parma: Philip was born at the Royal Alcazar in Madrid as Felipe de Borbón y Farnesio, the fourth child of Philip V of Spain and his second wife, Elisabeth Farnese. As a child he showed more interest in art than in politics. Like other children of the Spanish royal family he was raised in the Queen's household until the age of seven, with the Marchioness of Montehermoso as his governess. In 1724, when his father abdicated in favour of his son Louis, the four-year-old infante was given the Marquis of Surco as governor of his household. He also held the title of 12th Count of Chinchón, which he later ceded to his brother Luis in 1754.

His mother came from the Farnese family, which had ruled the Duchy of Parma, Piacenza and Guastalla for many generations. His elder brother Charles ruled it from 1731 to 1736, until it was exchanged with Austria for the Two Sicilies after the War of the Polish Succession.

Twelve years later, in the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, Austria lost the duchy and Philip became Duke of Parma on 18 October 1748, founding the House of Bourbon-Parma, a cadet line of the House of Bourbon. Under the Second Treaty of Versailles of 1757 between Austria and France he was meant to become king of the Southern Netherlands, in a deal that would have let French troops occupy key positions there. The Third Treaty of Versailles repudiated the arrangement, and Philip stayed in Parma.

The duchy had been ruined by years of warfare, and in 1759 Philip named the Frenchman Guillaume du Tillot as his minister to restore the economy. Philip was an enlightened ruler who stimulated education and philosophy and attracted figures such as Étienne Bonnot de Condillac and Alexandre Deleyre.

On 25 October 1739 Philip had married his first cousin once removed, Princess Louise Élisabeth of France, at Alcalá de Henares. The marriage was unhappy, and she died of smallpox at the age of 32 in 1759. They had three children: Isabella, who married the Archduke Joseph of Austria; Ferdinand, who succeeded his father as duke; and Luisa Maria, who married Charles IV of Spain.

Philip himself died unexpectedly of smallpox on 18 July 1765 at Alessandria, after accompanying his daughter on her way to Genoa, where she sailed for Spain to marry. Through her he is an ancestor of the Bourbons of Spain, the Bourbons of the Two Sicilies and the House of Orléans.
philip-i-count-of-flanders: Philip of Alsace was born in 1143, the second son of Count Thierry of Flanders and Sibylla of Anjou. His elder brother Baldwin died in 1150, which left him as his father's successor. His name appears on documents with the title of count as early as 1155, and in 1156 he married Elisabeth, elder daughter of Count Ralph I of Vermandois. At Arras at Easter 1157 his father transferred power to him before leaving with Sibylla on crusade. Thierry returned in 1159 and co-ruled with Philip, who focused on economic and judicial matters, until Thierry's death in 1168.

In his father's absence Floris III of Holland tried to take Zeeland and Waasland and laid heavy taxes on Flemish merchants on the river route to the Rhine. Philip's fleet defeated him in 1158, and in 1166 Philip captured him on the Scheldt and released him in 1167 under the treaty of Bruges, which recognised Flemish suzerainty over Zeeland and Waasland. When Elisabeth's brother Ralph II abdicated in 1167, the couple inherited Vermandois, which pushed Flemish authority further south than before. Philip governed with the aid of Robert d'Aire and mediated between Louis VII of France and Henry II of England.

Philip took the cross in 1175 and reached Palestine in 1177, intending to go as a pilgrim. He refused to command the planned invasion of Egypt proposed by King Baldwin IV of Jerusalem, and he refused the regency of Jerusalem. He joined the siege of Harim and, when Saladin sent reinforcements, accepted a ransom to lift it.

William of Tyre blamed him for the failure of the planned campaign, but historians hold that William did not write in good faith. In 1180 Philip had his ward, Philip II of France, marry his niece Isabelle of Hainaut, and war with France followed. After Elisabeth died in 1183, Philip II seized Vermandois. A later peace treaty recognised the cession of Vermandois to the king, though Philip kept the title of its count for life.

Philip took the cross again in 1190. At the siege of Acre he was stricken by the epidemic in the crusader camp and died on 1 August 1191. His wife Theresa, a daughter of Afonso I of Portugal, brought his body back to Flanders, and he was buried at Clairvaux Abbey. His sister Margaret I and her husband Baldwin VIII succeeded him. Philip's reign has been seen as the end of one kind of feudal world, as for the first time a king of France ruled over a count of Flanders. The economic expansion of Flanders continued, as the number of communal charters shows. Philip was patron of Chrétien de Troyes, who was writing his Perceval, the Story of the Grail.
philip-i-duke-of-burgundy: Philip of Rouvres was the only son of Philip, heir to the Duchy of Burgundy, and Joan I, heiress of Auvergne and Boulogne. His father died before the dukedom passed, and his grandparents were Odo IV, Duke of Burgundy, and Joan III, Countess of Burgundy and Artois. He succeeded his grandmother in the County of Burgundy, also called Franche-Comté, and in Artois in 1347, when he was only one year old. He is counted as Philip II of Burgundy and Philip III of Artois, and as Philip I of the duchy.

In 1349, aged three, he succeeded his grandfather as Duke of Burgundy. In 1355 he married Margaret, daughter of Louis de Mâle, Count of Flanders. Because she was heiress of Flanders, the match promised him the counties of Flanders, Nevers, Rethel and Antwerp and the duchies of Brabant and Limburg, most of them in the Low Countries. His mother Joanna, who had become Queen of France by remarrying King John II, governed Burgundy as his guardian until her death in September 1360. Philip was declared of age on 20 October of that year and in 1360 also inherited the counties of Auvergne and Boulogne from her.

Philip died on 21 November 1361, aged fifteen, before he could consummate his marriage to Margaret. With his death King John II of France claimed the duchy for the kingdom, and made his youngest son Philip the Bold royal lieutenant-general in 1363 and Duke of Burgundy soon afterwards. Philip had held the duchy for twelve years, and the lands he held in his own right, the duchy and the counties of Burgundy, Artois, Auvergne and Boulogne, had come to him through his grandparents and his mother.
philip-i-landgrave-of-hesse: Philip was the son of Landgrave William II of Hesse and his second wife, Anna of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. His father died when he was five, and in 1514 his mother became regent after a series of struggles with the Estates of Hesse. To end the quarrels over authority Philip was declared of age in 1518 and took up power the following year. His education had been imperfect, but he developed rapidly as a statesman. He first met Martin Luther in 1521 at the Diet of Worms, and he embraced Protestantism in 1524 after meeting Philipp Melanchthon. He then helped to suppress the German Peasants' War by defeating Thomas Müntzer at the Battle of Frankenhausen.

Philip organised the church in Hesse on Protestant principles, although there was no strong popular movement for it there. Monasteries and religious foundations were dissolved and their property was applied to charity and education, and the University of Marburg was founded in the summer of 1527 as a school for Protestant theologians. He allied with John, Elector of Saxony, at Gotha on 27 February 1526, and his efforts led through the League of Gotha and the League of Torgau to the Schmalkaldic League, which was joined by the Protestant powers in 1531. He also invited Huldrych Zwingli to Germany, which prepared the Marburg Colloquy, and he was suspected of Zwinglian leanings.

At the Battle of Lauffen on 13 May 1534 Philip took Württemberg from Archduke Ferdinand I of Austria. In 1540 he married a second wife, Margarethe von der Saale, while still married to Christine of Saxony. Luther and Melanchthon had given secret advice, and when the marriage became known it caused a scandal across Germany, and some allies refused to serve under him. He then made terms with Emperor Charles V and resigned the league's leadership in 1543. An imperial ban was declared against him and John Frederick of Saxony on 20 July 1546. After the defeat at the Battle of Mühlberg in 1547 he surrendered and, despite the promised terms, was held captive until the Peace of Passau in 1552.

Philip re-entered Kassel on 12 September 1552 and worked to restore order in Hesse. He urged mutual toleration between Calvinists and Lutherans and hoped for a great Protestant federation. He sent financial aid to the Huguenots, and Hessian troops fought beside them in the French religious civil wars. He gave the Hessian Church lasting form through the agenda of 1566–67. He died in 1567 and was buried in Kassel.

He had ten children with Christine of Saxony and nine with Margarethe. His territories were divided among his four sons by his first wife: William IV received Hesse-Kassel, Louis IV Hesse-Marburg, Philip II Hesse-Rheinfels and George I Hesse-Darmstadt.
philip-ii-of-france: Philip was born at Gonesse on 21 August 1165, the only son of King Louis VII and his third wife, Adela of Champagne. Because he was a first son born late in his father's life, he was nicknamed Dieudonné, God-given. When Louis VII's health declined, the 14-year-old Philip was crowned and anointed at Reims on 1 November 1179 by Archbishop William of the White Hands. On 28 April 1180 he married Isabella of Hainault, daughter of Count Baldwin V of Hainaut, who brought the County of Artois as her dowry.

From 1190 Philip styled himself King of France (rex Francie), where his predecessors had been kings of the Franks. The chronicler Rigord gave him the epithet Augustus for enlarging the crown lands. The royal demesne grew with the County of Amiens in 1185, Clermont-en-Beauvaisis in 1218 and Alençon in 1219. After a quarrel with Count Philip I of Flanders over the Vermandois, the Treaty of Boves in July 1185 gave the king Amiénois and Artois. He also built a French navy and, late in his reign, could muster some 3,000 knights.

He joined the Third Crusade with Richard I of England, leaving Vézelay on 4 July 1190 and reaching Acre on 20 April 1191; ill with dysentery when the city surrendered on 12 July, he lost zeal, and relations with Richard were strained. Back in France he worked to recover the Vexin. In May 1200 the Treaty of Le Goulet with King John settled Normandy's boundaries, but John's management of Aquitaine led to revolt, which Philip encouraged. In 1214 Philip defeated a coalition of his rivals, including John and the Emperor Otto IV, at the Battle of Bouvines, ending the Angevin Empire.

Philip expelled the Jews from the royal demesne in 1182 and confiscated their goods; ninety-nine were burned alive at Brie-Comte-Robert. In 1198 he allowed them to return. His marriage to Ingeborg of Denmark in 1193 led to his repudiating her the same day and a long dispute with the papacy; he later married Agnes of Merania.

Philip did not take part in the Albigensian Crusade proclaimed by Pope Innocent III in 1208, though he let his nobles join it; its fruits in southern France fell to his son Louis VIII and grandson Louis IX. In Paris he had the main streets paved, built the market of Les Halles, continued Notre-Dame de Paris, built the first Louvre as a fortress, raised a great wall around the city and gave a charter to the University of Paris in 1200. He died on 14 July 1223.
philip-ii-of-macedon: Philip was the youngest son of King Amyntas III and Eurydice of Lynkestis, born in 383 or 382 BCE. After the assassination of his brother Alexander II he was sent as a hostage to Illyria, and was later held at Thebes, then the leading city of Greece, from about 368 to 365 BCE, where he received a military and diplomatic education from Epaminondas. He returned to Macedon in 364 BCE. When his brother Perdiccas III died in battle against the Illyrians in 359 BCE, Philip was appointed regent for the infant Amyntas IV but took the kingdom for himself. He faced Paeonians and Thracians who had invaded the east and an Athenian force landed with a pretender.

Philip drove back the Paeonians and Thracians, defeated 3,000 Athenian hoplites and strengthened his army. Its cavalry grew from 600 to 4,000 men by 334 BCE, soldiers could be promoted and rewarded, and he created the Macedonian phalanx. He defeated the Illyrians in the Erigon Valley, besieged Amphipolis in 357 BCE and kept it, with Pydna, after promising them to Athens. He founded Philippi at Crenides, whose mines gave him much of his gold. At the siege of Methone he lost his right eye. He took Olynthus in 348 BCE and razed it.

As a leader of the Thessalian League, Philip entered the Third Sacred War and won at the Battle of Crocus Field. He made peace with Athens in 346 BCE. His sieges of Perinthus and Byzantium failed, but at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE he defeated Athens and Thebes and was recognised as military leader of the League of Corinth, a Greek confederation against Persia. In 336 BCE he sent Parmenion and 10,000 men into Asia Minor to prepare an invasion to free the Greeks of the western coast.

Philip was assassinated in October 336 BCE at Aigai, while entering the theatre during celebrations of the marriage of his daughter Cleopatra to Alexander I of Epirus. One of his bodyguards, Pausanias of Orestis, stabbed him. The motives are disputed. Aristotle says only that Pausanias had been offended by Attalus. Later writers link the killing with Alexander and Olympias, but some modern historians find these accounts improbable. Alexander succeeded him.

Philip had seven wives. In 1977 Manolis Andronikos excavated the Great Tumulus at Aigai near Vergina, and Tomb II is now generally held to be Philip's, partly because a skull shows damage to the right eye. He founded cities including Philippi and Philippopolis, today Plovdiv. Some Greeks honoured him with cult, such as an altar to Zeus Philippeios at Eresos and the Philippeion at Olympia.
philip-ii-of-spain: Philip was born in Valladolid on 21 May 1527, the son of Emperor Charles V and Isabella of Portugal, and belonged to the House of Habsburg. He was raised in the Castilian court and tutored by humanists, among them Juan Martínez Siliceo, the future archbishop of Toledo. He had a good command of Latin, Spanish and Portuguese but never equalled his father as a polyglot. Although an archduke of Austria, he felt himself culturally Spanish and was seen as a foreigner in the Holy Roman Empire, which ultimately impeded his succession to the imperial throne.

Philip was invested with the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily in 1554 and married Queen Mary I of England at Winchester Cathedral on 25 July 1554, becoming jure uxoris king of England and Ireland until her death in 1558. He considered himself the chief defender of Catholic Europe against the Ottoman Empire and the Protestant Reformation. His realms were a personal union of separate kingdoms, each guarding its own rights, so his authority was often overruled by local assemblies. Charles V had left him a debt of about 36 million ducats, and Philip defaulted on his loans several times, the first in 1557.

In the Netherlands, discontent over taxation and the persecution of Protestants led to the Iconoclast Fury of 1566 and open warfare in 1568. The Duke of Alba had Lamoral, Count of Egmont and Philip de Montmorency, Count of Horn executed in Brussels in 1568, and civilians were massacred at Mechelen, Naarden, Zutphen and Haarlem.

The conflicts lasted for the rest of his life. In 1584 he signed the Treaty of Joinville, funding the French Catholic League. In 1588 he sent an armada to invade England and overthrow Elizabeth I; it was repulsed in a skirmish and wrecked by storms on its return, and further armadas in 1596 and 1597 also failed.

Philip died on 13 September 1598 at El Escorial, aged 71, after a prolonged illness, likely cancer. His bed was placed so that he could watch the liturgy at the church's main altar, and despite severe pain he kept reviewing state papers to the end.

The Spanish conquest of the Philippines, named in his honour, was completed in his reign, and he finished building El Escorial in 1584. Historical opinion of him was heavily shaped by enemy propaganda, which he refused to answer, and his negative foreign reputation developed into the Spanish Black Legend. The historian Helmut Koenigsberger wrote that no personality in modern history had been as enigmatic and controversial.
philip-iii-of-france: Philip was born in Poissy on 1 May 1245, the second son of King Louis IX and Margaret of Provence. He became heir to the throne when his older brother Louis died in 1260. In 1262 he was married to Isabella of Aragon, in line with the Treaty of Corbeil, and his father knighted him on 5 June 1267. Louis IX also wrote the Enseignements for him, which presented justice as the first duty of a king.

Philip accompanied his father on the Eighth Crusade to Tunis in 1270. An epidemic of dysentery struck the army after it took Carthage, killing Philip's brother John Tristan on 3 August and Louis IX on 25 August. Philip, aged 25 and himself ill, was proclaimed king in Tunis. His uncle Charles I of Naples negotiated a treaty with the Hafsid caliph of Tunis on 5 November 1270. Philip's wife Isabella died after a fall from her horse while pregnant. He was crowned at Reims on 15 August 1271.

Philip kept most of his father's domestic policies, including the ordinances against seigneurial warfare, which he reinforced in October 1274. On 21 August 1271 his uncle Alphonse, Count of Poitiers and Toulouse, died childless, and Philip united his lands with the royal domain. In 1272 he campaigned against Roger-Bernard III, Count of Foix, who had invaded the County of Toulouse; the count surrendered and was imprisoned for a year, then freed. The Treaty of Orléans of 1275 gave France influence in Navarre by arranging a marriage between one of his sons and the heiress Joan, and French governors were sent there. A revolt in 1276 was put down by Robert II, Count of Artois.

After the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 Pope Martin IV granted Aragon to Philip's son Charles, and Philip launched the Aragonese Crusade, at the urging of his wife Marie of Brabant and of Charles of Naples. He took Girona on 7 September 1285, but dysentery struck the camp. The retreating French were defeated at the Col de Panissars on 1 October, and Philip died at Perpignan on 5 October 1285. His son Philip IV succeeded him. His reign added Toulouse, Auvergne, Guînes and Alençon to the royal domain, though the failed war nearly bankrupted the monarchy.
philip-iii-of-navarre: Philip was born on 27 March 1306, the son of Louis of Évreux, a younger son of Philip III of France, and founder of the Capetian House of Évreux. In 1318 he married his cousin Joan, the daughter of Louis X of France, who had died in 1316 leaving a four-year-old daughter. Philip V took the crown and Navarre instead, and an agreement of 27 March 1318 betrothed Joan to Philip of Évreux and gave her a dowry. Philip inherited Évreux in Normandy in 1319, and the marriage was not consummated until 1324.

When Charles IV died on 1 February 1328 the direct male line of the House of Capet ended. Philip of Évreux and his cousin Philip of Valois were the strongest Capetian candidates, and the 35-year-old Philip of Valois was preferred over the 23-year-old Philip of Évreux because of his age. Philip VI took Philip of Évreux onto his council, and Philip and Joan ceded Champagne and Brie to him for the counties of Angoulême, Mortain and Longueville.

Charles IV's death ended a union of France and Navarre of 44 years. The Navarrese assembly at Puente la Reina elected regents on 13 March 1328 and recognised Joan as sovereign in May. Philip was at first ignored, but Pope John XXII confirmed him as king on 22 August, and both were crowned and raised on the shield in Pamplona Cathedral on 5 March 1329, the first Navarrese monarchs to be crowned. A charter of May 1329 stated that Joan was the true and natural heir but that the kingdom would obey her consort as king, and that both would renounce the crown when their heir reached twenty-one.

Philip proved an effective ruler, and his best-known achievement was the improvement of the kingdom's law code in 1330. The couple lived mostly in France but visited Navarre several times. They built an irrigation system at Tudela, repaired castles, and condemned the perpetrators of anti-Jewish riots and compensated the victims. In August 1328 Philip fought for Philip VI at the battle of Cassel, and in 1339 and 1340 he served in the opening campaign of the Hundred Years' War. A war with Castile that began in 1335 ended with the treaty of Las Cuevas on 28 February 1336.

Philip joined the crusade against Granada and arrived at the siege of Algeciras in July 1343 with 100 knights and 300 infantrymen and a large quantity of provisions. In early September he fell ill, possibly after being wounded by an arrow, withdrew from the siege and died at Jerez de la Frontera on 16 September 1343. His body was buried at Pamplona and his heart in Paris. Joan reigned alone until her death in 1349, when their son Charles II succeeded.
philip-iii-of-spain: Philip was born in Madrid on 14 April 1578, the son of King Philip II of Spain and his fourth wife, Anna of Austria, who was his niece and cousin. After the death of his half-brother Don Carlos, Prince of Asturias, Philip II made closer arrangements for his other sons, appointing Juan de Zúñiga as Philip's governor and García de Loaysa as his tutor. The education followed guidelines set by Father Juan de Mariana, stressing moderation and personal discipline. Philip married his cousin Margaret of Austria, sister of the future Emperor Ferdinand II, on 18 April 1599, a year after becoming king.

Philip withdrew from his subjects to an unprecedented degree and left government to his favourite, the Duke of Lerma, who had been made a royal counsellor within hours of the accession and managed most audiences. Spanish representatives overseas, called proconsuls, increasingly followed independent policies. From 1612, and certainly by 1617, the Lerma administration was crumbling, as his enrichment in office became a scandal and his own son, the Duke of Uceda, grew alarmed at his spending. Philip remained close to Lerma and supported him in becoming a cardinal in March 1618.

Spain suffered serious economic problems. From 1599 to 1600 and for several years afterwards, bubonic plague killed over 10% of the population. In 1609 Philip decreed the expulsion of the Moriscos, descendants of Muslims who had converted to Christianity, of whom there were almost 200,000 in the south alone. The decree was timed to coincide with a truce in the Eighty Years' War.

Philip inherited the Dutch revolt and the Anglo–Spanish War. After the failure of the Spanish invasion of Ireland at the Battle of Kinsale he accepted that further attacks on England were unlikely to succeed. After the financial crisis of 1607 Spain could no longer pursue the war in the Netherlands, and with the accession of James I of England the war ended through the Treaty of London. The resulting period of peace, called the Pax Hispanica, lasted until Spain entered the Thirty Years' War in the final years of the reign.

In 1619 Philip travelled to Portugal, where he was received with enthusiasm, although nobles complained that they received no favours. He died in Madrid on 31 March 1621 and was succeeded by his son Philip IV, who swiftly removed the last remnants of the Sandoval regime from court. Known in Spain as Philip the Pious, he has generally left a poor legacy with historians, who have described him as an undistinguished man, though he ruled the Spanish Empire at its height.
philip-iv-of-france: Philip was born in 1268 at the fortress of Fontainebleau, the son of the future Philip III and his first wife, Isabella of Aragon. His grandfather Louis IX died on crusade in 1270, and his mother died in January 1271 after falling from a horse. In May 1276 his elder brother Louis died, and the eight-year-old Philip became heir apparent. Rumour held that Louis had been poisoned at the instigation of his stepmother, Marie of Brabant, whose own first son was born that month. His schooling was entrusted to Guillaume d'Ercuis, his father's almoner. Through his marriage to Joan I of Navarre he was also King of Navarre and Count of Champagne.

Philip was crowned at Reims on 6 January 1286, aged seventeen. He relied on a professional bureaucracy of legalists, such as Guillaume de Nogaret and Enguerrand de Marigny, and left unpopular policies to them. His reign saw the emergence or consolidation of the King's Council, the Parlement and the Court of Auditors. His opponent Bernard Saisset, bishop of Pamiers, said of him that he was neither man nor beast but a statue.

A feud between English and French sailors in 1293 led Philip to summon Edward I, as Duke of Aquitaine, to his court. Edward agreed to give up Gascony temporarily, but war followed from 1294. In Flanders, Count Guy of Dampierre renounced his fealty and the Franco-Flemish War began in 1297; Flemish town militias defeated the French at the Battle of the Golden Spurs on 11 July 1302, but Philip prevailed at Mons-en-Pévèle in 1304, and by the treaty of Athis-sur-Orge in 1305 Flanders lost Lille, Douai and Orchies. The wars drove him to debase the coinage, which brought unrest and rioting in Paris in December 1306.

Philip expelled the Jews from France on 22 July 1306 and confiscated their property. Deeply in debt to the Knights Templar, he had hundreds of them arrested in France on Friday 13 October 1307; they were tortured into admitting heresy, and many were burned at the stake. In March 1314 he had the last Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, burned. His taxation of the clergy led to a violent quarrel with Pope Boniface VIII, whose residence at Anagni was attacked by French forces in September 1303; this eventually led to the Avignon Papacy of 1309 to 1376.

In 1314 his daughters-in-law Margaret and Blanche of Burgundy were accused of adultery in the Tour de Nesle affair. Philip had a stroke while hunting and died at Fontainebleau on 29 November 1314; he is buried at Saint-Denis. His three sons reigned in turn as Louis X, Philip V and Charles IV, and their deaths without surviving sons began a succession crisis that led to the Hundred Years' War.
philip-iv-of-spain: Philip was born in the Royal Palace of Valladolid on 8 April 1605, the eldest son of Philip III and Margaret of Austria. In 1615, aged ten, he was married to the thirteen-year-old Elisabeth of France. Olivares, later his key minister, had been introduced to the prince by his uncle Baltasar de Zúñiga, who led a coalition against the Sandoval family that had dominated Philip III's court. Philip's diffidence was counteracted by Olivares' drive, and when he came to the throne in 1621, aged sixteen, he ordered that all papers needing his signature go first to the count-duke, who remained chief minister for twenty years.

Philip reigned through most of the Thirty Years' War. Zúñiga and Olivares persuaded him to commit Spain to an aggressive policy in alliance with the Holy Roman Empire, and hostilities with the Dutch were renewed in 1621. Spain was a loose collection of kingdoms and provinces with different taxes and privileges, and Olivares set up juntas, small committees that bypassed the slow royal councils but excluded many grandees and caused resentment. Philip doubled and then tripled the naval budget.

Elisabeth conspired with nobles to remove Olivares from court in 1643. Their only surviving son, Balthasar Charles, died in 1646, aged sixteen, and Philip was deeply shocked. In 1649 he married his fourteen-year-old niece Maria Anna to strengthen the tie with Austria. In 1640 the Iberian Union collapsed and John IV took the Portuguese throne. By Philip's death the empire covered about 12.2 million square kilometres, though in other respects Spain was in decline, a process to which his failure to achieve domestic and military reform contributed.

Philip collected art with astonishing enthusiasm and owned over 4,000 paintings at his death. He summoned Diego Velázquez to Madrid in 1624 and kept him for the rest of his career; the two shared an interest in horses, dogs and art. He also favoured the dramatists Lope de Vega and Pedro Calderón de la Barca. He died on 17 September 1665, hoping that his four-year-old son Charles II would be more fortunate than himself.

He left the regency to his wife Mariana, advised by a junta that excluded his illegitimate son John Joseph, which produced a power struggle between them until John Joseph's death in 1679. Known as the Planet King, Philip has been held responsible for Spain's decline, which was mainly due to causes largely beyond the control of any one ruler.
philip-melanchthon: Philipp Schwartzerdt was born on 16 February 1497 at Bretten, where his father, Georg Schwarzerdt, was armorer to Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine. His mother was Barbara Reuter. In 1507 he was sent to the Latin school at Pforzheim, where he was introduced to the Latin and Greek poets and to Aristotle. His great-uncle Johann Reuchlin, a Renaissance humanist, suggested that he follow a humanist custom and change his surname, literally black earth, to its Greek equivalent, Melanchthon. In 1508, when he was eleven, his father and grandfather died within eleven days of each other.

On Reuchlin's recommendation Melanchthon accepted a call from Martin Luther to the University of Wittenberg and became professor of Greek there in 1518, aged 21. He attended the Leipzig disputation of 1519 and replied to attacks by Johann Eck on the authority of Scripture. He married Katharina Krapp, the mayor's daughter, on 25 November 1520. His Loci communes of 1521 discussed the leading thoughts of Paul's Letter to the Romans and set out a doctrine in which faith in God counted for more than good deeds. He also worked with Luther on the translation of the Bible.

The Augsburg Confession, presented at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530, was based on Luther's Marburg and Schwabach articles but was mainly Melanchthon's work. He represented Luther at the Diet, since Luther was barred from attending, and Luther did not hide his dissatisfaction with its irenic tone. From 1531 he took part in discussions of the Lord's Supper with Martin Bucer. In 1547 he rejected the Augsburg Interim but made controversial concessions in the negotiations over the Leipzig Interim, which he later regretted. After Luther's death many saw him as the theological leader of the German Reformation, though the Gnesio-Lutherans led by Matthias Flacius accused him of heresy and apostasy.

Melanchthon's manuals were quickly taken up in schools and kept their place for more than a century. Through his Latin and Greek grammars and his work in educational institutions he became the founder of the learned schools of Evangelical Germany. Between 1536 and 1539 he was involved in the refoundation of Wittenberg, the reorganisation of Tübingen and the foundation of the University of Leipzig.

A severe cold caught on a journey to Leipzig in March 1560, followed by fever, led to Melanchthon's death on 19 April 1560. He was buried beside Luther in the Schloßkirche in Wittenberg. He is remembered as the man who systematised Luther's ideas, defended them in public and made them the basis of a religious education.
philip-of-swabia: Philip was born in or near Pavia in the Kingdom of Italy, the tenth child and eighth son of Frederick Barbarossa and his second wife Beatrice I, Countess of Burgundy. He was the fifth and youngest of the sons who survived. The origins of the Hohenstaufen, a name historians have given the dynasty since the 15th century, are unclear. Its prestige rested on descent from the Salian dynasty through Agnes, a daughter of Emperor Henry IV and the grandmother of Barbarossa. Conrad III was elected King of Germany in 1138 against fierce resistance from the House of Welf, and Barbarossa succeeded him in 1152.

Philip enjoyed his brother Henry VI's confidence to a great degree and appears to have been named guardian of Henry's underage son Frederick. In September 1197 he set out to fetch the boy from Apulia for coronation at Aachen. At Montefiascone he heard of Henry's sudden death in Messina on 28 September and returned at once to Germany. On 21 January 1198 he issued a charter for the citizens of Speyer in the name of King Frederick, but events overtook him. Reservations about a child as king led to two elections in 1198, which chose Philip and Otto of Brunswick, and so to the German throne dispute.

Kingship in this empire was exercised without a capital, and Philip had to travel the kingdom to give his rule authority. Of 28 known court days, only twelve took place within the Hohenstaufen sphere of influence. Philip increasingly asserted his kingship against Otto in the lands north of the Alps.

On 21 June 1208 Philip attended the wedding of his niece Countess Beatrice II of Burgundy to Duke Otto of Merania at Bamberg. In the afternoon, after retiring to his private apartments, he was murdered by Count Otto VIII of Wittelsbach. No chronicler witnessed it, and the sources disagree on its course. Most saw a withdrawn marriage promise as the motive: Philip had betrothed his daughter Kunigunde to Otto in 1203, then in November 1207 engaged her to Wenceslaus, son of King Ottokar I of Bohemia.
