Plotinus described three fundamental principles: the One, the Intellect and the Soul. The One is totally transcendent, without division or multiplicity, beyond being and non-being, and he identified it with the Good and with Beauty. All things flow from it by emanation without diminishing it.

He held that true happiness does not depend on worldly fortune. He died in seclusion on an estate in Campania left to him by his friend Zethos, and Eustochius reported his last words: Try to raise the divine in yourselves to the divine in the all. His thought influenced pagan, Jewish, Christian and Islamic thinkers, among them Augustine, the Fatimid teacher Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani and the Renaissance philosopher Marsilio Ficino.
plough: A plough, or plow in the US, is a farm tool for loosening or turning soil before sowing or planting. It may have a wooden, iron or steel frame with a blade attached to cut and loosen the soil, and the trenches it cuts are called furrows. Its main purpose is to turn over the uppermost soil, bringing fresh nutrients to the surface while burying weeds and crop remains. The earliest ploughs had no wheels, and the Romans called such a plough an aratrum. A Sumerian disputation poem of the 3rd millennium BCE personifies the plough in a debate with the hoe.

When agriculture began, soil was turned with digging sticks and hoes. The domestication of oxen in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley Civilisation, perhaps as early as the 6th millennium BCE, gave the draught power to develop the true ard, or scratch plough. A ploughed field of about 2800 BCE has been found at Kalibangan in India.

The heavy iron mould-board plough was invented in China under the Han Empire in the 1st and 2nd centuries and spread from there to the Netherlands. The first mould-board ploughs turned the soil in one direction only, so fields were worked in long strips, and their traditional size, a furlong by a chain, an area of one acre, is the origin of the acre.

The basic mould-board plough was unsuitable for the heavier soils of northern Europe. Wheels allowed heavier ploughs with a larger metal-faced mould board, and these led to greater food production, coinciding with a marked increase in the world's population in the second millennium CE. They needed up to eight oxen, so fields became long and narrow. Four to eight oxen were more than a typical peasant household could muster, so ploughing became a communal effort and contributed to the rise of the manorial system in northern Europe.

By 1837 John Deere, an Illinois blacksmith, was making polished cast steel ploughs for sticky soils. Riding ploughs with multiple mould boards soon followed, and steam engines and then tractors replaced animals as power.
plovdiv: Evidence of habitation in the area goes back to the 6th millennium BCE, when the first Neolithic settlements appeared, and the cultural layers in the city are twelve metres thick. A Thracian settlement named Pulpudeva was later conquered and ruled by Persians, Macedonians, Celts, Romans, Byzantines, Goths, Huns, Bulgarians and Ottoman Turks. Philip II of Macedon settled Thracians and 2,000 Macedonians there in 342 BCE and founded it as Philippopolis. The Roman Republic took it in 168 BCE, and it became the capital of the province of Thracia, at the centre of the road network of inland Thrace. Marcus Aurelius built a new wall around the city.

The Goths under Cniva sacked Philippopolis in 250, and the Huns did so in 441 or 442; the walls were rebuilt each time, and Justinian renewed them again. The city fell to the Bulgars of the First Bulgarian Empire in 863, in the reign of Boris I. Basil II used it as a strategic fortress in the wars against Bulgaria, and the Pechenegs occupied it briefly around 1090. Geoffrey of Villehardouin ranked it the third largest city of the Byzantine Empire after Constantinople and Thessalonica. Kaloyan of Bulgaria destroyed it in 1206, and in 1219 it became the capital of the Crusader Duchy of Philippopolis.

The Ottoman Turks under Lala Shahin Pasha took the city in 1364, though other accounts place its fall after the Battle of Maritsa in 1371. Over about five hundred years it was a sanjak centre at various times, one of the major economic centres of the Balkans beside Constantinople, Edirne, Thessaloniki and Sofia, and its richer citizens built the houses that still stand in the architectural reserve of Old Plovdiv.

The Treaty of San Stefano of 3 March 1878 chose Plovdiv as capital of a restored Bulgaria, but the Congress of Berlin separated the autonomous region of Eastern Rumelia from Bulgaria, and Plovdiv became its capital under a constitution made by the Ottoman Empire. In 1885 Eastern Rumelia joined Bulgaria. A railway linked the city with Constantinople in 1874 and with Sofia in 1888, and in 1892 it hosted the First Bulgarian Fair.

Plovdiv is the second largest city in Bulgaria, on the Maritsa river 144 km southeast of Sofia, spread over seven syenite hills that give it the name City of the Seven Hills. It had a population of 329,489 in 2024. It was the European Capital of Culture in 2019, and the city has more than 200 archaeological sites.
plutarch: Plutarch was born to a prominent family in the small town of Chaeronea, in the Greek region of Boeotia, about 30 kilometres east of Delphi. His family was long established there. His father was named Autobulus and his grandfather Lamprias, and his brothers Timon and Lamprias appear often in his essays and dialogues. He studied mathematics and philosophy in Athens under Ammonius from 66 to 67 CE. At some point he received Roman citizenship, sponsored by Lucius Mestrius Florus, an associate of the emperor Vespasian, and took the name Lucius Mestrius Plutarchus.

Plutarch lived most of his life at Chaeronea, where he served as a magistrate and held the office of archon,. He visited Rome about 70 CE with Florus, who served as a source for his Life of Otho, and he was on familiar terms with Roman nobles including Quintus Sosius Senecio. About 95 CE he became one of the two priests of the temple of Apollo at Delphi, a site that had declined considerably since the classical period. He was also epimeletes of the Amphictyonic League for at least five terms, from 107 to 127, organising the Pythian Games. Plutarch and his wife Timoxena had at least four sons and one daughter. The year of his death is not known.

His best-known work, the Parallel Lives, arranges biographies of illustrious Greeks and Romans in pairs to illuminate their shared virtues and vices. The surviving Lives contain 23 pairs and four single lives, though several others are lost and many survivors are truncated. Plutarch states in his Life of Alexander that he is writing lives and not histories, because a small thing such as a phrase or a jest often reveals character better than battles. His Life of Pyrrhus is the main account of Roman history from 293 to 264 BCE, for which the texts of Dionysius and Livy are lost.

The Moralia is a collection of seventy-eight essays and speeches. It includes a dialogue on the face seen in the orb of the Moon, which served as a source for Galileo, On the Worship of Isis and Osiris, a crucial source on ancient Egyptian religion, and philosophical treatises such as On the Decline of the Oracles. Some works printed with it, including the Lives of the Ten Orators, were falsely attributed to him and are credited to an unknown author called Pseudo-Plutarch.
plutarco-elias-calles: Calles was born Francisco Plutarco Elías Campuzano on 25 September 1877 in Sonora, one of two natural children of a bureaucrat father. He took the surname Calles from the uncle who raised him after his mother's death. The uncle was an atheist and instilled in him a commitment to secular education and disdain for the Roman Catholic Church.

In the Mexican Revolution he supported Francisco I. Madero and then joined the Constitutionalists of Venustiano Carranza, reaching the rank of general by 1915. That year his forces repelled the rival faction under Pancho Villa at the Battle of Agua Prieta, and he became governor of Sonora. In 1920 he joined Adolfo de la Huerta and Álvaro Obregón in the Plan of Agua Prieta, which overthrew Carranza, and served under Obregón as Secretary of the Interior.

Calles took office in 1924 in the first peaceful transfer of presidential power since 1884, backed by the labour confederation CROM and the Laborist Party. His government extended pensions to civil servants, created a cabinet-level ministry of public health, added two thousand rural schools to the thousand his predecessor had founded, and began a national road network, including the Mexican section of the Pan-American Highway, paid for by a gasoline tax. Its finance minister, Alberto J. Pani, advised founding the Banco de México. He also tried to professionalise the army under Joaquín Amaro.

He rejected the Bucareli Agreements of 1923 and began drafting an oil law that would strictly apply Article 27 of the constitution, which made everything under the soil the property of the state, in conflict with foreign oil companies. He also enforced the constitution's secular laws, which banned foreign priests, nationalised church property and let local governments limit the number of priests. Opposition to these anticlerical measures sparked the Cristero War.

Obregón won the 1928 election but was murdered before taking office by José de León Toral, a Catholic militant. Calles was ineligible to return to the presidency, and to avoid a vacuum he created the National Revolutionary Party in 1929, predecessor of the Institutional Revolutionary Party. From 1929 to 1934 he was Mexico's de facto leader, the period called the Maximato. After he backed Lázaro Cárdenas for president, the two quarrelled over labour unions and strikes, and Cárdenas exiled him. President Manuel Ávila Camacho allowed him to return in 1941. He died in Mexico City on 19 October 1945.

Supporters praise his reforms in health, infrastructure and education and his efforts to prevent instability after Obregón's murder, while detractors criticise the escalation of the Cristero War and his crackdowns on unions. His main legacy, in one account, was the pacification of Mexico through the creation of the party.
plymouth-montserrat: Plymouth lies on the lower south-western slope of the Soufrière Hills volcano, on the island of Montserrat in the Leeward Island chain of the Lesser Antilles. The town was laid out in the Georgian era on old lava deposits, close to a volcano that had been inactive for centuries. For centuries it was the only port of entry to the island, and it held almost all of Montserrat's shops and services as well as its seat of government.

After the first European colony on Montserrat was founded in 1632, St. Anthony's Church was established in Plymouth in 1636. It had to be rebuilt several times after earthquakes and hurricanes. On 17 September 1989 Hurricane Hugo destroyed a 55-metre stone jetty in the harbour and left many buildings, including the island's only hospital, unusable.

The volcano began erupting on 18 July 1995, and ash fell across the south of the island. Residents of Plymouth were evacuated in August 1995 and again on 1 December 1995, and for the third and final time on 3 April 1996. The island was divided into risk zones, with entry to the town sometimes banned. On 25 June 1997 an eruption produced pyroclastic surges that killed 19 people. Between 4 and 8 August 1997 further large eruptions destroyed about 80 per cent of the town and buried it under about 1.4 metres of ash, burning many buildings. The Royal Navy helped take the population to safety.

The southern half of the island was declared an exclusion zone. Plymouth, which had about 4,000 inhabitants, remains the de jure capital, while the government works from Brades in the north. The airport was buried in ash and a new one opened in 2005 near Brades. Between 1995 and 2000 two thirds of the island's population fled, many to the United Kingdom, leaving fewer than 1,200 residents in 1997. The volcanic deposits are hard, similar in density to concrete, so clearing the town was judged too costly.
plzen: Plzeň lies about 78 kilometres west of Prague, at the confluence of four rivers, the Mže, Úhlava, Úslava and Radbuza, which together form the Berounka. The first written mention of Plzeň Castle is from 976. King Wenceslaus II founded the city of New Plzeň nearby in 1295, and it quickly became an important place on the trade routes from Bohemia to Nuremberg and Regensburg. In the fourteenth century it had about 3,000 inhabitants, making it the third largest city in Bohemia after Prague and Kutná Hora.

The first written mention of beer brewing is from 1307. During the Hussite Wars Plzeň was the centre of Catholic resistance; Prokop the Great besieged it three times without success. In 1476 the city printed Statuta by Arnošt of Pardubice, the oldest book printed in Bohemia. In the Thirty Years' War Mansfeld took it in 1618, and Imperial troops did not recapture it until 1621.

From the second half of the nineteenth century the city industrialised rapidly. Emil Škoda founded the Škoda Works in 1869, which became the most important engineering company in the country and a crucial supplier of arms to the Austro-Hungarian Army. The Bavarian brewer Josef Groll produced the first batch of modern Pilsner beer on 5 October 1842, using soft local water, Saaz hops and Bavarian-style lagering. In April 1945 Allied bombing raids caused heavy damage, and on 6 May 1945 the 16th Armored Division of General George Patton's Third Army liberated the city.

Plzeň is the capital of the Plzeň Region, and its historic centre has been an urban monument reservation since 1989. The Cathedral of St Bartholomew, built in the Gothic style in the late thirteenth century, has the highest tower in the Czech Republic at 102.6 metres. Beneath the centre runs a labyrinth of tunnels and cellars with a length of 20 kilometres, partly open to visitors. The city was a European Capital of Culture in 2015, and the Pilsner Urquell Brewery is the largest brewery in the Czech Republic.
pocahontas: Pocahontas was born Amonute and was also known as Matoaka; Pocahontas was a childhood nickname that the colonist William Strachey translated as little wanton. Her birth year is unknown, with historians estimating about 1596. Her father was Powhatan, the Mamanatowick of the Powhatan Confederacy, an alliance of about thirty polities in the Tidewater region of Virginia. Her mother's name and origin are unknown. Although popular culture often calls her a princess, she was not in line to succeed her father, since Powhatan's brothers, sisters and his sisters' children stood in line to succeed him.

John Smith arrived in Virginia with 100 other settlers in April 1607. Pocahontas befriended the colonists and played games with the boys at the settlement, and early accounts say she brought food that saved many from starving. Smith's well-known story of her saving him from execution appears only in his 1616 letter to Queen Anne and his 1624 Generall Historie, and scholars dispute it: Karen Ordahl Kupperman sees embroidery, while Frederic W. Gleach suggests Smith misunderstood a ritual of adoption.

In March 1613, during the First Anglo-Powhatan War, Captain Samuel Argall learned that she was visiting the Patawomeck village of Passapatanzy. With the help of the weroance Iopassus he lured her onto his ship, the Treasurer, and held her for ransom. At Henricus the minister Alexander Whitaker taught her Christianity and she took the name Rebecca. She married the tobacco planter John Rolfe on 5 April 1614, and their son Thomas was born in January 1615. Their marriage began eight years of peace between the colonists and the Powhatan, known as the Peace of Pocahontas.

The London Company brought the Rolfes to England, where they arrived at Plymouth on 12 June 1616, to promote investment in Virginia. She was presented to English society as a princess, attended Ben Jonson's masque The Vision of Delight at Whitehall on 5 January 1617, and met Smith, who had been thought dead in Virginia. In March 1617 the Rolfes boarded a ship to return, but she fell gravely ill at Gravesend and died of unknown causes at about 21. She was buried on 21 March 1617 at St George's Church, whose later destruction by fire in 1727 left the grave's exact location unknown.

Many of the stories told of her have been romanticised, and contemporary sources support her friendship with Smith but not a romance, which first appears in 1803. Her descendants run through Thomas Rolfe and his daughter Jane. In 1907 she was the first Native American honoured on a United States stamp.
podgorica: Podgorica lies in central Montenegro, at the confluence of the Ribnica and Morača rivers, where the southern foothills of the Dinaric Alps meet the northernmost part of the Zeta Plain. The name means under the hill. The city is only 15 kilometres north of Lake Skadar and stands at the crossroads of several historically important routes, in fertile lowlands with a favourable climate.

The oldest physical remains in the area are from the late Stone Age. In the Iron Age the area between the Zeta and Bjelopavlići valleys was populated by two Illyrian tribes, the Labeates and the Docleatae, and the nearby town of Doclea had 8,000 to 10,000 inhabitants. The area later passed through many hands, among them the Roman Empire, the Byzantine Empire, the Serbian Empire and the Republic of Venice.

The Ottoman Empire captured Podgorica in 1474, and in 1479 built a large fortress there. The existing settlement, with its highly developed merchant connections, became the main Ottoman defensive and attacking bastion in the region. After the Congress of Berlin in 1878 the town was annexed to the Principality of Montenegro, ending four centuries of Ottoman rule. Roads were built to all neighbouring towns in 1902, and tobacco became its first significant commercial product.

In World War II Podgorica was bombed over 80 times, first by the Luftwaffe on 6 April 1941; an attack by the USAAF on 5 May 1944 killed about 400 civilians. It was liberated on 19 December 1944, and 1,691 people had been killed there in the course of the war. Josip Broz Tito promised on 12 July 1946 that the destroyed city would be rebuilt. It was renamed Titograd in 1946 and designated capital of the Socialist Republic of Montenegro, and rapid growth turned a small town into the country's primate city. Its original name was restored after a referendum on 2 April 1992.

Podgorica is the capital and largest city of Montenegro, capital of the independent state since 2006. It is a hub of the country's rail and road network and the centre of its education, science and healthcare. Cetinje, capital for much of Montenegrin history, preserves much of the national cultural heritage. Monuments in and around Podgorica include the Clock tower, the ruins of the Ribnica fortress and remnants of the ancient city of Doclea.
podhale: Podhale, in the Podhale dialect Podhole, meaning below the mountain pastures, is sometimes called the Polish Highlands and is Poland's southernmost region. It lies in the foothills of the Tatra range of the Carpathian Mountains and forms part of historic Lesser Poland. The Gorce Mountains mark its northern border, and its landscape includes extensive peat bogs and alluvial fans.

The southern part, from Brzegi and Bukowina to Zakopane, Kościelisko and Witów, is sometimes called Skalne Podhale, and the remainder Niżne Podhale. Its largest settlements include Nowy Targ, the historical capital of the region, Czarny Dunajec, Ludźmierz, Zakopane, Biały Dunajec, Szaflary and Poronin. The exact borders are disputed and unclear, because cultural expansion and blending in border areas with other Goral groups has shifted them.

Podhale is the best known of the Goral lands, and the region with which the Gorals are most commonly associated. Its folklore is distinct from other folk cultures in Poland. It was brought there mainly by settlers from Lesser Poland to the north and partly by Vlach settlers, who migrated into the region between the 14th and 17th centuries. Both the Podhale dialect and standard Polish are spoken, and the dialect is unusually alive compared with other Polish dialects, with a strong speaker base and a literary tradition in the region.

The region is known for its views, its nearness to the Tatra, its thermal baths and its romanticised culture, all of which make it a popular tourist destination. Among its attractions are the mountain resort of Zakopane and the lake Morskie Oko, the Eye of the Sea, which local legend holds is connected to the Adriatic by underground passages. Ludźmierz has the area's oldest shrine, Our Lady of Ludźmierz, called the Hostess of Podhale. Podhale is also known for oscypek, a cheese made from a mix of cow's and sheep's milk, for its music and for its ski slopes.
podlachia: The region lies along the middle stretch of the Bug River, between Mazovia in the west, Polesia and Volhynia in the east, the Narew River in the north and the Chełm Land in the south. Its largest city is Białystok and its historical capital is Drohiczyn. The name is probably from an East Slavic word for a Pole, meaning near Poland, from the period when the territory lay on the Mazovian border of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

Masovians settled the west before the 11th century, and Yotvingians held the north in the 12th until Bolesław V the Chaste and Leszek II the Black drove them out in the 13th and Poles from Masovia repopulated the land. Poland and Lithuania contested the region from then on, and in 1253 Pope Innocent IV recognized Polish sovereignty. It returned to the Grand Duchy in 1446. In 1513 King Sigismund I the Old formed the Podlaskie Voivodeship, with its capital at Drohiczyn, divided into the lands of Drohiczyn, Mielnik and Bielsk.

Knyszyn was the favourite residence of King Sigismund II Augustus, who died there in 1572, and Tykocin was the chief royal residence in the 17th and early 18th centuries. In the 18th and 19th centuries Białystok became the main centre, thanks to the Branicki family and its textile industry.

The Third Partition of 1795 divided Podlasie between Prussia and the Habsburg monarchy, with the Bug as the border. After the Treaties of Tilsit in 1807 part of it joined the Duchy of Warsaw and part, including Białystok, came under Russia, and in 1815 the Congress of Vienna placed all of it under Russian control. Two of the largest battles of the January Uprising, at Węgrów and Siemiatycze, were fought there in 1863. It became part of Poland after the Treaty of Riga of 1921, was split between Germany and the Soviet Union in 1939, and returned to Polish control in 1945.

The modern Podlaskie Voivodeship, established in 1999, covers the northern part of the historical region, including Białystok and Drohiczyn; Podlasie makes up 36% of it. The region is mostly inhabited by Poles, with many Belarusians in the east, and has long been considered Poland's most culturally diverse region. It is also a cultural centre of Poland's small Tatar minority, and it has its own folk costumes, traditional architecture and cuisine, of which potato babka is the best known dish.
podolia: Podolia lies in west-central and south-western Ukraine and north-eastern Moldova, in the northern part of Transnistria. It covers about 40,000 square kilometres of the East European Plain and is bordered on the south by the Dniester and crossed by the Southern Bug. Its elongated plateau, the Podolian Upland, rises to 144 m. Chernozem, black earth, predominates, making it very fertile farmland. The name derives from Proto-Slavic words meaning by or along and valley or lowland. The traditional capital is Kamianets-Podilskyi, and other chief settlements include Vinnytsia, Khmelnytskyi, Mohyliv-Podilskyi and Bar.

The region has had human inhabitants since the beginning of the Neolithic. Herodotus mentions it as the seat of the Graeco-Scythian Alazones, and the Romans left Trajan's Wall. In the 13th century the Mongols plundered the lowlands, then called Ponizie. Algirdas, Grand Duke of Lithuania, freed them after his victory over the Golden Horde at the Battle of Blue Waters in 1362 and annexed them to Lithuania as Podolia. In 1366 western Podolia with Kamieniec Podolski passed under Polish sovereignty, and after the death of Vytautas in 1430 it was incorporated into the Podolian Voivodeship of the Kingdom of Poland. The Union of Lublin of 1569 reunited western and eastern Podolia within the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.

Podolia was the target of frequent Tatar slave raids. From 1672 it was part of the Ottoman Empire as Podolia Eyalet, a province centred on Kamaniçe and divided into four sanjaks, and it returned to Poland in 1699 with the Treaty of Karlowitz. The Partitions of Poland of 1772 and 1793 gave the western and eastern parts to the Austrian and Russian empires. From 1793 to 1917 part of the region formed the Podolia Governorate of Russia, whose population in 1906 was estimated at 3,543,700, chiefly Ukrainians, with Polish and Jewish minorities.

After the First World War western Podolia came under Polish control, while the Soviet Union kept eastern Podolia. In 1939 the western area became part of Soviet Ukraine. From July 1941 German Einsatzgruppen carried out mass shootings of the Jewish inhabitants. In 1945, when Poland's eastern border was realigned along the Curzon line, the whole of Podolia remained in the Ukrainian and Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republics.

Podolia is known for its folk icon painting, whose long home iconostases on canvas of the late 19th and early 20th centuries are dominated by red, green and yellow; collections are held by the Vinnytsya Art Museum and the Museum of Ukrainian Home Icons in Radomysl Castle. The region is also the birthplace of the Baal Shem Tov, the founder of Hasidic Judaism.
poel: Poel forms the natural northern and eastern boundary of the Bay of Wismar on the German coast, and its northern shore lies on the south side of the Bay of Mecklenburg. It is close to Lübeck, Wismar and Schwerin and belongs to the Hamburg Metropolitan Region. The island is a municipality in the district of Nordwestmecklenburg, made up of the main places Kirchdorf and Oertzenhof and a number of smaller villages. It covers 36.02 square kilometres. The name derives from pole, the Common Slavic word for flat land or field. The Eleventh Edition of the Encyclopædia Britannica (1910 to 1911) cites Wismar Bay as the finest harbour on the Baltic.

The first inhabitants in historic times were Slavs of the Obotrite tribe. In the early 13th century the Slavic ruler Heinrich Borwin I brought German settlers from Dithmarschen and Holstein, who began building the island's church around 1210. Its Romanesque tower is 47 metres high and visible from almost every point on the island, and the nave was enlarged in the Gothic style around 1300. The church has been Lutheran since about 1535.

In 1614 Duke Adolf Friedrich I of Mecklenburg began a fortress near the church, completed in 1618. During the Thirty Years' War the duke had to yield it to imperial troops in 1628, and Swedish troops took it in 1635. After the Treaty of Westphalia in 1648 two-thirds of Poel, with Wismar and Neukloster, were granted to the King of Sweden, while the western third stayed with the Holy Spirit Hospital of Lübeck. The Swedes invested in making Wismar a military centre and neglected the castle, which was in ruins by 1740. In 1803 the Swedish portion was leased for 99 years to the Duke of Mecklenburg. Since 1927 a causeway has connected the island to the mainland.

Most of the island is farmland, and it is also a popular recreational area with fine beaches and sheltered harbours. Timmendorf harbour has a pilot's station and facilities for yachts and fishermen, and Kirchdorf has a yachting harbour and a boatyard. The earthen embankments and most of the moats of the 17th-century fortress can still be seen. The island has 2,873 inhabitants.
poggio-bracciolini: Poggio was born at Terranuova, near Arezzo in Tuscany, a village renamed Terranuova Bracciolini in 1862 in his honour. His father took him to Florence, where he studied Latin under Giovanni Malpaghino of Ravenna, a friend and protégé of Petrarch. His skill as a copyist brought him to the notice of Coluccio Salutati and Niccolò de' Niccoli, who befriended him. He studied notarial law and at twenty-one entered the Florentine notaries' guild. In 1403, on the recommendation of Salutati and Leonardo Bruni, he became secretary to Cardinal Landolfo Maramaldo, and soon joined the Chancery of Apostolic Briefs in the Roman Curia.

Over a career of about fifty years Poggio served seven popes, from Boniface IX to Nicholas V, rising from scriptor to abbreviator, scriptor apostolicus and, under Martin V, apostolic secretary. He remained a layman and considered himself a Florentine working for the papacy. After Martin V's election he spent five years in England, from 1418 until 1423, at the invitation of Cardinal Henry Beaufort, the least productive years of his career. In December 1435 he left his long-term mistress, with whom he had fourteen children, and married the teenage Selvaggia dei Buondelmonti; they had five sons and a daughter.

During the Council of Constance, from 1414, he explored the libraries of Swiss and Swabian abbeys, and his great finds date to 1415-1417. At St Gall he found Cicero's Pro Sexto Roscio, Quintilian, Statius' Silvae and Vitruvius's De architectura; at Cluny and Langres, more orations of Cicero. In January 1417 he found, in a German monastery probably Fulda, the only manuscript of Lucretius's De rerum natura then known, which he sent to Niccoli, whose copy became the model for more than fifty others. He bribed a monk to take a Livy and an Ammianus from the library of Hersfeld Abbey.

Poggio wrote only in Latin, in dialogues such as De avaritia, On Nobility, which defends nobility based on virtue rather than birth, and On the Vicissitudes of Fortune. His Liber Facetiarum, humorous and indecent tales that satirise the clergy, remained popular for centuries. His Historia Florentina continued Bruni's history to 1455. In 1452 he feuded with Lorenzo Valla over the Elegantiae, but they later reconciled. Poggio was a prolific scribe in Humanist minuscule, though later research showed that he did not invent it.

In April 1453 Cosimo de' Medici chose him as Chancellor of the Florentine Republic, in succession to Carlo Marsuppini. He died on 30 October 1459, before finishing his history, and was buried in Santa Croce, where a statue by Donatello stood.
pohnpei: Pohnpei, formerly Ponape or Ascension, is an island of the Senyavin Islands, part of the larger Caroline Islands group. Its name comes from the Pohnpeian language and means upon a stone altar. It belongs to Pohnpei State, one of the four states of the Federated States of Micronesia. It covers 334 square kilometres, rises to 782 metres and is the largest island of the federation. Palikir, the national capital, and Kolonia, the state capital, are on it. It is one of the wettest places on Earth, and it is home to the ka tree, found only on Pohnpei and Kosrae.

The earliest settlers were probably people of the Lapita culture from the south-eastern Solomon Islands or Vanuatu. Pohnpeian tradition divides the pre-colonial past into the Period of Building, before about 1100, the Period of the Lord of Deleur, about 1100 to about 1628, and the Period of the Nahnmwarki, about 1628 to about 1885. Legend says the Saudeleur rulers, the first to bring government to the island, were of foreign origin and that their centralised absolute rule grew more oppressive over generations. The dynasty ended with the invasion of Isokelekel, another semi-mythical foreigner, who replaced it with the more decentralised nahnmwarki system. Society was divided into five tribes, each headed by two principal chiefs.

The Spanish navigator Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón was the first European visitor, on 14 September 1529. The Russian explorer Fyodor Litke gave the first lengthy description in 1828. Whaling and trading ships followed, and a Protestant mission from New England settled permanently in 1852. A smallpox epidemic after 1854 caused a drastic fall in population. Spain claimed the Carolines by 1886 and founded Santiago de la Ascensión in what is now Kolonia. Germany bought the islands in 1899 after the Spanish–American War.

Under German rule, from 1907, individual land deeds gradually replaced the feudal system in which all land was held in fief. One work-for-taxes project on Sokehs Island sparked the Sokehs rebellion, in which nine people were murdered; 15 insurgents were executed and others banished to Palau. Japan took control after the First World War, and the United States bypassed Pohnpei in 1943–1945, although warships shelled it. It was administered by the United States under United Nations oversight from 1947, and the Federated States of Micronesia became independent in 1986. Pohnpeian is the indigenous language, and the island is the most ethnically diverse in the federation.
pointe-a-pitre: Pointe-à-Pitre stands on the southwest of Grande-Terre, facing the Caribbean Sea, near the Rivière Salée, the Salt River that separates Grande-Terre from Basse-Terre. It lies on a limestone plateau, which was a factor in the city's construction, and its bay, the Petit Cul-de-Sac Marin, offers a sheltered port. The name means headland of Pitre. It is popularly derived from a Dutch sailor or fisherman called Pieter who may have settled on a promontory in the 17th century, but linguists now question this and suggest the Spanish word pitera, a rope made from agave.

French colonial authorities had long thought of founding a city where Guadeloupe's two main districts meet, but attempts around 1713 to 1730 failed because the swampy ground was unhealthy. During the British occupation of Guadeloupe from 1759 to 1763 a settlement appeared on a hill overlooking the swamps. After Guadeloupe returned to France in 1763 the city was officially founded in 1764 by royal edict under the governor Gabriel de Clieu, and the swamps were drained in the following years, which allowed urban development.

Growth was relatively rapid, partly thanks to the corsairs. A great fire entirely destroyed the city in 1780, and an earthquake destroyed it again in 1843. Its history is marked by many disasters: fires in 1850, 1871 and 1931, earthquakes in 1851 and 1897, hurricanes in 1865 and 1928, and several cholera epidemics. After the 1928 hurricane the architect Ali Tur built much of the city's civil and religious heritage between 1930 and 1935, including the palais de justice, the hospice hospital, the fish hall, several schools and the fire station. Its location and large sheltered port nevertheless made it Guadeloupe's largest city and economic capital.

Pointe-à-Pitre is the second most populous commune of Guadeloupe after Les Abymes, and an economic capital though not the administrative capital, which is Basse-Terre. The commune itself is small, but it is the centre of an urban area of eleven communes holding about 65 percent of the island's population. The main seaport, Port de Jarry, lies across the bay in Baie-Mahault. The former cathedral of St Peter and Paul recalls that the town was the seat of a Roman Catholic diocese, united with Basse-Terre in 1951. Its monuments include the Place de la Victoire, the Schœlcher and Saint-John-Perse museums and the Mémorial ACTe.
pointe-noire: Pointe-Noire stands on a headland between Pointe-Noire Bay and the Atlantic Ocean, near the border with Angola. Before European contact the site was a region around the fishing village of Ndji-Ndji, under the Kingdom of Loango, about 20 kilometres south of its capital Buali. The name, meaning Black Point, comes from Portuguese navigators who in 1484 saw an outcrop of black rocks on the headland.

France acquired the land of the Loango kingdom on 12 March 1883 through a treaty negotiated between Lieutenant Cordier and the king, Manimacosso-Chicusso, and Pointe-Noire was founded that year. French Equatorial Africa was created in 1910, and French companies were allowed to exploit the Middle Congo. In 1923 Pointe-Noire was chosen as the terminus of the Congo-Ocean Railway, which was to link Brazzaville, where river navigation ended, to the coast. The site had to allow a deep-sea port, and it was preferred to Libreville, first proposed. The railway was completed in 1934.

Drinking water reached the city in 1927, when it had about 3,000 inhabitants. A first hospital was built in 1936, and a bank opened a branch that year. The harbour received its first ship in 1942. In 1950 the city had 20,000 inhabitants and became capital of the Middle Congo. After incidents during the 1958 elections, leaders of the Democratic Union for the Defence of African Interests moved the capital to Brazzaville, since Pointe-Noire was under the influence of the opposition.

Pointe-Noire was the most modern city in the country when Congo became independent in 1960. Oil discovered around 1980, exploited largely by the French company Elf Aquitaine, brought rapid growth: the population doubled by 1982 and reached 360,000 in 1994. The civil wars of 1997 and 1999 sent refugees from inland provinces, and the population passed one million. It is the second largest city of the Republic of the Congo, with its main port and fishing industry, and the terminus of the Congo-Ocean Railway.
poitiers: Poitiers stands on a vast promontory between the valleys of the Boivre and the Clain, on the Seuil du Poitou, a shallow gap that connects the Aquitaine Basin in the south to the Paris Basin in the north. The old town occupies a plateau rising about 40 metres above the streams around it, a strong tactical position that mattered especially before and throughout the Middle Ages.

The Celtic tribe of the Pictones founded the town and gave it its name; before Roman influence it was the oppidum of Lemonum, and after the conquest it was called Pictavium. The Romans built at least three aqueducts and an amphitheatre larger than the one at Nîmes. Hilary of Poitiers, the first bishop, held the see from 350 to 367 and evangelised the town; he was exiled by Constantius II and returned at risk of death. The Visigoths later made it one of their principal residences, until Clovis I defeated Alaric II at Vouillé, not far away, in 507, and the town came under Frankish rule.

In the Early Middle Ages Poitiers benefited from its defensible position far from the centre of Frankish power. It was the seat of a diocese from the 4th century and the capital of the county of Poitou. Charles Martel's troops fought an Umayyad army led by Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi near the city on 10 October 732, a battle also called the Battle of Tours. Eleanor of Aquitaine often lived there, embellished and fortified it, and in 1199 gave it communal rights; in 1152 she married the future Henry II of England in the cathedral.

On 19 September 1356 the English defeated a larger French royal army near the town in the Battle of Poitiers and captured King John II of France. From 1418, under Charles VII, the royal parliament sat in exile at Poitiers until 1436, and in 1429 the town was the site of the formal inquest into Joan of Arc. The university was founded in 1431. In 1569 it withstood a siege by Gaspard de Coligny during the Wars of Religion.

Poitiers is the capital of the Vienne department in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region and has a population of 89,427. It is a university town, and Descartes, Rabelais and Joachim du Bellay are among those associated with it. Its preserved buildings include the 4th-century baptistery of Saint-Jean, the 12th-century Church of Notre-Dame-la-Grande and the cathedral, completed at the end of the 12th century.
pokhran: Pokhran, officially spelled Pokaran, is a town and municipality in the Jaisalmer district of the Indian state of Rajasthan. It lies in the Thar Desert, 112 km east of the city of Jaisalmer, 172 km north-west of Jodhpur and 225 km south of Bikaner by road, on the railway line from Jaisalmer to Jodhpur. In Rajasthani the name means a place surrounded by five salt ranges. The climate is arid, with little rain in the monsoon months of July to September, extremely hot and dry summers in which daytime temperatures can reach 46°C, and very cold winters. The 2011 census gave the municipal board territory a population of 28,457.

Pokhran was the seat of the chief of the Champawats, a sub-clan of the Rathores of the state of Marwar-Jodhpur. The last jagirdar of Pokhran before Indian independence was Bhawani Singh of Pokhran, born in 1911. He served as a sessions judge and was elected as an independent to the first Lok Sabha from the Barmer-Jalore constituency in the general election of 1952.

The Pokhran Test Range, a key part of India's nuclear programme, lies outside the municipal board's jurisdiction and is controlled by the Indian Army. Its army base, built by the Army Corps of Engineers, stands 26 km north-west of the town and 4 km north of the village of Khetolai. It was built before May 1974, when, on the authorisation of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi to the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, it hosted the detonation of India's first nuclear device.

The Ministry of External Affairs designated the test of 18 May 1974 Pokhran-I, and it is also known as Smiling Buddha. The Indian Army detonated the bomb on the range under the supervision of several key generals. On 11 and 13 May 1998 the Defence Research and Development Organisation and the Atomic Energy Commission carried out five further tests there, called Pokhran-II: four devices of the Atomic Energy Commission and, under the codename Shakti, a thermonuclear device. The town and the test range are now known chiefly for these tests.
pol-pot: Pol Pot was born Saloth Sâr in the village of Prek Sbauv, outside Kampong Thom, the son of a prosperous farmer. He was educated at some of Cambodia's most elite schools, boarding from 1942 at a new junior middle school in Kampong Cham, where fellow pupils such as Hu Nim and Khieu Samphan later served in his government. He arrived in Paris on 1 October 1949 on a scholarship to study radio electronics, and joined the French Communist Party in 1951. He returned to Cambodia in 1953 and worked with the Khmer Việt Minh, then taught in Phnom Penh while remaining a central figure in the Marxist-Leninist movement.

In 1959 the movement was formalised as the Kampuchean Labour Party, later renamed the Communist Party of Kampuchea. To avoid repression by Norodom Sihanouk's government, Pol Pot moved to a jungle camp in 1962, and in February 1963 he was elected party secretary. The war against Sihanouk was launched in January 1968. After Lon Nol deposed Sihanouk in March 1970, Sihanouk allied with the Khmer Rouge, and his support greatly helped recruitment. In May 1973 Pol Pot ordered the collectivisation of villages in Khmer Rouge territory. Phnom Penh fell on 17 April 1975, and he secretly entered the abandoned city three days later.

In January 1976 a new constitution renamed the country Democratic Kampuchea. The Khmer Rouge emptied the cities and moved the urban population to collective farms and labour camps, where mass executions, torture, malnutrition and disease were rampant. Money, religion and private property were abolished, and more than 1.3 million people were executed and buried in mass graves. After repeated border clashes and massacres of Vietnamese villagers, Vietnam launched a full-scale invasion on 25 December 1978, and by January 1979 the Khmer Rouge were toppled.

The Khmer Rouge retreated to the jungles near the Thai border and kept fighting until the Vietnamese withdrew in 1989. In June 1997 Pol Pot ordered the killing of Son Sen, which prompted the commander Ta Mok to turn against him. Pol Pot was placed under house arrest and died shortly afterward in 1998. Some Cambodians still leave offerings at his grave in Anlong Veng, while many call the period samai a-Pot, the era of the contemptible Pot.
polabian-slavs: The Polabian Slavs, also known as Elbe Slavs and more broadly as Wends, were Lechitic, or West Slavic, tribes who lived along the Elbe in what is now eastern Germany. Their lands reached from the Baltic Sea in the north to the Ore Mountains in the south, and from the Saale in the west to medieval Poland in the east. They partly replaced Germanic tribes who had left the area by the 6th century. The Bavarian Geographer, compiled at Regensburg in 830, lists their tribes. Later writers group them into the Obotrites, the Veleti (also called Liutizians) and the Lusatian Sorbs.

In the 7th century the Chronicle of Fredegar names Dervan, duke of the Sorbs, first subordinate to the Franks and then a member of Prince Samo's union. Charlemagne used the Obotrites as allies against the Saxons and led an expedition against the Veleti in 798. German campaigns began in earnest under the Ottonian dynasty, with marches and bishoprics such as Magdeburg, Brandenburg and Havelberg to support conversion. In 983 the pagan Slavs rose in revolt, destroying Havelberg, Brandenburg and Hamburg, and imperial control between the Elbe and the Oder became nominal.

In the 11th century the Obotrite prince Udo and his son Gottschalk united the Obotrite tribes, but Gottschalk was killed in a revolt in 1066. Holsatian nobles settled in Wagria from 1140. The Wendish Crusade of 1147 was largely unsuccessful but devastated Liutizi lands, brought forced baptisms and secured Saxon control of Wagria and Polabia. From the late 1150s King Valdemar the Great of Denmark and Duke Henry the Lion of Saxony campaigned together, and the Obotrite prince Niklot died in 1160. The Danes took Rugia in 1168, and a Slavic fleet was crushed in the Bay of Greifswald in 1184. The Lusatian Sorbs were conquered in wars between 929 and 963.

A Polabian prince was called a knez. He led his tribe and its nobles, but his authority extended mainly over the territory of his governor, the voivod. River towns, which chroniclers call civitates, often limited princely power. Most people were peasants who grew grain and flax and kept cattle, and some fished or kept bees. Their towns were known for their longships. By the 14th century most Slavs in the area had been Germanized, but the Sorbs, descendants of the Milceni and the Lusici, kept their identity in Lusatia, and the two Sorbian languages are still spoken by roughly 22,000 to 30,000 people.
poland: Poland covers an administrative area of 312,722 square kilometres, the ninth-largest country in Europe. The central and northern parts bordering the Baltic Sea lie within the flat Central European Plain, while the south is hilly and mountainous. The Sudetes lie in the west and the Carpathians in the east, and the Tatra Mountains hold the highest point, the northwestern summit of Rysy at 2,500 metres. The coastline spans 770 kilometres. The longest rivers are the Vistula, the Oder, the Warta and the Bug, and the country has around ten thousand lakes, mostly in the north-eastern region of Masuria.

The first Stone Age archaic humans settled the area approximately 500,000 years ago. The earliest evidence of European cheesemaking, from 5500 BCE, was discovered in Kuyavia, and a fortified settlement at Biskupin is attributed to the Lusatian culture of the Late Bronze Age. In antiquity many peoples lived in the territory, among them Celtic, Scythian, Germanic, Sarmatian, Baltic and Slavic tribes. Poland began to form into a unitary and territorial entity around the middle of the 10th century under the Piast dynasty, and in 966 the ruler of the Polans, Mieszko I, accepted Western Christianity under the Roman Catholic Church. The Kingdom of Poland emerged in 1025.

In 1569 Poland cemented its long-standing association with Lithuania, forming the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which had an elective monarchy and adopted Europe's first modern constitution in 1791. The country was partitioned by neighbouring states at the end of the 18th century and regained independence in 1918 as the Second Polish Republic.

The invasion of Poland by Germany and by the Soviet Union in September 1939 marked the beginning of World War II, which resulted in the Holocaust and millions of Polish casualties. Forced into the Eastern Bloc, the Polish People's Republic was a signatory of the Warsaw Pact. The Solidarity movement emerged in 1980, and in 1989 Poland re-established itself as a liberal democracy and held free elections.

Poland has over 37 million people and is composed of sixteen voivodeships, with Warsaw as its capital and largest city. It is a unitary parliamentary republic with a bicameral legislature of the Sejm, with 460 members, and the Senate, with 100. The 2021 census found that ethnic Poles comprise 98.84% of the population. It keeps its own currency, the złoty. Poland has 18 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
poland-is-not-yet-lost: Poland Is Not Yet Lost, known in Polish as Mazurek Dąbrowskiego and originally as the Song of the Polish Legions in Italy, was written by Józef Wybicki in Reggio Emilia. In 1796 Wybicki, one of the moderate émigré politicians seeking French aid for Polish independence, proposed Polish Legions within the French Revolutionary Army and persuaded General Jan Henryk Dąbrowski, a veteran of the 1794 Kościuszko Uprising, to present the plan to the French Directory. A Polish legion was formed in January 1797 under the Cisalpine Republic. Its soldiers hoped to fight Austria under Napoleon Bonaparte and then march across Austrian territory to Poland to start a national uprising.

Wybicki arrived at Reggio in early July 1797 and wrote the song soon afterwards; it was probably first performed in public on 16 July during a military parade. The composer of the melody is unknown; it is most probably Wybicki's adaptation of a folk tune, a mazurka, long wrongly attributed to Michał Kleofas Ogiński.

The central idea, new in the age of early nationalism, is that a nation does not disappear for lack of political sovereignty. In 1842 Adam Mickiewicz explained that the opening words mean that a people who have in them what makes a nation can prolong their country's existence whatever its political circumstances. The song is also a call to arms, hoping that under Dąbrowski the legionaries will recover by force what foreign power has seized. It names military models: Dąbrowski, Napoleon, the 17th-century hetman Stefan Czarniecki and Tadeusz Kościuszko, recalled with the scythes of Racławice. Napoleon is the only non-Pole named.

The song was popular in Poland from late 1797 and was soon altered. The legions never returned as its verses promised; they were used to put down uprisings in Italy, Germany and Haiti, where disease decimated them. When Dąbrowski and Wybicki reached Poznań on 6 November 1806, locals greeted them singing it. It was sung in the November Uprising of 1830 to 1831, and between 1873 and 1911 German courts passed 20 sentences for singing it.

After the independence of the Second Polish Republic in 1918 it became the de facto anthem, and it was officially adopted in 1927. It inspired the Ukrainian anthem, the Hatikvah and the pan-Slavic Hey, Slavs. In 1945 Artur Rubinstein, finding no Polish delegation at the opening concert of the United Nations, played it loudly in protest.
polans-eastern: The Polans, also known as Polians, Polanians, Polianians or Eastern Polans, were an East Slavic tribe who lived on both sides of the Dnieper river from Liubech to Rodnia and down the lower courses of the rivers Ros', Sula, Stuhna, Teteriv, Irpin', Desna and Pripyat. Their name comes from the Old East Slavic word pole, meaning field, because according to the Primary Chronicle they lived in the fields. They are distinct from the western Polans of the Early Middle Ages, a West Slavic tribe who were ancestors of the Poles. At one stage the Polans were subjugated by the Khazars.

The land of the Polans lay at the crossroads of important trade routes and of territories inhabited by other East Slavic tribes, among them the Drevlians, Radimichs, Drehovians and Severians, and water routes connected them all. The Road from the Varangians to the Greeks, which linked northern Europe with the Black Sea and the Byzantine Empire, ran along the Dnieper through their land. This position allowed the Polans to play an organising role in the consolidation of the East Slavic tribes. According to the Primary Chronicle the tribe was headed by three brothers, Kyi, Shchek and Khoryv, who founded Kyiv, which became a tribal centre. Two Varangians, Askold and Dir, are considered the first rulers of Kyiv.

In the 860s the Varangians arrived and organised several military campaigns against the Byzantine Empire, which eventually defeated them and made peace. From the 9th century the Polans began to be known as Rus', and the region they inhabited as Rus' land, a name they presumably adopted from the Varangians. In the 880s Oleg the Wise conquered the land of the Polans, and from then on their territory became the political, cultural and economic centre of Kievan Rus'. In the 10th century the name Polans fell almost out of use, replaced by Rus', and they were last mentioned as a tribe in a chronicle of 944.

The chronicles repeatedly note that social and economic relations among the Polans were highly developed compared with those of neighbouring tribes. In the 9th and 10th centuries they practised well-developed arable farming, cattle breeding, hunting, fishing and wild-hive beekeeping, along with crafts such as blacksmithing, casting, pottery and goldsmithing. Thousands of kurgans from before the Polan period, found by archaeologists in their region, show that the land could support a relatively dense population. The Polans lived in small families in semi-dug-out earth houses and wore homespun clothes and modest jewellery. Before they converted to Christianity they burned their dead and raised kurgan-like embankments over them. According to chronicled legends, their largest cities were Kyiv, Pereiaslav, Rodnia, Vyshhorod, Bilhorod Kyivskyi and Kaniv.
polans-western: The name of Poland derives from that of the Polans, which in turn likely comes from the Polish word for field: the members of a Polan opole drew most of their income from the cultivated field. The chronicler Jan Długosz wrote that Lechites who lived on fields were called Polans by their compatriots in the forests. Zygmunt Gloger, in 1903, linked the name to a growing need for agriculture around the Warta.

The term is not well attested in the early Middle Ages. Its oldest known mention is in the first biography of Saint Adalbert, dated to 998–999, which calls Bolesław I the Brave Bolizlav Polanorum duce in the context of 995. Adam of Bremen, writing in 1075–1080, placed the Polans beside the Pomeranians on the Oder, bordering the Prussians, Czechs and the Rus. Modern historiography disputes the concept of a Polan tribe.

The usual account, called the Polan hypothesis, holds that the Polans were a powerful tribe in Greater Poland from the 8th century, led by the House of Piast, who united Poland by conquest in the 10th century under Mieszko I, baptised in 966. The historian Przemysław Urbańczyk has said the tribe did not exist, though this claim has been widely rejected. Their foremost gords were Gniezno, Grzybowo, Moraczewo, Giecz, Poznań, Bnin and Ląd; scholars debate whether Giecz or Kalisz was the original centre.

The Piast seizure of power probably came late, around the 940s, and was largely peaceful. The 930s and 940s saw an explosion of fort building that Andrzej Nowak called a Polan Big Bang. Archaeology then shows signs of violent conquest in Kuyavia, Lesser Poland and the Lublin Land. By the early 990s Mieszko controlled most of Greater Poland, Pomerania, much of Silesia and possibly Masovia.

Polan culture and society resembled those of the rest of early medieval Poland. The traveller Ibrahim ibn Yaqub, writing of his journeys in 962–964, described the realm of Mieszko, whom he called Mashaqqah, as the largest of the Slavic countries. He wrote that Mieszko paid three thousand mailed warriors from taxes collected in market weights, and that dowries were large, so a man with two or three daughters grew rich and one with two sons grew poor.

Urbańczyk describes early Polan society as egalitarian, a character others call democratic. Gniezno was a pagan cult site and a place of assemblies before the Piasts chose it as their capital. Excavations in the late 1990s and early 2000s showed that Ostrów Lednicki and Ląd existed before Piast rule.
policoro: Policoro is a comune on the Ionian coast, about 70 km from Taranto and 60 km from Matera. It is bounded by the towns of Rotondella, Scanzano Jonico and Tursi. The climate is hot Mediterranean, with mild winters and warm to hot, dry summers; snowfall is so rare that the townspeople remember it as a special event. The population swells in summer with tourists who come to the Lido di Policoro.

The ruins of the ancient Heraclea lie within the modern comune. The city was founded by colonists from Taras, present-day Taranto, and Thurii, and in very little time became richer and better known than the nearby town of Siris. In 280 BCE the Battle of Heraclea was fought there during the war between Taranto and Rome. The Tables of Heraclea date to this period; they are bronze tablets with texts in Greek and Latin on the public and constitutional rules and laws of the town, among them the Lex Iulia Municipalis, and are now in the Archeology Museum of Naples.

In the period of the Roman Empire the whole area depopulated and Heraclea lost its prestige, becoming a small village on a hill. The time and circumstances of its final extinction are wholly unknown. The site was desolate, and the neighbouring district, once regarded as one of the most fertile in Italy, was still almost uninhabited in the mid-19th century.

The present comune arose in the Middle Ages, in the 11th and 12th centuries, as a feudal estate and then a village. It developed around a baronial castle, used as a residence from about 1000 for hunting in the vast forests owned by local noble families such as the Berlingieri, and sheltered a population from nearby villages that were threatened by invasions and raids. Only after 1950, when the marshy and unhealthy land had been reclaimed and an agrarian reform had split and redistributed the land, did Policoro receive municipal autonomy. Families moved in from all parts of the region, producing a large demographic surge, and the town now has some 18,000 inhabitants.
polio-vaccine: Two kinds of polio vaccine are in use. The inactivated vaccine, IPV, is given by injection; after two doses 90% or more of recipients develop protective antibodies to all three serotypes of poliovirus, and at least 99% are immune after three. The oral vaccine, OPV, is an attenuated virus produced by passing it through nonhuman cells. It needs no sterile syringes and so suits mass campaigns, and it gives both humoral and cell-mediated immunity. Its drawback is a rare risk of vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis, about one case for every 2.7 million doses of the Sabin vaccine.

In 1948 a group led by John Enders at the Children's Hospital Boston cultivated poliovirus in human tissue in the laboratory, which made vaccine research practicable; Enders, Thomas H. Weller and Frederick C. Robbins received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1954. During the early 1950s United States polio cases ran above 25,000 a year, with 58,000 in 1952 and 35,000 in 1953.

Hilary Koprowski's attenuated vaccine, prepared by passing the virus through mouse brains, was first tested on 27 February 1950 on an eight-year-old boy at Letchworth Village, New York, and then on 19 other children. Jonas Salk's inactivated vaccine reached the market first. Because America was committed to Salk's vaccine, Albert Sabin and Koprowski tested their live vaccines elsewhere: Sabin in Mexico and the Soviet Union, Koprowski in the Congo and Poland.

In 1959 ten million children in the Soviet Union received the Sabin oral vaccine, and large trials there by Mikhail Chumakov and colleagues showed its safety and efficacy. The Sabin strains were chosen for worldwide distribution, and a trivalent oral vaccine was licensed in the United States in 1963. Between 1962 and 1965 about 100 million Americans received it.

A global eradication effort led by the World Health Organization, UNICEF and the Rotary Foundation began in 1988 and relied largely on the Sabin-Chumakov oral vaccine. Polio was eliminated in the Americas by 1994, in the Western Pacific in 2000 and in Europe in 2002, and India was declared polio-free in March 2014. The vaccine is on the WHO's List of Essential Medicines.
polis: The word polis had a different meaning in Ancient Greek than the Modern Greek word for city. In ancient Greece a polis was also considered a homeland, and it was autonomous, not necessarily belonging to any larger political entity. Poleis had their own constitutions and demanded loyalty from their citizens. About 1,500 such states are known to have existed, mainly in Greece and Asia Minor, with others founded throughout the Mediterranean and Black Sea regions.

Particularly during the Archaic period, poleis sent out settlers to found new colonies. These kept economic, cultural and military ties with their mother-city for centuries afterwards, and colonisation was the main method by which Greek language, religion and art spread. Ancient Greek writers also used the word for non-Greek cities: Aristotle discussed the Phoenician city of Carthage in comparing its constitution with Sparta's.

Aristotle's Politics is the only surviving ancient work that treats the polis at length. He held that a polis has a particular location, population and constitution (politeia), and that if it moves en masse, changes its form of government or takes in a new population, it is no longer the same polis. He described it as a community, built up from families and villages, which should be nearly self-sufficient.

The population was divided into citizens and non-citizens. A citizen, in Aristotle's words, is a person entitled to participate in government, and Xenophon reports that citizens on coming of age took an oath to uphold the law, usually as part of their military service. Poleis had ambassadors and could join or host the Hellenic Games. Plato, by contrast, wrote about an ideal polis ruled by a philosopher king, and listed its economic classes as producers, merchants, sailors, retail traders and wage earners.

Modern scholars often translate polis as city-state, a term applied to it by Herder in 1765 and anglicised by W. Warde Fowler in 1893. The translation has limits: many poleis were not city-states, and a polis need not be urban at all. Thucydides described the polis of the Lacedaemonians as composed of villages after the old fashion of Hellas, and the Perioeci around it were called poleis though they were subject to Dorian poleis.

Other models include the ancient city of Numa Denis Fustel de Coulanges, a 19th-century scholar who saw it as a confederacy of tribes that had grown from families and phratries. Studies of the last few decades have drawn on large databases of ancient sources to compare many poleis rather than rely on a single model.
polisario-front: In 1971 a group of young Sahrawi students in the universities of Morocco began organising what became the Embryonic Movement for the Liberation of Saguia el-Hamra and Río de Oro. It sought backing from Arab governments, including Algeria and Morocco, but drew only faint notice of support from Libya and Mauritania, and so moved to Spanish Sahara to begin an armed rebellion.

The Polisario Front was formally constituted on 10 May 1973 at Ain Bentili by several Sahrawi university students, survivors of the 1968 massacres in Zouérat and Sahrawi veterans of the Spanish Army. On 20 May it attacked El-Khanga, where a post of the Tropas Nómadas, Sahrawi-staffed auxiliary forces, was overrun and its rifles seized. Its power grew from early 1975 as the Tropas Nómadas began deserting to it. A United Nations visiting mission in June 1975 found an overwhelming consensus among Sahrawis for independence and judged the Polisario the most powerful political force in the territory.

After Morocco's Green March of 6 November 1975, Spain signed the Madrid Accords, ceding Spanish Sahara to Morocco and Mauritania. The Polisario proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic on 27 February 1976 and fought both armies. Moroccan air raids on refugee camps led it to move the refugees to Tindouf in Algeria. With arms and funds from Algeria and Libya its army grew to several thousand fighters using hit-and-run attacks.

A peace treaty of 5 August 1979 had Mauritania recognise Sahrawi rights and withdraw its forces; Morocco annexed the area Mauritania left. From the mid-1980s Morocco built a long sand wall, the Moroccan Wall, enclosing the economically useful parts of the territory, which stalemated the war. A ceasefire monitored by the United Nations mission MINURSO took effect on 6 September 1991 on the promise of a referendum, which stalled over who could vote. The ceasefire was ended in November 2020.

The Polisario describes itself as a front covering all political trends in Sahrawi society, not a party, and has no party programme. It is a Sahrawi nationalist and Arab socialist movement, and in 1991 it voted for free market economics and multi-party politics. Its secretary general is elected by a General Popular Congress, which meets every four years and draws delegates from the popular congresses of the refugee camps near Tindouf, from women's, youth and workers' organisations and from the army. Between congresses a National Secretariat is the supreme body. There is no formal membership: anyone who works with it or lives in the camps counts as a member. The United Nations considers it the legitimate representative of the Sahrawi people.
polish-corridor: The Polish Corridor, also called the Pomeranian Corridor, lay in the region of Pomerelia, or Eastern Pomerania, and gave the Second Polish Republic access to the Baltic Sea, dividing the bulk of Weimar Germany from the province of East Prussia. At its narrowest the Polish territory was only 30 kilometres wide. To its east lay the Free City of Danzig, now Gdańsk, a semi-independent city-state where German was spoken, under the protection of the League of Nations, united with Poland in customs, mail, foreign policy, railways and defence. The word corridor was regarded as offensive by interwar Polish diplomats, and Poles referred to the region as Pomorze or the Pomeranian Voivodeship.

Pomerelia was settled in the tenth century by Slavic Pomeranians, ancestors of the Kashubians, who were subdued by Bolesław I of Poland. Its dukes ruled until 1294. From 1308-1309 it fell to the Teutonic Knights, and in 1466, by the second Peace of Thorn, it became part of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth as part of autonomous Royal Prussia. Prussia annexed it in 1772 as West Prussia, and it became part of the German Empire in 1871. The corridor was therefore not an entirely new creation. Wilson's Fourteen Points of January 1918 proposed an independent Polish state with free and secure access to the sea, and Roman Dmowski argued that Poland could never be truly independent without it.

The corridor roused great resentment in Germany, and no Weimar government recognised the eastern borders set at Versailles. In 1922 Germany set up a ferry service to East Prussia to reduce its dependence on transit through Polish territory, and trains passed through with sealed carriages. In 1925 the Polish land reform listed 10,800 hectares from 32 German landowners and 950 hectares from seven Poles, though Germans owned 39 percent of the agricultural land. The census of 1910 counted 528,000 Poles, including Kashubians, and 385,000 Germans in the region.

Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. The German Fourth Army defeated the Polish Pomorze Army and captured the corridor in the Battle of Tuchola Forest by 5 September, and it was annexed by Germany until the Red Army took it at the end of the war. Poland's borders were reorganised at the 1945 Potsdam Conference, and the corridor became part of the reborn Polish state. Many German residents were executed and others expelled.
polish-lithuanian-commonwealth: Poland and Lithuania had been in a personal union since the Krewo Agreement of 1385 and the marriage of Queen Jadwiga of Poland to Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania, who was crowned Władysław II Jagiełło. Lithuania's vulnerable position persuaded its nobles to seek a closer bond with Poland.

Lesser Lithuanian nobles wanted to share the privileges of the Polish szlachta, but they refused Polish demands to incorporate the Grand Duchy as a mere province. Mikołaj Radziwiłł the Red and his cousin Mikołaj Radziwiłł the Black opposed the union. The Union of Lublin established the Commonwealth as a single entity on 1 July 1569, though Lithuania kept its own name, laws and territory.

Sigismund II Augustus died childless in 1572, ending the Jagiellonian dynasty, and monarchs were thereafter elected for life. On 11 May 1573 Henry de Valois was proclaimed king in the first royal election outside Warsaw, in which about 40,000 nobles voted. He signed the Pacta conventa and approved the Henrician Articles, but in June 1574 he left to claim the French crown, and the throne was declared vacant.

At its peak in the early 17th century the Commonwealth, spanned about 1,000,000 square kilometres and some 12 million people in 1618. Its stability then waned after a series of blows, as persecution of religious and ethnic minorities led several groups to rebel.

In the 18th century foreign powers interfered in royal elections and bribed nobles; Frederick Augustus of Saxony was elected in June 1697 with financing from Imperial Russia and Habsburg Austria and crowned Augustus II. In 1764 Stanisław August Poniatowski was elected with the support of Catherine the Great; in 1773 the king and parliament formed the Commission of National Education, the first Ministry of Education in European history. The Constitution of 3 May 1791 was a late reform effort, but the Commonwealth was partitioned among Austria, Prussia and Russia in the late 18th century.

The political system, called the Golden Liberty, had a bicameral parliament, the General Sejm, whose lower house was elected by the szlachta, about 10 percent of the population, and an elected king bound by the Henrician Articles and the pacta conventa. Power slipped increasingly from the central government to the nobility. The Commonwealth showed unusual ethnic diversity and religious tolerance by European standards, guaranteed by the Warsaw Confederation Act of 1573, though the practical degree of freedom varied.

Polish and Latin were the official languages, and Catholicism the state religion. The economy rested chiefly on agriculture and trade, with workshops such as paper mills, tanneries, ironworks and glassworks concentrated in the Kingdom of Poland. The Constitution of 3 May 1791 abolished the liberum veto, separated the powers of government and extended political rights beyond the nobility to the bourgeoisie.
polish-lithuanian-teutonic-war: In 1230 the Teutonic Knights moved to the Kulmerland and, at the request of Konrad I of Masovia, began the Prussian Crusade, conquering the Prussians by the 1280s. They then fought the Lithuanians for about a hundred years, raiding Samogitia, which separated their lands in Prussia from their branch in Livonia.

In 1385 Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania agreed in the Union of Kreva to marry Queen Jadwiga of Poland, converted to Christianity and was crowned King of Poland. Lithuania's conversion removed the religious reason for the Order's campaigns, but the Knights contested its sincerity before a papal court. Samogitia had been in Teutonic hands since the Peace of Raciąż of 1404, and the Knights also controlled the lower courses of the Neman, Vistula and Daugava.

An uprising began in Teutonic-held Samogitia in May 1409, supported by Lithuania and Poland. On 6 August 1409 the Grand Master, Ulrich von Jungingen, declared war and invaded Greater Poland and Kuyavia. Neither side was ready for a full war, and Wenceslaus, King of the Romans, mediated a truce signed on 8 October 1409 to expire on 24 June 1410. Jogaila and Vytautas agreed to unite their armies and march on Marienburg, and crossed the Vistula at Czerwinsk between 24 and 30 June 1410.

The Battle of Grunwald was fought on 15 July 1410. Estimates give 16,500 to 39,000 Polish–Lithuanian troops and 11,000 to 27,000 Teutonic. About 8,000 Teutonic soldiers were killed and 14,000 captured, and the Grand Master and most of the leadership died. The victors reached Marienburg only on 26 July, which gave Heinrich von Plauen time to organise a defence. Several cities surrendered, but the siege was lifted on 19 September, and the Knights quickly retook most of their castles.

The Peace of Thorn was signed on 1 February 1411. The Knights ceded Dobrzyń Land to Poland and gave up claims to Samogitia during the lifetimes of Jogaila and Vytautas. Further wars in 1414 and 1422 preceded the Treaty of Melno, which settled the territorial disputes. The Knights owed an indemnity in silver, estimated at ten times the annual income of the King of England, and met it by borrowing, taxing and confiscating church silver. Danzig and Thorn revolted against the taxes.
With Poland and Lithuania Christian, the Order struggled to recruit crusaders and relied on costly mercenaries. Unrest led to the Prussian Confederation in 1441 and the Thirteen Years' War in 1454.
polish-lithuanian-war: After the First World War, Lithuania, Poland and Soviet Russia competed for control of overlapping territories. The conflict between the first two centred on Vilnius, which the Council of Lithuania had declared the capital of the restored Lithuanian state. The Polish Army seized the city on 19 April 1919, and the first clashes between Polish and Lithuanian soldiers took place near Vievis in the spring of that year. The Entente drew demarcation lines that neither side accepted, and the front then stabilised until the summer of 1920, when the Polish-Soviet War turned against Poland.

In July 1920 Polish forces retreated before the Red Army, and the Lithuanians moved to secure territory the Poles left behind. The Soviets entered Vilnius first, on 14 July, and handed it to the Lithuanians on 26 August after their defeat in the Battle of Warsaw. Poland attacked Lithuanian units in the Suwałki region on 22 September. Under pressure from the League of Nations, it signed the Suwałki Agreement on 7 October 1920, which drew an incomplete demarcation line that left Vilnius open to a flanking move.

On 8 October the Polish general Lucjan Żeligowski staged a mutiny, secretly planned and authorised by the Polish chief of state, Józef Piłsudski. His division of 14,000 soldiers took Vilnius one day before the agreement was to take effect, against only two Lithuanian battalions. Poland officially called Żeligowski a deserter but supplied his units. On 12 October he proclaimed the Republic of Central Lithuania, with Vilnius as its capital. His offensive towards Kaunas was halted by the Lithuanians, and a ceasefire was signed on 29 November 1920.

The Republic of Central Lithuania was incorporated into Poland as the Wilno Voivodeship in 1922, and in March 1923 the Conference of Ambassadors recognised the armistice line as the Polish-Lithuanian border. The International Court of Justice in The Hague held in 1931 that Poland had broken international law by occupying Vilnius. Lithuania, which had defended its independence but lost a third of its territory and its capital, kept Vilnius as its constitutional capital and broke off relations with Poland until a Polish ultimatum in March 1938. It regained the city on 28 October 1939.
polish-muscovite-war-1605-1618: Russia had been in the Time of Troubles since the death of Tsar Feodor I in 1598, which ended the Rurik dynasty, and a famine from 1601 to 1603 deepened the crisis. In late 1600 a Polish mission led by Chancellor Lew Sapieha proposed an alliance with a future personal union, but Tsar Boris Godunov declined and instead extended the Treaty of Jam Zapolski to 1622. The impostor False Dmitry I appeared in Poland in 1603 and found backing among magnates such as Michał Wiśniowiecki and the Sapieha family. Sigismund III Vasa gave him only 4,000 zlotys, though Jesuits also funded him. In Polish historiography these first interventions, the First Dymitriad (1604–1606) and Second Dymitriad (1607–1609), are a conflict of their own.

In 1607 False Dmitry II appeared, again supported by Polish magnates, who supplied about 7,500 soldiers. On 28 February 1609 Tsar Vasili Shuysky allied with Charles IX of Sweden, and Sigismund, whose main aim was to regain the Swedish throne, obtained the Sejm's permission to declare war on Russia. Boyars opposed to Shuysky asked for Prince Władysław as tsar, and in September 1610 the Seven Boyars elected him. Sigismund refused to let his son take the throne unless the Muscovites converted to Catholicism, and the pro-Polish boyars withdrew their support.

A rising in Moscow against the Polish garrison in 1611 led to a siege of the Kremlin. Patriarch Hermogenes, who reportedly refused to order the attack called off, was starved to death. In 1611 Kuzma Minin and Prince Dmitry Pozharsky raised a new army, and the Poles were ousted from Moscow in September 1612, although they had taken Smolensk in June 1611. The front stayed quiet until a new campaign began on 6 April 1617, nominally under Władysław and in fact under Hetman Chodkiewicz. Cossacks under Petro Sahaidachny joined in 1618, and the siege of Moscow, begun on 2 October, was lifted after a night assault on 10–11 October failed.

A Russian assembly elected Michael Romanov tsar in 1613, beginning the Romanov dynasty, which ruled until the February Revolution of 1917. The Truce of Deulino, concluded on 11 December 1618, gave the Commonwealth Chernigov, Severia and Smolensk and set a fifteen-year truce. Władysław kept his claim to the Russian throne, though Sigismund had given it up. The victory was very costly in money and lives. Fighting resumed in 1632 in the Smolensk War, and by the Treaty of Polyanovka of 1634 Władysław renounced his claim. The war was the first major sign of a rivalry between Poland and Russia that lasted for centuries, and it inspired Pushkin's play Boris Godunov.
polish-soviet-war: After the collapse of the Central Powers and the Armistice of 11 November 1918, Vladimir Lenin's Soviet Russia annulled the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk and moved forces westward to reclaim the Ober Ost regions the Germans had abandoned. Lenin saw the newly independent Poland as a route for spreading communist revolution into Europe. Polish leaders, among them Józef Piłsudski, aimed to restore Poland's borders from before 1772. The lands in dispute, now in Ukraine and Belarus, had once belonged to Kievan Rus' and later to Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and many had passed to the Russian Empire in the Partitions of Poland-Lithuania.

The Red Army took Vilnius on 5 January 1919, and throughout that year Polish forces occupied much of present-day Lithuania and Belarus and won the Polish-Ukrainian War.
