On 21 April 1920 Piłsudski signed the Treaty of Warsaw with the Ukrainian leader Symon Petliura, whose government had in practice been defeated by the Bolsheviks. Piłsudski then launched the Kiev offensive, and Polish and allied Ukrainian forces captured the city on 7 May 1920. The offensive lacked local support, and many Ukrainians joined the Red Army rather than Petliura's forces.

A Soviet counteroffensive began in June 1920, and by August the Red Army had pushed the Poles back to Warsaw. In the Battle of Warsaw, fought between 12 and 25 August, Polish forces won an unexpected victory, often called the Miracle on the Vistula. Polish codebreakers, led by Jan Kowalewski and joined by mathematicians from Warsaw and Lwów, had broken Soviet ciphers, which let Polish commanders use their forces efficiently. Peace talks began in Minsk in mid-August and moved to Riga in September, and a ceasefire took effect on 18 October 1920.

The Peace of Riga, signed on 18 March 1921, set Poland's eastern border about 200 kilometres east of the Curzon Line. Poland received eastern Galicia and most of Volhynia and recognised the Ukrainian and Byelorussian Soviet republics, which ended Piłsudski's hope of a Polish-led federation. Of 80–85 thousand Soviet prisoners of war, 16–20 thousand died in Polish captivity, and of 51 thousand Polish prisoners, 20 thousand died. The reported pogroms of Jews by the Polish military led the United States to send a commission under Henry Morgenthau. Historians do not agree on who won: the war is seen as a Polish military victory but also as a political defeat.
polish-ukrainian-war: The war had roots in the ethnic, cultural and political differences between the Polish and Ukrainian populations of Galicia. The relative leniency of the House of Habsburg towards national minorities let both Polish and Ukrainian national movements develop in Austria-Hungary. After the 1848 Revolution the Austrians, concerned by Polish demands for greater autonomy, supported the Ruthenians, the East Slavic people later recognised as Ukrainians. The Ruthenian intelligentsia adopted the name Ukrainians, and in 1903 Poles and Ukrainians held separate conferences in Lviv. The two movements developed with contradictory goals, which caused the later clash.

On 18 October 1918 a Ukrainian National Council was formed, and during the night of 31 October to 1 November Ukrainian units of 1,400 soldiers and 60 officers, led by Captain Dmytro Vitovsky, took control of Lviv. The West Ukrainian People's Republic was proclaimed on 13 November 1918, with Lviv as its capital. Because the republic was not recognised internationally and Poland's boundaries had not yet been defined, the question was reduced to military control. Polish self-defence units held out until a relief force broke through on 21 November. Polish troops and criminals then looted the Jewish and Ukrainian quarters, killing up to 340 civilians.

Ukrainian forces, with a large numerical advantage until February 1919, held most of Eastern Galicia until May. A Polish offensive began on 14 May 1919 with the Blue Army of General Józef Haller, and Romania opened a second front on 23 May. A Ukrainian counter-offensive, the Chortkiv Offensive, under Oleksander Hrekov began on 8 June and came within two days' march of Lviv, but it ran short of ammunition, with only five to ten bullets for each soldier. Poland won the disputed territory on 18 July 1919. Both sides interned civilians in camps, where many died of cold, hunger and typhoid.

About 10,000 Poles and 15,000 Ukrainians, mostly soldiers, died. Britain under David Lloyd George and, to a lesser extent, Italy opposed Polish expansion, while France supported Poland with arms, officers and Haller's army. France later obtained control of the Eastern Galician oil fields. The Soviet Union annexed Galicia and Volhynia at the start of the Second World War, and after the war the region remained within Soviet Ukraine.

Although the 70 to 75 thousand men of the Ukrainian Galician Army lost, the experience of proclaiming a state and fighting for it deepened Ukrainian nationalism in Galicia. For Poles in Eastern Galicia, the victory ended 146 years of foreign domination, and the defence of Lviv, including the young defenders of the Łyczakowski Cemetery, was long remembered as an example of Polish heroism.
politburo: The English word comes from the Russian politbyuro, short for politicheskoye byuro, meaning political bureau. The concept was created during the Russian Revolution. On 23 October 1917 the Bolshevik Party Central Committee established a political bureau to direct the armed insurrection in Petrograd. It had seven members: Vladimir Lenin, Grigory Zinoviev, Lev Kamenev, Leon Trotsky, Joseph Stalin, Grigori Sokolnikov and Andrei Bubnov. This body was short-lived and ceased to operate soon after the Petrograd coup and the overthrow of the Provisional Government.

In March 1919, at the 8th Congress, the party formally established a permanent Politburo to make rapid decisions that could not wait for full sessions of the larger Central Committee. Its first full members were Lenin, Trotsky, Stalin, Kamenev and Nikolay Krestinsky.

After Lenin's death in 1924, authority in the Politburo was contested during the rise of Stalin, who used his post as General Secretary to eliminate dissenting members and made the body subordinate to his personal rule. In 1952 it was renamed the Presidium of the Central Committee and expanded, though real power stayed with a smaller inner leadership. It regained its old name in 1966 under Leonid Brezhnev, and it remained the supreme authority until the reforms of Mikhail Gorbachev and the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991.

The model spread. The Chinese Communist Party set up its Politburo in May 1927 at its 5th National Congress and later created an inner core, the Politburo Standing Committee. Following World War II the states of the Eastern Bloc and allied socialist regimes in Asia, Africa and Latin America adopted politburos on the Soviet pattern, including those of East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Vietnam and Cuba.

Each Party Congress elects a Central Committee, which elects the politburo, the secretariat and a general secretary. This process is called democratic centralism, a doctrine established by Lenin: members debate policy internally, but once a decision is taken all are bound to support it publicly. Membership has two tiers, full members with the vote and candidate members who attend and advise without voting. In practice the existing leadership controls nominations.

The Central Committee is the supreme body between congresses, but its size and infrequent meetings make the Politburo the continuous decision-making council, while the secretariat handles daily implementation and key leaders often sit on both. In Marxist–Leninist states the party is regarded as the vanguard of the people, and as the sole party its policy becomes national policy.
politics-aristotle: Aristotle was born in Stagira, attended Plato's Academy in Athens for about twenty years, tutored the young Alexander the Great in Macedonia and then founded his own school, the Lyceum. He lived in Athens as a metic and was never a fully fledged citizen of any Greek polis. At the end of the Nicomachean Ethics he declared that the inquiry into ethics leads into politics, and the two works are often seen as parts of one treatise on the philosophy of human affairs. The title means the things concerning the polis. For the work Aristotle collected 158 constitutions of city-states, an evidence-based method that contrasts with Plato's approach from first principles in the Republic.

A reference to the assassination of Philip II of Macedon in 336 BCE shows that at least part of the text was composed after that date. The text is not polished, and may have been assembled from shorter works and from notes taken by those who attended his lectures.

The work has eight books. Book I treats the polis as the highest form of community, since man is by nature a political animal. Book II examines the best regime, criticising the communal property of Plato's Republic and discussing the Spartan, Cretan and Carthaginian regimes, which were commonly held to be well managed. Book III considers who counts as a citizen and classifies constitutions as good, when rulers govern for the common good, or perverted, when they govern for themselves, according to whether one, a few or many rule.

Books IV to VI turn to real states, their instability and factionalism, and to democratic and oligarchic constitutions, including a mixed form blending the two. Book VII holds that the purpose of political association is human flourishing, and Book VIII covers education and music.

The order of the books is disputed. Book III ends with a sentence repeated almost verbatim at the start of Book VII, and some editors have moved Books VII and VIII after Book III. Werner Jaeger suggested that the work joins two treatises: Books I to III, VII and VIII, a less mature work with more emphasis on the best regime, and Books IV to VI, which are more empirical. The English word politics derives from its title, and translations include those of Benjamin Jowett (1885), Ernest Barker (1948) and Carnes Lord.
poll-tax: Poll is an archaic word for head, and the sense of counting heads survives in phrases such as polling place. Jewish law, as set out in Exodus, imposed a half-shekel on every man over twenty, rich and poor alike, first for the Tabernacle and later for the upkeep of the Temple of Jerusalem. Priests, women, slaves and minors were exempt. In Rome the tributum capitis fell on provincial subjects but not on Roman citizens. Tertullian called it a badge of slavery, and after the destruction of the Temple in 70 Vespasian imposed an extra poll tax of two denarii on Jews throughout the empire.
Under Islamic rule the jizya usually applied only to free, able-bodied adult men and could vary with income. The Ottoman Empire abolished it in 1855 and replaced it with a military-exemption tax.

In England a poll tax was first levied in 1377, at the request of John of Gaunt, to pay for the Hundred Years War, and in 1381 it is credited as one of the main causes of the Peasants' Revolt. The 17th-century poll taxes were assessed by rank, with dukes paying £100 and knights £20 in 1660, and were dropped after 1698 because collection was inefficient. In France the capitation fell on twenty-two classes, but the clergy bought permanent exemption in 1709 and nobles appointed their own assessors, so the burden fell on the lower classes. Russia imposed a poll tax in 1718 and abolished it in 1886.

Poll taxes are regressive, since the same sum is a smaller share of a larger income, and high amounts provoked revolts such as the Bambatha Rebellion in South Africa in 1906. Canada levied a head tax on Chinese immigrants from 1885 until 1923, and New Zealand taxed Chinese immigrants until 1944. In Britain the Community Charge, called the poll tax, replaced local rates in Scotland in 1988/89 and in England and Wales in 1990/91, and was met by mass nonpayment and riots, among them a protest of more than 200,000 in Trafalgar Square on 31 March 1990. John Major replaced it with the Council Tax.

In the United States, many Southern states used poll taxes after the Fifteenth Amendment to keep poor African Americans from voting. The Twenty-fourth Amendment of 1964 barred them in federal elections.
polonisation: Polonisation, or Polonization, is the acquisition or imposition of elements of Polish culture, in particular the Polish language. It happened in some historic periods among non-Polish populations in territories controlled by or under the influence of Poland. Like other examples of cultural assimilation, it could be voluntary or forced. It was most visible where Polish language or culture was dominant or where adopting it brought prestige or social status, as with the nobilities of Ruthenia and Lithuania. Political authorities have also promoted it administratively, particularly in the interwar period and after the Second World War.

Poles reached Lithuania long before the two countries were united. After the Union of Krewo (1386), when the Lithuanian Grand Duke Jogaila became the Polish king Władysław II Jagiełło, the gradual and voluntary Polonisation of the Lithuanian nobility began. Lithuanian nobles received privileges modelled on those of the Polish nobility, and 47 Lithuanian families were adopted by 45 Polish families and given Polish coats of arms. Lithuania took over Polish institutions such as voivodes, castellans and a Sejm.

Under the Union of Lublin in 1569 the Ukrainian territories of the Grand Duchy passed to the Crown of Poland. Many Ruthenian nobles adopted the Polish language and customs and some became Roman Catholics, and the concept of gente Ruthenus, natione Polonus arose. Conversion to Catholicism was often the most important part of the process, and the weakening of the Orthodox Church was what Belarusian and Ukrainian masses most resented.

In Royal Prussia, where German had been the language of the elite, the role of Polish grew from the early 16th century, and great families such as the Baysen took Polish names, becoming Bażyński. According to some scholars, the biggest successes in Polonisation came after the partitions, in times of persecution of Polishness. In the Vilnius region a mixed speech called simple speech opened the way for Lithuanians to adopt Polish.

In the Second Polish Republic, about 69 percent of the population was ethnically Polish in the census of 1921. National Democrats saw assimilation as a means of unifying the state, while centrist and leftist parties called for broad cultural autonomy in return for loyalty, a policy partly followed under Józef Piłsudski between 1926 and 1935. Belarusians lost most of their schools under the Law on Minority Education of 1924, and Ukrainian Greek Catholics met administrative restrictions. Many Lithuanian schools were closed in 1927 and after 1936. The policy also created an educated class among the minorities, who became instrumental in developing their own identities.
polonnaruwa: Polonnaruwa is the main town of Polonnaruwa District. The modern town, also called New Town, lies about 3 km south of the archaeological zone, and the other part of Polonnaruwa is the royal ancient city of the Kingdom of Polonnaruwa. In ancient times it was also called Pulathisipura and Vijayarajapura. The origin of the name is unknown; it was perhaps a contraction of Pulastya nagara, the city of the Hindu sage Pulastya.

The town lies in the low-country dry zone, with a tropical climate and seasonal rainfall brought by the monsoons. The district receives an average of about 1,584 mm of rain a year. The Mahaweli River and the region's irrigation reservoirs supply water for rice farming.

Polonnaruwa was first established as a military post by the Sinhalese kingdom. The Chola dynasty renamed it Jananathamangalam after invading the country, and Raja Raja Chola I built there a Shiva temple named after his queen, Vanavan Mahadevisvaram, now known as Siva Devale. The northern and central regions were governed directly as a Chola province under Rajendra Chola I. Chola rule ended after 1070, when Vijayabahu I, sending three armies against the city, besieged it for seven months and became its ruler.

Trade and agriculture flourished under his grandson Parakramabahu the Great, who insisted that not a single drop of water falling from the heavens should go to waste. Irrigation systems far superior to those of the Anuradhapura period were built, the largest being the Parakrama Samudra, the Sea of Parakrama. Apart from his immediate successor Nissankamalla I, later monarchs were less strong-willed and prone to quarrels within the court, and their marriage alliances with stronger South Indian kingdoms came to supersede the local royal line. This prompted an invasion by the warlord Kalinga Magha in 1214, which destroyed Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa by fire.

The ancient city of Polonnaruwa has been declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO. Toque macaques have lived in the ruins since the time of human occupation and have continued to thrive long after the humans departed.
polotsk: Polotsk is one of the earliest mentioned cities of the Eastern Slavs: the Primary Chronicle names it under 862, with Murom and Belozersk, and an archaeological expedition suggests it existed in the first half of the 9th century. The name may come from the Polota River, from a Russian word for marsh, or from a tribe, the Polochans. The first known prince was Rogvolod, who ruled from 945 to 978. He promised his daughter Rogneda to Yaropolk, prince of Kiev, but Yaropolk's brother Vladimir attacked Polotsk first, killed Rogvolod and his wife and sons, and married Rogneda. Their eldest son, Izyaslav, became prince of Polotsk and ruled from 989 to 1001.

Between the 10th and 12th centuries the Principality of Polotsk was the dominant centre of power in what is now Belarusian territory. It repeatedly asserted its sovereignty against other centres of Kievan Rus' and controlled vassal territories among the Balts in the west. Its most powerful ruler, Vseslav, reigned from 1044 to 1101.

During the Mongol invasion Polotsk avoided invasion and tribute to the Golden Horde, but became a vassal of the Lithuanian princes in 1240, and Vytenis annexed it by force in 1307. It received a charter of autonomy, the earliest of any city incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and adopted Magdeburg law in 1498. Ivan the Terrible's army captured it in 1563, and it returned to Lithuania 15 years later. Russia seized it in the First Partition in 1772.

Catherine II did not recognise the papal suppression of the Jesuits, so Polotsk became the European centre of the order, with a novitiate opening in 1780. The Jesuit college, opened in 1580, became the Polotsk Academy, which was closed in 1820 when Alexander I exiled the Jesuits; it then had 700 students.

The Saint Sophia Cathedral, built from 1044 to 1066, was a symbol of the independence of Polotsk and rivalled churches of the same name in Novgorod and Kyiv. Troops of Peter I of Russia ruined it, and the present baroque building by Johann Christoph Glaubitz dates from the mid-18th century. The Convent of Saint Euphrosyne keeps 12th-century architecture, notably the Transfiguration Church. The nun Euphrosyne of Polotsk, who lived from 1120 to 1173, built monasteries and promoted literacy, and the printer Francysk Skaryna, born in Polotsk around 1490, printed a Bible in Old Belarusian in 1517.
polyaenus: Polyaenus, whose Greek name Polyainos means much-praised, was a Roman Macedonian author and rhetorician of the 2nd century. The Suda calls him a rhetorician, and he writes that he was accustomed to plead causes before the Roman emperor. He dedicated his Stratagems in War to the two emperors Marcus Aurelius, who ruled from 161 to 180, and Lucius Verus, who ruled from 161 to 169, while they were engaged in the Roman–Parthian War of 161–166. The dedication dates from about 163, and Polyaenus says he was by then too old to accompany them on campaign.

The Stratagems is divided into eight books. The first six record the stratagems of the best-known Greek generals and rulers, the seventh those of non-Greeks, and the eighth those of the Romans and of illustrious women. Parts of the sixth and seventh books are lost, so that of the 900 stratagems he described, 833 survive. The book contains a vast number of anecdotes about many men of antiquity and has uniquely preserved many historical facts. It survives in a single full copy made in the 13th century, which once belonged to Michel Apostolios, and there are five abridged versions.

All his other works have perished. The Suda preserves the titles of two, On Thebes and Tactics, in three books. Stobaeus quotes from two further works, For the koinon of the Macedonians and For the Synedrion, and Polyaenus mentions his intention to write on the memorable actions of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. The Stratagems was first printed in a Latin translation by Justus Vulteius at Basel in 1549, and Isaac Casaubon published the first edition of the Greek text at Lyon in 1589. Further editions followed at Leyden in 1690, Berlin in 1756 and Paris in 1809 by Adamantios Korais. R. Shepherd translated it into English in 1793, and Seybold and Blume into German.
polybius: Polybius was born around 200 BCE in Megalopolis in Arcadia, then an active member of the Achaean League. His father, Lycortas, was a prominent landowning politician who became strategos, the commanding general, of the League. Polybius accompanied his father on embassies and gained experience of political and military affairs during his first thirty years.

Lycortas advocated neutrality during the Roman war against Perseus of Macedon, which aroused Roman suspicion. Polybius was one of 1,000 Achaean nobles sent to Rome as hostages in 167 BCE and was detained there for 17 years. His education won him entry to the leading houses, above all that of Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus, who entrusted him with the education of his sons, Fabius and Scipio Aemilianus.

Polybius wrote a biography of Philopoemen, a treatise called Tactics and a monograph on the Numantine War, all lost. His main work, the Histories, covers 264 to 146 BCE but concentrates on the years from 221 BCE, tracing how Rome overcame Carthage, Macedonia and the Seleucid Empire. Only books I to V survive in full, with a large part of book VI and fragments of the rest. He held that a historian needs political experience and knowledge of geography, and he interviewed participants in the Second Punic War, some of whom had known Hannibal.

Three books depart from the narrative. Book VI sets out the anacyclosis, a cycle of constitutions, and describes the Roman institutions that he believed let the Romans escape it, a mixed constitution in which monarchical, aristocratic and popular elements balanced one another. Book XII discusses how history should be written and criticises earlier historians such as Timaeus.

After the Achaean hostages were released in 150 BCE, Polybius went on campaign with Scipio Aemilianus to Africa and was present at the sack of Carthage in 146 BCE. When Corinth was destroyed in the same year he returned to Greece, used his Roman connections to ease conditions there and helped organise the new form of government in the Greek cities. The last event mentioned in the Histories seems to be the building of the Via Domitia in 118 BCE. Pseudo-Lucian states that he fell from his horse and died aged eighty-two.

The Histories is the only Hellenistic historical work to survive in any substantial form. Livy used it as a source, and its discussion of checks and balances influenced Montesquieu, John Locke and the framers of the United States Constitution. Modern historians admire his use of documents and his citation of sources.
polycrates: Polycrates was the son of Aeaces and ruled Samos until 522 BCE. His family background is not clearly known. J. P. Barron proposed that his ancestors ruled Samos as a dynasty from around 600 BCE, and an inscription of the mid-sixth century records an Aeaces dedicating plunder to Hera. His brothers Pantagnotus and Syloson were at first his co-rulers.

Herodotus reports that Polycrates took power with his two brothers and only fifteen men, after a period of civil strife on Samos. Soon he had Pantagnotus killed and Syloson exiled, and ruled alone. The Roman-period author Polyaenus tells of an armed procession to the Heraion during which the brothers murdered their enemies, though it is uncertain whether this describes the first coup or the later quarrel among the brothers.

Polycrates raised an army of 1,000 archers and a navy of 100 penteconters, the most powerful in the Greek world. Herodotus says he was the first Greek ruler to grasp the importance of sea power, and Thucydides lists him among the thalassocracies of the Aegean. He aimed to bring the Greek islands and the cities of Ionia under his rule, won a great naval victory off Miletus, and seized Delos, the key religious centre of the Aegean. He allied with Amasis of Egypt, but the ancient sources stress wide-ranging raiding more than conquest. Scholars debate whether his penteconters were a state navy or privately owned raiding ships.

Samos under Polycrates was a centre of engineering and culture. Herodotus presents three great Samian works: the 1,036-metre aqueduct tunnel known as the Tunnel of Eupalinos, a deep-water harbour mole and the temple of Hera, the Heraion, one of the three largest temples in the Greek world. He is vague about when they were made, and archaeology suggests the tunnel may be older than his rule. Polycrates was a patron of the poets Anacreon and Ibycus and founded a library.

Herodotus says that Polycrates sent forty triremes crewed by men he thought dangerous to the Persian king Cambyses, but that the crews turned back and attacked him. Modern scholars doubt the tale. Sparta and Corinth later besieged Samos for forty days without success. Around 522 BCE the Persian satrap of Sardis, Oroetes, lured him to Magnesia with a promise of money and had him assassinated. Herodotus does not say how he died, only that it was an undignified end for a glorious ruler.

Most later references to Polycrates concern his ring, thrown into the sea at the advice of Amasis and found again inside a fish, a story Herodotus uses to treat the mutability of fortune. Friedrich Schiller wrote a ballad on it in 1797.
polygnotus: Polygnotus was the son and pupil of the painter Aglaophon. He was a native of Thasos but was adopted by the Athenians and admitted to their citizenship. Later scholars of the classical world considered him one of the first great painters, and some even named him the inventor of the art. Theophrastus called him the inventor of painting, and Quintilian said he was one of the first great painters, whose works deserve inspection for something more than their mere antiquity.

During the time of Cimon, Polygnotus painted for the Athenians a picture of the taking of Troy on the walls of the Stoa Poikile and another, the marriage of the daughters of Leucippus, in the Anacaeum. Other works of his were preserved in the hall at the entrance to the Acropolis. Plutarch mentions that historians and the poet Melanthius attested that Polygnotus did not paint for money but out of goodwill towards the Athenian people.

His most important paintings were the frescoes in the Lesche of the Knidians, a building erected at Delphi by the people of Cnidus. Their subjects were the visit of Odysseus to Hades and the taking of Troy. The traveller Pausanias recorded a careful description of these paintings, figure by figure.

The foundations of the Lesche have been recovered in the French excavations at Delphi, and some archaeologists have tried to reconstruct the paintings from this evidence, though not their colours. The figures were detached and rarely overlapping, ranged in two or three rows one above another, and the further ones were not smaller or dimmer than the nearer. The paintings of this time therefore seem to have followed almost the same plan as contemporary sculptural reliefs.

Polygnotus was among the first Greek painters to produce large murals for public buildings. According to Aristotle, his excellence lay in the beauty of his drawing of individual figures, especially in the ethical and ideal character of his art. Earlier artists had set their figures on a simple groundline and treated the blank areas around them as empty space. Polygnotus arranged his figures on different levels, posing them in a landscape of transparent water and rocky land, and he was among the earliest painters to attempt three-dimensional scenes.
polykleitos: Latin authors including Pliny the Elder and Cicero call him Polykleitos the Sicyonian, while Plato and Pausanias call him the Argive. Modern scholars think Pliny conflated him with a lesser sculptor from Sikyon, a pupil of Pheidias. Pausanias insists the two were different men and that Polykleitos came from Argos, where he must have trained; he was a contemporary of Pheidias and may also have been taught by Ageladas. His son, Polykleitos the Younger, worked in the 4th century BCE, was also a sculptor of athletes and is best known as the architect of the great theatre at Epidaurus.

A figure of an Amazon he made for Ephesus was admired, and his colossal gold and ivory statue of Hera in the Heraion of Argos was compared favourably with Pheidias's Olympian Zeus. He made a bronze male nude, the Doryphoros, which survives in numerous Roman marble copies, as do the Diadumenos, a youth tying a headband, and other works attributed to him. Pliny names him among five major sculptors who competed to make a wounded Amazon for the temple of Artemis. None of his original sculptures is known to survive.

He wrote a treatise, now lost, the Canon, setting out a mathematical basis for an ideal male body. A saying of his is quoted: perfection comes about little by little through many numbers. According to Galen, the Canon took its name from the precise commensurability, symmetria, of all the parts to one another, from finger to finger and to the palm and wrist, and on to the forearm and upper arm. The Doryphoros probably embodied it. Scholars have never agreed on how the Canon was applied; in 1975 Richard Tobin conjectured a system built on the diagonal of a square, starting from the last joint of the little finger.

With Pheidias, Polykleitos created the Classical Greek style, and contrapposto, the pose that shows the body's weight shifting onto one leg, was a source of his fame. Plutarch repeats his remark that the work is hardest when the clay is under the fingernail. The art historian Kenneth Clark wrote that his aim was clarity, balance and completeness. His school lasted for at least three generations, and Pliny and Pausanias name about twenty sculptors in it; Skopas and Lysippus are among the best known of his successors.
polynesia: Polynesia has only about 300,000 to 310,000 square kilometres of land spread over a vast part of the central and southern Pacific, and more than 270,000 of them are in New Zealand. The Hawaiian archipelago makes up about half of the remainder. Most islands, including Hawaii and Samoa, are volcanic and built by hotspots, while New Zealand, Norfolk Island and Ouvéa are the unsubmerged portions of the largely sunken continent of Zealandia. The other main island groups within the triangle are Samoa, Tonga, the Cook Islands, Tuvalu, Tokelau, Niue, Wallis and Futuna and French Polynesia. The French writer Charles de Brosses first used the term Polynésie in 1756 for all the islands of the Pacific, and Jules Dumont d'Urville proposed a narrower definition in 1831.

By linguistic, archaeological and genetic evidence the Polynesians are a subset of the sea-migrating Austronesian people, whose languages trace back through Island Melanesia and Maritime Southeast Asia to Taiwan. The Express Train model, supported by most current data, holds that an expansion out of Taiwan reached Island Melanesia by roughly 1400 BCE and western Polynesia around 900 BCE, followed by a pause of about a thousand years before settlement of central and eastern Polynesia. Two other models, the Entangled Bank and the Slow Boat, stress longer interaction and admixture with peoples in Melanesia. Language, social life and material culture were distinctly Polynesian by 1000 BCE.

The sweet potato, native to the Americas, was widespread in Polynesia when Europeans arrived. Remains in the Cook Islands date to before 1400, and the present consensus is that Polynesians who travelled to South America and back brought it to central Polynesia around 1300. Whether Polynesians reached the Americas, and with what effects, remains contentious. Thor Heyerdahl's claim in the mid-20th century that Polynesians originated in the Americas is regarded as a misconception.

Polynesia is a cultural term for one of the three parts of Oceania, with Melanesia and Micronesia. It divides into West Polynesia, around Tonga and Samoa, and East Polynesia, which includes Tahiti, the Marquesas, Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand. Polynesian languages belong to the Oceanic branch of the Austronesian family and are similar to one another. The ancestral homeland, from a Proto-Nuclear Polynesian word, appears as Hawaiki in New Zealand and Havaiʻi in the Society Islands, and the largest islands of Hawaii and Samoa are called Hawaiʻi and Savaiʻi. Leaders were generally chosen by hereditary bloodline, though Samoa has a system, fa'amatai, that combines heredity with practical skills.
polynesians: Polynesians belong to the Austronesian peoples, who share their origins with the indigenous peoples of Taiwan, Maritime Southeast Asia, Micronesia and Madagascar, as genetic, linguistic and archaeological evidence indicates. The most widely accepted theory has Austronesians migrating out of Taiwan between 3000 and 1000 BCE in catamarans and outrigger boats with crab claw sails. Thor Heyerdahl's belief that Polynesians descended from people who sailed on rafts from South America has been rejected.

Their direct ancestors are thought to be the Lapita culture, which emerged in Island Melanesia and Micronesia around 1500 BCE and is distinguished by dentate-stamped pottery. Genetic studies find that about 79% of the Polynesian gene pool is Austronesian and 21% Australo-Melanesian, the result of limited admixture as the ancestors moved quickly through Melanesia.

The Lapita eastward expansion halted when it reached Fiji, Samoa and Tonga by around 900 BCE. For about 1,500 years it went no further, and in these islands the Lapita lost the technology of pottery-making for reasons that are unknown. Voyaging resumed around 700 CE, spreading to the Cook Islands, French Polynesia and the Marquesas, and from there to Hawaii by about 900, Easter Island by about 1000 and New Zealand by about 1200.

A study of 2020 found that Polynesians and the Indigenous peoples of South America came into contact around 1200, centuries before Europeans reached either. Navigators reached the farthest corners of the Pacific by reading stars, currents, clouds and the movements of birds, skills passed down through the generations.

Polynesian languages form a branch of the Oceanic subfamily of Austronesian. The Māori of New Zealand are the largest Polynesian population, followed by Samoans, Native Hawaiians, Tahitians, Tongans and Cook Islands Māori. There are an estimated 2 million ethnic Polynesians. Many live in the independent states of Samoa, Niue, the Cook Islands, Tonga and Tuvalu; others form minorities in Australia, Chile (Easter Island), New Zealand, France (French Polynesia and Wallis and Futuna) and the United States (Hawaii and American Samoa). Polynesian outliers lie in Micronesia, Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu and Fiji.
polyperchon: Polyperchon was a Macedonian Greek general whose father, Simmias, belonged to the aristocracy of Tymphaia in Upper Macedonia and was descended from the region's local kings. His brother Andromenes had four sons who became commanders under Alexander the Great. Claudius Aelian reports a rumour that Polyperchon was a bandit in his youth, but the passage is among many unreliable claims about the early years of well-known figures. He served Philip II and then accompanied Alexander on his long journeys.

After the Battle of Issus in 333 BCE Polyperchon took command of a battalion of the Macedonian phalanx in place of Ptolemy, who had fallen, and he held it at Gaugamela in 331 BCE. In 328 BCE he was left in Bactria to prevent rebellion, and at the Battle of the Hydaspes in 326 BCE he guarded the base camp with Alcetas and Craterus.

In August 324 BCE Alexander sent Craterus home with 10,000 veterans to replace Antipater as regent and made Polyperchon his deputy. Both were still in Cilicia when Alexander died in June 323 BCE. Polyperchon then governed Macedon and Greece while Antipater and Craterus crossed into Asia against Perdiccas, and he crushed an Aetolian force in Thessaly under Menon of Pharsalus.

In 319 BCE the aging Antipater named Polyperchon regent of the Macedonian Empire and made his own son Cassander chiliarch, second in command. Cassander, who had expected to succeed his father, refused the arrangement, and open hostility followed. Polyperchon allied with Eumenes and proclaimed the freedom of the Greek cities, but he suffered a defeat at Megalopolis in 317 BCE, his fleet was destroyed by Antigonus, and Cassander took Athens in 316 BCE and drove him from Macedon. Polyperchon joined Alexander's mother Olympias in Epirus. She led an army into Macedon and had King Philip murdered, but Cassander captured and killed her in 316 BCE and took Roxana and the boy king Alexander IV into custody.

Polyperchon withdrew to the Peloponnese, holding Corinth and Sicyon, and later put forward Heracles, a reputed son of Alexander, against Cassander. In 309 BCE he murdered the boy and reached a settlement in which Cassander recognised him as strategos of the Peloponnese with equal authority. After Ptolemy seized cities there in 308 BCE he reconquered much of the peninsula by 304 BCE, but in 303 BCE Demetrius Poliorcetes reversed many of these gains. After that he disappears from the record, though a passage of Plutarch suggests he may have lived into the early 3rd century BCE.
pomaks: The Pomaks are Bulgarian-speaking Muslims. Bulgarian, Greek and Turkish historians have interpreted their precise origin differently, but they are generally considered descendants of native Eastern Orthodox Bulgarians and of Paulicians who converted to Islam during Ottoman rule in the Balkans. The conversion was gradual. Under the millet system people were bound to their communities by religion rather than ethnic origin, and Ottoman law did not recognise ethnicity, so a Muslim of any background had the same rights and privileges.

In North Central Bulgaria the Ottoman authorities asked Paulicians in 1689, after the Chiprovtsi Uprising, to join one of the officially recognised religions. Some became Orthodox or Catholic and others became Muslim and were called Pomaks. In the Central Rhodopes a mass turn to Islam took place in the 16th and 17th centuries. Bulgarian tradition says Grand Vizier Köprülü Mehmed Pasha threatened the people of the Chepino Valley with death, but recent investigations hold that the theory of forced conversion lacks solid grounds, and some authors link the conversions to a tenfold increase of the jizya tax.

After the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878, Pomaks in the Vacha valley revolted against Eastern Rumelia and set up an autonomous state, the Republic of Tamrash. It ended in 1886 when the Ottoman government accepted Bulgarian rule over Eastern Rumelia. During the Balkan Wars an Islamic revolt began in 1913 in the Eastern Rhodopes and Western Thrace, and a Provisional Government of Western Thrace was set up in Komotini on 1 September 1913. Greece took over Western Thrace in June 1920. The Pomaks of Thrace were exempted, with Turks and Roma, from the population exchange provided by the Lausanne Treaty of 1923.

In Bulgaria, Pomaks were the subject of three state-sponsored assimilation campaigns in the 20th century, in 1912, the 1940s, and the 1960s and 1970s. They involved replacing Turkish-Arabic names with Bulgarian Christian ones and, in the first, conversion to Orthodoxy. Many Pomaks resisted. The third campaign was reversed in 1989.

Pomaks live mainly in the Rhodope Mountains of Bulgaria, in Western Thrace in Greece, and in Turkey, where most of them now live, mainly in Eastern Thrace. Bulgaria officially calls them Bulgarian Muslims and counts about 220,000. In Bulgaria they speak almost the same dialects as their Christian neighbours, while in Greece and Turkey they call their language Pomak. Today they declare a variety of identities, depending largely on the country they live in.
pomerania: Pomerania lies along the Bay of Pomerania on the southern Baltic shore, between the rivers Recknitz, Trebel, Tollense and Augraben in the west and the Vistula in the east. Its name is Slavic and means land by the sea. Most of it is coastal lowland on the Central European Plain, with a southern belt of hills and moraine-dammed lakes, the Pomeranian Lake District, and generally poor, sandy or marshy soil. The western coast is jagged, with the islands of Rügen, Usedom and Wolin and the Lagoon of Szczecin.

The term has no universally accepted definition. German usage means Hither and Farther Pomerania only, Polish usage adds Pomerelia, the eastern part, which includes Kashubia, Kociewie, the Tuchola Forest and Chełmno Land. It was first mentioned in an imperial document of 1046, naming Zemuzil, Duke of the Pomeranians.

People have lived in the area since the end of the Vistula Glacial Stage some 13,000 years ago; later peoples included Baltic and Germanic peoples and, in the Dark Ages, West Slavic tribes and Vikings. From the 10th century early Polish rulers subdued the region, and Gdańsk was established under Mieszko I. In the late 12th century the western part fell under the suzerainty of Denmark and the Holy Roman Empire, and the Duchy of Pomerania became Christian under Otto of Bamberg. In the early 14th century the Teutonic Knights annexed Pomerelia; it returned to the Polish Crown in 1466 after the Thirteen Years' War. The Duchy of Pomerania adopted the Reformation in 1534.

The Thirty Years' War ravaged and depopulated the duchy. When the Griffin house died out, the duchy was divided in 1648 between the Swedish Empire and Brandenburg-Prussia. Prussia gained southern Swedish Pomerania in 1720, annexed Pomerelia in 1772 and 1793, and received the rest of Swedish Pomerania in 1815. Both Pomeranian provinces joined the German Empire in 1871. After the First World War Pomerelia returned to Poland and Gdańsk became the Free City of Danzig.

The first battle of the Second World War was fought at Westerplatte in September 1939. Under German occupation more than 40,000 Poles died in executions, camps, prisons and forced labour, and the Stutthof concentration camp stood in the region. After 1945 the border moved west to the Oder–Neisse line and the German inhabitants were expelled; the area was resettled mainly by Poles.

Pomerania is split between Poland and Germany. Its largest cities are Gdańsk and Szczecin. The western part, Hither Pomerania, belongs to the German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania; most of the rest lies in the Polish West Pomeranian, Pomeranian and Kuyavian-Pomeranian voivodeships. Kashubians, descendants of the medieval West Slavic Pomeranians, are numerous in rural Pomerelia.
pomerelia: Pomerelia lies west of the Vistula and east of the Łeba, mostly within the Pomeranian Voivodeship. It is traditionally divided into Kashubia, Kociewie, Tuchola Forest, the Vistula Fens and Chełmno Land, inhabited by Kashubians, Kociewians, Borowians and Chełminians. The name means small Pomerania and has been used since the Late Middle Ages to distinguish it from Hither and Farther Pomerania to the west. Its earliest appearance is in the Pomerellische Handveste of 1441, issued by the Teutonic Grandmaster Konrad von Ehrlichshausen.

The area was settled by West Slavic and Lechitic tribes in the 7th and 8th centuries. In the tenth century it was incorporated into early Poland, by Mieszko I or perhaps by his father, and Mieszko founded Gdańsk between 970 and 980 to control the mouth of the Vistula. Its ties with Poland loosened in the eleventh century, and Bolesław III Wrymouth re-established direct control in 1116. After 1138 local governors of the Samborides dynasty became semi-independent, with Oliwa Abbey as the Christian centre.

In 1210 King Valdemar II of Denmark invaded and Mestwin I became his vassal, but Mestwin's son Swietopelk II gained full independence in 1227. He chartered Gdańsk with Lübeck law and settled his conflicts with the Teutonic Order, his eastern neighbour from 1230, in 1253. By the Treaty of Kępno of 15 February 1282 Mestwin II transferred suzerainty to Przemysł II of Poland, and kept control until his death in 1294.

After a revolt of the nobility in 1300 Wenceslaus II of Bohemia took the region, and Władysław I the Elbow-high recaptured it in 1306. The Teutonic Knights, called in against Brandenburg, kept it for themselves, and the dispute led to Polish–Teutonic Wars through the 14th and 15th centuries. In 1454 Casimir IV Jagiellon agreed to re-incorporate the region, and after the Thirteen Years' War (1454–1466) the Order renounced its claims. It became the Pomeranian Voivodeship within Royal Prussia, and Gdańsk was the largest port of Poland, exporting mostly grain.

Historic Pomerelia forms the bulk of the Pomeranian Voivodeship, with its southern part in the Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship and a small western fragment in the West Pomeranian Voivodeship. Its largest city is Gdańsk. Prussia annexed it in the Partitions of Poland, and most of it returned to Poland after 1918 and again in 1945.
pomorie: The town stands on a narrow rocky peninsula that extends 3.5 km into the Black Sea on the north-west coast of Burgas Bay, in Burgas Province. The sea surrounds it on the south, east and north-east, and Lake Pomorie, an ultrasaline lagoon and the northernmost of the Burgas Lakes, lies to the north. Only to the west-north-west does it join the Pomorie field, part of the Burgas lowland. The climate is humid subtropical, with winters milder than in the inland part of the country.

The name Anchialos comes from Ancient Greek words meaning near and sea, and the Bulgars called the town Tuthon. It was possibly founded in the 5th or 4th century BCE as a colony of Apollonia, today Sozopol, and Strabo's Geographica mentions it as a small town. Rome conquered the western Black Sea coast under Marcus Licinius Crassus in 29-28 BCE. Anchialos was formally proclaimed a city under Emperor Trajan and prospered in the 2nd and 3rd centuries under the Severan Dynasty as the most important import and export station of Thrace.

Barbarian invasions ended this prosperity in the middle of the 3rd century, and the Goths briefly captured the city around 270. Its closeness to Constantinople later made it a key food supply centre. After the First Bulgarian Empire formed in 681, Anchialos became a frontier fortress: Bulgar Khan Tervel defeated the forces of Justinian II near it in 708, Khan Krum took it in 812 and settled Slavs and Bulgars there, and the Byzantines restored their control in 864. Bulgaria held it again until 971, when Byzantium reconquered it and kept it for two centuries.

The town submitted to Ottoman rule in 1453, together with Constantinople, and as Ahyolu became the centre of a kaza and of an eparchy of the Patriarchate of Constantinople. Two patriarchs of Constantinople came from it. Anchialos was liberated from Ottoman rule on 27 January 1878 and joined Eastern Rumelia, then Bulgaria in 1885. In July 1906 the town was burnt down and over 300 Greeks were murdered by Bulgarian refugees from Macedonia, and European diplomacy compared the destruction to the anti-Jewish pogroms in Russia. It was renamed Pomorie in 1934 or 1935.

Pomorie is a seaside resort and the administrative centre of Pomorie Municipality, with a population of 13,926 at the 2020 count. It is known for wine and salt production, and its landmarks include a Salt Museum, a municipal museum and gallery, an ancient Thracian beehive tomb of the 3rd century CE, the Church of the Transfiguration of God (1765) and St George's Monastery (1856).
pompeii: Pompeii stood about 40 metres above sea level on a coastal lava plateau created by earlier eruptions of Mount Vesuvius, beside the mouth of the navigable Sarno River, which served early Greek and Phoenician sailors as a haven port. The first stable settlements on the site date to the 8th century BCE, when the Oscans founded five villages in the area. The Samnites conquered Greek Cumae between 423 and 420 BCE, and it is likely that Pompeii had already been conquered around 424 BCE.

Pompeii rebelled against Rome in the Social Wars, and in 89 BCE Sulla besieged it; the impact craters of thousands of ballista shots can still be seen in its walls. It surrendered and became a Roman colony, its people were granted Roman citizenship and quickly assimilated, and Latin became the main language. Urban development accelerated from about 30 BCE, with an amphitheatre, two theatres and at least four public baths. The city was home to some 11,000 people, and it had at least 31 bakeries.

Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE in one of the deadliest eruptions in history, which lasted two days. The first phase was a rain of pumice lasting about 18 hours, which allowed most inhabitants to escape; only about 1,150 bodies have been found on the site. In the night or early the next day pyroclastic flows began, scorching clouds of ash that knocked down structures in their path and incinerated or suffocated the remaining population. Pompeii lay buried under 4 to 6 metres of ash and pumice. Titus donated large sums to the victims, but no recovery work was done. Survivors reoccupied the site as a small informal settlement that lasted until the fifth century.

The site's name and location were forgotten, though it appeared on the Tabula Peutingeriana of the 4th century. It remained largely undisturbed until its rediscovery in the late 16th century, and major excavations began in the mid-18th century, marking the emergence of modern archaeology. Early efforts were haphazard or marred by looting. Organic remains decayed within the ash, allowing archaeologists to make moulds of figures in their final moments, and graffiti on walls preserve the colloquial Vulgar Latin of the time. Two-thirds of the city has been excavated, and Pompeii is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
pompeius-trogus: Pompeius Trogus was a Gallo-Roman historian from the Celtic Vocontii of Narbonese Gaul who lived under the emperor Augustus and was therefore a contemporary of Livy. His grandfather served under Pompey in his war against Sertorius and, through Pompey's influence, obtained Roman citizenship, so the family took their patron's praenomen and nomen, Gnaeus Pompeius, as was customary. Trogus's father served under Julius Caesar as his secretary and interpreter. Trogus seems to have been a polymath, and following Aristotle and Theophrastus he wrote books on the natural history of animals and plants.

His principal work was the Philippic Histories and the Origin of the Whole World and the Places of the Earth, in 44 volumes. According to its surviving epitome, its main theme was the Macedonian Empire founded by Philip II, but it functioned as a general history of the parts of the world that fell under Alexander the Great and his successors, with extensive ethnographical and geographical digressions. Trogus began with Ninus, the traditional founder of Nineveh, and ended at about the same point as Livy, in 9 CE. The development of the East from the Assyrians to the Parthians is covered extensively, while early Roman history and the history of the Iberian Peninsula are briefly treated in the last two books.

The work drew on earlier Greek historians such as Theopompus, whose Philippica may have suggested the title, Ephorus, Timaeus and Polybius. Because such a work was thought beyond the ability of a Gallo-Roman, it is generally assumed that he used a Greek compilation such as the Universal History of Timagenes of Alexandria. Trogus criticised Sallust and Livy for putting elaborate speeches into the mouths of their characters.

The Philippic Histories is lost and survives in excerpts by other authors, including Jerome and Augustine, and in a loose epitome by Justin, who preserved the parts he found most important or interesting. The last event Justin records is the recovery of Roman standards from the Parthians in 20 BCE. Separate summaries of the books, the prologi, are preserved in the manuscripts of Justin. Even in this mutilated state the work is an important authority for the ancient history of the East. Trogus's books on animals and plants were quoted extensively by Pliny the Elder. His account of the Jews, set in the history of the Seleucid Empire, is, with the passages in Tacitus, the most extensive description of the Jews in classical Latin literature.
pompey: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus was born in Picenum, the eldest son of Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo, who was the first of his family branch to reach senatorial status and became consul in 89 BCE. Pompey began his career serving with his father in the Social War. After Strabo died in 87 BCE, Pompey stood trial for his father's alleged embezzlement and was acquitted. In 83 BCE he raised a legion from his father's clients and veterans and joined Sulla, who greeted him with the title imperator.

In Sulla's civil war Pompey defeated the Marian forces in Sicily and Africa. His opponents nicknamed him adulescentulus carnifex, the young butcher, for the execution of Carbo, while his troops called him Magnus, after Alexander the Great. He later commanded in Spain against Quintus Sertorius and arrived in Italy in time to massacre 6,000 fugitives from the army of Spartacus. He was consul with Marcus Licinius Crassus in 70 BCE, when the tribunes recovered powers Sulla had removed.

Under the Lex Gabinia he was given wide powers to suppress the pirates of the Mediterranean, and under the lex Manilia he took over the war against Mithridates VI of Pontus. He then reorganised the East and intervened in Judea, backing Hyrcanus II against his brother Aristobulus II. Back in Rome he held a third triumph in 61 BCE, but the Senate refused to ratify his eastern settlement. In 60 BCE he joined Crassus and Julius Caesar in the First Triumvirate and married Caesar's daughter Julia.

Julia died in 54 BCE and Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BCE, removing the ties that held the alliance. Pompey aligned himself with the optimates, was elected sole consul in 52 BCE, and in 49 BCE war broke out with Caesar. Defeated at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE, he fled to Egypt and was killed on 28 September 48 BCE at Pelusium by Lucius Septimius, a Roman officer serving the Egyptian army.

Ancient and later writers treated his fall as a great subject. Lucan retold the civil war in his epic De Bello Civili, now known as the Pharsalia, and Renaissance English and French dramatists returned to the story, among them George Chapman and Pierre Corneille. Pompey's money also built the Theatre of Pompey, one of the best known structures of ancient Rome.
pomponius-mela: Little is known of Pomponius Mela beyond his name and birthplace, the small town of Tingentera or Cingentera on Algeciras Bay in southern Spain, identified as Iulia Traducta. The text naming it is corrupt. He wrote under the emperor Claudius: his allusion to a proposed British expedition by the reigning emperor is almost certainly to that of Claudius in 43 CE, and several references to events of the reign of Augustus, especially new names given to Spanish towns, show it cannot refer to Julius Caesar. Mela belonged to the Italic communities settled in Spain, like the two Senecas, Lucan, Martial and Quintilian. It has been conjectured that he was related to Marcus Annaeus Mela, son of Seneca the Elder and father of Lucan.

His short work, De situ orbis in three books, fills less than a hundred pages of ordinary print. Apart from the geographical parts of Pliny's Historia naturalis, which cites Mela as an important authority, it is the only formal treatise on the subject in Classical Latin. It mainly agrees with Greek writers from Eratosthenes to Strabo. Mela describes the coasts in the manner of a periplus, probably because his material came from navigators. He begins at the Straits of Gibraltar, follows the south coast of the Mediterranean, goes round Syria, Asia Minor and the Black Sea and returns to Spain, then follows the ocean coast from Spain and Gaul round to India and back.

He divides the Earth into five zones, of which only two are habitable, and uniquely among ancient geographers asserts that antichthones live in the southern temperate zone, cut off by the torrid zone. Like most classical geographers he regards the Caspian Sea as an inlet of the Northern Ocean. His knowledge of western Europe was ahead of the Greek writers: he defines the coasts of Spain and Gaul and the Bay of Biscay more accurately than Eratosthenes or Strabo, and he is the first to name the Orcades, or Orkney Islands. He also speaks of a great northern bay, the Codanus sinus, with a large island called Codanovia.

The work remained in use nearly to the year 1500. The first printed edition appeared at Milan in 1471, and the first critical edition was by Joachim Vadian in 1518. Johann Friedrich Gronovius edited it in 1685 and 1696, Arthur Golding's English translation appeared in 1585, and F. E. Romer published a recent English translation in 1998.
ponary-massacre: Ponary, now Paneriai, is a suburb of Vilnius. After the Soviet invasion of Poland in September 1939 the region was occupied and, on 10 October, transferred to Lithuania under the Soviet-Lithuanian Mutual Assistance Treaty. Following the Soviet annexation of Lithuania in June 1940, work began near Ponary on an oil storage facility for a future military airfield. It was never completed, and the Wehrmacht took the area in June 1941 during Operation Barbarossa. The killing squads used the six large pits dug for the storage tanks to hide the bodies of those they killed.

The killings began as soon as SS Einsatzkommando 9 reached Vilna on 2 July 1941. Most were carried out by the Ypatingasis burys, a Lithuanian volunteer unit eighty men strong. The Vilna Ghetto was established in September, and that month 3,700 Jews were shot in one operation and 6,000 in another, after being rounded up in the city and walked to Paneriai. Most victims were stripped before being shot. By the end of 1941 about 50,000 to 60,000 Vilna Jews had been killed, though estimates for this period differ widely. The pace slowed in 1942, when the Wehrmacht took on the ghettoised Jewish workers as slave labour.

As Soviet troops advanced in 1943, the Nazi units tried to hide the crime under the directive known as Aktion 1005. Eighty prisoners from the Stutthof concentration camp were forced to dig up the bodies and burn them. On 19 April 1944 the prisoners escaped through a tunnel dug with spoons, and the eleven who survived the war helped reveal the massacre.

The total number of victims is put at up to 100,000, of whom about 70,000 were Jews. Among the others were Polish intellectuals, including the professor Kazimierz Pelczar and the priest Romuald Świrkowski, members of the Armia Krajowa resistance, Soviet prisoners of war and Romani people. Under Soviet rule the official line was that the site held only Soviet citizens. The Polish journalist Kazimierz Sakowicz recorded the killings in a diary kept in hiding, which Rahel Margolis found and published in 1999. The site has monuments to Holocaust victims, erected in 1991, and to Polish victims, erected in 1990 and rebuilt in 2000, and a small museum.
ponce-puerto-rico: Ponce lies on the southern coastal plain of Puerto Rico, on the shore of the Caribbean Sea, south of Adjuntas, Utuado and Jayuya and between Peñuelas and Juana Díaz. The municipality has 31 barrios, 12 of them in the urban area, and is the second largest on the island by land area. It includes Cerro de Punta, the island's highest peak at 1,340 metres, and part of the Toro Negro Forest. Its historic district, Ponce Pueblo, lies about 4.8 kilometres inland from the coast.

The region belonged to the Taíno territory of Guaynia. Agüeybaná, a cacique who led it, was among those who greeted Juan Ponce de León when he came to the island in 1508. Four archaeological sites in the municipality are significant: Canas, Tibes, Caracoles and El Bronce. The city was founded on 12 August 1692 and is named after Juan Ponce de León y Loayza, great-grandson of the conquistador. Its first mayor was Pedro Sánchez de Matos. In the early 19th century Ponce was still one of dozens of hamlets on the island, whose people lived on subsistence agriculture, cattle raising and maritime contraband with foreigners.

During the 19th century a new architectural style, later called Ponce Creole, was born in the city, and architects mixed Art Nouveau and neoclassical styles. The Teatro La Perla was built in 1864. Ponce was the first city in Puerto Rico where Protestant churches were built, and the Ponce Cathedral dates from 1839. When the United States invaded Puerto Rico in 1898, Ponce was the largest city on the island, with a population of 22,000, and it had the best road to San Juan and underwater telegraph cables to Jamaica and the West Indies.

The taking of the port by American troops was a turning point in the campaign, since it let them bring in men and war material. Bomba and Plena music grew up mainly in the south of the island, and Ponce, especially Barrio San Antón, is known as a birthplace of these rhythms.

Ponce became the first municipality in Puerto Rico to obtain autonomy, on 27 October 1992, under the Autonomous Municipalities Act. Its historic centre has been revitalised under the Ponce en Marcha project, and it has many museums. The economy was long based on sugarcane and now rests on manufacturing, retail and tourism, and the Port of Ponce is the island's chief Caribbean port. Ponce has 166,327 inhabitants according to the 2010 census, and March 21 is observed each year in memory of the Ponce massacre.
pondicherry: Pondicherry stands on the south-east coast of India, with the Bay of Bengal to the east and the state of Tamil Nadu around it. Its name comes from the Tamil putu-cēri, new village, and the French first spelt it Poudichéry. The u was later misread as n, and the spelling Pondichéry stuck. It was also known as Vedapuri, as the settlement was once the home of scholars versed in the Vedas. A marketplace called Poduke, mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea as a port for Roman trade, has been identified with Arikamedu, about 3 kilometres from the modern city.

Before the Europeans came, the area was ruled in turn by the Pallavas, the Cholas, the Pandya dynasty, the Nayaks of Gingee under the Vijayanagara Empire, and from 1614 to 1638 by the Sultan of Bijapur. Portuguese traders came in 1521, followed by the Dutch and the Danes in the 17th century. In 1674 the French East India Company set up a trading centre, and François Martin turned it into the chief French settlement in India. He dealt with the sultans of Golconda, traded in jewellery and precious stones, and faced strong opposition from the Dutch and the English. A canal divided the city into a French Quarter and an Indian Quarter.

The Dutch captured Pondicherry on 21 August 1693, during the Nine Years' War, after a fleet of seventeen ships under Laurens Pit the Younger bombarded it for two weeks until Martin surrendered. It was handed back to the French in 1699 under the Peace of Ryswick. The British took it on 16 January 1761 and returned it by the Treaty of Paris of 1763, took it again in 1793 and returned it in 1814. France added Mahé in 1720, Yanam in 1731 and Karaikal in 1738.

In March 1954 the municipalities of Pondicherry and Karaikal, representing roughly 90 per cent of the people of the French possessions, called for a merger with India. A vote of 178 councillors on 18 October 1954 gave 170 votes in favour. The de facto transfer took place on 1 November 1954, and the treaty for the de jure transfer, signed in 1956, was ratified by the French National Assembly only on 16 August 1962.

Pondicherry, officially Puducherry, is the capital of the Union Territory of Puducherry, and most of its people speak Tamil. Its old districts keep colonial buildings, churches and French-style avenues. The Sri Aurobindo Ashram on Rue de la Marine is one of the most important ashrams in India, and the township of Auroville lies about 8 kilometres to the north-west. The French Institute of Pondicherry and a French consulate are among the French institutions in the city.
pont-du-gard: Nemausus was awkwardly placed for a water supply. Plains to its south and east lay too low for water to flow to the city, and the hills to the west were too difficult for engineers, so the only real alternative was the springs of the Fontaine d'Eure near Ucetia (Uzès). The straight-line distance is only about 20 km, but the aqueduct winds for around 50 km to get round the Garrigues de Nîmes, since a tunnel through them would have been 8 to 10 kilometres long.

The spring lies only 17 m above the distribution basin in Nîmes, giving an average gradient of about 1 in 3,000. Newer excavations suggest construction took place between 40 and 60 CE: coins found in the outflow at Nîmes are no older than the reign of Claudius (41–54 CE). It is believed to have taken about fifteen years and 800 to 1,000 workers.

The bridge is 274 m long, with three recessed levels of arches whose main piers stand in line one above another. Its width varies from 9 m at the bottom to 3 m at the top. It was built largely without mortar or clamps, from an estimated 50,400 tons of local shelly limestone; some blocks weigh up to 6 tons. Many blocks carry numbers and inscriptions such as fronte dextra, guiding the builders to their places.

The water conduit runs along the top. Its walls are dressed masonry and its floor concrete, covered with a stucco containing shards of pottery and tile and sealed with maltha, a mixture of slaked lime, pork grease and the juice of unripe figs. The aqueduct is estimated to have supplied about 40,000 cubic metres of water a day, which took nearly 27 hours to reach the city. Constant cleaning by workers called circitores was needed to remove mineral deposits and roots.

Maintenance was neglected from the 4th century, and the aqueduct had probably gone out of use by about the 6th century. The bridge survived largely because it served as a toll bridge: in the 13th century the French king granted the seigneurs of Uzès the right to levy tolls, which later passed to the Bishops of Uzès, who were responsible for its upkeep. In the 1620s the Duke of Rohan had one side of the second row of arches cut back to move his artillery across, weakening it severely.

A road bridge by the engineer Henri Pitot was added in 1743–47, and Napoleon III backed repairs carried out between 1855 and 1858. Jean-Jacques Rousseau, visiting in 1738, wrote that it was the only time in his life that an object surpassed his expectation. UNESCO listed the site in 1985, and from 1996 a four-year project removed traffic and built a visitor centre.
pontic-caspian-steppe: The steppe stretches from the northern shores of the Black Sea, the Pontus Euxinus of antiquity, to the northern area around the Caspian Sea, where it ends at the Ural-Caspian narrowing and joins the Kazakh Steppe of Central Asia as part of the larger Eurasian Steppe. It covers about 994,000 km2 across north-eastern Bulgaria, south-eastern Romania, Moldova, southern and eastern Ukraine, the North Caucasus and the Lower Volga region. The East European forest steppe bounds it on the north, and the drier Caspian lowland desert lies between it and the Caspian Sea. Its flora and fauna are distinctive, and the Ponto-Caspian seas are the remains of the Turgai Sea, an extension of the Paratethys.

The area corresponds to the Cimmeria, Scythia and Sarmatia of classical antiquity. Across several millennia numerous tribes of nomadic horsemen used the steppe, and many went on to conquer lands in the settled regions of Central and Eastern Europe, West Asia and South Asia. Genetic research has identified the region as the most probable place where horses were first domesticated. The Kurgan hypothesis, the most prevalent theory in Indo-European studies, places the homeland of the speakers of Proto-Indo-European on the steppe.

A sequence of prehistoric cultures is listed for the region, among them the Khvalynsk culture (5000-3500 BCE), the Sredny Stog culture (4500-3500 BCE), the Yamnaya or Kurgan cultures (3500-2300 BCE), the Catacomb culture (3000-2200 BCE) and the Srubna culture (1600-1200 BCE). Peoples and states with origins on the steppe include the Cimmerians, Scythians and Sarmatians, then the Ostrogoths, Alans, Huns, Avars, Khazars and Pechenegs, the Kipchaks and Cumans of the 11th to 13th centuries and the Golden Horde of the 13th to 15th. Kievan Rus', the Cossacks, Kalmyks, Nogais, the Crimean Khanate and the Russian Empire belong to its later history.
pontifical-swiss-guard: The Guard has its origins in the 15th century. Pope Sixtus IV allied with the Swiss Confederacy and built barracks in Via Pellegrino, foreseeing the recruiting of Swiss mercenaries. Innocent VIII renewed the pact to use Swiss troops against the Duke of Milan, and Alexander VI used them in his alliance with the King of France. During the Italian Wars the Swiss were a fixture on the front lines among the warring factions. Cardinal Giuliano della Rovere, who had been Bishop of Lausanne and knew the Swiss well, became Pope Julius II in 1503 and asked the Swiss Diet for a constant corps of 200 mercenaries, financed by the Augsburg merchants Ulrich and Jacob Fugger.
The first contingent of 150 soldiers left on foot in September 1505 under Kaspar von Silenen and entered Rome on 22 January 1506, now regarded as the official date of the Guard's foundation.

Its most significant hostile engagement came on 6 May 1527 during the Sack of Rome. As the troops of Emperor Charles V advanced, 147 of the 189 Guards, including their commander Caspar Röist, died fighting so that Clement VII could escape through the Passetto di Borgo, escorted by the other 42. Clement replaced the depleted Guard with 200 German mercenaries, and in 1537 Paul III ordered it reinstated; anti-papal sentiment in Switzerland hindered recruitment.

After the Italian Wars the Guard ceased to serve as a combat unit and became mostly a protection and honour guard, though twelve members served at the Battle of Lepanto in 1571. It was disbanded and reinstated in 1800, 1814 and 1849, and in the later 19th century it declined into a ceremonial body with low standards. The modern Guard is the product of reforms by its commander Jules Repond from 1910 to 1921, who recruited only native Swiss, introduced rigorous exercises and designed the Renaissance-style uniform, completed in May 1914. His strictness led to a week of open mutiny in July 1913.

The Guard protects the Pope and the Apostolic Palace in Vatican City and accompanies the Pope on journeys abroad. Overall security in the city-state is the work of a separate body, the Corps of Gendarmerie of Vatican City. After the attempt on the life of Pope John Paul II on 13 May 1981 the Guard placed greater emphasis on its non-ceremonial roles and equipped itself with modern small arms, though its dress uniform of striped red, dark blue and yellow, high plumed helmet and halberd remain. Recruits must be unmarried Swiss Catholic men between 19 and 30 who have completed basic training with the Swiss Armed Forces.
popayan: Popayán lies in the Pubenza Valley in southwestern Colombia, between two mountain ranges, at 1,760 metres above sea level, with an average temperature of 18 °C. The city is known as the white city for the colour of its colonial buildings and as the University City, since the University of Cauca, founded in 1827 by decree of General Francisco de Paula Santander, is based there. The origin of the name is uncertain: one theory reads it as two villages with reed roofs, another derives it from a cacique named Payán, and a third from the Quechua for the valley of the river.

Nothing is recorded of the pre-Hispanic village of Popayán. El Morro del Tulcán, a truncated pyramid built between 500 and 1600 CE, was already abandoned when the Spanish arrived, and analysis of dental samples suggests that those buried there probably belonged to the upper class. The conquistador Sebastián de Belalcázar arrived on 13 January 1537. In the 16th and 17th centuries Popayán was governed by an appointed governor under the Royal Audience of Quito, part of the Viceroyalty of Peru.

Its position between Lima, Quito and Cartagena made it important, and even after the Pacific was reached it remained a transfer point for gold and other riches going to Cartagena on their way to Spain. It also served as a colonial mint, producing gold escudo coins and silver reales from 1760 through 1819, and it continued to strike coins for the Republic of Colombia after 1826. A battle for independence was fought at the country house of Calibio on 15 January 1814. During that struggle Antonio Nariño had the lead weights of the cathedral clock tower's English clock, installed in 1737, changed to supply metal for ammunition. In 1873 the Humilladero Bridge was built over a fault, and it has stayed intact through many earthquakes.

Popayán is the capital of the department of Cauca, with a municipal population of 318,059 and an area of 483 square kilometres. It has been the home of seventeen Colombian presidents. An earthquake of 31 March 1983, lasting eighteen seconds, toppled many of the city's buildings; reconstruction took more than ten years, and the quake led to Colombia's first seismic design code. The historic centre keeps its baroque architecture and its churches, among them San Francisco, Santo Domingo and the cathedral. In 2005 UNESCO named Popayán its first city of gastronomy, and in 2009 it declared the Easter Week processions of Semana Santa a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Patrimony of Humanity.
pope-adrian-i: Adrian came from a family of the Roman military aristocracy known as the domini de via Lata. His father, Theodore, died while Adrian was very young, and he was taken in by his paternal uncle Theodotus, a consul, dux and primicerius. He was bishop of Rome from 1 February 772 until his death on 25 December 795. The popes then had to contend with repeated Lombard attempts to expand in Italy at the expense of the papacy. Receiving no support from Constantinople, they looked to the Franks.

When Carloman I died in December 771 and Charlemagne took his lands, Carloman's widow Gerberga and her sons fled to the Lombard court at Pavia. King Desiderius asked Adrian to crown the boys Kings of the Franks. The pope refused, and Desiderius invaded the Duchy of the Pentapolis, which Charlemagne's father had given to the papacy in 756.

Charlemagne crossed the Alps in 773 and besieged Pavia. The Lombards surrendered in exchange for their lives, Desiderius was sent to the abbey of Corbie, and Charlemagne took the title King of the Lombards. The pope received additions to the Duchy of Rome, the Exarchate of Ravenna and the Pentapolis. Adrian struck the earliest papal coin, gave Charlemagne the title Patrician of Rome and from 781 dated papal documents by Charlemagne's reign instead of the Byzantine emperor's.

Adrian approved the Second Council of Nicaea of 787, which confirmed the veneration of icons. Charlemagne, who had received its decisions in a poor Latin translation, answered with the Capitulare contra synodum of 792, and his theologians wrote the Libri Carolini; a synod at Frankfurt in 794 refused to receive them. In 787 Adrian raised the diocese of Lichfield to an archdiocese at the request of King Offa of Mercia. He restored Roman aqueducts and rebuilt the churches of Santa Maria in Cosmedin and San Marco.

His pontificate was the longest since Saint Peter until that of Pius VI in the late 18th century. Charlemagne commissioned Adrian's epitaph in 796 and held a competition for its text, which Alcuin won. Carved in Roman square capitals on black limestone, it is now in the portico of St Peter's, a notable example of Carolingian monumental script.
pope-adrian-iv: Nicholas Breakspear was the son of Richard Breakspear, from a relatively humble family, and was probably born in or near St Albans in Hertfordshire. The year of his birth is unknown; he was probably about 55 when elected. Much of what is told of his youth comes from writers working more than thirty years after his death. He studied canon law at Arles, then became a canon regular at the Abbey of Saint-Ruf at Avignon, where he rose to abbot; the monks complained that he was overly strict. Pope Eugene III made him Cardinal-Bishop of Albano, and he met his lasting friend John of Salisbury.

In 1152 Breakspear went as legate to Scandinavia. Norway was in civil war and King Inge I's authority was weak; he reconciled the warring factions, if only for a time, and reorganised the church there before moving to Sweden, where he was acclaimed and chroniclers later called him a saint. He was elected pope on 4 December 1154. He was the only pope born in England until the election of a pope from the United States in 2025.

Rome was unsettled by the republican commune and by Arnold, who was captured by imperial troops in summer 1155 and hanged. Frederick Barbarossa was crowned emperor on 18 June 1155, secretly, to mislead the Romans. Adrian then allied with the Byzantine emperor Manuel I and southern Italian rebels against William I of Sicily, whom he had excommunicated, but William won decisive victories in 1156, and at the Concordat of Benevento the pope had to invest him with his lands, receiving homage and an annual tribute.

The pact with William angered Frederick. In 1157 a letter used the Latin word beneficium of the imperial crown, which some of Frederick's councillors translated as fief, implying that the emperor held it from the pope; Adrian explained it meant a good deed. In 1159 Frederick claimed extensive lands in northern Italy, and Adrian gave him forty days to withdraw on pain of excommunication. He died at Anagni on 1 September 1159.

The cardinals then split, electing Alexander III and the antipope Victor IV, which began a long schism. Adrian is said to have granted Henry II the bull Laudabiliter authorising the invasion of Ireland, but scholars are uncertain whether it ever existed. His decretal Dignum est allowed serfs to marry without their lord's consent.
pope-alexander-iii: Rolando was born in Siena. From the 14th century he was said to belong to the aristocratic family of Bandinelli, though this has not been proven. He is not the canonist Master Roland of Bologna, as was once thought. He probably studied at Bologna, where he taught theology.

In October 1150 Pope Eugene III made him Cardinal-Deacon of Santi Cosma e Damiano, and he later became Cardinal-Priest of St Mark. In 1153 he became papal chancellor and led the cardinals opposed to Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa. In 1156 he negotiated the Treaty of Benevento, which restored peaceful relations between Rome and the Kingdom of Sicily.

After Adrian IV died on 1 September 1159, Rolando was elected on 7 September and took the name Alexander III. A minority of cardinals chose Octavian instead, who became Victor IV and Frederick's antipope. Alexander refused to attend Frederick's council at Pavia, stating that a pope can be judged only by God, and the council recognised Victor in February 1160. Alexander excommunicated Victor and Frederick, and monarchs such as Géza II of Hungary, the king of France and Henry II of England came to recognise him. Because of imperial strength in Italy he spent much of his pontificate outside Rome, leaving it between 1162 and 1165 and again in 1167.
