In 1281 they sold the territory to the Bishop of Basel, but the Counts of Montbéliard refused to hand over the town.

Bishop Henry of Isny asked King Rudolph I of Habsburg for support, and after six weeks under siege the count gave way. On 20 April 1283 the king asked the bishop to grant the town a charter. The bishop sold Ajoie back to Montbéliard in 1386, but the town was again subject to the bishop from 1461.

The Reformation in Basel led the bishopric to move its headquarters to Porrentruy in 1527. Under Bishop Jakob Christoph Blarer von Wartensee, who reigned from 1575 to 1608, the town reached the height of its importance, with the castle enlarged and a Jesuit college built, and this prosperity ended with the outbreak of the Thirty Years' War in 1618, when the town was repeatedly occupied, besieged and plundered. On 27 April 1792 French Revolutionary troops drove out the bishop.

Porrentruy became the capital of a dependent republic, which France incorporated in 1793 as the Département du Mont-Terrible. In 1815 the town was given to the Canton of Bern. In the 19th century politics was marked by conflict between Liberal-Radicals and Catholic Conservatives, and the Radicals held the mayor's office from 1860 until 1972. The Canton of Jura, created on 1 January 1979, chose Delémont rather than Porrentruy as its capital.

Porrentruy had 6,675 inhabitants in 2018, most of whom speak French. It houses the cantonal courts, the archives of the former episcopal see of Basel and the cantonal library. The old town, with Gothic, Baroque and neoclassical buildings, is part of the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites, and the castle, the Jesuit church and college and the Church of Saint-Pierre are listed as sites of national significance. The Porte de France, built in 1563, is the only medieval city gate left. In 1988 the town won the Wakker Prize for its architectural heritage.
port-arthur-tasmania: Port Arthur lies on the Tasman Peninsula, about 97 kilometres south-east of Hobart. The peninsula was a naturally secure site, surrounded by water that the administration rumoured to be shark-infested. The only link to the mainland was the isthmus of Eaglehawk Neck, 30 metres wide, which was fenced and guarded by soldiers, traps and dogs. Many attempts at escape were made all the same, and some succeeded. Martin Cash escaped with two others.

The settlement was named after George Arthur, the lieutenant governor of Van Diemen's Land, and began in September 1830 as a timber-getting camp. From 1833 until 1877 it received the convicts judged most hardened, the secondary offenders who had persistently reoffended in Australia. Security was among the strictest in the British penal system, yet the regime rested on the idea that prisoners could be reformed while punished. Boys, some as young as nine, were held apart at Point Puer, the second boys' prison of the British Empire, and put to stone cutting and construction.

The Separate Prison, completed in 1853 and extended in 1855, grew out of Jeremy Bentham's theories. Its wings could all be seen from a central hub, though individual cells could not. It marked a shift from physical to psychological punishment: food served as reward or penalty, and under the Silent System prisoners were hooded and kept silent. Many developed mental illness. Critics held that Port Arthur was as harsh as other penal settlements, or worse. The Isle of the Dead received those who died; of 1,646 recorded graves only 180, those of staff and military, are marked.

After the prison closed in 1877 much of the property was auctioned, though most was not sold until 1889. Buildings decayed, owners pulled some down, and fires in 1895 and 1897 and earth tremors did further damage. The town of Carnarvon replaced the prison settlement, and in 1927 the name Port Arthur was restored as tourism grew. Novels such as Marcus Clarke's For the Term of His Natural Life of 1874 kept the convict past before the public.

Since 1987 the Port Arthur Historic Site Management Authority has run the site. It was inscribed with the Coal Mines Historic Site on the World Heritage Register on 31 July 2010 as part of the Australian Convict Sites. On 28 April 1996 Martin Bryant murdered 35 people and wounded 23 at the site, which led to a national restriction on high-capacity semi-automatic shotguns and rifles.
port-au-prince: Port-au-Prince lies on the Gulf of Gonâve, whose bay acts as a natural harbour and has sustained economic activity since the Taíno. The city's layout resembles an amphitheatre, with commercial districts near the water and residential neighbourhoods on the hills above. The name means 'Prince's Port', but it is unclear which prince was meant: one theory points to Le Prince, a ship that arrived in 1706, though the islets in the bay were called les îlets du Prince as early as 1680.

The area was part of the Taíno chiefdom of Xaragua. Under Spanish rule the governor Nicolas Ovando, from 1503, had Taíno leaders killed at a feast, and violence and disease decimated the native population. The Spanish administration abandoned the region in 1606, and French filibusters arrived around 1650, setting up a hospital that gave the region the name Hôpital. Spain renounced its claims in 1697. Petit-Goâve was too malarial and Léogâne hard to defend, so Port-au-Prince was built in 1749, and in 1770 it replaced Cap-Français as capital of Saint-Domingue.

In 1804 it became the capital of independent Haiti. After the assassination of Jean-Jacques Dessalines in 1806 it was capital of the southern republic under Alexandre Pétion, and it became capital of all Haiti when the country was unified in 1820. American forces occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934. On 12 January 2010 a magnitude 7.0 earthquake destroyed most of the central historic area, including the cathedral and the National Palace; Haiti's government estimated the death toll at 230,000.

Port-au-Prince is the capital and most populous city of Haiti, with a population estimated at 1,200,000 in 2022. It is the seat of the State University of Haiti, established in 1920, and the Presidential Palace stands on the Champ de Mars. Its cultural sites include the National Museum, founded in 1938, the National Archives and the National Library. Each November the national cemetery fills with people celebrating Fet Gede, a Vodou festival of the dead.
port-louis: Dutch settlers used the site as a harbour from 1606 and called the area the Harbour of Tortoises. Under French government it became the administrative centre of Mauritius, then called Ile de France, and a major reprovisioning halt for French ships passing between Asia and Europe around the Cape of Good Hope. The port is named in honour of King Louis XV, and the French governor Bertrand-François Mahé de La Bourdonnais contributed to the development of the city. Because the Moka Mountain Range shelters it from cyclone winds, it was chosen to house both the main harbour and the fort.

The port kept its value during the British occupation of the island in the Napoleonic Wars, when it helped Britain control the Indian Ocean. Port calls fell drastically after the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, but rose during the canal's seven-year closure from 1967. Modernisation in the late 1970s helped it remain the central point for all imports and exports of Mauritius.

Port Louis is the capital and most populous city of Mauritius, with 147,066 inhabitants at the 2018 census. The main harbour is the only official port of entry and exit for sea vessels in the country, and ships must be cleared there before visiting any other anchorage. It is the biggest port facility in the Indian Ocean region, with specialised terminals for sugar, fish and containers.

Many buildings reflect the city's colonial history, among them French colonial buildings of the 18th century such as Government House, the Jummah Mosque, Saint James Cathedral, a Tamil temple and the five-tier Port Louis Theatre. The Aapravasi Ghat is the remains of the immigration depot built by the British government to import labourers from India, Eastern Africa, Madagascar, China and Southeast Asia to work on the island's sugar estates. The Intercontinental Slavery Museum deals with slavery and indentured labour.
port-moresby: Port Moresby lies on the shores of the Coral Sea, on the south-western coast of the Papuan Peninsula of the island of New Guinea. The place where the city was founded has been inhabited by the Motu-Koitabu people for centuries. When Europeans first came, the largest settlement, Hanuabada, consisted of five villages of Motu and Koita people, who were organised into units called iduhu, somewhat like clans. Port Moresby was already an important centre of trade, visited by distant tribes of New Guinea.

In February 1873 the crew of HMS Basilisk, surveying the southern shore of New Guinea, reached the harbour. Captain John Moresby named it for his father, Admiral of the Fleet Sir Fairfax Moresby. Missionaries of the London Missionary Society arrived in 1873 and 1874. In 1883 the Premier of Queensland ordered the police magistrate Henry Chester to take possession of the eastern half of New Guinea, and on 4 April the Union Jack was raised at Port Moresby. A protectorate over the south-eastern coast was proclaimed in October 1884, and Special Commissioner Peter Scratchley chose the site as the colonial capital.

In 1906 the Papua Act transferred Papua, with Port Moresby as capital, to direct Australian rule. In the Second World War it was a prime objective of Imperial Japanese forces in 1942 and 1943, and by September 1942 it was an important Allied complex of bases. General Douglas MacArthur had his headquarters there from November 1942 to October 1944. It was granted city status in 1972 and became the capital of independent Papua New Guinea in September 1975.

Port Moresby is the capital and largest city of Papua New Guinea, with 756,754 inhabitants at the 2024 census. Although surrounded by Central Province, it forms its own National Capital District, and the Motu and Koitabu landowners are represented by the Motu Koita Assembly. The National Parliament Building, opened in 1984, and the National Museum and National Library stand in the suburb of Waigani.
port-of-spain: Port of Spain measures about 10.4 square kilometres and lies in the north-west of the island of Trinidad, between the Gulf of Paria, the Northern Range and the Caroni Swamp. The Laventille Hills form its eastern boundary. The climate is tropical monsoon, with little seasonal variation, a wet season from May to December and a dry season from January to April. The city proper is small. It forms the western end of a continuous built-up area, the East-West Corridor, which runs about 24 kilometres east to Arima.

The Spanish founded the town as Puerto España. The first settlement stood near an Amerindian fishing village called Cumucurapo, meaning place of the silk cotton trees, in the area now known as Mucurapo. The name Conquerabia is also recorded for an Amerindian settlement here. It may have been a separate village, another name for Cumucurapo, or the result of a misunderstanding by early Spanish settlers, who set up a port called Puerto de los Españoles, later Puerto de España. In 1560 a Spanish garrison was posted near the foot of the Laventille Hills.

Queen's Park Savannah, once sugar land, was bought by the town council in 1817 from the Peschier family. After an election in 1887 Michel Maxwell Philip became mayor, a post previously held only by white men, which the historian Bridget Brereton wrote perhaps marked the emergence of the coloured man as a political force in Trinidad. The city was also the de facto capital of the short-lived West Indies Federation.

Port of Spain is the capital and chief port of Trinidad and Tobago, with a municipal population of 49,867 in 2017. It is a retail and administrative centre, with most government offices, and a financial centre for the Caribbean. The Trinidad and Tobago Stock Exchange, the Central Bank, the Red House and Independence Square are in the downtown district. Queen's Park Savannah, about 110 hectares, is the largest open space. The pre-Lenten Carnival is the city's main annual festival, and the city was among the hosts of the 2007 Cricket World Cup.
port-vila: Port Vila lies on the west coast of the island of Efate, in Shefa Province, and is the capital and largest city of Vanuatu. Locally it is called simply Vila. The name of the area is Efil in the native South Efate language and Ifira in the neighbouring Mele-Fila language, of which Vila is a variant. Ifira is a small island in Vila Harbour where many traditional landowners live. The climate is tropical and maritime, with nearly constant trade winds, a wettest month in March and a driest in September.

Port Vila is the most important harbour and the centre of trade of Vanuatu. It is home to many languages: the daily lingua franca is Bislama, English and French are widely spoken, and many of Vanuatu's 138 indigenous languages are heard as people from rural areas move to the city.

Melanesian people have occupied the area for thousands of years. In 2004 an archaeological expedition at Teouma found a burial site of 25 tombs holding about three dozen skeletons of members of the Lapita culture; ceramics from the site were dated to the 13th century BCE. James Cook charted Efate in 1774 and named it Sandwich Island. His expedition did not land, but noted the good harbours and land suitable for European settlement.

In the late 19th century, when the islands were known as the New Hebrides, the economic balance began to favour the French by the 1890s, and they established large plantations. The French citizen Ferdinand Chevillard bought and cleared land around Port Vila for what was to be the largest French plantation on the island; it became instead the municipality of Franceville, which declared independence on 9 August 1889 and lasted only until June of the following year. After 1887 the territory was jointly administered by the French and the British, formalised in 1906 as an Anglo-French Condominium. During the Second World War Port Vila was an American and Australian airbase.

Port Vila had 49,034 inhabitants at the 2020 census, 16.3 per cent of the population of Vanuatu. The people are predominantly Melanesian, with small Polynesian, Asian, Australian and European populations. Christianity is the main religion in Vanuatu, and the city has a Roman Catholic cathedral, the Cathédrale du Sacré-Cœur, seat of the Diocese of Port Vila.

The Vanuatu Cultural Centre, which hosts the Vanuatu National Museum and the National Audiovisual Archives, stands at Saralana Park in front of the National Parliament. The city is one location of the University of the South Pacific, and is served by Bauerfield International Airport. It has been damaged by cyclones: Cyclone Uma in 1987 and Cyclone Pam on 13 March 2015, whose eye wall passed just east of the town.
portland-cement: Portland cement developed from natural cements made in Britain from the middle of the 18th century. In 1756 John Smeaton experimented with combinations of limestones and additives, including trass and pozzolanas, for the lighthouse now known as Smeaton's Tower. James Parker patented Roman cement in 1796; it became popular but was largely replaced by Portland cement in the 1850s. Louis Vicat's artificial hydraulic lime is considered the principal forerunner of Portland cement. The name is recorded in a directory of 1823, and in his patent of 1824 Joseph Aspdin used it because the hardened cement resembled Portland stone, quarried on the Isle of Portland in Dorset. His product was nothing like modern Portland cement and has been called proto-Portland cement.

His son William Aspdin, who left his father's company, apparently produced calcium silicates by accident in the 1840s, set up a plant at Rotherhithe in 1843 and improved his cement in 1848. In 1853 he moved to Germany. Isaac Charles Johnson refined the product further and claimed to be its real father. In 1859 John Grant set requirements for the cement used in the London sewer project, which became a specification, and Frederick Ransome patented the rotary kiln in 1885, allowing a continuous process.

Portland cement is made by heating limestone and a clay source in a kiln to form clinker, at about 1,450 °C for modern cements, and then grinding the clinker with about 5 per cent gypsum. The gypsum prevents flash setting. Ordinary Portland cement is grey, and white Portland cement needs raw materials very low in iron and a hotter kiln.

Its most common use is in concrete, a composite of gravel, sand, cement and water that can be cast in almost any shape and used for roads, dams and structural elements. It is also used in mortars, plasters and grouts. A typical concrete sets in about six hours and reaches a compressive strength of 8 MPa in 24 hours and 41 MPa at three months. Manufacture releases carbon dioxide from the raw materials and from fuel, and its quarries and kilns have environmental effects.
portlaoise: The Annals of the Four Masters, written in the 1630s, call the site Port Laoighisi. The town grew around the Fort of Leix, or Fort Protector, whose construction began in 1548 under the Lord Deputy, Sir Edward Bellingham, to secure English control of the county after the exile of Gaelic chieftains the year before. The fort stood on rising ground, protected to the south and east by the River Triogue and an esker known as the Ridge.

An Act of Parliament in the reign of Mary I established the town proper, named Maryborough in her honour, and the county became Queen's County. The area had been a focus of the rebellion of Ruairí Óg Ó Mórdha, who lost his lands, which the Crown wanted settled by reliable landowners. For some fifty years the settlers fought a continual low-scale war against Gaelic chieftains who opposed the settlement, and the town was burnt several times by the end of the 16th century.

Maryborough received a market in 1567, and in 1570 a charter of Elizabeth I raised it to a borough. It sent two members to the Irish Parliament until 1800. Its Court House was built in 1805 and its County Gaol in 1830. In 1929, a few years after the foundation of the Irish Free State, the town was renamed Portlaoighise, later simplified to Port Laoise, and the county became County Laois.

Portlaoise is the county town of County Laois, in the South Midlands of the province of Leinster, 94 km west-southwest of Dublin on the M7 motorway. The Slieve Bloom mountains lie to the west and the Great Heath of Maryborough to the east. It had 23,494 inhabitants at the 2022 census. Remains of Fort Protector can still be seen in the town centre. The first aeroplane made in Ireland was assembled in the town, and its first flight was reported on 4 November 1909.
porto: Porto stands on the Douro River estuary in northern Portugal, about 280 kilometres north of Lisbon, and its western part reaches the Atlantic coast. It is the capital of the Porto District. Its historic core, with the Luiz I Bridge and the Monastery of Serra do Pilar, was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996, and has been a National Monument since 2001.

Before the Roman conquest the region was inhabited by the Gallaeci, a Celtic people, and findings suggest settlement at the mouth of the Douro as early as the eighth century BCE. As Portus Cale the town became a significant commercial hub under the Roman Empire, and its combined Celtic-Latin name has been cited as the origin of the name Portugal. In the Suebian and Visigothic periods it was a key centre for the spread of Christianity.

The Methuen Treaty of 1703 strengthened ties with England, and by 1717 English firms dominated the port wine trade. The Marquis of Pombal created a state-controlled wine company and demarcated the Douro, Europe's first protected wine region, which led in 1757 to the Revolta dos Borrachos, suppressed brutally by the authorities.

On 29 March 1809, during the Peninsular War, the Ponte das Barcas, a pontoon bridge, collapsed as civilians fled French forces, with an estimated 4,000 deaths. Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, then retook the city, crossing the Douro in wine barges. On 19 January 1919 monarchists declared the Monarchy of the North in Porto, which briefly served as the capital of the restored monarchy.

Porto is the second-largest city in Portugal, after Lisbon, with a metropolitan area of about 1.9 million people. Port wine takes its name from the city, since the cellars of Vila Nova de Gaia packaged and exported the fortified wine. In 2001 it shared the title of European Capital of Culture with Rotterdam.
porto-novo: Porto-Novo lies in the south of Benin on an inlet of the Gulf of Guinea, 13 kilometres from the Atlantic, from which it is separated by a lagoon. It stands about 30 kilometres east of Cotonou and 12 kilometres from the Nigerian border. Its commune covers 52 square kilometres. The city sits at the edge of the Dahomey Gap, which makes its climate drier than its nearness to the equator would suggest.

Porto-Novo was once a tributary of the Yoruba Oyo Empire, which offered it protection from the neighbouring Fon, who were expanding their power. The Yoruba called the city Ajashe, and the Gun called it Hogbonu. The first inhabitants were Yoruba-speaking, but a wave of migration from the region of Allada in the 1600s brought Te-Agbalin and his group to Ajashe in the late 16th century. In 1730 the Portuguese Eucaristo de Campos named the city Porto-Novo, because it resembled the city of Porto. It developed as a port for the transatlantic slave trade led by the Portuguese Empire.

In 1861 the British, who were active in nearby Nigeria, bombarded the city, and in 1863 the Kingdom of Porto-Novo accepted a French offer of protection. The neighbouring Kingdom of Dahomey objected to French involvement, and war broke out between the two states. In 1883 Porto-Novo was incorporated into the French colony of Dahomey and its dependencies, and in 1900 it became Dahomey's capital. The French sought to impose their language in every sphere of life and to stamp out the indigenous languages. Kings continued to rule in the city, officially and unofficially, until the death of the last, Alohinto Gbeffa, in 1976; from 1908 the king held the title of Chef supérieur.

Many Afro-Brazilians settled in Porto-Novo after returning to Africa following emancipation in Brazil, and Brazilian architecture and foods remain important to its cultural life. Under French rule, people often fled across the new border into British-ruled Nigeria to avoid harsh taxation, military service and forced labour. The border cuts through contiguous Yoruba- and Egun-speaking areas.

Porto-Novo is the official capital of Benin and the second-largest city, with 264,320 people at the census of 2013. The national parliament sits there, while the presidency and most other government institutions are in Cotonou. Its residents are mostly Yoruba and Gun. King Toffa's Palace, now a museum, and its surrounding district were added to UNESCO's Tentative List in 1996. The Da Silva Museum tells of the returning Afro-Brazilians, and the Alexandre Sènou Adandé Ethnographic Museum holds a large collection of Yoruba masks.
porto-torres: Porto Torres lies on the north-west coast of Sardinia, in the centre of the Gulf of Asinara, about 25 kilometres east of Cape Falcone and 15 kilometres from Sassari. It is a comune in the Metropolitan City of Sassari. The municipality is split into two parts of almost equal size: the town, with its industrial area and Roman ruins, on the flat Nurra plain, and the islands of Asinara and Isola Piana, which since 1997 form the Asinara National Park. Its full Latin name was Colonia Iulia Turris Libisonis, where Turris, tower, probably refers to a nuraghe or to Monte d'Accoddi.

Traces of human presence include the altar of Monte d'Accoddi, necropolises and, from the Bronze and Nuragic ages, the necropolis of Su Crucifissu Mannu, where two skulls show signs of surgery, possibly for relieving migraines and tumours or for religious reasons.

The town was founded in the 1st century BCE as Colonia Iulia Turris Libisonis, apparently by Julius Caesar, and was the first Roman colony on the whole island. Pliny calls it the only colony on Sardinia in his time, which suggests that there had been merely a fort before. The main road across the island ran from Caralis, Cagliari, to Turris, and a second road ran along the west coast. Remains include a temple dedicated to Fortune, baths, a basilica, an aqueduct and a bridge. It was an episcopal see in the early Middle Ages. The Romanesque basilica of San Gavino, built between 1065 and 1080, honours three saints said to have been beheaded in 303 under Diocletian and Maximian.

The city was inhabited until the 11th century, when most people moved to Sassari. In the Judicate of Logudoro its name became Torres. It was partly under Genoese hands until the early 15th century, when the Aragonese took it, and later it became part of the Kingdom of Sardinia. Torres was separated from Sassari in 1842, when the area around the basilica joined the fishermen's community by the port to form Porto Torres. It was bombed by the Allies on 18 April 1943.

Porto Torres is the second biggest seaport on the island after Olbia. The basilica of San Gavino, the largest Romanesque church in Sardinia, has two apses instead of the usual western facade and eastern apse, and its crypt holds several Roman sarcophagi; it was the main cathedral of the archdiocese of Sassari until 1441.
portobelo: Portobelo lies on the northern part of the Isthmus of Panama, in Colón Province, 32 km northeast of the modern port of Colón at the Atlantic entrance of the Panama Canal. It was chosen for its deep natural harbour. Tradition holds that Christopher Columbus named it Puerto Bello, meaning beautiful port, in 1502. After the English privateer Francis Drake died of dysentery in 1596, he was buried at sea in a lead coffin off Portobelo, and Drake Island at the mouth of the harbour commemorates him.

The Spanish explorer Francisco Velarde y Mercado founded Portobelo in 1597, and it quickly replaced Nombre de Dios as the major local port for Peruvian silver. With Veracruz it was one of the two Atlantic ports on the route of the Spanish treasure fleet, and the Spanish built fortifications to protect it. English privateers led by William Parker captured it in 1601. Henry Morgan did so in 1668 with 450 privateers and plundered it for 14 days; the English pirate John Coxon took it again in 1680.

In 1726 the Royal Navy under Admiral Francis Hosier blockaded the port to stop the treasure fleet returning to Spain; Hosier and many of his sailors died of tropical disease at Bastimentos. On 21 November 1739 a British squadron under Admiral Edward Vernon captured it in the War of Jenkins' Ear. More medals were struck for Vernon than for any other 18th-century British figure, and places across the British Isles were named Portobello, among them Portobello Road in London, a district of Edinburgh and the Portobello Barracks in Dublin.

The Spanish recovered Portobelo in 1741 after their victory at the Battle of Cartagena de Indias. British efforts to gain a foothold on the Spanish Main and disrupt the galleon trade failed. Afterwards the Spanish used small fleets trading at many ports, which made them less open to attack, and ships began to sail around Cape Horn to trade directly on the western coast.

Portobelo is the seat of Portobelo District, and its economy received a boost in the late 19th century during the construction of the Panama Canal. In 1980 UNESCO designated the Fortifications on the Caribbean Side of Panama: Portobelo-San Lorenzo, the ruins of the Spanish colonial fortifications and nearby Fort San Lorenzo, a World Heritage Site. In July 2012 the World Heritage Committee placed the site on the List of World Heritage in Danger, citing environmental factors, lack of maintenance and uncontrolled urban development.
portoferraio: Portoferraio is a town and comune on the edge of the harbour of the island of Elba, in the province of Livorno in Tuscany, and is the island's largest municipality. Many of its buildings stand on the slopes of a tiny hill bordered on three sides by the sea, and the town centre is crowded around the small marina in a natural cove. The name has changed over time: Ferraia in Etruscan times, Fabricia under the Romans and Ferraio under the Grand Duchy of Tuscany.

Cosimo I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, founded the town in 1548 as Cosmopoli, meaning Cosimo's City, to balance the presence of the Spanish citadel at Porto Azzurro. It had three forts, Forte Stella, Forte Falcone and Forte Inglese, and a massive line of walls, all still visible today. An edict of 1556 gave special privileges to all who settled in Cosmopoli, and the first Jews arrived at the beginning of the 17th century. A synagogue was built in 1631-1632, and in 1702 the Grand Duke ordered the Jews to live on a designated street, a small ghetto they could not leave after one in the morning.

The town remained with the Grand Duchy of Tuscany until the late 18th century, when its strategic position brought it into contention with France, Great Britain and Austria. A British garrison withstood the Siege of Porto Ferrajo in 1801, but the Treaty of Amiens in 1802 transferred the town to France. In 1814 it was handed over to Napoleon Bonaparte as the seat of his first exile. It grew quickly in the 19th century as the main port for shipping iron ore from Rio Marina to the mainland, whence its present name, meaning Iron Port. In 1860 it became part of the Kingdom of Italy.

In the Second World War German forces occupied Elba, and in late June 1944 an Allied force composed mainly of Free French troops liberated the island in a fight that lasted two days; Portoferraio was damaged by the fighting and bombing. Mining ended from the 1970s, and the town became an internationally known seaside destination. Its main sights are the three forts, an archaeological museum and Napoleon's house.
portoviejo: The Spanish captain Francisco Pacheco founded the town on 12 March 1535 near the coast as Villa Nueva de San Gregorio de Portoviejo. In 1628 it was moved inland to its present site because of Indian attacks. It is still known as the city of the Royal Tamarind Trees, after the tamarind plantations that once stood around it. Its Spanish name, San Gregorio de Portoviejo, survives in the private university that bears it.
An earthquake of magnitude 7.8 struck the region on 16 and 17 April 2016, and Portoviejo suffered over 300 deaths and heavy damage to buildings. The airport served as a shelter for those affected.

Portoviejo is the capital of Manabí Province, about 30 kilometres from the Pacific coast. It is the political and economic centre of the valley of the Portoviejo River, which also takes in the cantons of Santa Ana and Rocafuerte. About 110 square kilometres of that valley are cultivated every year. The city is important for coffee, cattle and fishing, has an agricultural-processing industry and has good road connections to Quito and Guayaquil.

Its cooking uses peanuts, bananas, cheese, corn and yucca, with dishes such as biche de pescado, corviche and bolón de verde. Ecuador has declared its gastronomy intangible heritage, and UNESCO has admitted the city to its Creative Cities Network in the category of gastronomy. Among its sights are the Mamey Ecological Park, a botanical garden of 50 hectares owned by the Technical University of Manabí, founded in 1952, the Metropolitan Cathedral of Jesus the Good Shepherd and the archaeological park of Cerro Jaboncillo outside the city.
portsmouth-new-hampshire: The Piscataqua River is a tidal estuary with a swift current, but it forms a good natural harbour, and it is the boundary between New Hampshire and Maine. The first European to explore and write about the area was Martin Pring in 1603. Colonists settled the west bank in 1630 and named the place Strawbery Banke after the wild strawberries growing there. Fort William and Mary, on what is now New Castle Island, protected the village. Fishing, lumber and shipbuilding were the principal businesses, and the port prospered as a link between upstream industries and merchants abroad.

Enslaved Africans were imported as labourers as early as 1645 and were integral to the city's prosperity, and Portsmouth took part in the Triangle Trade. The town was incorporated in 1653 and named after the colony's founder, John Mason, who had been captain of the English port of Portsmouth in Hampshire. Its shipyard completed its first ship for the Royal Navy, HMS Falkland, in 1696. After Queen Anne's War, Governor Joseph Dudley chose the town to host the negotiations for the 1713 Treaty of Portsmouth, which temporarily ended hostilities between the Abenaki and the colonies of Massachusetts Bay and New Hampshire.

In 1774 Paul Revere rode to Portsmouth to warn that the Royal Navy was coming to capture the port, and the Patriot government later moved the capital inland to Exeter. In 1779 nineteen enslaved African Americans of Portsmouth petitioned the state legislature for the abolition of slavery, citing the principles of the Revolution; the legislature tabled it, and New Hampshire abolished slavery in 1857. Portsmouth was incorporated as a city in 1849. A fire in 1813 burned 244 buildings, and the fire district created afterwards required brick walls and slate roofs, which gave the downtown its distinctive look. As mill towns grew on river power, Portsmouth's port declined.

Portsmouth is a city in Rockingham County, New Hampshire, with a population of 21,956 at the 2020 census. It keeps many Colonial, Georgian and Federal style houses, some now museums, and a Historic District Commission protects its architecture. The Captain Gregory Purcell house, where John Paul Jones boarded in 1781–1782 while his ship Ranger was built on Badger's Island in Kittery, is the only surviving property in the United States associated with him. The Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, founded in 1800 as the first federal navy yard, stands on Seavey's Island in Kittery, Maine, and was where the 1905 treaty ending the Russo-Japanese War was signed.
portsmouth-rhode-island: Portsmouth is a town in Newport County, Rhode Island. It has a total area of 59.3 square miles (154 square kilometres), of which about 39 per cent is land and the rest water. Most of its land lies on Aquidneck Island, which it shares with Middletown and Newport. The town also includes smaller islands, among them Prudence Island, Patience Island, Hope Island and Hog Island.

Portsmouth was settled in 1638 by a group of religious dissenters from the Massachusetts Bay Colony, among them Dr. John Clarke, William Coddington and Anne Hutchinson. It is named after Portsmouth in Hampshire, England. Roger Williams convinced the settlers to go there instead of to the Province of New Jersey, where they had first planned to settle. The town was founded by the signers of the Portsmouth Compact. Its original name was Pocasset, and it was officially named Portsmouth on 12 May 1639.

It is the second-oldest municipality in Rhode Island, after Providence, and was one of the four colonies that merged to form the Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, the others being Providence, Newport and Warwick. It later became part of the State of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations. Jeremy Clarke, an early settler who lived from 1605 to 1652, served as the second governor of the colony, and his wife Frances Latham was known as the mother of governors.

The population was 17,871 at the 2020 census. The town is the headquarters of US Sailing, the national governing body of sailing, and hosts the Newport International Polo Series at Glen Farm. Its historic sites include the Battle of Rhode Island site, the Green Animals Topiary Garden, the Portsmouth Friends Meetinghouse Parsonage and Cemetery, dating from about 1699, the Prudence Island Lighthouse of 1823 and the Hog Island Shoal Lighthouse of 1901, as well as the wreck sites of H.M.S. Cerberus and H.M.S. Lark, dated 1778. Julia Ward Howe, author of The Battle Hymn of the Republic, is among its notable people.
portuguese-empire: The Kingdom of Portugal arose from the Reconquista, the gradual reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula from the Moors. It became a separate kingdom in 1139, completed its reconquest of Moorish territory by reaching the Algarve in 1249, and was freed from the threat of Castile by the Treaty of Ayllón in 1411. Portuguese attention then turned overseas, first to the Marinid Sultanate in North Africa. Historians point to the chance to continue the crusade against Islam, the promise of glory and spoils for the military class, and the hope of expanding trade and addressing Portugal's economic decline.

Ceuta proved a disappointment, but Portugal held it and explored the Atlantic coast of Africa under Infante Henry the Navigator, who led and financed exploration until his death in 1460. Gil Eanes rounded Cape Bojador in 1434. The Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 divided the world outside Europe between Portugal and Spain along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in May 1498 and in 1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral made landfall on the Brazilian coast. Albuquerque captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate in 1510 and made it the capital of the East Indies.

In 1580 Philip II of Spain seized the Portuguese crown, beginning the Iberian Union, and the colonies were attacked by the Dutch Republic, England and France. Portugal had a smaller population and could not defend its overstretched trading posts, and the empire began a slow decline. After the Restoration War began in 1640, the gold of Minas Gerais, discovered in 1693, became the economic focus of the empire. In 1808, after a French invasion, John VI moved the royal court to Brazil, which became independent in the 1820s. The remaining colonies were forts and plantations on the African coast, Portuguese Timor and enclaves in India and Macau; the British Ultimatum of 1890 ended Portugal's Pink Map project to join Angola and Mozambique.

Under António de Oliveira Salazar the Estado Novo resisted decolonisation and renamed the colonies overseas provinces. Macau was returned to China on 20 December 1999. Eight former colonies have Portuguese as their official language, and with Portugal they belong to the Community of Portuguese Language Countries, which is the cultural and intergovernmental successor of the empire. Portuguese remains co-official with Cantonese in Macau. The Azores and Madeira are the only overseas territories still politically linked to Portugal.
portuguese-house-of-burgundy: Henry, Count of Portugal, a grandson in the senior line of Robert I, Duke of Burgundy, joined the Reconquista in the Iberian Peninsula in the late 11th century. After conquering parts of Galicia and northern Portugal on behalf of Alfonso VI of León, he married Alfonso's illegitimate daughter Teresa and received the County of Portugal as a fief under the Kingdom of León, becoming count in 1096.

His son Afonso Henriques defeated his mother in the Battle of São Mamede in 1128 and was proclaimed King of Portugal after his victory at the Battle of Ourique in 1139, founding the Afonsine dynasty. Pope Alexander III recognised Portugal as an independent state only in 1179. Through his mother Afonso descended from the Jiménez dynasty and the Astur-Leonese line; through his father he was connected to the Capetian dynasty.

The kings who followed Afonso I continued the Reconquista against the Moors. Under Afonso II Portugal held its first parliament, and Afonso III conquered the Kingdom of the Algarve and took the title King of Portugal and the Algarve. His son Denis I, who formalised the Portuguese language, developed the kingdom's land, and the borders of Portugal were fixed by the Treaty of Alcañices in 1297.

Princes of the house took thrones elsewhere in Europe, among them Ferdinand I, Count of Flanders, and Peter I, Count of Urgell. Princesses became royal consorts, including Berengaria, Queen of Denmark, and Leonor, Queen of Aragon.

In 1383 Beatrice, princess of Portugal and heir to the throne, married John I of Castile. When her father Ferdinand I died in the same year, the kingdom fell into anarchy in the crisis of 1383 to 1385, threatened with annexation by Castile. The crisis ended in 1385 with the Portuguese victory at the Battle of Aljubarrota and the accession of John, Master of Aviz, an illegitimate son of Peter I, who began the House of Aviz.
portuguese-language: Portuguese belongs to the Ibero-Romance group, which evolved from several dialects of Vulgar Latin in the medieval Kingdom of Galicia and the County of Portugal. Before the Roman conquest the territory of modern Portugal was inhabited by the Gallaeci, Lusitanians, Celts, Iberians, Phoenicians, Greeks and Ligurians, whose languages were gradually replaced but left words behind, many of them about nature, agriculture and material culture. The Roman presence began in 218 BCE and full consolidation came in 19 BCE under Augustus. Latin spread outward from the cities and was tied to Roman citizenship. In the 5th century the Suebi and Visigoths conquered the peninsula and contributed about 500 Germanic words, many to do with warfare.

Portuguese has a rich system of nasal vowels, and its spelling is largely phonemic but shaped by etymology and tradition. Its verbs have kept more inflections from classical Latin than any other major Romance language, and it has features that other Romance languages, except Galician and Fala, lack, among them the future subjunctive and the personal infinitive. Its lexicon of around 228,500 entries comes largely from Latin, with more than 3,000 words traced to pre-Roman Celtic sources and loanwords from Germanic, Arabic, African, Amerindian and Asian languages. It is fully mutually intelligible with Galician, with which it shares its origin in the medieval language Galician-Portuguese. Two standard varieties are used for learning, European and Brazilian Portuguese.

Colonial expansion carried Portuguese across the world. It is the official language of eight countries: Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe and Timor-Leste, and shares official status in Macau and Equatorial Guinea. There are about 267 million speakers in all, some 200 million of them in South America and 30 million in Africa. In Cape Verde and Guinea-Bissau a Portuguese-based creole is also widely spoken. The Community of Portuguese Language Countries unites all the officially Lusophone nations, and recent spelling agreements have tried to give the language one spelling everywhere.
portuguese-restoration-war: The succession crisis of 1580 created the Iberian Union, a personal union of Habsburg Spain and Portugal. After Philip IV succeeded his father in 1621, Portuguese merchants paid higher taxes, the nobility lost influence in the Cortes Generales, and appointments went increasingly to Spanish outsiders. Spanish involvement in the Eighty Years' War brought Dutch attacks on Portuguese colonies. With Spanish resources absorbed by the Thirty Years' War and a revolt in Catalonia, conspirators known as the Forty Conspirators struck on 1 December 1640. They killed the Secretary of State, Miguel de Vasconcelos, and imprisoned the Vicereine, Margaret of Savoy, and John, 8th Duke of Braganza, was acclaimed King John IV.

The war consisted mainly of border skirmishes and cavalry raids, with only five major battles in twenty-eight years. John IV created a Council of War on 11 December 1640 and sought alliances: France signed on 1 June 1641, since Cardinal Richelieu wanted Portuguese resistance to drain Spanish resources. France abandoned the alliance in the Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659. Meanwhile the Dutch seized Angola, São Tomé and Malacca in 1641, and Portugal regained Angola in 1648, São Tomé in 1649 and Brazil in 1654.

The first stage (1640–1646) included the Portuguese victory at Montijo on 26 May 1644, and the second (1646–1660) was a standoff of small raids. In 1662 Charles II of England married Catherine of Braganza, and an English brigade of about 3,000 arrived under Friedrich Hermann von Schönberg. In 1663 John of Austria the Younger took Évora, but the Portuguese defeated him at Ameixial on 8 June. After Castelo Rodrigo on 7 July 1664, the Spanish lost over 10,000 men at Montes Claros on 17 June 1665.

With English mediation, the Treaty of Lisbon of 1668 recognised the House of Braganza as Portugal's ruling dynasty. Independence freed Portugal to pursue its colonial trade, and after 1668 it cultivated intellectual ties with France and England. The memory of Spanish invasion remained a strong support for Portuguese nationalism.
porus: Porus is known only from Greek sources. His kingdom lay between the Hydaspes (Jhelum) and Acesines (Chenab) rivers, and Strabo noted that it held almost 300 cities. Scholars differ on who he was. Michael Witzel conjectures that he was a king of the Pūrus, a Vedic tribe, and Hem Chandra Raychaudhuri largely agreed. Ishwari Prasad and others argue that he was a Shurasena, because Quintus Curtius Rufus says his vanguard carried a banner of Herakles.

Porus was hostile to the neighbouring polity of Taxila, whose earlier ruler Ambhiraj, his maternal uncle, he had assassinated. When Alexander the Great crossed the Indus, Omphis, the ruler of Taxila and son of Ambhiraj, greeted him and hoped to use his forces to bring Porus and Abisares to submission. Abisares offered submission, but Porus refused.

At the Battle of the Hydaspes in 326 BCE, Alexander crossed the river on a stormy night just before dawn, while the rest of his forces were spread along the bank to distract Porus. Porus took a defensive position on the plain, with infantry and elephants in front and cavalry and chariots on the wings. Alexander's cavalry charged his left wing, and his cavalry was driven back into the infantry lines, causing confusion.

The mahouts were killed with sarissas and the elephants pushed back into Porus' own columns. Porus refused to surrender and wandered on an elephant until he was wounded and his force routed. The exact site and strengths are unknown because the sources differ widely, and A. B. Bosworth warns that they are highly exaggerated. Alexander founded Nicaea at the site of the victory and Bucephalous in memory of his horse.

Alexander, impressed by Porus, did not depose him. He restored and enlarged his territory, annexing that of Glausaes, and Omphis was reconciled with him. Porus joined a campaign east of the Acesines against a cousin of his and took part in the siege of Sangala. When Alexander turned back at the Hyphasis, Porus was left as de facto ruler of the entire territory east of the Hydaspes, with no European satrap beside him.

After Alexander died in 323 BCE and Perdiccas was murdered in 321 BCE, the regent Antipater, according to Diodorus, recognised Porus' authority over the territories along the Indus. Eudemus, who had been Alexander's satrap in the Punjab, killed him. Porus reportedly died sometime between 321 and 315 BCE. In the medieval Alexander Romance he is defeated by Alexander in single combat, and he has appeared in many later films, series and games.
poseidon: The earliest attested form of the god's name is written in Linear B as Po-se-da-o and Po-se-da-wo-ne. If the surviving tablets can be trusted, these names occur more often than that of Zeus. A feminine variant, po-se-de-ia, suggests a lost consort goddess, in effect the precursor of Amphitrite.

Poseidon was the chief god at Pylos and Thebes, and carried the title wanax, meaning king or protector, and the title Earth-shaker. He had a chthonic aspect, being called Lord of the Underworld, and in the Mycenaean period his cult was probably tied to protecting the palace. In a culture that depended heavily on the sea, there is not enough evidence that he was then linked with it.

Poseidon is one of the twelve Olympians. In the standard myth he was born to the Titans Cronus and Rhea and swallowed by his father, then freed when Zeus gave Cronus an emetic. According to Homer and Apollodorus, Zeus, Poseidon and Hades divided the world by lot: Zeus received the sky, Poseidon the sea and Hades the Underworld.

His weapon was a trident forged by the Cyclopes. In Arcadia he was related to Demeter and Despoina and worshipped as a horse and a god of waters, and most Greeks saw him as tamer or father of horses who struck the ground with his trident to create springs.

Several myths tell of his contests for cities. Athena became patron of Athens after a competition in which Poseidon struck the Acropolis with his trident and raised a salt spring, while he remained present there through his surrogate Erechtheus. He fathered Theseus with Aethra, and in the Odyssey he punished Odysseus for blinding his son Polyphemus, delaying his return by ten years.

His worship spread over Greece and southern Italy, and he was specially honoured in the Peloponnese and the Ionic cities. The city names Poteidaia in the Chalkidiki peninsula and Poseidonia, a Greek colony in Italy later known as Paestum, show the weight of his cult. The Panhellenic Isthmian Games at Corinth were held in his honour and included athletic and musical contests and horseracing.

At Mycale in Ionia, representatives of twelve cities held the Panionia, a festival of Poseidon Helikonios that became the meeting place of the Ionian League. Athens had a month named Poseidaon in its calendar. A Homeric Hymn addresses him as tamer of horses and saviour of ships. His Roman equivalent is Neptune.
posidonius: Posidonius, nicknamed the Athlete, was born around 135 BCE into a Greek family in Apamea, a Hellenistic city on the Orontes River in northern Syria. As a young man he moved to Athens and studied under Panaetius, the leading Stoic philosopher of the age. After Panaetius died in 110 BCE he settled in Rhodes, gained citizenship, and kept a school there that became the leading institution of its time.

From about the 90s BCE he made voyages round the Mediterranean to gather scientific data and observe peoples. At Gades on the Atlantic coast of Hispania he saw tides much higher than in the Mediterranean and held that daily tides follow the Moon's orbit. In Gaul he studied the Celts and noted that they honoured the Druids, whom he saw as philosophers.

On Rhodes Posidonius held office as one of the Prytaneis, the most important political office there. He was chosen for at least one embassy to Rome, in 87–86 BCE, during the First Mithridatic War. Under him Rhodes eclipsed Athens as the centre of Stoic philosophy, drawing Greek and Roman students.

Pompey attended a lecture in 66 BCE and again in 62 BCE, when Posidonius, suffering from gout, answered his pain by declaring that it would never persuade him it was an evil. Cicero attended his lectures in his twenties and called him 'my teacher'; Posidonius politely declined to write on Cicero's consulship. His grandson Jason of Nysa succeeded him as head of the school.

His works survive only in fragments, though the titles of more than twenty are known. He wrote on physics, astronomy, geography, history, ethics and mathematics, and held that philosophy was the master art that alone could explain the cosmos. A Stoic who also drew on Plato and Aristotle, he saw the universe as an interconnected whole. He estimated the Sun's distance at 9,893 times the Earth's radius and reasoned that the Moon causes the tides.

In his Histories he continued Polybius's account of Roman expansion, covering 146–88 BCE in 52 volumes. His lost geography of the Celts was a main source for Diodorus Siculus, Strabo, Caesar and Tacitus. Strabo called him the most learned of the philosophers of his time.
positivism: Positivism holds that all genuine knowledge is either true by definition or positive, meaning facts derived by reason and logic from sensory experience. It rejects other ways of knowing, such as intuition, introspection or religious faith. Although the approach has recurred in Western thought, modern positivism was first set out in the early nineteenth century by Auguste Comte. Massive advances in the natural sciences then encouraged thinkers such as Henri de Saint-Simon, Pierre-Simon Laplace and Comte to believe that the scientific method should replace metaphysics.

Comte first described the outlook in The Course in Positive Philosophy, published between 1830 and 1842, and followed it in 1844 with A General View of Positivism. The first three volumes of the Course dealt with the existing physical sciences, and the last two stressed the coming of a science of society. For Comte the physical sciences had to arrive first, before humanity could turn to the complex science of society itself.

Comte's sociological positivism holds that society, like the physical world, operates according to scientific laws. Fabien Magnin, the first working-class adherent, led a movement called Proletarian Positivism, and Comte named him his successor as president of the Positive Society. Eugène Sémérie described positivism as a political party that aimed to reconcile order with progress.

Émile Durkheim rejected much of Comte's philosophy but kept its method, holding that the social sciences continue the natural sciences into human conduct. He set up the first European department of sociology, at the University of Bordeaux in 1895, and published Suicide in 1897, in which he compared suicide rates among Catholic and Protestant populations. Logical positivism grew from the Vienna Circle, whose doctrines Otto Neurath, Hans Hahn and Rudolf Carnap summarised in a pamphlet of 1929.

Positivism has been criticised for reductionism. Giambattista Vico asserted in 1725 the superiority of the science of the human mind, and Wilhelm Dilthey argued that only humanistic knowledge gives insight into thoughts, feelings and desires. At the turn of the twentieth century German sociologists, among them Max Weber, introduced methodological antipositivism, which concentrates on cultural norms and values seen from a subjective perspective. In 1934 Karl Popper argued in The Logic of Scientific Discovery against verificationism, holding that an observation can at best falsify a statement. It remains popular, but it has declined since the turn of the twentieth century under criticism from antipositivists and critical theorists.
postumus: Little is known of the early life of Marcus Cassianius Latinius Postumus. He is claimed to be of Batavian origin, since his coinage honours the deities Hercules Magusanus and Hercules Deusoniensis, who would have been popular among the Batavians. He probably rose through the army to command the Roman forces among the Celts, and he may have been made imperial legate of Germania Inferior by the emperor Valerian.

By 259 Valerian was campaigning against the Persians, and his son and co-emperor Gallienus was occupied on the Danubian frontier, so Gallienus left his son Saloninus and military commanders, among them Postumus, to protect the Rhine. In 260 the army defeated a Juthungian army returning from Italy with prisoners, and Postumus distributed the captured spoils to his legions. Saloninus, advised by his praetorian prefect Silvanus, demanded the booty at Cologne. Postumus made a show of reluctantly enforcing the order, and his troops instead proclaimed him emperor and besieged Cologne. After the walls were breached, Silvanus and Saloninus were killed.

Postumus was recognised in Gaul, Germania Superior and Inferior and Raetia, and by 261 also in Britannia and Hispania. His capital was in northern Gaul, probably at Cologne or Trier, and he gave his government the traditional Roman offices, taking the consulship, the title of pontifex maximus and tribunician power. His coins call him the restorer of the Gauls, and he fought successful campaigns against the Franks and Alemanni in 262 and 263. Scholars debate whether he meant to remove Gallienus; his forms and titles remained conventionally Roman. Gallienus attacked in 265, but his first attempt failed, and in a second campaign he was wounded while besieging a Gallic city and withdrew.

In 268 the coinage was suddenly debased, which suggests financial difficulties. The same year Aureolus, commanding Milan for Gallienus, declared for Postumus, who failed to support him. In early 269 Laelianus, governor of Germania Superior, was proclaimed emperor at Mainz. Postumus captured the city and killed him, but when he tried to restrain his army from sacking it, the soldiers killed him. The Gallic Empire survived him under Marius and then Victorinus, though it lost Hispania. His coinage, notably the Labours of Hercules series of gold coins, is of particular interest to numismatists.
potala-palace: The palace is named after Mount Potalaka, regarded in Buddhist tradition as the abode of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. It stands on Marpo Ri, the Red Hill, in the centre of the Lhasa Valley, on the site of an earlier palace attributed to Songtsen Gampo and traditionally dated to 637. Two chapels at its northwest corner, the Phakpa Lhakhang and the Chogyel Drupuk, preserve parts of that palace; the second is a cavern identified as Songtsen Gampo's meditation cave.

Ngawang Lozang Gyatso, the Fifth Dalai Lama, began the present building in 1645 after his adviser Konchog Chophel, Thirty-fifth Ganden Tripa of the Gelug school, pointed out that the site lay between Drepung and Sera monasteries and the old city of Lhasa and suited a seat of government. The outer structure took three years, the interior and its furnishings 45. The Dalai Lama and his government moved into the White Palace in 1649, and the Red Palace was added between 1690 and 1694.

The Potala is built in the dzong style at about 3,700 metres and measures 400 metres from east to west and 350 from north to south. Its sloping stone walls average 3 metres thick and 5 at the base, and copper was poured into the foundations as protection against earthquakes. The complex rises thirteen stories and holds more than 1,000 rooms, 10,000 shrines and some 200,000 statues. The crimson Red Palace contains the principal halls, chapels and shrines of past Dalai Lamas, and a Kalachakra Mandala was made there in the 1690s.

From 1649 until 1959 the palace was the residence of the Dalai Lamas. It was damaged in the Tibetan uprising of 1959, when Chinese shells were fired into its windows, and it became a museum complex after the annexation of Tibet by the People's Republic of China. It escaped damage in the Cultural Revolution in 1966 through the intervention of Zhou Enlai. The Potala Palace was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1994, after a restoration in 1989–1994.
potato: The potato is the underground stem tuber of Solanum tuberosum, a perennial in the nightshade family. Its tubers are not roots but stems that form from thickened rhizomes at the tips of long thin stolons. Wild potato species occur from the southern United States to southern Chile. Genetic studies show that the cultivated potato has a single origin, in the area of present-day southern Peru and extreme northwestern Bolivia, around Lake Titicaca, where pre-Columbian farmers domesticated it about 7,000 to 10,000 years ago from a species in the Solanum brevicaule complex.

The earliest archaeologically verified tuber remains come from the coastal site of Ancon in central Peru and date to 2500 BCE. The most widely cultivated variety, Solanum tuberosum tuberosum, is indigenous to the Chiloé Archipelago and has been grown by the local indigenous people since before the Spanish conquest.

The English word potato comes from the Spanish patata, in turn from the Taíno batata, which meant sweet potato and not the plant now called simply the potato. The name spud comes from spudde, a short and stout knife or dagger in the 15th century, and was transferred to the tuber from around 1840.

The Spanish introduced potatoes to Europe in the second half of the 16th century. Selective breeding has since produced over 5,000 varieties, about 3,000 of them in the Andes, mainly in Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Chile and Colombia. Over 100 cultivars might be found in a single valley, and a dozen or more might be maintained by a single agricultural household. Most potatoes are self-incompatible and bear no useful fruit when self-pollinated, which makes crop breeding difficult, since all sexually produced plants must be hybrids.

The potato has been an essential crop in the Andes since the pre-Columbian era. The Moche culture of northern Peru represented it in ceramics, both naturally and as human figures. In Inca mythology Axomamma, a daughter of the earth mother Pachamama, is the goddess of potatoes, who ensured the fertility of the soil and the growth of the tubers. In Haudenosaunee mythology the first potatoes grew out of the feet of Earth Woman after she died giving birth to her twin sons, Sapling and Flint. Chuño, a freeze-dried potato product, is traditionally made by Quechua and Aymara communities of Peru and Bolivia.

In Europe the potato became an essential crop, especially in Northern and Eastern Europe. In the late 19th century numerous images of potato harvesting appeared in European art, including the works of Willem Witsen and Anton Mauve. Raw potatoes contain toxic glycoalkaloids, chiefly solanine and chaconine, and tubers exposed to light can become toxic.
potawatomi: The Potawatomi call themselves Neshnabé, a cognate of Anishinaabe, meaning original people. They are part of a long-term alliance, the Council of Three Fires, with the Ojibwe and the Odawa, and are regarded as its youngest brother. In that context they are called Bodéwadmi, keepers of the fire, because they tend the council fire.

They traditionally speak Potawatomi, a Central Algonquian language most similar to Odawa. Children are instructed in the Seven Grandfather Teachings of wisdom, respect, love, honesty, humility, bravery and truth, and in the story of the Water Spider, who weaves a bowl from her web and sails across the water to bring back fire for the other animals.

Early 17th-century French records suggest that the Potawatomi lived in what is now southwestern Michigan. During the Beaver Wars they fled to the area around Green Bay to escape the expansion of the Iroquois and the Neutral Confederacy, and they numbered about 3,000 in 1658. Historians divide their post-contact history into French contact, British contact, the United States treaty period and Removal. After France ceded its lands to Britain, the Potawatomi took every British frontier garrison except Detroit in Pontiac's Rebellion, and they expanded west from Detroit and south along the shore of Lake Michigan.

They were an important part of Tecumseh's Confederacy, fought in Tecumseh's War and the War of 1812, and switched sides between Britain and the United States as power and their trade and land interests shifted. Chiefs Blackbird and Nuscotomeg led about 500 warriors against the evacuation column at the Battle of Fort Dearborn, killing most of the civilians and 54 of Captain Nathan Heald's force, while Mucktypoke had counselled against the attack and later saved some captives.

Treaties of the late 1820s created reservations, and in the Second Treaty of Prairie du Chien of 1829 the Chippewa, Ottawa and Potawatomi ceded most of their lands in Wisconsin and Michigan. By the Treaty of Chicago of 1833 the United States promised new lands, annuities and supplies in return for further cessions.

The Illinois Potawatomi were removed to Nebraska and the Indiana Potawatomi to Kansas, and those in Kansas were later moved to Indian Territory. Annuities were often reduced or late, and many suffered. The Catholic priest Benjamin Petit documented the Trail of Death of 1838. Many Potawatomi, mostly in Michigan, found ways to stay, and others fled to the Odawa or to Canada.

Today federally recognised Potawatomi tribes include the Forest County Potawatomi Community, the Hannahville Indian Community, the Pokagon Band, the Prairie Band of Potawatomi Nation and the Citizen Potawatomi Nation in Oklahoma, and communities in Ontario. Most first-language speakers are elderly, and the people are working to revitalise the language. Place names such as Waukegan, Muskegon, Kalamazoo and Skokie come from it.
potchefstroom: Potchefstroom, known colloquially as Potch, lies on the Mooi River, Afrikaans for pretty river, about 120 km west-southwest of Johannesburg and 45 km east-northeast of Klerksdorp. Several theories explain its name. One derives it from Potgieter, the Voortrekker leader and founder Andries Potgieter, with chef marking him as leader and stroom the river. Others point to the word Potscherf, a shard of a broken pot, because the soil of the valley cracks in drought. The scholar M. L. Fick suggested that Potgieterstroom was shortened to Potgerstroom and then Potchefstroom.

The Voortrekkers proclaimed the town in December 1838, and settlement began around June 1839. Until 1840 Potchefstroom and Winburg, with their territories, formed the Republic of Winburg-Potchefstroom, with Potgieter as chief commandant. In October 1840 Potgieter, Andries Pretorius and G. R. van Rooyen decided that it would unite with Pietermaritzburg. On 17 January 1852 the Sand River Convention, signed by Pretorius and a British delegation, granted independence to the farmers north of the Vaal, leading to the Transvaal. The republic's 1858 constitution named Potchefstroom as capital and Pretoria as seat of government, and in May 1860 Potchefstroom became the chief city while the capital moved to Pretoria.

On 16 December 1880 the First Boer War began when Boer forces besieged the old fort, held by British troops; the siege ended amicably on 23 March 1881. In the Second Boer War the British pursued a scorched-earth policy, destroying some 30,000 Boer farmhouses by one museum's account, and set up a concentration camp for Afrikaner civilians at Potchefstroom, which the historian G. N. van den Bergh called the first and largest in the Transvaal.

At the opening of the city hall in 1909, the Colonial Secretary Jan Smuts was asked whether Potchefstroom might become the capital of the Union of South Africa. He replied that it had no chance and should aim to be the country's largest educational centre, which gave rise to its reputation as the city of expertise. North-West University was formally established on 1 January 2004 by a merger, and its largest campus and head office are at Potchefstroom. The Aardklop Arts Festival, mainly in Afrikaans, has been held in late September since 1997. The city is the seat of the JB Marks Local Municipality, and its heritage sites include the old fort and cemetery of 1881 and the Town Hall of 1909.
potomac-river: The Potomac has two sources. The North Branch rises at the Fairfax Stone in West Virginia and the South Branch near Hightown in Highland County, Virginia, and the two meet just east of Green Spring in Hampshire County, West Virginia. From there the river flows towards Washington, D.C. and the Chesapeake Bay, passing through five geological provinces: the Appalachian Plateau, the Ridge and Valley, the Blue Ridge, the Piedmont Plateau and the Atlantic coastal plain.

At Little Falls the river drops from the Piedmont to the coastal plain at the Atlantic Seaboard fall line, and below it the tides reach the river. The estuary widens until it is 11 statute miles wide at its mouth between Point Lookout, Maryland, and Smith Point, Virginia. The river's drainage area is about 14,700 square miles, and it forms the boundary between Maryland and Washington, D.C. on one bank and West Virginia and Virginia on the other.

The Potomac has long been inhabited by Native Americans. Before European contact the region was governed by the Algonquian Piscataway confederacy and its allies, under a leader called the Tayac, until power shifted south to the Powhatan confederacy. The name is a European spelling of Patawomeck, the name of a village on the southern bank. Captain John Smith explored the river in 1608, and his map was published in London in 1612.

George Washington was born in, surveyed and spent most of his life within the Potomac basin. He intended the Patowmack Canal to link the Tidewater region near Georgetown with Cumberland, Maryland. It was begun in 1785, completed in 1802 and closed in 1830. The Chesapeake and Ohio Canal then ran along the Maryland bank from 1831 to 1924. The First United States Congress stated by an act of 16 July 1790 that the capital should be on the river.

In the American Civil War the river was a boundary between the Union and the Confederacy, and the Union's largest army was named the Army of the Potomac. Robert E. Lee crossed it twice to invade the North, in the campaigns that ended at Antietam on 17 September 1862 and Gettysburg on 1 to 3 July 1863. Maryland and Virginia long disputed control of the river; the 1877 Black-Jenkins Award gave Maryland the river as far as the low-water mark on the Virginia side.

Washington, D.C. lies entirely on its banks, as does Mount Vernon, the home of George Washington, and the river is nicknamed the Nation's River. The Washington Aqueduct began drawing the capital's drinking water from the Potomac in 1864, and the river supplies about 78 per cent of the water used in the Washington area. Its navigable parts were designated a National Recreation Trail in 2006.
potosi: Potosí lies at a nominal 4,067 metres above sea level, one of the highest cities in the world, at the foot of the Cerro de Potosí, also called the Cerro Rico or rich mountain, whose peak reaches 4,824 metres. The mountain is a dacite volcanic dome with silver-bearing veins and is honeycombed by workings that reach depths of 1,150 metres. At peak production in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries the ore contained up to 40 per cent silver.

The city was founded in 1545 as a mining town, and the indigenous prospector Diego Huallpa is traditionally credited with discovering the Cerro Rico. In the second half of the 16th century the mountain produced an estimated 60 per cent of all silver mined in the world. The easily smelted ore was exhausted by 1565, and output recovered through mercury amalgamation, first the patio process of Bartolomé de Medina and from 1609 a pan process invented at Potosí. The crown licensed private miners and taxed them, with a 20 per cent levy called the quinto. By about 1603 there were roughly 6,000 Europeans, 5,000 Africans and at least 120,000 native Andeans in the city, the second largest in the world after London.

Indigenous workers were drafted into the mines under the mita, based on an older Andean system of labour for public works. Thirteen thousand men a year were conscripted, about one in seven adult men of the indigenous population in the area covered. They carried ore up ladders in shafts lit by candles and died from falls and pneumonia, while mercury poisoned many in refining. Historians differ on the mita's weight: Noble David Cook notes that in 1603 only 5,100 of 58,800 indigenous workers were mitayos, whereas Peter Bakewell stresses that many other workers were former mitayos or mitayos in their off weeks.

Potosí is the capital of the Department of Potosí in Bolivia. Its historic centre, with a large amount of preserved colonial architecture, forms with the Cerro Rico a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Mining changed from silver to tin in 1891 and continued in tin until 1985, and the city is still a mining centre.
potsdam: Potsdam lies on the River Havel, a tributary of the Elbe, about 25 kilometres south-west of Berlin's city centre. The area was formed from a series of large moraines left after the last glacial period, and the hilly landscape holds about 20 lakes and rivers in and around the city, among them the Griebnitzsee, Templiner See and Jungfernsee. Only a quarter of the city is built up, the rest remaining green space. The highest point is the Kleiner Ravensberg, at 114 metres. The name of the city and of many of its boroughs is of Slavic origin; it seems originally to have been Poztupimi, perhaps from a West Slavonic term meaning beneath the oaks.

The area shows signs of occupation since the Bronze Age. After the migrations of the Germanic peoples, Slavs moved in, and Potsdam was probably founded after the 7th century as a settlement of the Hevelli tribe centred on a castle. It was first mentioned in 993, when Emperor Otto III gave the territory to Quedlinburg Abbey, and it received its town charter in 1345. In 1573 it was still a small market town of about 2,000 people, and the Thirty Years' War cost it nearly half its population. It had been a Hohenzollern possession since 1415, and in 1660 the Elector of Brandenburg chose it as a hunting residence.

The Edict of Potsdam of 1685 offered religious freedom and made the city a centre of European immigration, drawing Huguenots and settlers from Russia, the Netherlands and Bohemia. The royal residences were built mainly under Frederick the Great, including Sanssouci, by Georg Wenzeslaus von Knobelsdorff, in 1744.

When Berlin was capital of Prussia and then of the German Empire, the court remained in Potsdam, and in 1914 Emperor Wilhelm II signed the Declaration of War in the New Palace. The city lost its status as a second capital in 1918. On 21 March 1933 Paul von Hindenburg and Adolf Hitler shook hands in Potsdam's Garrison Church in the ceremony known as the Day of Potsdam. Allied bombing raids, notably on the Old Town on 14 April 1945, severely damaged the city.

Potsdam is the capital and largest city of the German state of Brandenburg and part of the Berlin/Brandenburg Metropolitan Region. Its parks and palaces, among them Sanssouci and Cecilienhof Palace, form Germany's largest World Heritage Site. Babelsberg in the south-east has a film studio founded in 1912, the oldest large-scale film studio in the world, and Potsdam was named a UNESCO City of Film in 2019. The city became a centre of science in the 19th century, and it has the University of Potsdam and more than 30 research institutes.
potsdam-agreement: After the end of the war in Europe, the Allies assumed supreme authority over Germany by the Berlin Declaration of 5 June 1945. The Potsdam Conference ran from 17 July to 2 August 1945 and was attended by Joseph Stalin, President Harry S. Truman and Prime Minister Clement Attlee, who replaced Winston Churchill after the British general election. At the conference the Western Allies were presented with Stalin's fait accompli awarding Soviet-occupied Poland the river Oder as its western border. France was not invited, and its provisional government accepted a seat on the Council of Foreign Ministers with the reservation that it would not accept in advance any commitment to a central German government.

The agreement divided Germany into four occupation zones, with the commanders-in-chief exercising authority within their zones and jointly through the Allied Control Council for Germany as a whole. Its principles were democratisation, treatment of Germany as a single unit, disarmament and demilitarisation, and the removal of Nazi influence. Civilian heavy industry with war potential was to be reduced or destroyed and the economy turned towards agriculture and light industry. The Soviet Union received reparations from its own zone, and 10 per cent of the western zones' unnecessary industrial capacity was to be transferred to it. All but thirty German submarines were to be sunk and the rest of the navy divided equally.

The United States and the United Kingdom promised to support the transfer of Königsberg to the Soviet Union. Poland's provisional western border was set at the Oder–Neisse line, with the final delimitation awaiting a peace settlement. The three governments also recognised that German populations remaining in Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary would have to be transferred to Germany, and agreed that this should be done in an orderly and humane manner. Other clauses concerned the trial of war criminals, Austria, peace treaties with Italy and the former Axis states in Europe, and the withdrawal of troops from Iran.

The Allied Control Council was constituted in Berlin on 30 July 1945 to carry out the Four Ds of denazification, demilitarisation, democratisation and decentralisation. The Cold War soon led to German rearmament, and dismantling stopped in West Germany in 1951.

France resisted implementing the agreement in its zone and refused to resettle expelled Germans. The transfer clause was used to legitimise the expulsion of Germans from Poland, Czechoslovakia and the lands placed under Polish administration, and expulsions also occurred in Romania and Yugoslavia. The agreement was a communiqué and not a peace treaty in international law. The Oder–Neisse line became Poland's permanent border only in the 1990 German–Polish Border Treaty, and the Treaty on the Final Settlement with Respect to Germany of 12 September 1990 superseded the agreement.
potsdam-declaration: At the start of the Potsdam Conference the United States delegation considered a proclamation demanding Japan's unconditional surrender in the name of the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union and China. The text went through many drafts. Joseph Stalin declined to endorse it, since the Soviet Union was not yet at war with Japan, and committed instead to subscribing once it entered the war. On 24 July President Harry S. Truman gave Winston Churchill a draft, and the American delegation adopted all the British amendments.

Chiang Kai-shek was not at the conference, so China was asked by telegram. He agreed to one amendment, listing the President of the National Government of the Republic of China before the British prime minister. Churchill authorised the text on 26 July before submitting his resignation that evening, after his unexpected election defeat. The signatures of Chiang and Churchill were in fact in Truman's handwriting.

The declaration demanded the elimination for all time of the authority of those who had misled the Japanese people into world conquest, the occupation of points in Japanese territory to be designated by the Allies, and the limiting of Japanese sovereignty to Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, Shikoku and minor islands. Japanese forces were to be disarmed and sent home. It stated that the Allies did not intend the Japanese to be enslaved as a race or destroyed as a nation, but that war criminals would receive stern justice.

It also offered the revival of democratic tendencies, freedom of speech, religion and thought, industries that would sustain the economy but not rearmament, and the withdrawal of occupying forces once a peaceful and responsible government had been established. It never mentioned the emperor, and left unstated the number of occupation points, the fate of the minor islands and the form of Allied control. The warning of prompt and utter destruction has been read as a veiled reference to the atomic bomb, which was not named.

The declaration was broadcast to Japan and more than 3 million leaflets describing it were dropped, but it was never sent through diplomatic channels. In Tokyo, Foreign Minister Shigenori Tōgō and others felt it must be accepted, but the war minister and the chiefs of staff opposed it.
