Ptolemy made Egypt a closed monetary zone, requiring foreign coins to be exchanged at its borders. He commanded the building of the Library of Alexandria and of the Lighthouse of Alexandria. He made his son Ptolemy II his co-regent in 285 BCE, and died in 282 BCE.

Ptolemy left what the sources describe as a compact, well-ordered realm after forty years of war. His reputation for good nature and generosity attached Macedonian and Greek soldiers to his service, and he was a patron of letters. His last wife was Berenice I, and her son succeeded him as Ptolemy II, while his sons by Eurydice, Ptolemy Keraunos and Meleager, ruled in turn as kings of Macedon. The dynasty ruled Egypt until the death of Cleopatra VII in 30 BCE. According to Proclus, Ptolemy sponsored the mathematician Euclid, and told him that he found the Elements too difficult; Euclid replied that there is no royal road to geometry.
ptolemy-ii-philadelphus: Ptolemy II was the son of Ptolemy I, the Macedonian general of Alexander the Great who founded the Ptolemaic Kingdom, and of his third wife, Berenice I. He was born on Kos in 309 or 308 BCE, during his father's invasion of the Aegean in the Fourth Diadoch War, and had two full sisters, Arsinoe II and Philotera. He was educated by distinguished intellectuals, among them Philitas of Cos and Strato of Lampsacus. His older half-brother Ptolemy Keraunos was heir presumptive at his birth, and a struggle for the succession ended with Keraunos leaving Egypt around 287 BCE. Ptolemy I had Ptolemy II declared king and co-regent on 28 March 284 BCE, and the co-regency lasted until his father's death in 282 BCE.

He pursued an aggressive foreign policy with mixed success. Around 275 BCE Ptolemaic forces invaded Nubia and annexed the northern twelve miles of the Triakontaschoinos, the stretch of the Nile between the First and Second Cataract, whose gold mines helped the prosperity of the kingdom. In the First Syrian War, from 274 to 271 BCE, he invaded Seleucid Syria, was defeated by Antiochus I and retreated, but Antiochus abandoned the war and agreed to peace. About 270 BCE he cleared the old canal from the Nile to the Gulf of Suez, and two missions went down the Red Sea coasts and set up a chain of harbour bases.

In the Chremonidean War, about 267 to 261 BCE, he confronted Antigonid Macedonia for control of the Aegean and suffered serious setbacks. The Second Syrian War, from 260 to 253 BCE, lost many of the gains of the first, including sections of Pamphylia and Cilicia. He died on 28 January 246 BCE.

Ptolemy II transformed the cult of Alexander the Great into a state cult of the dynasty. He deified his father and, after her death, his mother Berenice I, and about 272 BCE made himself and his sister-wife Arsinoe II divine as the Theoi Adelphoi. He also presented himself as a traditional pharaoh and financed temple building across Egypt, including the core of the Temple of Isis at Philae. He was an eager patron of scholarship, funding the expansion of the Library of Alexandria. The poets Callimachus, Theocritus, Apollonius of Rhodes and Posidippus received stipends, and the mathematician Euclid worked under his patronage. The tradition that he prompted the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible is unlikely to be true.
ptolemy-iii-euergetes: Ptolemy III was the eldest son of Ptolemy II and his first wife Arsinoe I, daughter of King Lysimachus of Thrace. After a conflict with Ptolemy II's sister Arsinoe II, Arsinoe I was exiled to Coptos, and her children seem to have been removed from the succession. Ptolemy III appears to have been raised on Thera, and his tutors included the poet Apollonius of Rhodes. In the late 250s BCE Ptolemy II arranged his engagement to Berenice, only child of King Magas of Cyrene, which shows that he was by then heir presumptive. He took the throne on 28 January 246 BCE.

Magas had declared himself king of Cyrenaica in 276 BCE. After his death his widow Apame invited an Antigonid prince, Demetrius the Fair, to marry Berenice instead, but Berenice had him assassinated. Only on Ptolemy III's accession did his wedding with Berenice seem to take place. Ptolemaic authority over Cyrene was reasserted, and two port cities were founded and named Ptolemais and Berenice.

In the Third Syrian War (246–241 BCE) he invaded Syria in support of his sister Berenice and her infant son, only to find at Antioch that both had been murdered. He pressed on into Mesopotamia and conquered Babylon, but a revolt in Egypt forced him home. Peace in 241 BCE left him the conquered lands in Asia Minor and northern Syria, including Seleucia Pieria, the port of Antioch. In the Aegean a Ptolemaic fleet was defeated by Antigonus II of Macedon at Andros, but he went on funding Macedon's opponents in Greece, notably the Achaean League.

The Canopus decree of 238 BCE, issued by a synod of all the priests of Egypt, was the first known trilingual decree in Greek, hieroglyphs and demotic. It formed a partnership between the pharaoh and the priestly elite that lasted to the end of the dynasty. In 243 BCE Ptolemy and Berenice were made objects of worship as the Theoi Euergetai, the Benefactor Gods, and in 224 BCE Athens honoured him with a new tribe named Ptolemais.

Ptolemy III died of natural causes in November or December 222 BCE, and his son Ptolemy IV succeeded him without incident. The Ptolemaic Kingdom reached the height of its military and economic power during his kingship.
ptolemy-iv-philopator: Ptolemy IV was the second child and eldest son of Ptolemy III and Berenice II. He had an older sister, Arsinoe III, and three younger brothers, Lysimachus, Alexander and Magas, all born in the 240s BCE. Under Ptolemy III the kingdom had reached its height, though that reign had also seen the first native Egyptian revolt, in 245 BCE.

The new king was about twenty and under the strong influence of the aristocrats Sosibius and Agathocles, brother of the king's mistress Agathoclea. Sosibius engineered a purge of the royal family. His uncle Lysimachus was probably murdered, and his brother Magas, popular with the army, was scalded to death in his bath. Ptolemy married Arsinoe III by 220 BCE.

Antiochus III, who had taken the Seleucid throne in 222 BCE, invaded Coele-Syria and in 219 BCE captured Seleucia Pieria. In early 218 BCE he destroyed Ptolemaic forces at Berytus. On 22 June 217 BCE, Ptolemy and Arsinoe led the Egyptian army against him at Raphia, one of the largest battles of the Hellenistic Age, with over 150,000 soldiers. Polybius, generally hostile to Ptolemy, presents the king's sudden appearance on the front line as the turning point. Antiochus retreated, and the peace left Ptolemy with the territories he had held at the start, apparently except Seleucia Pieria. A priestly synod at Memphis issued the Raphia decree.

Ptolemy proclaimed himself a god, the Theos Philopator, and systematised the dynastic cult. He promoted the cult of Dionysus, and was called the Neos Dionysos. He supported Egyptian temples, notably the Temple of Horus at Edfu, and is said to have built a huge galley, the tessarakonteres. In Greece he helped broker the Peace of Naupactus in 217 BCE.

After the war a great revolt broke out in Egypt. In October or November 205 BCE the leader of the southern rebels took Thebes and was crowned pharaoh as Horwennefer, and he kept his independence for nearly twenty years, until captured in August 186 BCE. Polybius held that the revolts resulted from arming Egyptians for the war.

Ptolemy died in July or August 204 BCE in unclear circumstances, and Arsinoe III died at about the same time. His six-year-old son Ptolemy V, co-regent since 210 BCE, was proclaimed king with Sosibius and Agathocles as regents. Polybius, the main source, portrays Ptolemy as a bad king absorbed in luxury, but he was not his contemporary, and luxury was often counted a virtue by those who lived then.
ptolemy-keraunos: Ptolemy was the eldest son of Ptolemy I Soter and his first wife Eurydice, daughter of Antipater, regent of Macedon, and was probably born in 319 BCE. His epithet Keraunos is Greek for thunderbolt and referred to an impatient, impetuous and destructive character. Between 317 and 314 BCE his father married Berenice, one of Eurydice's ladies-in-waiting, and had further children, among them the future Ptolemy II Philadelphus. At first Ptolemy was heir presumptive, but as Berenice's son grew older a power struggle developed between the half-brothers, and Ptolemy left Egypt around 287 BCE. Ptolemy II was made co-regent on 28 March 284 BCE.

Ptolemy went to the court of Lysimachus, who ruled Macedon, Thrace and western Asia Minor. The court was divided: Lysimachus was married to Ptolemy II's full sister Arsinoe II, while his heir Agathocles was married to Ptolemy's full sister Lysandra. The sisters were already in conflict over the succession. Lysimachus chose to back Ptolemy II. When Agathocles was executed in 282 BCE, the historian Memnon names Ptolemy as the murderer, but all other sources place him on Agathocles' side and have him accompany Lysandra to the court of Seleucus I. Seleucus invaded early in 281 BCE and Lysimachus was killed at the Battle of Corupedium.

Ptolemy came under Seleucus' control and joined his inner circle. In September 281 BCE, as Seleucus sacrificed at a place called Argos before crossing the Hellespont, Ptolemy murdered him, intending to take the territories of his protector. He was thus responsible for the death of the last of the Diadochi, Alexander's successors. He was acclaimed king by part of Seleucus' army at Lysimachia and formally gave up his claim to Egypt.

As king of Macedon Ptolemy defeated Antigonos Gonatas in a naval battle and confined him to Demetrias in Thessaly. He allied with Pyrrhus of Epirus, which freed Pyrrhus to invade Italy. Justin reports that he gave Pyrrhus troops and elephants and a daughter in marriage, though some scholars doubt this. He proposed marriage to his half-sister Arsinoe II, widow of Lysimachus, who agreed on condition that her young sons be kept safe. On the wedding day he murdered the two younger sons, and she fled to Samothrace and then Egypt. A war with Arsinoe's eldest son, probably Ptolemy Epigonos, and an Illyrian king, Monunius, occupied most of 280 BCE.

In January or February 279 BCE Gauls led by Bolgius invaded Macedon. Ptolemy refused to wait for his full force and rejected help from 20,000 Dardanians. He was wounded and captured and the Gauls killed him. After his death anarchy followed until Antigonos Gonatas defeated the Gauls near Lysimachia in 277 BCE and was recognised as king.
ptolemy-of-mauretania: Ptolemy was probably born between 13 and 9 BCE, the child of Juba II of Numidia and Cleopatra Selene II, who had been appointed rulers of Mauretania by the emperor Augustus in 25 BCE. Their court at Caesarea promoted Greek and Egyptian culture through art, building and a royal library. His mother gave him the name Ptolemy, as was traditional for male members of the Ptolemaic dynasty, rather than a Numidian or Roman one. He was probably educated in Athens, where he was honoured with a statue at the Gymnasium of Ptolemy, and he probably held Roman citizenship.

From 17 CE Juba II faced a revolt led by Tacfarinas, a Gaetulian who had once served as a Roman auxiliary, and by 21 CE Ptolemy was co-regent. When Juba died, Ptolemy became sole ruler. He assisted the Roman proconsul of Africa, Publius Cornelius Dolabella, in the campaign in which Tacfarinas was killed at Augea. The Senate named him a friend and ally of the Roman people and in 24 CE sent him an ivory sceptre, a gold crown, a curule seat and a toga picta, all of which appear on his coins. Duane W. Roller regarded the war as a showcase of his competence, while Anthony A. Barrett suggested that he contributed little.

Mauretania prospered under him by exporting grain, olive oil, garum, Tyrian purple dye and luxury woods to Rome, along with animals for spectacles in the Colosseum. Unlike his scholarly father, he was reputed to be an immature ruler controlled by members of his court. Near the end of his reign he began to act independently of Rome and issued gold coins, which he may not have been permitted to do.

In late 39 or early 40 CE Caligula summoned Ptolemy to Rome. According to Suetonius he was meant to receive honours but was arrested instead and later executed. Cassius Dio claimed that the emperor envied his wealth, and Suetonius that his purple attire drew admiration in the amphitheatre. Modern historians suggest that Caligula saw him as a political threat, or that he was suspected in the conspiracy of Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Gaetulicus; Duncan Fishwick and Brent Shaw thought him almost certainly innocent.

Caligula tried to annex the kingdom but met a rebellion led by Aedemon, which destroyed Tamuda and partly destroyed Volubilis and Lixus. It was suppressed shortly before Claudius became emperor in 41. After another rising in 42, Claudius sent Gaius Suetonius Paulinus and Gnaeus Hosidius Geta to establish Roman control, and he separated the country into Mauretania Tingitana and Mauretania Caesariensis.
ptolemy-vi-philometor: Ptolemy VI was the eldest son of Ptolemy V and Cleopatra I. His father's reign was dominated by the Fifth Syrian War (204–198 BCE), in which the Seleucid king Antiochus III defeated the Ptolemaic forces, annexed Coele-Syria and Judaea, and reduced Egypt to a subordinate position. Ptolemy VI was born in 186 BCE, probably in May or June, and had a sister, Cleopatra II, and a younger brother, Ptolemy VIII.

When Ptolemy V died unexpectedly in September 180 BCE, the six-year-old boy was crowned at once, with his mother as co-regent. The epithet Philometor, 'lover of his mother', reflects her unusual place in the documents of the time. After her death in 178 or 177 BCE, two of her associates, Eulaeus and Lenaeus, acted as regents. In early 175 BCE they married the king to his sister Cleopatra II, following the Ptolemaic custom of brother-sister marriage.

The Sixth Syrian War began probably in early 169 BCE. The Ptolemaic army set out from Pelusium to invade Palestine but was defeated in the Sinai by Antiochus IV, who seized Pelusium. Ptolemy VI then negotiated an agreement that in effect made him a Seleucid client, and the Alexandrians responded by declaring Ptolemy VIII sole king. Antiochus besieged Alexandria without taking it and withdrew in September 169 BCE. The brothers soon reconciled, and Antiochus invaded again in the spring of 168 BCE. A Roman embassy led by Gaius Popillius Laenas confronted him at Eleusis and forced a settlement.

The rift between the brothers outlasted the war. Late in 164 BCE Ptolemy VIII expelled Ptolemy VI, who went to Rome and then to Cyprus. In summer 163 BCE the people of Alexandria rose against Ptolemy VIII and recalled Ptolemy VI, who granted his brother Cyrenaica. Ptolemy VIII appealed to Rome for Cyprus as well, but the Senate gave him no real support, and in 154 BCE Ptolemy VI besieged him at Lapethus and captured him. He also allowed a group of Jewish immigrants led by Onias IV to settle at Leontopolis and build a temple there.

Ptolemy VI supported a series of rival claimants to the Seleucid throne. In 145 BCE he invaded Syria, took the coastal cities and was crowned king of Asia at Antioch, but he abandoned the title, fearing that a union of the two kingdoms would bring Roman intervention. With Demetrius II he defeated Alexander Balas at the Oenoparas river; Alexander fled to Arabia and was killed. Ptolemy VI had been wounded in the battle and died three days later. Demetrius II soon expelled the Ptolemaic troops from Syria, and the Alexandrians invited Ptolemy VIII to take the throne.
ptolemy-viii-physcon: Ptolemy VIII was the younger son of Ptolemy V and Cleopatra I, the daughter of the Seleucid king Antiochus III, whom Ptolemy V had married in 194 BCE as part of a peace treaty after the Fifth Syrian War. His elder brother Ptolemy VI was the heir from birth, and he also had a sister, Cleopatra II. In October 170 BCE, now about sixteen, he was made co-regent with his brother and sister, who were by then married to one another, in the run-up to the Sixth Syrian War. The regents Eulaeus and Lenaeus remained in charge of the government in practice.

The failure of Egyptian forces in the Sixth Syrian War damaged the monarchy's prestige and caused a lasting rift between the brothers. In 165 BCE the courtier Dionysius Petosarapis tried to exploit it and stirred up a revolt in the Fayyum. In 164 BCE Ptolemy VIII drove out his brother and became sole king, but he was expelled in 163 BCE and took control of Cyrenaica. Dissatisfied, he went to Rome, where the Senate declared that he should have Cyprus as well, though Polybius believed it wished to weaken Ptolemaic power. From 162 BCE he was an official friend and ally of the Roman Republic. As king in Cyrene he held the priesthood of Apollo, hosted lavish feasts and built widely.

When Ptolemy VI died on campaign in Syria in 145 BCE, the Alexandrians called Ptolemy VIII back to marry his sister Cleopatra II. His cruel treatment of opponents, and his marriage to his niece Cleopatra III, led to a civil war from 132 BCE to 127 or 126 BCE, in which Cleopatra II held Alexandria with Greek support and he held most of the rest of Egypt with native Egyptian support. Native Egyptians rose to the highest posts of the government for the first time. He won, and in 118 BCE the royal trio announced a reconciliation in the Amnesty decree.

Ptolemy VIII took part in Greek scholarship, especially philology. He is reported to have written a study of Homer and twenty-four books of Hypomnemata, or Notes, a miscellany of stories about monarchs and exotic wildlife. Yet Alexandria declined as an intellectual centre in his reign, partly because of the massacres he carried out in 145 and 126 BCE. Among his victims were Aristarchus of Samothrace and Apollodorus of Athens, and other scholars went into exile in Athens or Rhodes. Ancient Greek sources are extremely hostile to him, and the historian Günther Hölbl calls him one of the most brutal and at the same time one of the shrewdest politicians of the Hellenistic age. In his last years Eudoxus of Cyzicus travelled to India.
ptolemy-xii-auletes: Ptolemy XII was the oldest son of Ptolemy IX, by a mother whose identity is uncertain. Cicero and other ancient sources call him illegitimate, and some scholars propose that his mother was a concubine. His grandmother Cleopatra III sent him and his brother, later Ptolemy of Cyprus, to the island of Kos in 103 BCE.

Mithridates VI of Pontus seems to have captured them in 88 BCE, and held them as hostages until 80 BCE. After the killing of his cousin Ptolemy XI in 80 BCE, Ptolemy XII was recalled and proclaimed king in Alexandria in April of that year. He was known as Auletes, meaning the flautist, for playing the flute at Dionysian festivals.

Ptolemy X had left Egypt to Rome in his will if he had no surviving heirs, so Ptolemy XII followed a respectful policy towards Rome. In 65 BCE the censor Marcus Licinius Crassus proposed to annex Egypt, but Quintus Lutatius Catulus and Cicero opposed it. Ptolemy began to bribe Roman politicians, funding this by raising taxes and by loans from Roman bankers such as Gaius Rabirius Postumus.

In 60 BCE he went to Rome, where he paid Pompey and Caesar six thousand talents, equal to the total annual revenue of Egypt. The Senate recognised him as king, and in 59 BCE Caesar passed a law that named him a friend and ally of the Roman people.

In 58 BCE Rome took Cyprus, and his brother committed suicide. Ptolemy took no action, and the court at Alexandria forced him to leave Egypt. His daughter Berenice IV took the throne. He went to Rome, where Pompey housed him. In 55 BCE he paid Aulus Gabinius 10,000 talents to invade Egypt, and Gabinius defeated the frontier forces and took the palace. Ptolemy had Berenice and her supporters executed, and ruled with the help of around two thousand Roman soldiers and mercenaries, the Gabiniani. He made Rabirius his finance minister to put popular anger at the taxes on a Roman, and later had to imprison him to protect his life.

Ptolemy XII died before 22 March 51 BCE, after falling ill. His daughter Cleopatra VII had been named his regent. In his will he made her and her brother Ptolemy XIII joint rulers and the people of Rome the executors, and Pompey approved the will. Ancient and modern writers portray him as weak and self-indulgent.

Strabo calls him the worst of the later Ptolemies and says he took such pride in playing the flute that he held contests in the royal palace. Mary Siani-Davies writes that his aim throughout was to keep the throne for his heirs, at the cost of lands, wealth and, according to Cicero, the dignity of kingship.
publius-quinctilius-varus: Varus was a patrician by birth, but his family, the Quinctilii Vari, had long been impoverished and unimportant. His father, Sextus Quinctilius Varus, a senator, sided with the Senatorial Party against Julius Caesar and killed himself after the Battle of Philippi in 42 BCE. Varus had three sisters, who made advantageous marriages. He married Vipsania, daughter of Marcus Agrippa, before 13 BCE, and was a personal friend of Agrippa and Tiberius. He later married Claudia Pulchra, a grand-niece of Augustus, who bore him a son, also named Publius Quinctilius Varus. Despite his father's allegiance he became a supporter of Augustus.

Varus accompanied Augustus on a three-year tour of the eastern provinces between 22 and 19 BCE. Around 15 BCE he served for a year or more as legate of the 19th Legion at Dangstetten, shown by a luggage tag found there. When Agrippa died in 12 BCE, Varus delivered the funeral eulogy with Tiberius, and in 13 BCE he was consul as Tiberius's colleague. He governed Africa in 8 to 7 BCE and then Syria and Judaea, with four legions, until 4 BCE, and was known for harsh rule and high taxes.

After the death of Herod the Great in 4 BCE, Josephus tells that Varus acted swiftly against a messianic revolt, occupied Jerusalem and crucified 2,000 Jews. Archaeological evidence suggests that people in Judaea boycotted Roman red slipware pottery in protest.

Tiberius declared Germania pacified in 6 CE and left to suppress the Great Illyrian Revolt, and Augustus made Varus the first officially appointed governor of the new province in 7 CE. In September 9 CE he prepared to march the Seventeenth, Eighteenth and Nineteenth Legions from Vetera to Moguntiacum. Arminius, a Germanic prince who was a Roman citizen and led an auxiliary cavalry unit, reported a revolt, and Varus followed his lead, ignoring a warning from Segestes. The legions marched into an ambush near Kalkriese, north of Osnabrück. The forest and swampy ground made their manoeuvres impossible, and on the third day the Germanic fighters overwhelmed them.

Varus took his own life by falling on his sword. Arminius sent his head to Maroboduus of the Marcomanni, who refused the alliance and sent it to Rome for burial. Some captured Romans were enslaved or ransomed, while Tacitus and Florus report that officers were sacrificed on altars. The three legions were never again listed in the Roman army, and the Romans later recovered their eagles. Suetonius says Augustus tore his clothes and for years cried out, Quinctilius Varus, give me back my legions. The government blamed Varus, and his son's prospects were ruined. Roman writers called the defeat the Varian disaster.
publius-sulpicius-quirinius: Quirinius was born around 51 BCE into an undistinguished family at Lanuvium, a Latin town near Rome, the son and grandson of men named Publius Sulpicius Quirinius. He followed the usual path of service for an ambitious young man of his class. According to the historian Florus, he defeated the Marmaridae, a tribe of desert raiders from Cyrenaica, around 14 BCE, possibly while governor of Crete and Cyrene, but declined the honorific name Marmaricus. His election as consul in 12 BCE was a sign of the favour of Augustus.

Around 5 to 3 BCE Quirinius led a campaign, probably as legate of Galatia, against the Homonadenses, a tribe of the mountains of Galatia and Cilicia. He reduced their strongholds and starved out the defenders, and was awarded a triumph and elected duumvir by the colony of Antioch of Pisidia. By 1 CE he was tutor to Augustus' grandson Gaius Caesar, and when Augustus' support shifted to his stepson Tiberius, Quirinius changed allegiance too. His first marriage, to Claudia Appia, ended in divorce, as did his second, to Aemilia Lepida, in 20 CE he accused Lepida of falsely claiming that he had fathered her son and of trying to poison him. Tacitus says she was popular and the public saw his prosecution as spiteful.

After Herod Archelaus was banished in 6 CE, Judaea came under direct Roman rule with Coponius as prefect, and Quirinius was appointed legate of Syria with instructions to assess Judaea for taxation, beginning with a census. Censuses were forbidden under Jewish law and the assessment was greatly resented. Open revolt was prevented only by the high priest Joazar, but according to Josephus and the Acts of the Apostles the census led to the revolt of Judas of Galilee and the party of the Zealots.

Quirinius governed Syria, with authority over Judaea, until 12 CE and then returned to Rome as a close associate of Tiberius. He died nine years later. Tiberius asked the Senate for a public funeral, and Tacitus calls him a tireless soldier who became consul under Augustus. His governorship is confirmed by coins of his administration dated to the 36th year of Caesar, and the Stele of Quintus Aemilius Secundus, an officer who served under him, records a census of the city of Apamea ordered by Quirinius.

The Gospel of Luke, chapter 2, links the birth of Jesus with the census of Quirinius. This is widely held to contradict the Gospel of Matthew, which places the birth in the reign of Herod the Great, who died in 4 BCE, and most critical scholars judge Luke inconsistent with the historical evidence.
puducherry-union-territory: The Union Territory of Puducherry lies on the southern part of the Indian Peninsula and consists of four small districts that do not touch one another. Puducherry and Karaikal, on the Bay of Bengal, are enclaves of Tamil Nadu; Yanam, also on the Bay of Bengal, is an enclave of Andhra Pradesh; and Mahé, on the Laccadive Sea, is an enclave of Kerala. Together they cover 483 square kilometres. Some regions are themselves made of separate pockets: Puducherry has eleven and Mahé three. This unusual geography is a legacy of the colonial period, since the territory keeps the borders of former French India. Its name comes from the Tamil putu-cheri, meaning new village, first spelt Poudichéry by the French.

The earliest recorded history of the area goes back to the second century CE, when the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea mentions a marketplace called Poduke. Excavations at Arikamedu, a site possibly connected with it, found Roman pottery; later investigation placed the occupation of the site from the third or second century BCE to the eighth century CE.

In 1674 Pondicherry became a French colony. With Chandernagor, French since 1673, Mahé (since 1721), Yanam (since 1723), Karaikal (since 1739) and Masulipatam (1760) it formed French India under a single governor in Pondicherry, although British occupations repeatedly interrupted French rule over one or more of these enclaves. The territories passed to the Republic of India de facto on 1 November 1954 and de jure on 16 August 1962. Chandannagar merged with West Bengal in 1954. The remaining four became the State of Pondicherry, and on 1 July 1963 the Union Territory of Pondicherry; the name was officially changed to Puducherry on 1 October 2006.

Under the Treaty of Cession of 1956 the four territories kept the special administrative status they had before 1 November 1954, and any constitutional change to it was to follow consultation of the population. The treaty also kept French as an official language for as long as the elected representatives did not decide otherwise.

Puducherry is governed as a union territory, with a Lieutenant Governor representing the central government and an elected legislative assembly. At the 2011 census its population was 1,394,467. Tamil is the first language of most people, with Telugu and Malayalam spoken in Yanam and Mahé; the official languages are French, Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and English. The city of Puducherry was the residence of Sri Aurobindo, and the Sri Aurobindo Ashram and the experimental city of Auroville lie in and beside it.
puebla-state: Puebla lies in the central highlands of Mexico between the Sierra Nevada and the Sierra Madre Oriental, and covers 33,919 square kilometres. It has a triangular shape with its narrow part to the north. It borders Veracruz, Oaxaca, Guerrero, Morelos, the State of Mexico, Tlaxcala and Hidalgo. Its highest elevations are volcanoes on its borders: Pico de Orizaba, at 5,747 metres, on the border with Veracruz, Popocatépetl at 5,452 metres and Iztaccíhuatl at 5,286 metres. Five major indigenous groups live in the state: the Nahuas, Totonacs, Mixtecs, Popolocas and Otomi, mostly in the far north and far south.

The territory was among the first in present-day Mexico to be inhabited. The earliest settlements are in the valley of Tehuacán, the oldest near the Agujereado Mountain, dating to about 10,000 BCE, and more than 450 prehistoric sites are known in that valley alone. Evidence of agriculture dates to between 3500 and 2000 BCE, by 900 BCE corn, beans, squash, chili peppers and cotton were widely grown, and city states had appeared by 700 BCE. The site of Cantona, occupied between the 7th and 11th centuries CE, reached its height when many other Classic centres were declining.

Hernán Cortés entered the area in 1519 with indigenous allies on his way to Tlaxcala. Many peoples there were under Aztec domination and saw the Spanish as a way to escape it. At Cholula, Cortés was told of a plot against him and ordered the Massacre of Cholula on 12 October 1519, which frightened others into submission. The city of Puebla was founded by the Spanish in 1531 to secure the trade route between Mexico City and the port of Veracruz.

During the Mexican War of Independence the city remained loyal to the viceroy, while much of the south was in insurgent hands. The first governor of the state was Carlos García Arriaga in 1821, and the first state congress sat in 1824, the year of the first state constitution. In 1912 the Zapatistas took over a number of communities, and the state was re-established under the Constitution of 1917.

Puebla is one of the 31 states that with Mexico City make up the federal entities of Mexico. Its capital is Puebla City, and it is divided into 217 municipalities. The historic centre of the capital was named a World Heritage Site in 1987. Talavera pottery, a type of maiolica brought to Mexico by the Spanish, is the state's best-known craft, and its dishes include mole poblano. Cinco de Mayo is observed throughout the state.
pueblo-peoples: Pueblo is a Spanish word meaning 'village' and 'people', first used by Spanish explorers for the peoples' style of dwelling. In the twentieth century archaeologists often called the ancestors of the Pueblo peoples Anasazi, a word introduced by Alfred V. Kidder from a Navajo term meaning 'enemy ancestors'. Contemporary Pueblo people object to it as derogatory, and the term Ancestral Puebloan is now preferred.

Pueblo societies contain elements of three cultures that dominated the Southwest before European contact: the Mogollon, whose people lived near the Gila Wilderness; the Hohokam; and the Ancestral Puebloan culture of the Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde regions. The first evidence of maize cultivation in the Southwest dates from about 2100 BCE. By about 700 to 900 CE people had begun to leave pit houses for connected rectangular rooms of adobe, and by 1050 they had built planned villages of large terraced buildings.

Pueblo Bonito in Chaco Canyon, the largest of these villages, held around 700 rooms in five stories and may have housed as many as 1,000 people. The Tiwa people fought the Coronado Expedition in the Tiguex War of 1540–41, and a group led by Juan de Oñate arrived in 1598. Spanish efforts to replace Pueblo religion with Catholicism grew steadily harsher.

In the 1670s a severe drought brought famine and more frequent Apache raids. Growing resentment of Spanish abuses led to the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, the first uprising led by a Native American group to expel colonists from North America for a considerable time. In 1970 the United States returned the 48,000 acres of Blue Lake mountain land to Taos Pueblo.

Pueblo peoples speak languages of four distinct families, so that speakers of one are not easily understood by speakers of another. Keresan is spoken at Acoma, Laguna and several other pueblos; Tanoan includes Tewa, Towa at Jemez and the Tiwa languages; Hopi is spoken on the Hopi Reservation in Arizona. Communities are organised around family clans. Corn is the staple food. The Zuni and Hopi practise dry farming, while the River Pueblos irrigate.

Many Pueblo people hold beliefs in Katsinas, supernatural beings regarded as representatives of the ancestors, who bring rain and can heal or cause disease. Pueblo communities have preserved much of their culture, including a syncretic Pueblo Christianity. About 75,000 Pueblo people live chiefly in New Mexico and Arizona.
puerto-cabello: Puerto Cabello lies on the north coast of Venezuela in Carabobo State, about 210 km west of Caracas. The word cabello means hair, and the Spanish used to say that the sea was so calm there that a ship could be moored to the dock with a single hair. Its climate is a borderline tropical savanna, almost dry enough to be a hot semi-arid one. The date of its foundation is not known. Its name is first documented on the map of the province of Caracas prepared in 1578 by Juan de Pimentel.

The location made the port easy prey for buccaneers, and in the 17th century it was a popular trading post for Dutch smugglers, whose contraband trade consisted mostly of cocoa exchanged with the Dutch colony of Curaçao. The Spanish took over the port in 1730, after the Real Compañía Guipuzcoana had moved in. The company built warehouses, wharves and an array of forts, and by the 1770s Puerto Cabello was the most fortified town on the Venezuelan coast. The San Felipe castle and the Solano fortress remain from that period.

During the War of Jenkins' Ear the port was the company's careening harbour. In 1743 the British Commodore Charles Knowles attacked La Guaira on 18 February and Puerto Cabello on 15 and 24 April, and the defenders under Governor Gabriel de Zuluaga beat him off each time. On 25 October 1799 Captain Edward Hamilton of HMS Surprise cut the frigate Santa Cecilia, the former HMS Hermione, out of the harbour. In 1812 Simón Bolívar was appointed commander of the town but left after a royalist rebellion. The Spanish retreated to the castle after the Battle of Carabobo in 1821, and Puerto Cabello was the last royalist stronghold of Venezuela's war of independence, captured by José Antonio Páez on 8 November 1823.

British and German ships attacked the harbour in the Venezuelan crisis of 1902–03. In 1940 six Italian ships and one German ship took refuge in the bay as Venezuela was neutral, and on the night of 31 March their crews set them on fire on the orders of the Axis naval command. In 1962 pro-Castro naval officers, marines and members of the FALN rose in an uprising known as El Porteñazo, and loyal National Guard and army forces retook the city after house-to-house fighting.

Puerto Cabello is Venezuela's largest seaport, and the UCOCAR shipyards there have built patrol vessels for the Venezuelan Navy. The Solano fortress, part of the San Esteban National Park, and the San Felipe castle are among its attractions. The soldier Juan José Flores, who served as president of Ecuador, was born in the city.
puerto-cortes: Puerto Cortés, originally known as Puerto de Caballos, is a port city and municipality on the north Caribbean coast of Honduras. It lies on the Laguna de Alvarado, with a natural bay, north of San Pedro Sula and east of Omoa. The city holds a local patronal festival for two weeks in August, whose last Saturday is called Noche Veneciana, and 15 August is a local holiday for its patroness, the Virgen de la Asunción.

Gil González Dávila founded a settlement in 1524 and called it Villa de la Natividad de Nuestra Señora, now known as Cieneguita. In 1526 Hernán Cortés came from Mexico to punish González Dávila, and several horses drowned as he unloaded his ships, so he named the place Puerto Caballos. By 1533 a local leader called Çiçumba, whose name the Spanish recorded in many variants, had destroyed the town. After his defeat in 1536 by Pedro de Alvarado, a new Puerto de Caballos was founded on the southern shore of the Laguna de Alvarado.

Because pirates threatened it until the Spanish fort at Omoa was built in the 18th century, it had few permanent residents in the 16th and 17th centuries, and Christopher Newport briefly occupied it during the Anglo-Spanish War. In 1869 it took the name Puerto Cortés in honour of Hernán Cortés.

A plan of 1850 for an inter-oceanic railway, prompted by the demand for transport across Central America after the gold rush of 1849, anchored the line at Puerto Cortés. President Marco Aurelio Soto nationalised the railroad in 1876, but it reached only San Pedro Sula, and the plan was abandoned when the Panama Canal was completed in 1903. The region became an early centre of banana production. Samuel Zemurray's Cuyamel Fruit Company bought land near Omoa in 1910, came to dominate the port, built a rail spur into the town in 1918 and gained effective control of the National Railroad in 1920. After he sold the company to United Fruit in 1929, that firm held great influence in the town and in Honduras.

The Empresa Nacional Portuaria was created in 1966 and a free trade zone in 1976. The first four-lane highway in Honduras, opened in 1996, joined the port to San Pedro Sula. The town counted 73,150 people in a 2023 calculation, and its port is among the busiest in Central America.
puerto-limon: Limón lies on a cape on the Caribbean coast of Costa Rica. South of National Route 32 the Limoncito and Cieneguita rivers converge before reaching the sea. Uvita Island lies less than a kilometre east of downtown. The climate is tropical rainforest and nearly 3,600 millimetres of rain a year.

Puerto Limón is Spanish for 'port lemon'. The earlier name was Cariay or Cariai, used by the indigenous peoples until the arrival of Christopher Columbus. The origin of the name Limón is unknown, but by 1852 President Juan Rafael Mora Porras was calling the port Puerto del Limón.

Columbus anchored off the coast at Isla Uvita in 1502, and on 25 September he recalled landing at a town the locals called Cariay. The Atlantic coast was left largely unexplored by Spanish settlers until the 19th century, though from 1569 grants of land at Matina were worked with enslaved Africans to grow cacao, which drew pirates. Edward Mansvelt and his vice admiral Henry Morgan landed at Portete in 1666 and marched inland to Cartago, but the inhabitants drove them back at Turrialba on 15 April.

The town was founded in 1854 by Philipp J. J. Valentini under government auspices and made a district in 1870. In 1867 work began on a railway from the highlands to the sea, and Limón was chosen as the site of a major port to ship coffee from the Central Valley. In the second half of the 19th century hired workers arrived from Jamaica, with smaller groups from Barbados and Trinidad and Tobago. On 3 July 1942 the German submarine U-161 attacked the ship San Pablo while it was being unloaded, killing twenty-three dockers and one crew member.

Limón is the capital of its province and canton, and nearly 90 per cent of Costa Rica's imports and exports pass through the two harbours at Moín. Spanish is the main language, but many people of Afro-Caribbean origin speak an English-based creole, Limonese Creole or Mekatelyu, which has around 60,000 speakers. The cuisine has close ties to Jamaica; rice and beans and the patty are staples. The city's carnival, held in the week of 12 October, was first organised in 1949 by the community leader Alfred Josiah Henry Smith.
puerto-rico: Puerto Rico consists of a main island and smaller islands, including Vieques, Culebra and Mona. It lies about 1,000 miles south-east of Miami, between the Dominican Republic and the U.S. Virgin Islands, and is the smallest of the Greater Antilles. The Cordillera Central crosses the island from east to west. Puerto Rico is Spanish for rich port. Columbus named the island San Juan Bautista and the capital Ciudad de Puerto Rico, but traders came to call the whole island Puerto Rico, and San Juan became the name of the port and capital.

The island's history began with the Ortoiroid culture, an Archaic hunter-gatherer population present as early as about 4,000 years ago. Around 500–200 BCE Saladoid peoples from the Orinoco River basin migrated there, bringing sedentary agriculture and ceramics, and their ancestry became predominant in the populations that developed into the Taíno. The Taíno were the dominant Indigenous people when Columbus arrived in 1493. Their numbers fell sharply in the 16th century through introduced infectious diseases, exploitation by Spanish settlers and warfare.

Spain claimed the island after Columbus's arrival and Juan Ponce de León colonised it in 1508. It was a major military post in the wars between Spain and other European powers in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, and in 1593 Portuguese soldiers formed the first garrison of the San Felipe del Morro fortress. Spanish settlers, mainly from the Canary Islands and Andalusia, and African slaves changed the cultural and demographic landscape. By the late 19th century a distinct Puerto Rican identity, combining European, African and Indigenous elements, had begun to emerge.

In the 19th century Puerto Rico and Cuba were Spain's last two colonies in the New World. The Crown revived the Royal Decree of Graces of 1815, offering free land to those who swore loyalty to the Crown and the Catholic Church, in the hope that independence movements would lose strength. The United States acquired Puerto Rico in 1898 after the Spanish–American War. Puerto Ricans have been U.S. citizens since 1917, and Congress approved a territorial constitution in 1952.

Puerto Rico is officially the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, an unincorporated territory of the United States, and its political status is a continuing subject of debate. San Juan is the capital. Spanish and English are the official languages, though Spanish predominates. Old San Juan has the Cathedral of San Juan Bautista, which holds the tomb of Juan Ponce de León.
pula: Pula, also called Pola in Italian, is the largest city in Istria County, at the southern tip of the Istrian peninsula in western Croatia. It lies on and beneath seven hills, on the inner part of a wide gulf with a naturally well-protected port up to 38 metres deep, which is open to the northwest. It was the administrative centre of Istria from Roman times until Pazin took that role in 1991.

Greek tradition attributed the foundation of Polai to Colchians who had chased Jason into the northern Adriatic and settled in a place they called the city of refuge. In antiquity the Histri, a Venetic or Illyrian tribe, lived there. The Romans conquered Istria in 177 BCE, and the town was raised to colonial rank between 46 and 45 BCE under Julius Caesar. At its height it had about 30,000 people. It took the side of Cassius in the civil war of 42 BCE, and was demolished after Octavian's victory, but was rebuilt at the request of Octavian's daughter Iulia, as Colonia Pietas Iulia Pola Pollentia Herculanea.

Odoacer virtually destroyed Pula in 476 CE, and the Ostrogoths ruled it from 493 to 538. Under the Exarchate of Ravenna, from 540 to 751, it prospered as the major port of the Byzantine fleet, and the Basilica of Saint Mary Formosa was built in the 6th century. The Franks took it in 788. The Venetians took it in 1148 and it swore allegiance to Venice in 1150, and they ruled it from 1331 until 1797. Plague, malaria and typhoid, along with attacks by Genoese, Hungarian and Habsburg forces, left only 3,000 inhabitants by the 1750s.

After the collapse of Venice in 1797 it passed to the Habsburgs, and it became the premier naval port of the Austrian empire in the late 1850s, chosen as the base in 1859 by the Danish admiral Hans Birch Dahlerup. Pola grew from a fading provincial town into an industrial city. In 1910 it had 58,562 inhabitants, 45.8 per cent Italian speaking. After World War II the Istrian Italians of Pula left for Italy in large numbers, and Istria was united with Yugoslavia on 15 September 1947.

Pula is the seventh-largest city of Croatia, with a population of 52,220 in 2021. It is known for its ancient Roman buildings, above all the 1st-century amphitheatre, one of the six largest surviving Roman arenas, still used for summer film festivals. The Arch of the Sergii and the Temple of Augustus also survive, and the city is officially bilingual, in Croatian and Italian.
punakha: Punakha is the administrative centre of Punakha dzongkhag, one of the 20 districts of Bhutan. It lies at an elevation of 1,200 metres above sea level, about 72 km from Thimphu, a journey of about three hours by car. Unlike Thimphu, it is quite warm in winter and hot in summer. Rice is the main crop along the valleys of the Pho Chhu and Mo Chhu, the two main rivers of Bhutan, and Dzongkha is widely spoken in the district.

Punakha was the capital of Bhutan and the seat of government until 1955, when the capital was moved to Thimphu. Its great fortress, Pungthang Dewachen Phodrang (Palace of Great Happiness), better known as Punakha Dzong, was constructed under the command of Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal and is believed to have taken about two years to complete. It is the winter residence of Bhutan's Central Monastic Body, led by the Je Khenpo, and houses the most sacred relics of the Southern Drukpa Kagyu school, including the Rangjung Kasarpani, and the sacred remains of Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal and Tertön Padma Lingpa.

In 1907 the dzong was the site of the coronation of Ugyen Wangchuck as the first King of Bhutan. Three years later a treaty was signed at Punakha by which the British agreed not to interfere in Bhutanese internal affairs, while Bhutan allowed Britain to direct its foreign affairs. The dzong has suffered repeatedly. It was partially destroyed by fire in 1780, 1789, 1802, 1831, 1849 and 1986, and it experienced an earthquake in 1897 and a flood in 1994. Standing at the confluence of the two rivers, it is vulnerable to flash floods caused by glacier lakes, and flood damage is recorded in 1957, 1960 and 1994.

A covered wooden cantilever bridge over the Mo Chhu was built together with the dzong in the 17th century and was washed away by a flash flood in 1957 or 1958. A new bridge of traditional construction, with a free span of 55 metres, was begun in 2006 and completed in 2008 with help from Germany. The valley is known in Bhutan for rice farming, both red and white, and the village of Ritsha, with its two-storey houses of pounded mud on stone foundations, is often called the rice bowl of Bhutan. Punakha Domchoe, held in the first month of the Bhutanese year, is an important festival combining ritual with a display of horsemanship and sword play.
punctation-of-olmutz: The German Confederation, dominated by Austria, had been dissolved in the Revolutions of 1848 and partially succeeded by the Frankfurt Assembly. After the assembly failed, Prussia took the initiative in early 1850 with the Erfurt Union, a federation of most of the German states under its own lead. The two powers were thus in conflict over the leadership of Germany.

A dispute between the Elector of Hesse and his subjects gave the Austrian chancellor Felix zu Schwarzenberg the occasion to isolate Prussia further. Austrian and allied armies advanced into the Electorate of Hesse, and on 8 November 1850 the Prussian army came close to war with Bavaria, an ally of Austria, near Fulda-Bronnzell. In the Warsaw negotiations of October 1850 Tsar Nicholas I of Russia had already taken Austria's side, which was part of the reason why Prussia decided to give in.

The agreement, also called the Agreement of Olmütz, came out of a conference held in the town, now Olomouc in the Czech Republic, and closed the Autumn Crisis of 1850. Prussia gave up its claim to lead the German states and submitted to Austrian leadership of the restored confederation. It agreed to demobilise, to take part in the intervention of the German Diet in Hesse and in Holstein, and renounced any resumption of the Erfurt Union. Austria for its part agreed to call a conference of ministers to discuss a reform of the confederation.

The ministerial conference that Austria had promised met in Dresden the following year and ended without result, so that the confederation continued unreformed under Austrian leadership. The name of humiliation was given to the treaty because many saw in it a capitulation of the Prussians to the Austrians.
pune: Pune lies on the western margin of the Deccan Plateau at about 560 metres above sea level, on the leeward side of the Sahyadri range, and is about 149 kilometres by road south-east of Mumbai. The old city, with its many peths, stands on the east bank of the Mutha river, while the cantonment areas of Khadki and Camp were laid out by the British. The earliest reference to the town is a Rashtrakuta dynasty copper plate of 937 CE, which names it Punya-vishaya. Copper plates of 858 and 868 CE show an agricultural settlement called Punnaka on the site, and the Pataleshwar Caves, a rock-cut temple complex, date from the same era.

The Seuna Yadavas of Devagiri held Pune from the 9th century to 1327, and Muslim sultanates held it until the late 1600s. In 1599 the Ahmadnagar Sultanate granted it as a jagir to Maloji Bhosale, who passed it to his son Shahaji. Shahaji chose the town as the residence of his wife Jijabai and young son Shivaji, the future founder of the Maratha empire, and the Lal Mahal, where Shivaji spent his youth, was completed in 1640. Baji Rao I, appointed Peshwa in 1720, moved his base to Pune in 1728 and began Shaniwar Wada, finished in 1730, which turned a kasbah into a city.

After the Peshwas were defeated at the Battle of Khadki on 5 November 1817 the British seized the city and placed it under the Bombay Presidency. They built a large military cantonment to the east, while the old city kept narrow lanes and districts divided by caste and religion. Pune became the monsoon capital of the Governor of Bombay, and the Southern Command of the Indian Army was established there in 1895.

Pune is the administrative headquarters of Pune district in Maharashtra, with 3,124,458 people in the city at the 2011 census. Marathi is the official and most spoken language. The University of Pune, now Savitribai Phule Pune University, was founded in 1949, the National Chemical Laboratory in 1950 and the National Defence Academy in 1955. Among historic sites are Shaniwar Wada and the Aga Khan Palace, where Mahatma Gandhi was interned during the Quit India movement. The first rules of modern badminton were drawn up in Pune in 1873.
punic-wars: For a century before the First Punic War the Roman Republic had expanded in southern Italy, and by 270 BCE, when the last Greek cities of Magna Graecia submitted at the end of the Pyrrhic War, it had conquered all of peninsular Italy south of the Arno. Carthage, with its capital in what is now Tunisia, ruled a maritime empire that covered southern Iberia, much of the North African coast, the Balearic Islands, Corsica, Sardinia and the western half of Sicily. The most reliable source is the Greek historian Polybius, whom modern historians accept largely at face value despite his favourable treatment of Scipio Aemilianus.

The First Punic War began in 264 BCE over control of the Sicilian city of Messana, when Rome had a strong army but no navy. It lasted twenty-three years and was fought mostly on and around Sicily. After Carthage was defeated in 241 BCE it paid large reparations and Sicily became the first Roman province. Hamilcar then took his army to Iberia in 237 BCE and built a largely autonomous state in the south-east, with silver mines and manpower.

The Second Punic War began in 218 BCE after Hannibal captured Saguntum. Hannibal crossed the Alps and campaigned in Italy for fourteen years, repeatedly defeating Roman legions. A Roman invasion of Africa in 204 BCE led to his recall, and he was defeated at Zama in 202 BCE. The treaty of 201 BCE stripped Carthage of its overseas territories, imposed an indemnity and forbade it to wage war without Rome's permission. The Third Punic War began in 149 BCE, after Carthage, harried by the Numidians under Masinissa, raised an army against the treaty. Elements of the Senate led by Cato the Elder had long wished to destroy Carthage.

In 146 BCE the Romans stormed Carthage, sacked it, slaughtered or enslaved its population and demolished the city. A curse was placed on anyone who might resettle the site, which was confiscated as public land. The remaining Carthaginian territory became the Roman province of Africa, with Utica as its capital, a major source of grain for Rome. Punic cities elsewhere, such as those in Mauretania, kept their own government and culture, and the Punic language continued to be spoken in North Africa until the 7th century CE.
punjab: Punjab is a geographical, ethnolinguistic and historical region in the north-west of South Asia, within modern Pakistan and north-western India. Its name comes from the Persian panj, five, and āb, water, and means the land of five waters: the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Sutlej and Beas, all tributaries of the Indus. The Mahabharata names a region Panchanada, and the ancient Greeks called it Pentapotamía. The Rigveda knew a land of seven rivers, Sapta Sindhu, which also counted the Indus and the Kabul. Its boundaries are imprecisely defined: in the sixteenth-century Mughal Empire the term meant a smaller area between the Indus and the Sutlej.

Settlements grew along the five rivers as early as the Indus Valley civilisation, which flourished from about 3000 BCE. Indo-Aryan migrations passed through the region in waves between 1500 BCE and 500 BCE, and the bulk of the Rigveda was composed there between about 1500 and 1200 BCE. Local kingdoms known as Mahajanapadas arose. In the ninth century the Odi Shahi dynasty from Gandhara, called the Hindu Shahis, ruled western Punjab along with Kabulistan. The Mughals gained power in the early sixteenth century and gradually controlled the whole region from their capital at Lahore, until the dynasty weakened in the eighteenth century and Afghan rulers took the region.

Maharajah Ranjit Singh founded the Sikh Empire, which lasted from 1799, when he captured Lahore, until 1849, when it was conquered in the Second Anglo-Sikh War. It stretched from the Khyber Pass in the west to western Tibet in the east and from Mithankot in the south to Kashmir in the north, with Lahore as its capital. It had about 3.5 million people in 1831 and was the last major region of the subcontinent annexed by the British Empire. The British Punjab Province was one of the largest provinces of the British Raj. After the Partition of British India in 1947 the region was divided into West and East Punjab, and in 1966 India divided East Punjab into Punjab, Haryana and Himachal Pradesh.

Lahore is the largest city and historic capital, and other major cities include Faisalabad, Rawalpindi, Multan, Amritsar, Ludhiana and Chandigarh. The Punjabi people speak Punjabi, written in the Gurmukhi script in India and in Shahmukhi in Pakistan. Muslims are the majority in Pakistani Punjab and Sikhs in Indian Punjab, with Hindu, Christian, Jain and other communities. Islam arrived through southern Punjab in the eighth century and became the majority religion by the sixteenth, largely through Sufi missionaries. Agriculture has been central to the economy, and wheat, rice, cotton and sugarcane are grown; the Green Revolution of the mid-1960s to the mid-1970s made the region a major food producer.
puno-region: Puno lies in the south-east of Peru and is the fifth largest department of the country, after Cuzco, Madre de Dios, Ucayali and Loreto. It is bordered by Bolivia to the east and by the departments of Madre de Dios, Cusco, Arequipa, Moquegua and Tacna. Its capital, the city of Puno, stands on Lake Titicaca in the Altiplano, or high sierra, on the Collao Plateau. The Andean mountains make up 70 per cent of the territory and the rest is covered by Amazon rainforest.

The western part of Lake Titicaca, the world's highest navigable lake, lies in the department. Its islands include Taquile, Suasi and Amantaní, known for weaving and pre-Columbian constructions. The Uros live on floating islands made of totora reeds and travel in boats of the same material. The Titicaca National Reserve protects extensive stretches of reeds and many species. The climate is cold and dry with a four-month rainy season, while the rainforest is warm.

In ancient times the Collao plateau was inhabited by Aymara groups, among them the Collas, Zapanas, Kallahuayos and Lupacas, and the Quechuas came later. The area was the territory of the Tiahuanacos, between 800 and 1200 CE, who were the highest cultural expression of the Aymara people in what is now Peru and Bolivia. The Incas took over these lands in the fifteenth century. The chronicler Inca Garcilaso de la Vega places the legend of Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo, who emerged from the waters of Lake Titicaca to found the Inca Empire, in these ancient times.

Under Spanish rule Puno was the obligatory route for travellers to Potosí in Bolivia, and the Spanish, drawn by mining, left an important colonial legacy. In 1668 the viceroy, the Conde de Lemos, established San Juan Bautista de Puno as capital of the province of Paucarcolla; it was later called San Carlos de Puno after Charles II of Spain and became capital of the Intendancy of Puno. The department was created by the Reglamento Provisional de Elecciones of 26 April 1822. In 1870 the Arequipa to Puno railway was installed and navigation began on Lake Titicaca.

The department is divided into 13 provinces and 107 districts, and is run by a regional government. Indigenous people are the majority. In the 2007 census the language first learnt by most residents was Quechua (38.01 per cent), followed by Spanish (34.81 per cent) and Aymara (26.93 per cent). The Quechua spoken is the Cusco-Collao variety.
puntarenas: Puntarenas is a city on the Pacific coast of Costa Rica and the seat of the Puntarenas canton, which is the first canton of the province of the same name, so the city is also the provincial capital. The city comprises the districts of Puntarenas, Chacarita and El Roble. The name joins punta and arenas, meaning point and sands, and is first recorded in February 1720, when the pirate John Clipperton noted in his journals that he had come to a Punta de Arena, the needle-like strip of land on which the city stands. The province is the most extensive in the country, with its largest section in the south, far from the city.

The first European to reach the site was Gil González Dávila in 1522. The Gulf of Nicoya served as an entryway to the interior of Costa Rica, but the port of Puntarenas was not developed until 1840, when coffee production in the highlands reached exportable volumes. In 1845 the Congress of the Republic declared it a duty-free port, with the exception of cognac and hard liquor.

At first the coffee came down to the port in oxcarts along a trail through the mountains. In 1859 a stretch of railway was completed between Puntarenas and Esparza, one of the country's earliest Spanish settlements, founded in 1574. The line was eventually built through to San José and opened in 1910.

The railway kept the Pacific port at the centre of the regional economy throughout the 20th century. The old port facilities aged and could not take the much larger ships of modern fleets, so in the 1980s a new port was built to the south at Caldera, where ships had anchored in colonial times and which had been the first port site used since 1522.

Puntarenas has some 100,000 inhabitants with its surrounding neighbourhoods. Its Pacific beaches attract tourists, especially surfers, and regular ferries cross to the Nicoya Peninsula. Seafood such as ceviche characterises its cooking.
puntland: Puntland occupies the north-eastern portion of Somalia, about 212,510 square kilometres or roughly one third of the country. It borders Somaliland to the west, the Gulf of Aden to the north, the Guardafui Channel and the Indian Ocean to the east, Galmudug State to the south and Ethiopia to the south-west. Cape Guardafui forms the tip of the Horn of Africa, and Ras Hafun is the easternmost point on the African continent. The Golis Mountains, Galgala and Al Madow are among its mountains.

The climate is semi-arid and warm, favouring pastoralism, and no area receives more than 400 millimetres of rain a year. The name derives from the Land of Punt mentioned in ancient Egyptian sources, whose exact location is still unknown. Many studies place Punt in present-day Somalia, while others place it elsewhere.

The Majeerteen Sultanate was founded in the mid-18th century and rose to prominence the next century under Boqor Osman Mahamuud. Centred on Alula, it controlled much of northern and central Somalia in the 19th and early 20th centuries and ruled the towns of Alula, Bargaal, Bosaso and Hafun. It traded widely and made treaties with foreign powers. A struggle between Boqor Osman and his cousin Yusuf Ali Kenadid nearly destroyed it; Kenadid was forced into exile in Yemen, then returned in the 1870s with Hadhrami musketeers and established the Sultanate of Hobyo in 1878.

After the Somali Civil War began in 1991, a constitutional conference was held in Garoowe in 1998 over three months. Political leaders, traditional elders, business people and civil society representatives took part, and the autonomous Puntland State of Somalia was established to provide services and security and to facilitate trade. Abdullahi Yusuf Ahmed was its founding president. A new regional constitution was passed on 15 June 2009, and in January 2009 the short-lived quasi-state of Maakhir was incorporated into Puntland. Control of the Sool, Sanaag and Ayn provinces in the west has been disputed with Somaliland.

Puntland is a federal member state of Somalia with its capital at Garoowe, and Bosaso is its commercial capital. Its president and vice president are elected by a unicameral parliament. About 39 per cent of its people were estimated to be nomads in 2016, and the population is mainly Somali, with the Darod especially well represented and a number of Mehri residents. Islam is the main religion.

The coastline is 1,600 kilometres long and rich in fish. Livestock, fishing, frankincense, myrrh, gum arabic and trade are the main sources of income, and the key trading centres are Bosaso and Galkayo. Puntland also has its own security force and its own public broadcaster, Puntland TV and Radio, founded in April 2013.
puranas: Tradition credits Vyasa, the narrator of the Mahabharata, with compiling the Puranas. An old account holds that there was originally a single Purana: the Vishnu Purana says Vyasa entrusted his Puranasamhita to his disciple Lomaharshana, who passed it to disciples whose collections, together with his own, formed the Mulasamhita from which the later eighteen Puranas were derived. Many scholars instead consider the Mahapuranas the work of multiple authors over several centuries.

The word purana appears in the Vedic texts, for example in the Atharva Veda. The texts existed in oral form before they were written down, so the date of a written copy does not give the date of origin. Ludo Rocher states that no Purana can be given a specific date as a whole; Wendy Doniger assigns approximate dates, such as c. 250 CE for the Markandeya Purana and c. 450 CE for the Vishnu Purana.

The eighteen Mahapuranas, the major Puranas, are traditionally divided into three groups of six according to the three qualities of existence: purity, passion and inertia. Each group centres mainly, but not only, on one deity. There are also eighteen Upapuranas, or minor Puranas, though lists disagree on which titles belong among them. The Skanda Purana, with 81,000 verses, is the largest. Together the texts run to over 400,000 verses.

Several Puranas name five characteristics of a Purana: the creation of the world, its further creation and cosmology, the genealogies of gods, sages and kings, the cosmic ages of each patriarch, and accounts of royal dynasties. The Bhagavata Purana adds five more. In practice the range is wider. Some, such as the Agni Purana and Matsya Purana, treat subjects from astronomy and cosmetics to philosophy and festivals, while the Skanda, Padma and Bhavishya Puranas are largely pilgrimage guides.

The Puranas are classed as Smriti and do not have the authority of scripture in Hinduism. Scholars have nevertheless seen in them a process of cultural synthesis, in which the beliefs of many local traditions were woven into the Vedic and Brahmanic fold. Greg Bailey describes them as records of cultural adaptation over some 2,000 years.

Their manuscripts differ greatly. A palm-leaf manuscript of the Skanda Purana found in Nepal, dated to 810 CE, is entirely different from the versions in circulation since the colonial period, and later finds suggest major rewritings before the 12th century and again in the 15th to 16th centuries. Because the texts record neither authors nor dates and are inconsistent with one another, Rocher states that attempts to use them as history have had limited success unless supported by inscriptions, archaeology and other independent evidence. Horace Hayman Wilson published an English translation of the Vishnu Purana in 1840.
purandar-singha: Purandar Singha was born in 1807 at Silmari in British-ruled Bengal, a great-great-grandson of the Ahom king Rajeswar Singha. His grandfather and his father Brajanath Gohain had conspired against reigning kings and lived there as exiled princes in poverty. In 1818 Ruchinath Burhagohain, who held King Chandrakanta Singha responsible for bringing in the Burmese, invited Brajanath to claim the throne, and their force entered the capital Jorhat on 17 February 1818. Brajanath had coins struck in his own name, but the mutilation of one of his ears barred him from kingship, since an Ahom king had to be without blemish. His son, then ten years old, was acclaimed instead.

Real authority lay with Brajanath and Ruchinath, who removed the officers suspected of loyalty to Chandrakanta. A Burmese army of 30,000 sent by King Bodawpaya defeated the Assamese on 17 February 1819; Purandar, his father and Ruchinath fled to Guwahati with the valuables of the royal treasury, worth 3.5 million rupees. After a second defeat on 11 June 1819 they escaped to Bengal. The Governor-General Lord Hastings refused to help. They recruited soldiers in Goalpara, Bengal and Bhutan, armed with the aid of a British trader, Robert Bruce, and fought both Chandrakanta and the Burmese before withdrawing in 1822.

After the Treaty of Yandabo of 24 February 1826 the British held the Brahmaputra valley. Sensing discontent, they considered in 1832 restoring Upper Assam as a tributary princedom and chose Purandar over Chandrakanta; some historians think they expected a long-exiled prince to be the more grateful and submissive. From April 1833 he ruled from Jorhat, without Sadiya and Matak, for a tribute of 50,000 rupees. Within three years he fell behind in his payments and asked for a reduction. An enquiry by Captain Francis Jenkins found corruption and oppression, and the king himself amassing a personal fortune.

The kingdom was placed under direct British control in September 1838. Purandar stayed in Jorhat and refused the pension of 1,000 rupees a month granted in October 1838, hoping that a petition to the Governor-General would restore his state; it was turned down. When officials and adventurers dug into the royal tombs, the maidams, at Charaideo in search of treasure, he first protested and then opened many tombs himself. He died on 1 October 1846 and was entombed at Jorhat, at the place now called Raja Maidam.
puritans: The Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559 established the Church of England as a Protestant church and closed the English Reformation. Under Elizabeth I the church was widely considered Reformed, and Calvinists held the best bishoprics and deaneries, yet it kept cathedrals, choirs, a formal liturgy in the Book of Common Prayer, traditional vestments and bishops. The Puritans were dissatisfied with this limited reform. The word Puritan began as a term of abuse, dated by Thomas Fuller to 1564, and the people it described called themselves the godly, saints or God's children.

They adopted a covenant theology and in that sense were Calvinists. Divided in church polity between episcopal, presbyterian and congregational views, some wanted the established church reformed throughout, while others favoured separation. At the Hampton Court Conference of 1604 James I largely sided with his bishops.

Under Charles I the Puritans became a political force. Opponents of the royal prerogative allied with reformers who saw the church moving in the wrong direction and objected to growing Catholic influence at court. By the late 1630s they were allied with the commercial world, with parliamentary opposition and with the Scottish Presbyterians, and the First English Civil War of 1642 to 1646 brought them to power. Some Puritans left for New England between 1629 and 1640, supporting the founding of the Massachusetts Bay Colony. The migration ceased by 1641.

At the Restoration of 1660 and under the Act of Uniformity of 1662, the Church of England returned to its pre-war form. Historian Edmund Calamy estimated that about 2,400 Puritan clergy left it in the Great Ejection of 1662. They were thereafter included among Dissenters.

In colonial New England, Puritan leaders worked for universal literacy so that people could read the Bible. In 1642 Massachusetts required heads of households to teach their children and servants to read. In 1647 Parliament banned Christmas, Easter and Whitsuntide. New England Puritans were intolerant of Quaker, Anglican and Baptist beliefs, and those of Massachusetts Bay were the most active persecutors of Quakers.

Puritanism was never a formally defined division of Protestantism, and the term was rarely used after the turn of the 18th century. Congregationalist churches are descended from the Puritans, and their beliefs appear in the Savoy Declaration. Many Dissenters formed the basis of later Congregationalist, Baptist and Presbyterian traditions. Writers such as John Milton, John Bunyan and Anne Bradstreet are still read.
pushyamitra-shunga: Pushyamitra Shunga, also written Pushpamitra, was the founder and first ruler of the Shunga Empire, which he established to succeed the Maurya Empire. He took power after assassinating the last Mauryan emperor, Brihadratha. He is said to have driven out the Greeks in a Shunga-Greek war and to have ruled for 36 years. The Buddhist Ashokavadana names him as the last Mauryan emperor, which appears to confuse him with Brihadratha. Inscriptions of the Shungas have been found as far as Ayodhya, and the Divyavadana says his realm reached Sakala, now Sialkot in Pakistan.

He performed the Vedic Ashvamedha sacrifice to legitimise his rule, as the Dhanadeva-Ayodhya inscription records. Michael Witzel states that the Manu Smriti, which stresses orthodox faith in statecraft, was first compiled under his rule, and Kaushik Roy sees it as a Brahmanical reaction to the rise of Buddhism and Jainism. His history is also recorded in Banabhatta's Harshacharita.

Buddhist texts accuse Pushyamitra of persecuting Buddhists. The earliest, the Ashokavadana of the 4th or 5th century CE, says his advisers told him he could rival Ashoka's fame by destroying Buddhism. He tried to destroy the Kukkutarama monastery, then offered a hundred coins for every monk's head at Sakala, and was killed by a Buddhist yaksha. Later texts, among them the Vibhasa, the Arya-Manjushri-Mula-Kalpa and Taranatha's history of the 16th century, tell similar stories with different places and deaths. Many historians regard them as exaggerated.

Scholars are divided. John Marshall found evidence of damage to Buddhist sites at Takshashila and thought the Sanchi stupa vandalised in the 2nd century BCE, and others date damage at Kaushambi and Deur Kothar to his time. H. Bhattacharya suggested political motives, since Buddhists may have favoured his Indo-Greek rivals. Others reject the claim. Etienne Lamotte notes that the legends disagree on where he campaigned and died, and that the dinara named in the Ashokavadana was not in general use before the 1st century BCE. Romila Thapar and Eric Seldeslachts find no firm evidence, and the Buddhist monuments of Bharhut and Sanchi were improved under Shunga rule, though N. N. Ghosh dates Bharhut to later Shunga kings. Pushyamitra was succeeded by his son Agnimitra.
puster-valley: The Puster Valley is one of the largest longitudinal valleys in the Alps, running east to west between Lienz in East Tyrol, Austria, and Mühlbach near Brixen in South Tyrol, Italy. It lies in the western part of the Periadriatic Seam, which separates the Southern Limestone Alps from the Central Eastern Alps. Half of the valley drains westward to the Adriatic through the Adige, the other half eastward to the Black Sea through the Danube, with the watershed on the shallow Toblacher Feld. The Rienz flows west and the Drau east into East Tyrol. Its towns lie between 750 and 1,180 metres above sea level, and the largest side valley is the Tauferer Ahrntal.

The valley has been inhabited since prehistoric times, and Iron Age finds are known. The Romans called its Illyrian inhabitants Saevates, and used the Rienz valley as a main road to the north-eastern regions of the Empire. It belonged to the province of Noricum, and over four centuries its people took on Roman customs, language and the Christian religion. In the 5th century Goths, Baiuvarii and Slavs came down into the area, and the Baiuvarii won out over the Slavs, who left traces in the place names of East Tyrol.

From the 10th century it formed the Pustrissa countship, first mentioned in 974. Emperor Henry IV ceded it to the Bishop of Brixen in 1091, and the Hapsburg took possession of it in the 16th century. After the Austrian defeat at Austerlitz and the Treaty of Pressburg in 1805 the region passed to Bavaria, and Tyroleans under Andreas Hofer repeatedly fought Bavarian rule. After Napoleon's fall it rejoined Austria, and after the First World War the South Tyrolean part was assigned to Italy. The Puster Valley Railway opened in 1871.

The South Tyrolean part forms the Puster Valley District, founded in 1969 from 26 municipalities, with an area of 2,071 square kilometres and more than 73,000 people. Bruneck is its main town. The 2001 census recorded German as the native language of 80.96 per cent of its people, Ladin of 13.40 per cent and Italian of 5.64 per cent.
putrajaya: Putrajaya is an enclave within the state of Selangor on the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia. It covers 4,931 hectares, divided into 20 precincts. The central Core Island, Nusa Perdana, holds the ministerial headquarters, civic squares, courts and ceremonial boulevards, while the outer precincts hold housing, schools, shops and recreation grounds. The master plan reserved nearly 40 per cent of the territory for parks, water bodies and landscaped open space, including the Putrajaya Lake and its wetlands. The city was named in honour of Malaysia's first prime minister, Tunku Abdul Rahman Putra Al-Haj; putra means prince or son and jaya success or victory in Sanskrit.

The site was originally Prang Besar, established in 1921 as a rubber estate by British veterans of World War I, which grew from 800 acres to 8,000 by taking in surrounding plantations. In the late 1980s the federal government sought to gather ministries scattered across congested Kuala Lumpur into a dedicated administrative capital. Prang Besar was chosen over an alternative site at Janda Baik in Pahang because it lay midway between central Kuala Lumpur and the planned Kuala Lumpur International Airport at Sepang. The federal government acquired about 11,320 acres from the Selangor state government.

The city was conceived in the 1990s by Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad and the Kuala Lumpur mayor Elyas Omar as a garden city and intelligent city. Construction began in August 1995, one of the largest infrastructure undertakings in Southeast Asia, at an estimated cost of US$8.1 billion, with designs mostly by Malaysian firms. The Asian financial crisis of 1997 moderately slowed it. Much of the monumental architecture draws on regional Islamic motifs, including Arabesque, Persian and Central Asian styles. The Prime Minister's Department moved there in 1999, and most federal civil servants followed between 2000 and 2005. On 1 February 2001 Selangor formally ceded the territory, which became Malaysia's third federal territory after Kuala Lumpur in 1974 and Labuan in 1984.

Putrajaya is the administrative centre of Malaysia and houses the executive and judicial branches of the federal government, the judiciary having moved there in 2003. Kuala Lumpur remains the national capital under the federal constitution, and continues to be the seat of the Yang di-Pertuan Agong and of Parliament. Local administration lies with the Putrajaya Corporation, a statutory body under the Prime Minister's Department.
puyang: Puyang lies on the northern shore of the Yellow River in north-eastern Henan. It borders Anyang to the west and Xinxiang to the south-west, and the provinces of Shandong and Hebei to the east and north. Its climate is a warm temperate continental monsoon one, with a dry, windy spring, a hot and rainy summer and a winter with little snow or rain. The surrounding land is farmed, and the adequate sunshine suits crops.

A burial site of the Yangshao culture in the area has a depiction believed to be an ancient cosmogram of the round Heaven and the square Earth. In 1987 a group of clams arranged in dragon patterns was unearthed there and dated to more than 6,400 years ago. It earned the city the name of the First Dragon of China, and a Chinese research association has named Puyang the Hometown of Chinese Dragons. Many Chinese scholars regard it as one of the important birthplaces of Chinese civilization.

The Classic of Poetry, the earliest collection of verses in China, includes poems that depict the countryside of Puyang. Wu Qi, the military strategist, Shang Yang, the statesman, and Lu Buwei, the thinker, are among the historical figures from the city.

In the Three Kingdoms era Puyang was Cao Cao's headquarters in Yan Province from 191 until 196 CE, and the battlefield of the Battle of Yan Province from 194 to 195.
