Under the Qing and the Republic of China it was a county of Daming Prefecture in Zhili province; in 1928 Zhili was abolished and Puyang joined Henan. In August 1949 it was taken from Henan into the experimental province of Pingyuan, and in November 1953 it was finally returned to Henan.

Puyang is a prefecture-level city that administers one district and five counties. Its 2020 census recorded 3,772,088 people. It has four national cultural relics protection units, among them the Qicheng relics, and a larger number of provincial and local sites, including the Cangjie mausoleum site and the Nanle Confucius temple. Petroleum and natural gas are its main mineral resources, and the Zhongyuan Oilfield and other petrochemical enterprises are established there.
puyi: Puyi was born in Beijing on 7 February 1906, the son of the Manchu prince Zaifeng, Prince Chun, and of Youlan, daughter of Ronglu, an ally of Empress Dowager Cixi. His uncle, the Guangxu Emperor, was his predecessor. In 1908 Cixi chose him to succeed the childless Guangxu, and he ascended the throne at the age of two with his father as regent. After the garrison at Wuhan mutinied on 10 October 1911, the general Yuan Shikai was sent to crush the revolt but could not, since opinion had turned against a dynasty that many believed had lost the mandate of heaven.

Empress Dowager Longyu, regent from 6 December 1911, endorsed the edict of abdication on 12 February 1912 under a deal brokered by Yuan. Under the Articles of Favourable Treatment Puyi kept his imperial title and remained in the northern half of the Forbidden City. The general Zhang Xun restored him to the throne from 1 to 12 July 1917, and from 1919 the Scottish scholar Reginald Johnston tutored him. On 5 November 1924 the warlord Feng Yuxiang abolished his title and expelled him from the palace, and in 1925 he moved to Tianjin.

After the Mukden incident of 18 September 1931 the Japanese Kwantung Army proposed that he head a Manchurian state. He was installed as Chief Executive of Manchukuo on 1 March 1932 and crowned Emperor of Manchukuo, with the regnal title Kangde, on 1 March 1934. On 9 August 1945 the Soviet Union entered Manchukuo and its armies overwhelmed the Kwantung Army.

The Soviets took Puyi to Siberia, and in 1946 he testified at the Tokyo War Crimes Tribunal. He was repatriated to China in 1950 and, after his release in 1959, published an autobiography ghostwritten by Li Wenda and worked as a gardener and then as a researcher. Red Guards burned copies of his book during the Cultural Revolution, but Premier Zhou Enlai protected him. Puyi died in Beijing on 17 October 1967, aged 61, of kidney cancer and heart disease.
pyongyang: Pyongyang lies in the west-central part of North Korea on a flat plain, about 50 kilometres east of Korea Bay, an arm of the Yellow Sea. The Taedong River flows southwestward through the city, about 109 kilometres upstream from its mouth. The Pyongyang plain is one of the two large plains on the western coast of the Korean peninsula, the other being the Chaeryong plain, each of about 500 square kilometres.

The name comes from the Sino-Korean words for flat and land. In native Korean the city was called Buruna or, less commonly, Barana, which may mean land of the field. Its other historic names include Ryugyong, Kisong, Hwangsong, Rakrang, Sŏgyong, Sodo, Hogyong, Changan and, under Japanese rule, Heijō. Early in the 20th century missionaries called it the Jerusalem of the East, because it was a stronghold of Protestant Christianity, especially during the Pyongyang Revival of 1907.

In 1955 archaeologists excavated prehistoric dwellings in a large ancient village at Kŭmtan-ni in the Pyongyang area, dating to the Jeulmun and Mumun pottery periods. According to legend the city was founded in 1122 BCE on the site of the capital of the traditional king Tan'gun. Korean historiography beginning with the 13th-century Samguk yusa links it to Asadal, or Wanggeom-seong, the first capital of Gojoseon. Historians reject this because earlier Chinese works such as the Records of the Grand Historian mention a much later Joseon, so the link may have been asserted by North Korea for propaganda, though Pyongyang did become a major city in old Joseon.

Wanggeom-seong, on the site of modern Pyongyang, served as the capital of Gojoseon from 194 to 108 BCE and fell in the Han conquest of 108 BCE. Emperor Wu of Han ordered four commanderies set up, with Lelang Commandery at the centre and its capital, called Joseon, at the location of Pyongyang. Pyongyang was also the capital of Goguryeo and later served as a secondary capital of Goryeo. Until 1946 it was the provincial capital of South Pyongan Province.

Pyongyang is the capital and largest city of North Korea, a directly administered city with a status equal to the provinces. It became the de facto capital after the state's founding in 1948 and was declared the official capital by the 1972 Constitution. The 2008 census counted 3,255,288 people. The city was devastated in the Korean War and quickly rebuilt with Soviet assistance. Kim Il Sung University, the country's oldest, was founded there in 1946. The best-known local dish is Pyongyang raengmyŏn, thin buckwheat noodles in a cold meat broth with watery kimchi and a slice of sweet Korean pear.
pyotr-ilyich-tchaikovsky: Tchaikovsky was born on 7 May 1840 in Votkinsk, a small town in Vyatka Governorate near the Kama River. His father, Ilya Petrovich Tchaikovsky, was a lieutenant colonel and engineer in the Department of Mines and managed the Ironworks in Kamsko-Votkinsk. Although musically precocious, he was educated for a career as a civil servant, since there was little opportunity for a musical career in Russia and no institutional music education. On 10 June 1859, aged 19, he graduated as a titular counselor, a low rung on the civil service ladder, and spent three years in the Ministry of Justice. He then entered the new Saint Petersburg Conservatory, from which he graduated in 1865.

The Western-oriented teaching he received at the conservatory set him apart from the nationalist composers of The Five, Mily Balakirev, César Cui, Modest Mussorgsky, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov and Alexander Borodin, who thought conservatories unnecessary. Tchaikovsky and his fellow students were caught between them and Anton Rubinstein, who defended professional training. His successes came infrequently and with great effort, and he was lifelong sensitive to criticism; Nikolai Rubinstein attacked the First Piano Concerto in private fits of rage. Hans von Bülow premiered it and championed other works. From 1867 the publication of his songs and piano music for the home market helped his popularity.

In March 1884 Emperor Alexander III conferred on him the Order of Saint Vladimir, which carried hereditary nobility and a personal audience with the Tsar. In 1885 the emperor requested a new production of Eugene Onegin at the Bolshoi Kamenny Theatre, signalling that his music was replacing Italian opera as the official imperial art, and awarded him a lifetime annual pension of 3,000 rubles. In his last years he grew at ease with the Belyayev circle around Rimsky-Korsakov. In 1892 he was voted a member of the Académie des Beaux-Arts in France, and in 1893 the University of Cambridge gave him an honorary Doctor of Music degree.

Tchaikovsky died in Saint Petersburg on 6 November 1893, aged 53, and was interred in Tikhvin Cemetery at the Alexander Nevsky Monastery. His death is attributed to cholera, caused by drinking unboiled water at a local restaurant. In the 1980s there was academic speculation in Britain that he killed himself, and Roland John Wiley wrote that we do not know how he died and may never find out. His music has remained popular, though critics were initially divided: some Russians thought it insufficiently Russian, while some Europeans praised it for offering more than exoticism.
pyotr-krasnov: Pyotr Nikolayevich Krasnov was born in Saint Petersburg on 22 September 1869 (10 September, old style), the son of Lieutenant General Nikolay Krasnov and grandson of General Ivan Krasnov. In 1888 he graduated from the Pavlovsk Military School and joined the Ataman regiment of the Life Guards. In 1902 the army newspaper Russkii Invalid published his articles from a trip to Mongolia, China and Japan, among them one on the Japanese army that a staff officer called poorly founded, hasty and far from the truth.

In the First World War Krasnov commanded the 2nd Combined Cossack Division from 1915 to 1917. In the summer of 1916 it was the first unit to break through Austro-Hungarian positions at the Battle of Lutsk, and he was wounded in the leg. In September 1917 he took command of the 3rd Cavalry Corps. After the October Revolution, Alexander Kerensky appointed him commander of the 700 Cossacks who marched on Petrograd. Bolshevik troops surrounded them at Gatchina on 15 November, and Krasnov was taken prisoner but soon released by Leon Trotsky, after which he made his way to the Don.

In May 1918 he was elected Ataman of the Don Cossack Host at Novocherkassk. He negotiated with the Germans occupying Ukraine and, with their support, equipped an army that drove the Soviets from the Don region in May and June 1918. By the middle of June a Don Army of 40,000 men, 56 guns and 179 machine guns was in the field. The historian Richard Pipes described him as an opportunist and an adventurer, and his German orientation made the Allied governments distrust him. On 19 February 1919 he left for Western Europe, and Afrikan P. Bogaewsky succeeded him as Don Ataman. He lived in Germany, then in France from 1923, where he helped found the anti-communist Brotherhood of Russian Truth, and he wrote novels.

During World War II Krasnov sought an alliance with Nazi Germany, motivated in part by Soviet repression of the Cossacks and the Russian Orthodox Church. After the invasion of 22 June 1941 he spoke regularly on Radio Berlin in Russian, in antisemitic broadcasts that presented the German advance as a liberation, and he worked with officials of Alfred Rosenberg's ministry for the occupied eastern territories.

The British handed him to the Soviets on 28 May 1945. He was held in the Lubyanka prison in Moscow, tried by the Military Collegium of the Supreme Court and sentenced to death with Andrei Shkuro and others. He was hanged on 17 January 1947. In 1997 Russia's Military Collegium confirmed that he had been justly convicted and was not to be rehabilitated, and in 2008 the council of Don atamans refused a petition for his rehabilitation, citing his collaboration with Germany.
pyotr-rumyantsev: Pyotr Alexandrovich Rumyantsev came from the Russian noble Rumyantsev family and was the only son of Count Alexander Rumyantsev. He is said to have been born at Stroiești, in present-day Moldova or Transnistria, although other accounts place his birth in Moscow. Because his mother spent much time in the company of Peter the Great, rumours made him the emperor's illegitimate son. Peter was his godfather and he was named after him. He first saw military service under his father in the war with Sweden of 1741–1743 and carried the Treaty of Åbo to the Empress, for which he was promoted to colonel.

His first military glory came in the Seven Years' War at Gross-Jägersdorf in 1757 and Kunersdorf in 1759. In 1761 he took the Pomeranian fortress of Kolberg, which other Russian commanders had twice besieged without success, and in doing so used troops in battalion columns combined with a scattered formation of jaegers. He used mobile divisional squares in place of linear battle orders, and began the formation of light jaeger battalions in the Russian Army.

After the Cossack Hetmanate was abolished in 1764, he governed Little Russia for Catherine the Great until her death 32 years later, working to remove any autonomy of the hetmans and to incorporate the new territories fully into the empire. In the Russo-Turkish War that began in 1768 he commanded the army sent to capture Azov. He defeated the Turks at Ryabaya Mogila, Larga and Kagul, crossed the Danube and advanced into Romania, and became field marshal with the victory title Zadunaisky, meaning Trans-Danubian. When his forces approached Shumla in 1774 the new sultan, Abdul Hamid I, sued for peace, and Rumyantsev signed it on a military tambourine at Küçük Kaynarca.

Rumyantsev set out his views on the art of war in the Instructions of 1761, the Customs of Military Service of 1770 and the Thoughts of 1777, which gave a theoretical base for the reorganisation of the army undertaken by Potemkin. In the Second Russo-Turkish War he suspected Potemkin of curtailing his supplies and resigned his command. In the Polish campaign of 1794 he was again named commander-in-chief, but Suvorov led the armies in battle, while Rumyantsev stayed at his Ukrainian manor at Tashan, which he had rebuilt as a fortress.

He died there on 19 December 1796, just over a month after Catherine, and was buried in the Kiev Pechersk Lavra. The Kagul Obelisk at Tsarskoye Selo and the Rumyantsev Obelisk on Vasilievsky Island commemorate his victories. His sons Sergey and Nikolay never married, and the comital branch of the family became extinct on their deaths.
pyotr-wrangel: Wrangel was born in Novoalexandrovsk in the Kovno Governorate, now Zarasai in Lithuania, into a Baltic German noble house that had served the rulers of Sweden, Prussia, Austria and Russia for over 700 years. At his father's wish he trained as a mining engineer and graduated first in his class from the School of Mines in Saint Petersburg. His compulsory service in the Horse Guards began in 1901, but he was blackballed when he sought a permanent commission and went to work as an engineer in Siberia.

The Russo-Japanese War of 1904 changed his course. He volunteered, served with a Cossack regiment and won his first decorations. In the First World War he led a cavalry charge on a German battery at Kaushen in East Prussia on 6 August 1914 and was one of the first Russian officers awarded the Order of St. George. He rose to major general.

After the October Revolution he went to Yalta, where Red sailors arrested him in early 1918 and he was nearly executed. In August 1918 he joined the Volunteer Army under General Anton Denikin, won victories in the Northern Caucasus and in June 1919 captured Tsaritsyn. He then clashed with Denikin over the Moscow Directive and was dismissed in December 1919. After one battle he ordered 370 captured Red officers and non-commissioned officers shot.

On 4 April 1920 a military council elected him commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces of Southern Russia, confined to Crimea. He renamed it the Russian Army and set up a civil government that proposed a land reform recognising the peasants' seizures of 1917; it came too late to win them over. In June 1920 his forces broke out in the Northern Taurida Operation, but when Poland signed an armistice in October the Red Army turned on him. On 14 November 1920 ships evacuated his soldiers and civilians from Crimea.

His army was interned at Gallipoli and on Lemnos, then resettled in Yugoslavia and Bulgaria. In 1924 he founded the Russian All-Military Union and led it from Brussels until he died suddenly in 1928 after a short illness. His family believed he had been poisoned by a Soviet agent; the historian Richard Luckett thinks a natural death more probable. He was buried in Belgrade in 1929.

Peter Kenez judges him abler as politician, diplomat and general than Denikin, but holds that he took command when the White cause was already lost. His supporters credit him with leading his army out of a hopeless position without loss of honour.
pyramid-of-djoser: The Pyramid of Djoser stands in the Saqqara necropolis northwest of the ruins of Memphis, and it was the first Egyptian pyramid to be built. Djoser, known in his tomb by his Horus name Netjerikhet, was the first or second king of the 3rd Dynasty. Most Egyptologists credit his vizier Imhotep with the design, on the strength of a statue of Imhotep in the complex, his title of overseer of sculptors and painters, and a remark by the historian Manetho that he invented building in stone. An earlier mastaba at Saqqara, S3038, with mudbrick walls built out into eight shallow steps, was a precedent.

The pyramid rises in six steps to between 60 and 62.5 m, with a base of 109 m by 121 m, and was cased in polished white limestone. It was built in phases, labelled M1 to M3 and P1 to P2 after the excavator Jean-Philippe Lauer. It began as a square mastaba 63 m wide, was enlarged with new casings and an eastern extension over eleven shafts leading to the burial chambers of Djoser's family, then became a four-step pyramid and finally a six-step one. Egyptologists disagree on why: Lauer thought the change made the tomb visible from Memphis, while Rainer Stadelmann suggested it was planned as a pyramid from the start.

Beneath it lies a labyrinth of tunnels and galleries nearly 6 km long, running from a central shaft 28 m deep. Some walls are inlaid with blue faience tile in imitation of reed matting. The burial chamber was a vault of granite closed with a block of 3.5 tons; no body was found, since the tomb had been extensively robbed. More than 40,000 stone vessels were found in the galleries, many bearing the names of earlier kings.

The pyramid stands in a mortuary complex of about 15 hectares, enclosed by a niched limestone wall 10.5 m high and over 1.6 km long and surrounded by a rock-cut trench 750 m long. Its builders carved 1,680 niches in the wall by hand, copying forms that earlier builders had made from wood, rope and reed mats. The stone work implies that the royal government now controlled far more material and human resources, and from this reign the kings of the Old Kingdom were buried in the north rather than at Abydos.

The step pyramid set the stage for the pyramids of the 4th, 5th and 6th Dynasties, including those of Giza. Imhotep was later deified and known to the Greeks as Asclepios. The monument was reopened to visitors in March 2020 after a restoration of 14 years.
pyramid-of-the-moon: The pyramid stands in the western part of the ancient city of Teotihuacan, in what is now San Martín de las Pirámides, Mexico. It mimics the contours of the mountain Cerro Gordo, just to the north, which may have been called Tenan, in Nahuatl 'mother or protective stone'. Between 150 BCE and 500 CE a Mesoamerican culture built a city on a plateau of about 22 square kilometres here, and the ethnicity of its inhabitants is debated. Construction of the pyramid, between 100 and 450 CE, completed the bilateral symmetry of the temple complex.

The pyramid consists of seven buildings, each covering the one before. Building 1, from about 100 CE, was a square platform with sloping sides about 23.5 metres long. Building 4, completed about 250 CE, was a substantial enlargement, and Building 5 introduced the talud-tablero style. The last, Building 7, was built about 400 CE and is the one visible today, 43 metres tall on a base of 147 by about 130 metres.

Its main function was public ritual sacrifice. A platform on top was used for ceremonies in honour of the Great Goddess of Teotihuacan, a goddess of water, fertility, the earth and creation. A stone figure of the goddess weighing 22 tonnes was uncovered, and the Aztecs said that a huge stone figure related to the moon had once stood on the pyramid. Opposite the goddess's altar lies the Plaza of the Moon, which was also used for astronomical observation and calendar-related activities.

Five burial complexes lie within the layers, none before Building 4. Burial 2, from about 250 CE, held a man of about 40 to 50 years, seated and probably bound, with ear flares, beads, figurines, obsidian blades and the remains of pumas, eagles and rattlesnakes. Burial 4 held seventeen human heads, and Burial 6 twelve skeletons with bound hands. Isotope studies suggest that some victims were not from Teotihuacan.

From 1998 archaeologists excavated beneath the pyramid by tunnelling into it, and the layers gave the first timeline for the history of Teotihuacan. A team led by Saburo Sugiyama and Rubén Cabrera found tombs with sacrificial victims, animal bones, greenstone figures, obsidian blades and other offerings. Sugiyama and Leonardo López Luján proposed that the burials were cosmograms, laid out by priests according to set patterns. The preferred victims were adult and sub-adult males from elsewhere, perhaps war captives, and Sugiyama has suggested that sacrifice and large-scale construction correlated with the growth of state and military power.
pyramid-of-the-sun: The Pyramid of the Sun stands along the Avenue of the Dead at Teotihuacan, between the Pyramid of the Moon and the Ciudadela, in the shadow of the mountain Cerro Gordo. The name comes from the Aztecs, who visited the city centuries after it was abandoned; the name the Teotihuacanos gave it is unknown. It was built in two phases. The first brought it nearly to its present size, and the second gave it its completed width of 225 metres and added an altar on top, which has not survived.

The structure was finished with lime plaster brought from surrounding areas and painted with brightly coloured murals. Neither paint nor plaster remains visible. Jaguar heads and paws, stars and snake rattles are among the few images associated with the pyramid. It is thought that the pyramid honoured a deity of Teotihuacan society, but little evidence supports this, and the destruction of the temple on top, by deliberate and natural forces, has prevented identification with any particular god.

The pyramid was built on a carefully chosen spot, from which it could be aligned with Cerro Gordo to the north and, at right angles, with sunrises and sunsets on specific dates. The central part of the city's grid, including the Avenue of the Dead, repeats its orientation, while the southern part follows a slightly different one dictated by the Ciudadela.

In 1959 the archaeologist Rene Millon and his team were among the first to study the tunnels beneath the pyramid. Most of the main tunnels had been sealed, though whether on purpose is open to interpretation. They yielded pottery, hearths and other artefacts, and Millon's team rejected the older theory that slaves built the pyramids, arguing that the craftsmanship suggests motivated builders.

In 1971 Ernesto Taboada found the entrance to a seven-metre pit at the foot of the main staircase, leading to a cave about six metres beneath the centre of the structure. It was first thought to be a natural lava tube and possibly Chicomoztoc, the place of origin in Nahua legend. Later excavations suggest it is man-made and could have served as a royal tomb. Only a few caches of artefacts have been found, including obsidian arrowheads and human figurines, and children's burials lay at the corners of the pyramid, probably part of a rite dedicating its construction. The Teotihuacan Ocelot, found near its foot in the late nineteenth century, is in the British Museum.
pyramid-texts: The Pyramid Texts are written in Old Egyptian and were carved in vertical columns of hieroglyphs on the subterranean walls and sarcophagi of pyramids at Saqqara. Unlike the later Coffin Texts and Book of the Dead they were reserved for the king, with the exception of three queens, Wedjebten, Neith and Iput, and they carry no illustrations. Their spells, called utterances, were chiefly concerned with the transformation of the deceased into an akh. They fall into two broad groups: sacerdotal texts, ritual in nature and spoken by a lector priest, such as offering spells and the Resurrection Ritual, and personal texts that guide the spirit out of the tomb. The personal texts include provisioning, transition and protective spells.

Kurt Sethe's first edition counted 714 distinct spells, and later discoveries brought the total to 759. No single edition contains every recorded spell. The spells describe the king's routes to the sky by ramps, stairs, ladders, ferry and flight, and they can call on the gods for help or threaten them. Utterances 273 and 274, the so-called Cannibal Hymn, show the king taking the powers of the gods by slaughtering and eating them.

The Pyramid Texts first appear in the pyramid of Unas, where 283 spells cover the walls of the antechamber, burial chamber and part of the passage. The walls around the sarcophagus are not inscribed. The pyramid of Unas was the smallest built in the Old Kingdom, and its layout was copied and expanded in later pyramids. The texts continued through the Sixth Dynasty and into the Eighth. In the Middle Kingdom kings had the Coffin Texts inscribed on their own coffins instead, though the spells continued to be practised, and a near-complete copy of the texts from Unas was inscribed in the tomb of Senwosretankh at El-Lisht. By the New Kingdom the texts had lost their exclusivity and appear in the tombs of officials.

Gaston Maspero, who reached Egypt in 1880, found the texts at South Saqqara in the pyramid of Pepi I and then in that of Merenre I. Auguste Mariette rejected the findings, since no writing had previously been found inside a pyramid. In 1881 Maspero found more in the pyramids of Unas, Teti and Pepi II, and in 1894 he published the first corpus. Sethe's edition and concordance of 1908 to 1910 became the standard version. Raymond O. Faulkner published an English translation in 1969, and Gustave Jéquier published the corpus of five further pyramids after excavations between 1926 and 1932.
pyrenees: The Pyrenees extend nearly 500 kilometres from their union with the Cantabrian Mountains to Cap de Creus on the Mediterranean coast, and reach their highest point at the peak of Aneto, 3,404 metres, in Huesca. They are older than the Alps: their sediments were first deposited in coastal basins in the Paleozoic and Mesozoic eras, and between 100 and 150 million years ago the opening of the Bay of Biscay pushed present-day Spain against France and compressed the rock layers. Low passes are lacking, and the main roads and railways between France and Spain run in the lowlands at the western and eastern ends, near sea level.

Classical writers explained the name in two ways. In one account Pyrene was the daughter of a king in Mediterranean Gaul who gave hospitality to Hercules; the hero wronged her, and after she died in the woods he laid her to rest and called her name across the mountains, which kept it. Pliny the Elder connected the story with Lusitania but rejected it as fabulosa, highly fictional. Other classical sources derived the name from the Greek word for fire, and Diodorus Siculus related that herdsmen once left a fire that burned over the whole mountain area.

The Romans opened many of the marble quarries, which supplied the Grand Antique marble used in Rome and Constantinople and later the coloured marbles used to decorate the Louvre, Versailles and the Royal Palace of Madrid. Old Roman roads ran over the Col de Somport. Historically the Crown of Aragon and the Kingdom of Navarre extended on both sides of the range. The Roncevaux Pass, entirely in Navarre, is an important point on the Camino de Santiago pilgrimage route, and according to legend the gap in the ridge known as the Brèche de Roland was made by Roland.

The main crest mostly forms the border between France and Spain, with the principality of Andorra between them in the east. The languages spoken include Spanish, French, Aragonese, Catalan, Basque and Occitan. Transhumance, the moving of livestock to high pastures in May or June and back in September or October, long shaped rural life, with families living in stone cabins during the summer. In 1997 part of the range, including the Ordesa y Monte Perdido National Park, was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List for its geological landforms and for the transhumance system.
pyrrhic-war: Rome had expanded steadily down the Italian peninsula, defeating the Samnites and their allies in the Third Samnite War (298 to 290 BCE). The Greek city of Thurii allied itself to Rome in 285 BCE, and in 282 BCE a force of Samnites, Lucanians and Bruttians besieged it. The consul Gaius Fabricius Luscinus relieved the city. Tarentum, which had aligned itself with the Lucanians, saw the Roman alliance with Thurii as a challenge to its leadership of the Greek cities and feared that Rome would replace its democracy with a pro-Roman oligarchy. It attacked a Roman fleet in its waters, and a Roman army under the consul Lucius Aemilius Barbula invaded its territory. Judging itself too weak, Tarentum invited Pyrrhus, king of Epirus.

Pyrrhus, whose aims were probably a hegemony over Magna Graecia, made peace with Macedon and sent troops to Tarentum. In 280 BCE he met the consul Publius Valerius Laevinus near Heraclea, where both armies probably numbered a little over 20,000 men, and his war elephants helped to defeat the Romans. In 279 BCE the Romans were defeated again at Asculum. Pyrrhus is said to have exclaimed there "Another such victory and we are lost!", which gave rise to the phrase Pyrrhic victory.

He then went to Sicily at the invitation of Syracuse and drove the Carthaginians from much of the island, but could not take their stronghold of Lilybaeum, which their navy kept supplied. Meanwhile the Romans recovered much of Calabria. Pyrrhus returned to Italy in early 276 BCE, losing some ships to the Carthaginian fleet on the way. In 275 BCE he fought the consul Manius Curius Dentatus at Beneventum. Ancient sources say he was defeated, but some modern historians think the battle a draw. Either way he was forced onto the defensive and withdrew to Epirus, leaving a garrison at Tarentum.

Tarentum fell to the Romans in 272 BCE, when its Epirote garrison surrendered in exchange for safe passage home, and the remaining Italiot Greek cities sought terms. Pyrrhus died the same year at Argos, struck by a roof tile during street fighting. Rome founded colonies at Paestum, Beneventum and Aesernia in 273, 268 and 263 BCE, and armed resistance in the south would wait for Hannibal. The war raised Rome's standing across the Mediterranean, and the historian Florus marked it as the start of Roman ambitions beyond Italy. Later Roman writers embellished the war with prophecies and duels, and the story was shaped by the later Punic wars.
pyrrho: Pyrrho came from Elis, on the Ionian Sea. He was likely a member of the Klytidiai, a clan of seers in Elis who interpreted the oracles of the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, where Pyrrho served as a high priest. The Klytidiai were descendants of Klytios, the son of Alcmaeon and the grandson of Amphiaraus. In a poem called the Python, his pupil Timon of Phlius describes first meeting him on the grounds of an Amphiareion, a temple of Amphiaraus, while both were on a pilgrimage to Delphi.

Most biographical information comes from Diogenes Laertius, who drew chiefly on the mid-third-century BCE biographer Antigonus of Carystus. Unlike the founders of other Hellenistic philosophies, Pyrrho was not substantively influenced by Socrates. He travelled with Anaxarchus on Alexander the Great's Indian campaign, which Diogenes dates to 327 to 325 BCE, and is said to have gone as far as the gymnosophists in India and the Magi in Persia. How much he took from this journey is disputed. Richard Bett heavily discounts Indian influence, noting that conversation with the gymnosophists needed three translators, while Johannes Bronkhorst sees no link between early Buddhism and Pyrrho's thought. It has also been suggested that the gymnosophists were Jains or Ajnanins.

Pyrrho wrote nothing. Most of what is known of his philosophy comes from Timon, whose fragments were preserved mostly by Sextus Empiricus, Diogenes Laertius and Eusebius. Much of what is now called Pyrrhonism comes from the Outlines of Pyrrhonism by Sextus Empiricus, written over 400 years after Pyrrho's death, so little is certain about how his own views differed from the later school.

Most sources agree that his aim was ataraxia, freedom from mental disturbance, reached by giving up beliefs about thoughts and perceptions. A summary preserved by Eusebius, quoting Aristocles, quoting Timon, holds that things are equally indifferent, unstable and indeterminate, so that neither senses nor opinions are true or false and one should be without opinions, saying of each thing that it no more is than is not. Interpretations of this passage conflict. Many suggest Pyrrho held reality to be inherently indeterminate, which Sextus would have counted as a negative dogmatic belief.

It is uncertain whether Pyrrhonism continued without a break or died out and was revived; several centuries after Pyrrho, Aenesidemus led a revival. It was one of two major schools of scepticism of the Hellenistic period, the other being Academic scepticism. Pyrrhonists treat their philosophy as a way of life with Pyrrho as its model, seeking ataraxia through epoché, the suspension of judgement, by setting arguments of equal strength against each other.
pyrrhus-of-epirus: Pyrrhus was the son of the Epirote prince Aeacides and Phthia, a Thessalian noblewoman. Aeacides was a cousin of Olympias, which made Pyrrhus a second cousin of Alexander the Great. Aeacides supported Olympias against Cassander and was dethroned when his soldiers mutinied. Pyrrhus's family fled north to Glaucias of the Taulantians, an Illyrian tribe, and Pyrrhus was raised by Glaucias's wife Beroea, a Molossian of the Aeacid dynasty. Glaucias refused to give him up to Cassander. He then served his brother-in-law Demetrius Poliorcetes, fought at Ipsus in 302 BCE, and in 298 BCE was taken hostage to Alexandria under a treaty between Demetrius and Ptolemy I Soter.

In Alexandria Pyrrhus married Antigone, Ptolemy's stepdaughter. After Cassander died in 297 BCE, Ptolemy gave him men and money and sent him back to Epirus. He ruled jointly with Neoptolemus, then had him murdered at a dinner after learning of a plot against his life. He co-ruled Macedon with Lysimachus after driving out Demetrius, and was himself driven out in 284 BCE. Tarentum asked him to lead its war against Rome, and he arrived in Italy in 280 BCE with 20,000 infantry, 3,000 cavalry and 20 war elephants. His costly victories at Heraclea and Asculum gave rise to the phrase Pyrrhic victory.

In 278 BCE the Greek cities of Sicily asked him to drive out Carthage, and he lifted the siege of Syracuse and was proclaimed king of Sicily. His assaults on Lilybaeum failed, and compulsory contributions and garrisons angered the Sicilians. In 275 BCE the consul Manius Curius Dentatus repulsed his attack near Beneventum, where he lost half of his elephants. He gave up the campaign in Italy and returned to Epirus, keeping only Tarentum.

Pyrrhus seized the Macedonian throne from Antigonus II Gonatas in 274 BCE, but made himself unpopular by letting his Gauls plunder the royal tombs at Aegae. In 272 BCE the Spartan Cleonymus asked him to attack Sparta. The assault was thwarted, and Pyrrhus was killed in a street battle at Argos. Plutarch records that Hannibal ranked him first among commanders, or in another passage second only to Alexander. The phrase Pyrrhic victory comes from his reported remark after Asculum that another such victory over the Romans would ruin him utterly.
pyrzyce: Pyrzyce, called Pyritz in German and Përzëca in Kashubian, is a town in Pomerania, north-western Poland, and the capital of Pyrzyce County in West Pomeranian Voivodeship. It grew from an early medieval tribal stronghold that became a castellan seat and a centre of the grain trade. The town has largely preserved its medieval defensive walls with several gates and towers, several medieval churches and a regional museum. Since 1994 it has had a geothermal plant, one of the oldest in Poland, which draws on Lower Jurassic thermal waters.

An anonymous document of around 850, the Bavarian Geographer, mentions the tribe of the Prissani with 70 strongholds. The territory became part of the emerging Polish state under Mieszko I around 967. The settlement was first mentioned in 1124 by Bishop Otto of Bamberg, who baptised the first Pomeranians here on a mission entrusted to him by Bolesław III Wrymouth. It was among the first towns of Western Pomerania to convert. A church was founded in 1140, and a castle is first mentioned then.

After Poland fragmented, Pyrzyce became part of the Duchy of Pomerania. A new layout with two parallel main streets was established around 1240, and in 1263 Duke Barnim I granted Magdeburg town rights. Dukes Otto I and Barnim III exempted the burghers from customs duties in 1320 and confirmed the right to mint coins in 1326. By the Contract of Pyritz of 1493 the Dukes of Pomerania recognised the succession rights of the House of Brandenburg. A fire destroyed most of the town in 1496, and in 1524 it was the first town in Pomerania to adopt the Lutheran Reformation.

During the Thirty Years' War imperial and Swedish forces occupied it in turn, and fire largely destroyed it in 1634. In 1653 it passed to the Brandenburg-Prussian province of Pomerania. In 1945 the Red Army captured the town, and Soviet artillery in February destroyed much of the old town. Pyrzyce was restored to Poland, its German population was expelled under the Potsdam Agreement and Poles, among them people displaced from former eastern Poland, settled there.
pythagoras: No authentic writings of Pythagoras survive, and almost nothing is known for certain about his life. The earliest sources, from Xenophanes, Heraclitus, Empedocles, Ion of Chios and Herodotus, are brief, ambiguous and often satirical. The main biographies, by Diogenes Laërtius, Porphyry and Iamblichus, date from late antiquity and are filled with myths and legends, which grow more fantastic the later the writer.

Herodotus and Isocrates agree that Pythagoras was the son of Mnesarchus and was born on the island of Samos in the eastern Aegean. Aristoxenus stated that Pythagoras left Samos in the reign of Polycrates at the age of 40, which gives a birth date around 570 BCE. Most scholars agree that he travelled to Croton in southern Italy around 530 BCE, where he founded a school.

The teaching most securely linked to Pythagoras is metempsychosis, the belief that every soul is immortal and enters a new body after death. The earliest source is a satirical poem by Xenophanes, who describes Pythagoras interceding for a beaten dog, in whose cries he recognised the voice of a dead friend. He may also have devised the harmony of the spheres, by which the planets move according to mathematical ratios and produce an inaudible music.

The school at Croton resembled a monastery. Its members were bound by a vow to Pythagoras and each other, shared their possessions and ate meals in common. Pythagoras was credited in antiquity with the Pythagorean theorem and with discoveries in music and astronomy, but historians debate whether he made them. The geometric principles were known in Babylonian mathematics and in ancient India, and Burkert notes that antiquity never credited Pythagoras with proving any theorem.

After the decisive victory of Croton over Sybaris around 510 BCE, Pythagoras's followers came into conflict with supporters of democracy, and their meeting houses were burned. Pythagoras may have been killed in this persecution, or he may have escaped to Metapontum and died there.

Pythagoras influenced Plato, whose dialogues, especially the Timaeus, show Pythagorean ideas. His teachings revived in the first century BCE among Middle Platonists, and in the Middle Ages he was revered as the founder of mathematics and music. Nicolaus Copernicus cited Pythagoreans as influences on his heliocentric model, and Johannes Kepler, who considered himself a Pythagorean, took the title of his Harmonices Mundi from the doctrine of the harmony of the spheres.
pytheas: Pytheas came from the Greek colony of Massalia, modern Marseille, and worked as a geographer, explorer and astronomer. His own account of his voyage did not survive. Only quotations and summaries remain in later writers, notably Strabo's Geographica, Diodorus of Sicily and Pliny's Natural History. Strabo tried to discredit him. Dicaearchus, who died about 285 BCE, distrusted his stories, while Aristotle and Ephorus do not mention him, which helps to date the voyage.

Pytheas made his voyage to northern Europe in about 325 BCE and was the first documented Mediterranean mariner to reach the British Isles. Where it began is unknown. The Carthaginians had closed the Strait of Gibraltar to ships of other nations, so some historians think he went overland to the Loire or the Garonne, while others think he hugged the coast. Strabo reports that he travelled over the whole of Britain that was accessible. He called the island Prettanike, the earliest known form of the name Britain, and named its corners Kantion, Belerion and Orkas, taken to be Kent, Cornwall and Orkney.

In Cornwall, Diodorus says, people mined tin, smelted it and shaped it into pieces like knucklebones, which were carried at low tide to the island of Ictis and then on horses for 30 days to the Rhône. Pytheas also described Thule, and a frozen sea one day's sail beyond it.

Pytheas was the first known Greek to describe the Arctic, polar ice and the Celtic and Germanic tribes, and the first on record to describe the midnight sun. He measured latitudes with the gnomon, and his account of the tides is the earliest known to suggest that the moon causes them. Pliny reports his claim that the tide in Britain rose 80 cubits, far beyond any known British tide. Dicaearchus, Timaeus, Eratosthenes, Hipparchus, Polybius, Artemidorus and Posidonius are among the ancient authors known to have seen his text, so he was a central source for the North Sea and the subarctic lands of western Europe.
pythia: The name Pythia comes from pythia hiereia, 'priestess of the Pythian Apollo'. Pythios is an epithet of Apollo, derived from Pytho, in myth the original name of Delphi, and so related to Python, the snake Apollo slew there. The Greeks derived the place name from the verb for 'to rot', referring to the smell of the decomposing monster.

The oracle was established by the 8th century BCE at the latest, though some estimates place the shrine as early as 1400 BCE, and there is evidence that Apollo took the shrine over from an earlier dedication to Gaia. The Homeric Hymn to Delphic Apollo, dated to about 580-570 BCE, tells how Apollo, in the form of a dolphin, chose Cretan sailors from Knossos as his first priests.

The oracle gave prophecies during the nine warmest months of the year. In winter Apollo was said to leave his temple to his half-brother Dionysus, and he returned on the seventh day of the month of Bysios, his birthday. Once a month the Pythia underwent purification, including fasting, and on the seventh day she was led, veiled in purple, to the Castallian Spring. Those who consulted her went through an interview with the priests, framed their questions, presented gifts and walked the Sacred Way carrying laurel before they entered the adyton, the chamber of the oracle, to put their question.

Other officials served beside her. After 200 BCE two priests of Apollo, chosen for life from the leading citizens of Delphi, ran the sanctuary; Plutarch served as one. There were also five hosioi and the prophetai, whose duties are unclear. Later authors say the Pythia spoke in a frenzy and that priests recast her words as dactylic hexameter, but Joseph Fontenrose and Lisa Maurizio argue that the sources show her speaking intelligibly in her own voice. The temple whose ruins survive dates from the 4th century BCE; the earlier one was destroyed by an earthquake in 373 BCE.

The Delphic oracle was the most prestigious and authoritative of the Greek oracles, and is among the best documented religious institutions of the classical Greeks. Its maxim 'Know thyself' was carved in the temple. The Roman emperor Theodosius I silenced it in 390 CE by destroying the temple and most of its statues.

Plutarch tied the Pythia's inspiration to vapours from the Kerna spring beneath the temple. The French excavation led by Théophile Homolle from 1892 found no fissure, and in 1904 Adolphe Paul Oppé denied that any chasm or vapour had existed. Later geological studies proposed gas emissions from a chasm, with ethylene suggested by de Boer and others, while Lehoux calls ethylene impossible. Methane, carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide have also been proposed.
pythian-games: In Greek myth the games began with Apollo's slaying of the serpent Python, as he looked for a place to found his temple. After burying the body, he founded the oracle of Delphi. In some versions Apollo was guilty of a crime by killing Python and Zeus ordered him to make amends, so he founded the games; in others he founded them to celebrate his victory.

Originally the Pythian Games were a musical event built around the singing of a hymn to Apollo, held every eight years. Administration then passed to the Delphic Amphictyony, a council of twelve Greek tribes, which reorganised them around the end of the First Sacred War. New events were added, music was expanded and athletics eventually introduced, and the festival came every four years, two years before and after the Olympic Games, near the end of August.

Preparations began six months ahead, when nine Delphian theoroi were sent to the Greek cities to announce the games and declare the Sacred Truce, the Hieromenia. A city that fought or robbed during the truce was barred from the sanctuary, the games and the oracle. The festival lasted six to eight days and opened with a reenactment of Apollo's victory over Python, a procession and a sacrifice in the Temple of Apollo.

Athletic contests took place in the Stadium and at their peak included the stade, diaulos, dolichos, the armed race, wrestling, boxing, pankration and the pentathlon. Equestrian races on the last day ran in the hippodrome on the plain of Krisa; unlike the Olympics, the games had no four-horse chariot race for adults and instead added running races for boys. The first games under the Amphictyony included singing to the cithara, and contests for aulos playing, poetry, prose and tragic acting followed. Painting contests came in the mid-5th century BCE, and theatrical competitions in Roman times.

In the early years winners may have received prizes such as golden tripods, but once the games became stephanitic, or crown games, the victor received a wreath of bay laurel from the Vale of Tempe in Thessaly. Women were allowed to compete at Delphi in both athletic and artistic events; the only surviving record of a woman victor is Tryphosa, who won the girls' stadion race.

The Theban poet Pindar wrote twelve odes for Pythian victors, called Pythionikoi, among them those for Hippokles of Thessaly in 498 BCE, Midas of Akragas in 490 BCE and Hieron of Syracuse in the 470s BCE. They praise the winners' families and show the aristocratic ideals of the late archaic period. Delphi remained an active pagan site despite the rise of Christianity, and the games continued into the late Roman Empire.
